I love this author and have been reading her for years. Real life family situations-demanding relatives, sibling, etc. trouble that entertain.

Even though the visions she sees through her fingers can knock her off her feet, Everly still is willing to work to stop criminals so she can protect herself and her friends. I like the mix of paranormal and government agencies securing our country by working together in these stories. The characters are the heroes we wish we all could be, using their brains to solve crimes. The people are "real" in that the stories give their phobias and insecurities about themselves that we as people suffer through in our lives. They have flaws like we do and still come through the trials and stresses to figure out who did it in the end. They, also, struggle through how to have a relationship with someone special while letting them be who they are.

Exciting hard to put down, but not the everyday stories we are taught about Angels. In the end, you see God from a different point of view. I may not agree with it all, but it is a very exciting story!

Adopted into a happy family, Jill still wants to know her birth mom. Until she was on her death bed, however, she refused. She calls her daughter a witch then dies. New family is revealed and competes with her investigation. All this is written with humorous characters: one-eyed cat, scarf obsessed knitting receptionist, etc. Entertaining mystery!

I loved the flow of the book. If you love intrigue and romance, this is a great one. The only problem I have is the way the killer gets his hands on the last victim. Smart people don't make such a stupid mistake after doing so many things right.
I like the humor between the actions of the PI and the deputy and the ending fits perfectly with their crazy interaction. I strongly recommend the book.
Loved the pace of disclosure. Enjoyed the characters and their growth during the story. I liked the new take on angel/demon hierarchy.

What a wait to start a mystery! This may be for teens, but I loved it. Veronica Mars move over. Losing your mom young can cause girls to have a different mind set than their peers. Everyone knows kids conform or become the target of peers who like to exploit others flaws.
This shows that Kait maybe different, but she has a real part to play in the world, even at 16. Meeting the top man in her class, while crashing his sister's funeral, may not sound promising, but it gives them a mission. The story, also, points out others that would be overlooked in the normal high school crowd. Kait manages to show their true place while solving a drug case that the police don't have the full picture on.

The book was dark, but the mystery and writing kept me hanging in to the end. I have a love/dislike with this story because it shows gambling in all it's ugliness. The rest of the story is so intriguing, however, I could not put it down. Great story and believable.
I would have liked it better without the sexual details. Storyline is interesting and the characters are explained as you go along so you can understand the psychology of the action.

At first, the story lines were a little disconcerting, but as the became connected it was a funny and interesting mix. When the global warming was first introduced, I thought-Not again. As the story continued to unfold, however, I loved the approach. It plays well to the conspiracy theorist in all of us.

Really enjoyed this. Christian Fiction is so much easier to read since I don't have to skip uncomfortable sexual content or overly graphic crime scenes. This author had a good story without anything being added to detract from the story line.

This book is an uncomfortable read at times, but they fit the characters that the author creates so I easy myself through them. I like the Lei and she has had a painful life so I can get past some of the more graphic details to continue to get to know her better. She is a determined and tough lady worth meeting.
Great momentum to the story. Funny and interesting start to finish. Good, clear characters.

Like most modern women Angie knows there is no such thing as ghosts, but . . . That is the point of the story. Is there truth to the paranormal we like to read about? She is getting married and now  worries about living in her father's building with her new husband. As her fianc struggles with one then 2 people from a company that are found dead, she begins to house hunt with her realtor sister. It is easy to demand to see a house that is way under priced, but as she keeps including friends and family in the return trips to a house she loves, things get spooky. It turns out not one but 3 people who lived there died right outside the house. Who is haunting the house and what really happened there? Very entertaining!
This book casts a spell with the amazing characters that draw you into the story. I felt the indecision, love, dan
Juggling her family and her job keeps this housewife on her toes. Throw in romance, swingers and a big school project for the moms to plan and set up, you can expect a very active, never dull, story.

When a Westmound Summit turns deadly, the on-site Scooby-Doo fans are told by the police to not be seen investigating. With the help of Moo, the company Great Dane, they begin snooping and fined everyone of the suspects has a good motive. Moo is allowed to take down the murderer at the end.
The detective work is more straight forward conversations and the police attitude is more don't let me see you interviewing suspects. It makes a more relaxed mystery and Moo adds humor with the normal Great Dane clumsiness to keep things entertaining.

Emily Parker lost her husband, Evan, in more just the physical absence from her life after his murder. His secrets began to come out slowly and now in the middle of her investigation of an Asian "family" briefly encountered in a public restroom, a missing teenage friend, and possible prostitution in their small town, it all seems to be getting ready to come out so they can solve his murder, too. What an emotional ride Debra takes us on! This was the first I read from the series and I was easy to follow and keep up with all the action. Well done!

Women are dying and being attacked. Magick is real and practiced by True Witches. Can they find the villain before he gets the next victim? Interesting book, but a little too much descriptive sex for my taste.

users.query: This book (and the last) were a drag. This author needs some serious editing! Seems like he is getting lost in the descriptive part of the narrative and the thrust and direction are too diluted by far. Also, we are running out of original protagonists, and I find myself becoming detached from the characters. There are only two I care about any more, and it is getting hard to wade through pages and pages of descriptive nothingness to keep up with them. Not sure I will continue with the series. I feel kind of abused!

cands.text: I wish I could give two ratings to this book, one for the memoir and another for the resources section. The first part of the book, the memoir, is alternately touching and frustrating. The writing can only be described as florid! Every word has numerous modifiers and the descriptions go on and on and on. I found myself skipping a lot, trying to stay with the story. That said, I have enormous admiration for the author, having traveled a similar road myself. The losses associated with Lyme only start with physical health. I admire her courage and determination, and most of all I admire that she found a new and unshakable identity as Lyme took away all the conventional ways we value ourselves. I thank her for sharing that journey. I also appreciated Part 2 of the book which is the factual part about Lyme and presents many resources useful to Lyme sufferers. All in all, this was a worthwhile read.

I loved this novel. It is a mystery told with sweetness and charm. The characters are well-developed, the descriptions captivating without being too long. The setting is very atmospheric. "Ordinary Grace" is one of those books you treasure as you read it, and long after too.

Got this book because the setting is in my neighborhood. Both my husband and I read this book and enjoyed it. It holds your attention, the descriptions are good and the characters not bad for a "whodunit"!

This is an important book, filled with insights! What I especially liked was how this book helped me to analyze what is going on with difficult people in my life, AND offers ways to help me improve the relationship. It also gave me some insight into myself ( I didn't especially enjoy that part!!) which also makes this book valuable. I look forward to Sarah/Sam's next book!

I have read all the Mitch Rapp books, mainly because my brother shares them with me. I have never been over-awed by the one dimensional sang-froid of Mr. Rapp, but this book was a BIG disappointment! Aside from bad proof-reading, the major flaw in the book is the ending. For an author who lovingly details spy-craft, torture, and location, he certainly failed to connect the dots between the last two chapters. Penultimate chapter: Rapp is a hero, saves his comrades and escapes from the bad guys. Ultimate chapter: he is a hero on another continent, everyone who should have been rescued was safe, rescued from different locations in the city of Beirut, the bad guys captured. How did that happen? The author doesn't tell us. Did Mr. Flynn have a deadline? Did he write himself into a corner and took the cheap way out? Not Mr. Vince Flynn's best effort!
This is a lovely book. We have given copies to each of our grandchildren as keepsakes honoring their christenings. The subject matter, quality and colors are perfect.

Got this for my husband who enjoys following ANYthing about golf. He enjoys watching the women's tour. He was disappointed with this book because it was too much about her, and not enough about the big picture.

While this book helps to understand intermittent fasting, I was disappointed. I am a well educated person, and I found the way the medical research was presented was a bit confusing. I felt that this book was written for a target audience of body building types and was not too simpatico for a 69 year old woman! I had lots of questions that I couldn't find answers to. I think the author did a good job explaining the many ways to do the actual fasting. I thought this book was WAAAAY to expensive for what it is.

I was afraid to watch this movie, having heard that it is quite violent. But on the strength of its winning an academy award, I was persuaded to watch it. Well, it is extremely violent, and I find that I am mystified by its academy award. I really didn't care for it at all. It was dark...the film itself, the story and the characters. I didn't feel uplifted, better informed, or particularly entertained when it was over. Just was relieved it was over. I guess everyone has their own tastes. Not my kind of movie.

I really enjoyed this book! There is a lot to learn from the author about these amazing creatures. The octopus is a fascinating animal. I confess that I got a bit weary with all the hanging out over barrels and tanks at the aquarium, but on the other hand, the author's wonder and enthusiasm as she got to know the various octopi (octopusses?) was kind of infectious. All in all, I am glad I read it.

The premise of this movie is good and the descriptions make it sound quite different than it really is! Star-studded. Yes. But what promised to be an enchanting story became silly and goofy. Too many things were annoying--sailboats that moved like speedboats, floods that weren't really floods, ridiculous and unbelievable people....The young stars and their trajectory was good and touching. Otherwise it was a waste of my time and $$. This seems to be one of those movies that is hyped, only to leave you feeling like a sucker for reviews.

This book should be required reading for ANYone who eats! Dr. Davis does a great job of giving the history of wheat, the alterations made in it by man. It is pretty clear that wheat today is not the wheat our grandparents ate, nor any of our forebears ate for thousands of years. If you are overweight and can't seem to fight it, if you can't stop eating, if you are hungry all the time if you have an auto-immune disease, if you live in a brain fog, if you have type 2 diabetes or are "pre-diabetic", this is a must read. The author writes very clearly as he explains the many aspects of the "wheat problem" and has documented his case very thoroughly. I had already given up eating grain, this book affirms my choice!

This documentary is at once hopeful, appalling, infuriating, sad, AND important! If you wonder why "the war on cancer" isn't getting won, you will learn why when you watch this movie. There is a lot of money in the status quo, and there are a lot of corrupt folks who are working hard to keep it that way. I admire the aplomb and determination of Dr. Burzynski. Just think. He started as a brilliant researcher, became a miracle worker, then got to be a crusader, legal expert and hero. What a life. Thanks to Eric Merola for making the movie. Thanks to Dr. Burzynski for his courage. Thanks to all the people who worked to help him fight back!

LATER REVIEW: In 2015 we purchased this item on February 15. It was for our winter home. We used it several times until we left for the season and left it in Florida. We returned in Early December, got our our Whitmor Drying Rack, hung wet tee shirts and polo shirts on it. A few hours later the arms had collapsed. There is a little, tiny, locking button that broke. My husband happened to find the broken piece (small, very small). What we saw made us pretty angry. The button is a miniscule screw, covered in plastic. The diameter is pathetic. Did Whitmor engineers really think that size screw was adequate? I am angry. We did not misuse this rack. It is just a good looking piece of junk. Not only am I angry, but disappointed. Whitmor saved a bit on screws. I am out nearly $30! Meanwhile, hubby got a hose clamp and our drying rack is functional enough.

i have had this watch for several months now. i wear it daily. a long time ago, i had another automatic seiko divers watch, but stopped wearing it because it started losing 2 minutes per day, and i didn't want to send it off to be fixed. for a long time, i have been pulling my cell out of my pocket to check the time, and eventually i just got tired of it. this watch reminds me of the previous seiko i had (except this has the metal band). adjusting the band when i got it was not as hard as i feared. i found that using a push pin allowed me to remove a link, and adjust the clasp. the watch seems to slowly lose 2 minutes, and then maintain that offset (hence the comment about accuracy versus precision). one thing i really like about this watch is a trait it shares with the old one, the crystal is recessed behind the betzel, which means that if the watch hits something, it is much less likely that the glass gets scratched. it is a large watch, one of the largest diver's watches seiko makes, but it seems to fit my wrist. definitely worth the 150$ i paid for it.

UPDATE: (feb2015, changed from 5 to 3 starts)

i have had the watch just over two years. cosmetically it has held up great. there is a little scuffing on the bottom of the band, but the face and bezel have held up great, and show almost no signs of wear.

the issue is the accuracy. at this point, it loses about a minute a day. i wear it every day, for about 16 hours. having to add back 5 or 10 minutes every week or two is getting old. as much as i like the watch, i am thinking about replacing it. i don't want to get a freaking rolex, but i don't want a battery either.

it is really too bad, i like the look, the fit, and how it has held up physically so far. but i need it to tell time with a bit more accuracy.

this is an interesting product. it leaves off the smallest two or three sockets i have in each of metric or SAE. it also stores the short sockets upside down, so the engraving on them cannot be "read" easily. it would be easiest to place this with a short end towards you to use this as intended, with metric along one side, and SAE on the other. there is room for the second short socket (often you have both 6 and 12 point sockets), but only room for one deep socket (a problem if you have both 6 and 12 point deep sockets too), if you intend to use the other side for metric.

on the plus side, the outermost short sockets are held in place by plugs that directly fit them, so they are snug, and misplaced sockets are easily to identify.

i think if i decided to go down this road, i would get a black one to go with this, and place metric in one, and SAE in the other. they offer other tool storage products, also in red and black, so you could also store your wrenches in matching black and red holders.

users.query:
This wonderful bit of nonsense features beloved characters from book 3, Ice Blue -- my favorite in the series, so far, starring Taka and Summer. The heroine of this book is Summer's sister, Jillian (Jilly), and the hero is Taka's cousin Reno, newest operative for the Committee, and another ice-cold anti-hero, but not quite as gamma as Peter Bastien, from Book 1. Jilly is 20 and Reno about 28, I think (discrepancy with book 3), so they both seem less mature than the other couples in the series.

This book is set in winter in Tokyo, and also in Los Angeles. The Committee plays only a small role.

When the story begins, Jilly has arrived in Tokyo unexpectedly, to cry on her sister's shoulder, hoping also to catch a glimpse of Reno, the exotic subject of all her secret virginal daydreams. However, danger waits for the unsuspecting brainiac. Because of Sir Harry Thomason's residual murder contract (see book 4), Russian mercenaries are trying to kill Taka and Summer, so they are hiding away. (We see little of Summer, but more of Taka.)

So, as a matter of family honor, Reno must keep Jilly safe from the thugs who would use her as bait to lure Taka back to Tokyo. And he must keep his hands off her, having promised Summer and Taka that he won't play into Jilly's infatuation for him. Keeping his hands off Jilly, resisting his attraction to her -- that's the central theme of this book. The suspense itself is a bit over-the-top, but heh...it worked. From Jilly's first day in Tokyo, the action is non stop, as Reno keeps his "Ji-chan" on the run from murderous Russian hit men, and even more treachery closer to home.

They spend every second together, even sleeping squeezed together in a tube hotel. Reno has promised to stay away from Jilly, and he has every intention of doing so, but ... easier said than done! He blows hot and cold, and sometimes terribly cold, attempting to stifle his intense feelings for her. He doesn't know what's wrong with him--he doesn't do love! Only sex.

If he can just get Jilly safely out of the country and back to LA, he could move on, and find someone else to screw. Right?

Over the course of this story, Reno grows up a lot, facing some heavy family issues, falling in love, even getting rid of his exotic camouflage, to large extent, by the end of the book. I look forward to seeing him in book 6.

I loved Jillian almost more than Reno, which is unusual for me. I usually bond with the hero more. Jilly held her own very nicely, and did what she had to do, even killing. Loved Reno's worried concern when Jilly went into a shocked daze after she shot someone's head off (a bit graphic, eeew). Jilly stayed strong and held it together even when Reno was a complete jerk, twisting the knife to break the growing emotional bond that scared him into a cold sweat. Loved the scene in Grandfather's compound, when Jilly realized how much Reno cared for her, despite his careless and cruel words. He says "No, Ji-chan, I don't love you" even as he's pulling her close, ready to die for her. Haha!

As I said, the non-stop action and never-ending danger is over the top, and when evil follows Jilly home to Los Angeles, I was rolling my eyes. But what fun! Jolly good story!

cands.text:
Bring ice water! This one is hot!

Warning-- she has sex with him in were form one time.

The  3 stars are for the erotic aspects of the book. If I were to rate the book on plot and character development, I would give it 2 stars, for the reasons below.

Most of the book is devoted to sex scenes.

Sometimes the author got her timeline wrong. She would refer to the "mate hunt" happening Thursday night, and then on the same page, it's happening tonight, then a few days later it's back to Thursday. Confusing! This kind of thing happened a few times, with other events, too.

Graham, as the wolf pack Alpha, allowed his evil cousin to get away with too much, including intent to kill Missy. That seemed out of character. And the likelihood of a human running in a race against wolves? Didn't buy it. And as Alpha, Graham could have found a way around it, to be consistent with his supposedly strong, protective, and authoritative character.

I never really fell in love with Graham. I never felt drawn to Missy, either. They were okay, but the author gave me no reason to care deeply about them.

Not much of a story line, and what there was had some major improbabilities.

Republished as an e-book recently,  I read the paperback eons ago and kept it -- along with every book this author has written. I  love how Jessica Steele creates conflict in her heroes, who end up wholeheartedly adoring the very one they initially distrusted and/or despised. Then they must grovel a little.  :-)  Her heroes can be ruthless, rude, insulting...and tender, charming, hot. Her heroines are not doormats.

Jessica Steele is now about 80 years old, sad to say. She is one of the worst writers, in terms of syntax. Her sentence construction is ... unusual. She missed a lot of school as a sickly child, and dropped out when TB developed. But IMO, she is among the best authors at Harlequin for developing conflict, snappy dialogue, and sexual awareness, with bits of humor.

With His Ring:

Yorke is a wealthy, debonaire Brit (think Cary Grant) who gets into conflict with Sabina, a secretary. She is single and a virgin (of course).

Sabina won't give Yorke the emerald ring that she is safeguarding for Natalie, her best friend who is backpacking in Brazil. York insists the ring belongs to his grandmother, and that Natalie's fiance stole it, but Sabina has no proof of this, so she digs her heels in. Yorke tries to bully her into giving him the family heirloom (by being rude, commanding, bossy), then tries to explain the situation, and then tries to charm and coax her, but Sabina won't budge. When nothing works, he realizes he's dealing with an Unusual Woman -- beautiful and spunky and loyal, with a sense of humor and a soft spot for old ladies -- especially frail old ladies who are recovering from major heart surgery.

As these two go toe-to-toe, an attraction builds, but neither will admit it. Yorke starts telling a few white lies to keep Sabina at his side. They are harmless, but he's never been prone to fibbing. On top of that, he finds himself surly and possessive because Sabina goes out with Oliver. Jealousy!? This "most eligible Englishman" can't believe the welter he's in.

Steele is pretty good at building chemistry and emotional intensity. Her love scenes -- even getting only to 2nd or 3rd base -- are more sizzling than some erotica I've read. Excerpt:

"Sweet love," he groaned, and caressed her, moulding her breasts, teasing... And Sabina was reduced, seduced into just holding onto him, while his mouth and tongue and gentle teeth teased and tormented each hard, throbbing nipple....and as one of his hands caressed down to her thigh..."

But, wait! She's a virgin (!!) and he's a honorable man! (No!!!) I didn't like the way Yorke coldly stopped the loving.

 In some of Steele's Hqn Presents, they go all the way, and in only a few Hqn Romances. For example, see Wife in Waiting for tender sizzling sex scenes, fully completed.

******

I was intrigued by the plot synopsis, but I didn't like the heroine, Astrid Honeywell. She is 26 years old and the eldest sibling, serving as default parent to her three younger sisters, Alice (23), Antonia, and Ardyce (the girls are about 8 and 10). Sadly, Astrid came across as childish, stupid, and unworthy of her siblings. She employed juvenile methods for dealing with the duke's ownership of what she viewed as Honeywell property. The author doubtless meant to portray Astrid as an independent woman of character --  "feisty"  but to me, Astrid seemed idiotic. A moron.

Slapstick humor. Some readers say this book is funny. To each her own, but it's not my style of comedy. It's slapstick, unkind, juvenile, and repetitive. For example, characters repeatedly fall in the mud while running from Petunia, the rampaging pig. It wasn't funny the first time, and became annoying with each new mention of Petunia. I didn't like the heroine laughing at the poor valet when he finally had enough and -- covered in mud -- decided to quit his job.

I didn't much like the hero, either. The Duke let his valet quit after years of service, showing no signs of maturity or good humored patience when confronted with the poor maddened mud-man.  Furthermore, the Duke had never seen a pig in his life before, except on a dinner platter??? He got motion sickness in the carriage and retched 50 times en route to Yorkshire. 50 times!!! His OCD-driven need for order and control was not funny. It was sad. And such an intense level of compulsion would not be so easily overcome.

3.5 stars -- and all for Drew!

Okay, so Drew and Indigo are wolf changelings in the Snow Dancer Pack. They lust after each other, but idiotic Indigo is stubbornly wary of mating with someone of lower rank than herself. Drew changes Indigo's silly mind. That's the book. Plus a thin Psy plot.
---
I was gonna give it 2 stars, because Indigo was irritatingly stupid and the plot was too thin...

... but my inner wolf howled "5 stars for Drew!" -- cuz she loved all the licking, the nipping, the petting, the sucking, the biting. Plus  talking sexy, thinking sexy, panting for sex, having sex!! All the cuddling, and courting, with roses, more roses, and cheesecake,  more cheesecake, and chocolate kisses, more kisses....yummy Drew.

I argued with my animal ego, explaining that Indigo irritated me, and there was simply not enough action. All that sex eventually got boring, without a nicely paced plot. I wanted more suspense, I said.

My wolf snarled at me, her claws poking under my skin, arguing that there was plenty of action: In the first third of the story,  the wolves find hidden Psy devices (*Yawn). In the second chunk, the wolves rescue someone from a fall. (**Howdy-do) In the final third, the wolves fight the bad Psy guys (**but the battle was soon over. Predictable.)

Wolfie snapped at me again, growling "5 stars for my Drew!"

Ok, fine! So 3.5 stars. But not for the plot. Not for the action. Not for the annoyingly cryptic and brief Psy Council meetings. The stars are for Drew. All for Drew.

My wolf and I agree --  Drew is yummy. Dreamy, dreamy, Drew.
---

Snarky, but I've read so many Psy books, and this time I grew annoyed whenever the wolves, especially Indigo, referred to themselves alternatively as a wolf or a human, changing persona every other second. Patricia Briggs does a better job of keeping the wolf dormant, unless a particular type of situation occurs. For example, there is more rhyme and reason to the shifting dominance of Charles versus his animal ego, Brother Wolf, in the Alpha and Omega series.

Many will disagree, but I think 3 stars is generous.  Pleasant enough, but not my style. Absurd. The romance is fine, the passion steamy, and I even sympathized with some of the characters. But the plot is ridiculously silly. At the same time, it's needlessly complex, due to the widely varied species of characters and the overlapping series.

Kenyon breaks the KISS rule (keep it simple, sweetie). She's got one series layered upon another series, and eventually, even a third overlapping series. She's got organizations piled upon societies and species. Yikes!  Dark-Hunters, Were-Hunters, Dream-Hunters, daemons, demons, Arcadians, Kategorians (sp?), Apollites, Romans, Greeks, vampires, werewolves, all kinds of shape-shifters, the Fates and other Greek gods, and...humans.

Not to mention the character names: Fury, Vane, Fang...Bride.  LOL!!

Lots of improbabilities:

We have Vane, a shapeshifter wolf who only left the wild 8 months ago, having spent his entire life (almost 5 centuries)  in a wolf den, apart from humans, but who dresses in leathers, can handle a motorcycle, manages an investment portfolio and is on good terms with the Wichovia bank president, knows his salad fork from his steak knife, is a wine connoisseur, drives several hot sports cars..... Imagine shapeshifter bears celebrating Thanksgiving. Silly.

What are the chances that Bride's ex-boyfriend would be SUCH an overt jerk with a capital B. I mean he was over the top.  What motivated him, after 5 years of dating, to be so unwarrantedly cruel? Who knows. Who cares. Plot device.

Our hero Vane can magically makes clothes, cell phones, and roses instantly appear,  and he knows that his human mate and his comatose brother are on a high priority hit list from his vile pack, but he LEAVES THEM UNPROTECTED TO GO GET A DRINK??  Even though his enemies appeared in that very same room only a few days ago??? (obviously, Kenyon needed to steer the plot. Who cares if we sacrifice all respect for Vane's intelligence, if not his SHORT TERM MEMORY!!)

Gads.

Vane tells Bride that he is 460 years old. That would mean he was born around 1550. Shakespearian days.  But when they go back in time to England to see his mother, to a time AFTER he was born, and AFTER his brothers were grown up, they go to -- wait for it --  the 5th Century, referencing King Arthur. (I really must have missed something, because no way does that add up.)

I'm in the minority. Many readers lap it up. Read this book for the romance, not for a coherent, compelling story.

======================

I enjoyed the beginning (up until they arrive at Fort Edward) and the ending better than the middle section. It got too dark and unpleasant. Too melodramatic and overblown. The villain is soooo evil. Pamela Clare is a favorite author, but I prefer her contemporary I-Team series. My favorites are Unlawful Contact (I-Team Series, Book 3) and Skin Deep (I-Team After Hours). Back to this book: No synopsis. No spoilers. I Iain, The McKinnon. Love all his Ranger brothers and friends. Love Annie, too. As for secondary characters, I got a kick out of Joseph and Lieutenant Cooke. William Wentworth is an odd mix, and thus interesting. Uncle Bain was not interesting. One dimensional. But I didn't laugh once. And I do like to laugh. I only smiled a few times, primarily the scenes with secondary characters (Killy, Dougie, Joseph, Cooke, etc.) I did quite a bit at the end. What a beautiful ending. I loved it. My favorite part of the book! Also, too much time spent in the mind, rehashing what just happened. We read about it happening, then we read about Iain or Annie or William thinking it over, fretting about it. Slows the pace. The lashing went on too long, including the tension-laden pages before the whipping. I just felt icky that whole time. This was my main complaint with book three, Defiant (MacKinnon's Rangers, Book 3) -- but it was MUCH worse in that book. Ugh. Loved the tender smexy scenes, including the hot scene in the sweat lodge, but I thought the sex scenes were absurd. Annie is a virgin. It would never have occurred to her to go down on Iain, especially since he had not gone done on her... yet. And the part with the razor? Totally improbable for that setting. Bottom line, this one is not for me. I know many of my friends love this series, though. I am in the minority.

Way too dark for me. A serial killer. A mad doctor. Two evil woman. Gross human experiments in some Russian underground complex with a bunch of totally vile psychopaths. I couldn't take any more of that Spider creature. She totally creeped me out. The imprisonment began early in the book and the torture contined for MUCH too long. The character didn't break out until 42% into the book (not page 42, reading status was set wrong). Even once they were out, the creepoids followed them and continue to pop up and gross me out. Throughout at least half the book, Artur keeps remembering "Marilyn weeping" as he mentally replayed her violent mutilation. No no no no no. Just no.

And too much introspection, bogging down the pace severely. Introspection in the midst of conversation even -- sometimes going on for more than a page!!!

Apart from that, the romance didn't do anything for me. Artur basically took one look and fell in love. Why? No reasons given.

Also, why did Rictor feel so protective of Eleni? What is he, anyway? What kind of being? and what about the couple who killed Ms. Graves and her goons? What are they? What is this "other" organization? Just too many threads left open for the next book in the series, making this one unsatisfying.

The heroine was sometimes clever, but at one point she took off alone, knowing the serial killer was after her. TSTL.

What did I like: I liked it when Eleni barfed all over her captor. Twice. On purpose. I liked it whenever Eleni or Artur broke the psychic bonds of Spider woman, Ms Weave. I liked the camaraderie that grew between the four escapees. Also, I liked the two shape shifters, especially the jaguar.

Minor nit-picks:

Shapeshifter Koni is a raven in book 1, but now he is a crow.

Setting in the seaside port Vladivostok seemed vivid. I've never been there, but it felt real. However, Artur lives in a 2-story BRICK townhouse in San Francisco suburb. Brick not allowed, due to earthquake-safety building code.

Artur said the days were long because it was summer, yet the rain was ice cold? It hailed, and the heater on the train was on. She wore a turtleneck sweater? In summer? How about a scarf around the neck, to hide the bruising.

Book 1 characters did not appear in this book at all, but they were mentioned once or twice.

Content: Sex, gruesome murder, lots of violence and bloody savagery, some swearing, a little profanity

4.75 stars, rounded to , because Ice Blue is indeed totally cool, keeping me up all night, java in hand. It's in the midst of ashes, bones, urns, and potential Armageddon. Yup! Never a dull moment, right up until the Lunar New Year -- oh, no!! It's well-paced, suspenseful, a little scary, and soooo sexy. The story flows, from winter in Santa Monica, California to rain-swept Bainbridge Island in Washington State, to frozen Tokyo and the cleverly conceived confrontation with evil, and finally to London, on the verge of spring. Granted, there are a few bald spots in the plot, and half a dozen typos or so, but this book is a KICK! It's a mix of Bourne and Bond, with a luscious anti-hero. I liked the first book in the series, Black Ice with Chloe and Bastien, but I love this one. (Actually, Black Ice had a more textured villain, whereas this villain was a one-dimensional religious lunatic.) The POV shifts constantly (sometimes too much) from Dr. Summer Hawthorne to Takashi (Taka) O'Brien to His Holiness, the Shirosama, guru of the True Realization Fellowship, to Madame Isobel Lambert, the Judi Dench-like Director of The Committee, a London-based covert special-ops group, and Taka's boss. The PLOT: Taka, a half-Japanese / half-American assassin, is conflicted about Lambert's order to kill Summer, to save the world from chemical and biological mass murder (not beyond the realm of possibility, considering the noxious gassing of the trains in Japan several years ago). Contrived! There was no need for the (mostly benign) Committee to kill an innocent citizen. They could have simply kidnapped Summer and hidden her safely away, keeping her memories and her urn from the Shirosama. But I went along for the ride. And what a ride it was! Summer's POV: "Even in the shadows she could see that he was exquisitely beautiful. High, perfect cheekbones, exotic eyes of an indeterminate shade, narrow face and rich, full mouth. His hair was long and silky, black, and he was at least part Asian, despite the fact that he towered over her." Taka's POV: "She had blue eyes, and she was prettier than he'd realized. She didn't wear make up, and she had a sprinkling of freckles across her nose. He'd never killed anyone with freckles before." *Evil chuckle* Isn't he just adorable?! Cruel, ice cold, and eventually so damn crazy about her! It's just driving him nuts. He ties himself into KNOTS, haha, but once he makes up his mind that he is NOT gonna kill her, he goes all alpha, protective, hot, and sexy. It's not love at first sight. Taka thinks Summer is frumpy and annoyingly stupid. And she sometimes is! He's cruel sometimes, but then he's sorry. And so so hot! That scene in the bathroom!!! The bedroom! And in the end, the sweetest -melting scene, with Taka holding Summer "so tightly a weaker woman might break, whispering to her in Japanese, sweet, loving words, letting her cry." Awwww!! HEA for all. Hugs all round! Great secondary characters, especially red-haired bad-boy Reno (Taka's younger cousin) and Jilly (Summer's teenage sister), the stars of book 5, Fire and Ice. I really liked Jilly, so here is an excerpt showing her personality: Genevieve breezed into the kitchen... "Tea in the garden, I think. Peter will be home early, and he'll probably bring Isobel. We all need frocks." "Frocks?" Jilly echoed with a laugh. "You're not putting me into Laura Ashley -- I'm bigger than you and I fight dirty." Haha! Just one example of some of the humorous dialogue. Content: Explicit sex scenes (three). Violence. Lots of cussing and profanity (not my cuppa). Several typos.

This book could be for Young Adults, but be aware there is some swearing, including the F-bomb, lots of dismemberment and mutilation, and some sexual references.

The perspective is constantly shifting, from Selia to Jaden to Keldar to Nathan. Too much head-hopping.

Ahoy! *mild spoilers* (I keep it vague)

This book is difficult to classify. It purports to be a fantasy, but nothing is truly fantastic. There is no high fantasy -- no dragons, elves, or sorcerers. The rest could be explained away as genetics and skill -- skill in using herbs to heal, skill in following tracks and in warfare, and genetically-developed ability to smell odors across long distances, especially useful when scenting humans. Everything could be real, and found here on Earth, from the blood-eating, cannibal-like Svistra race to the "White Forest" that devours humans and animals alike (Earth has similar carnivorous plants). Even the wasteland known as the Dead Lands struck me as similar to the kind of decay brought on by a nuclear bomb or the salting of the earth.

So, it didn't feel much like a fantasy, despite the "About the Author " section where Thomas refers to reading about Narnia and Middle Earth as a girl. No. It felt like a grim post-apocalyptic political piece. This dark tone was reinforced when one of the most lovable characters was written out midway. A mistake! From treacherous human kings to butchering barbaric Svistras, there were few characters to like, much less love. (Nathan was cool, though.)

At the same time, Altered Destiny purports to be a romance -- and it did feel like a mild romance between Selia, the warrior human, and Jaden, her handsome Svistra prince. But yet.... Where's the Happy Ever After? For one thing, the ending was written without even a kiss !!! (and they never made love either, even though we got the "joy" of watching the evil Keldar start to mate with Noe). On the up side, midway through the book there are one or two scenes involving kissing and cuddling between Jaden and Selia.

But even more worrisome, I did NOT close the book assured of a fine future for this couple, even though Selia rather carelessly assures Jaden that people will get used to him. Um...how likely is that? The Svistra have been viciously and horrendously mutilating, murdering -- and feeding on-- innocent men, women, and children from all the surrounding villages. Jaden is a Svistra.

Plus, why should I even LIKE the Svistra race as a whole? The author portrayed only one !!! likable member of this race, Jaden. The rest are repulsive, engaging voluntarily and even gleefully in vampiric blood-sucking, patricide, infanticide, mutilation, etc. Very gory!

As though to make me sympathetic to this bloody Orc-like culture, Jaden tells some long sob story about their history. Then, Shawna Thomas tosses a bone in the last section -- a friend of Jaden's appears suddenly in the cast. Apparently, he's a likable fellow -- a nice Svistra -- but how would I know? He virtually walked across the stage, and that's it, but I am to believe in his ability to command during this critical period of potential peace? Poorly developed.

There is also mention of Jaden's mother, a kinder, gentler Svistra who became a healer, but we never actually meet her. (Also, we never find out why Nathan thought the old male healer looked like Jaden.)

Bottom line, I don't recommend this book. While Jaden and Selia were awfully sweet together, I was ultimately disappointed and even disturbed by it. Altered Destiny held my attention fairly well, with a balance of scary, suspenseful, and sweet parts, but in the final analysis, it read like a gruesome analogy to the Israeli / Palestinian conflicts over land -- or the "Manifest Destiny" conflict between the pioneering settlers and the Native Americans, but set in some mythical place at some ancient time.

Horrifyingly gruesome at times, this is an absorbing, suspenseful, and detailed survival story with strong themes of tenacity, trust, and passionate unyielding commitment. Dare and Angie get my vote for most likely to succeed at ... anything and everything!

I liked this book better the second time around (but this time I totally skipped over the truly gory scenes and the pages wih the bear's point of view).  The first time I read it, the survival aspects overwhelmed the romance, so I would rate it 3 stars, at best.

However, on the second read, I concentrated mainly on Dare and Angie. I felt like I really got to know the characters -- and more importantly, they began to bond with each other. A trusting, devoted relationship developed nicely, even though the entire book -- except for the epilogue -- takes place in about 48 hours.

Umm. No. Dare has had his eye on Angie for the past two years. Actually, he's had "his eyes on her world-class ass" since the first time they met. But she wanted nothing to do with the guy who was "stealing customers" from under her nose. As you might guess, the course of true love (yada yada yada).

Now, two years later, Dare goes up the mountain to keep covert watch over his hostile love, who is leading a hunting expedition with two men. Good thing, too. He found her crawling in the mud, at night, in the icy rain, with her ankle on fire and two killers behind her, one with two feet, the other four.

Dare -- a former army sergeant -- is alpha all the way. He rescues her. It's soooo not easy, but Angie is alpha, too -- never a quitter and stubborn to the core, despite suffering pain, fatigue, shock, and borderline hypothermia.  Lots of intense  survivalist stuff goes on for many pages, but I liked that. So many of these modern romantic suspense books make the life-or-death rescue look like a piece of cake (not a piece of wedding cake, though -- that will give Angie nightmares).

Once the immediate danger is alleviated, they recuperate for a while. In a snug cabin, amidst torrential rains, Dare FINALLY gets the girl to look at him, talk to him!! So...lots of lovely relation-shipping (J) is packed into two cloistered days in a cabin, leading to a fabulously passionate love scene. Dare is also tender, and funny. I chuckled at their sexy banter.

But...the danger is still there, and they gotta get off that mountain.

In the epilogue, they get married (of course) and celebrate with a "big-ass wedding cake"  (you'll see, the white icing is important).

I read all 4 books of the Esri series over a long weekend a month ago. My most favorite was book 2, Dark Deceiver, and this was my second most favorite. I liked the developing relationship between the special-ops warrior and the somewhat dumpy and submissive dwarf, who, as she responds to various challenges in a dangerous other world, gradually reveals her true self-- unknown even to her. She morphs into a woman of beauty, wisdom, skill, and strength (but still just barely 5 feet). Surprisingly, it was a wonderfully well-told tale, with some sophisticated plotting and surprising revelations. This is better than standard Harlequin fare, in my view. Some fun sex, too! :-) On the down side, at least for me, this book had religious swear words--according to my kindle, 11 occurrences. Distracting and annoying.

************* CONTENTS: About four explicit sex scenes, several scenes of murder and mayhem, including violence against a ten-year-old boy, minimal or no profanity (much appreciated), minimal or no typos (yay!) ************* I'd go as high as 4 stars. Those who love Pamela Clare's like-titled book Surrender might really like this book -- the first in a series of three, and Farrelly's debut novel. For me, there was a little too much grim villainy. Too many mayhem scenes. As soon as something good would happen, it would be followed by something violent. Up-down-up-down, like a yo-yo. I could feel a pattern in the flow. Yet well done, for all that. WRITING SKILL: The writing is of decent quality. The plot is coherent, at times poignant, and the smexy times sizzle -- especially in the hot springs. The historical aspects felt authentic, too. More so than most books of this genre. However, I felt the author reveals too much. I predicted *almost* every single bad thing that happened. She needs to keep her cards a little closer to her chest, instead of revealing everything the villains are up to, as the third-person POV switched from hero to heroine to villains. But to her credit, Farrelly doesn't slow the pace and fill the pages with repetitive internal reflection. There is some of that, but not too much. Further, she portrays children fairly authentically. The ten-year-old boy is credible. Also, the dialogue includes the idiomatic expressions of the past. AUDIO: I listened to this book and also read it, switching between kindle book and audio. The narrator is Keith Tracton. See audio review at the bottom. His narration gets 3 or 4 stars, I'd say. STORY IN BRIEF, NO MAJOR SPOILERS, WITH MY COMMENTS: Set in Wyoming just after the Civil War, the story spans 1865-1867. It begins with Confederate Captain Michael Cantrell, our hero, listening to his beloved General Robert E. Lee address the troops with a "farewell to arms" speech. The author made this authentic historically, including the papers Michael carries, stating that he will never bear arms against his own country again (something like that). Michael lost his entire family and is heartbroken, so he leaves Dixie and heads west on his black steed, Jet. A year later, he happens upon Annie Devlin and her ten-year-old brother Robbie, losing ground fast under deadly attack. The siblings are alone in the world, because their schoolteacher mother died six years ago, and their horse-breeder father died one year ago. A corrupt landowner wants the Devlin ranch, but Annie stubbornly won't sell and won't cave to threats and bully tactics, so the corrupt Colonel sends out his worst thugs, including a nasty piece of work named Skinner. In the nick of time, Michael rescues Annie and Robbie, but he gets badly wounded. Annie takes him home and nurses his wounds. This happens early in the story. At first, Michael is aloof and distant, because he doesn't ever want to feel any more loss or pain. However, the Devlins win his heart. He becomes a brother to Robbie, helping him with homework and horses, etc. Eventually, Annie and Michael become lovers and get married. SOUNDS LOVELY, RIGHT? Well, yes and no. It's a fairly grim story, with splashes of joy. Like a Pamela Clare historical romance, there is no surcease fom the wicked schemes of amoral men. All three protagonists -- even Robbie -- must repeatedly battle various vicious villains. Too many times, in my opinion. However, there are some brief joyous scenes in between the mayhem. Some laughter. Some warmhearted at-home scenes, bonding with Robbie and Annie. Some fairly humorous banter between Annie and Michael, and I loved the comaraderie between Michael and his older roommate from West Point, the local Calvary Major he calls "Chief" (and Chief calls Michael "The Brat"). Eventually, some sizzling sexy times. Then a wedding at the Fort. The reception scene was quite something! Chuckles all around! There is also a lot of "coming to terms" with past deaths, and with all the Yankee men in blue -- especially the horde at the military outpost. The author neatly portrayed Michael's sense of anxiety and unease around the Yankee regiment, and his slow adjustment to them, and inclusion back into the fold. CHARACTERIZED BY GUILT: Michael Cantrell, only 24, was a prime cadet at West Point Academy before war broke out: top of his class, tall, strong, lethal. Dark blond hair and deep blue eyes. He was born into a prosperous and loving Virginia family that didn't approve of slavery, but did uphold states rights. During the war, he lost his entire family, especially his little brother Gavin. Michael blames himself for Gavin's death. I really dislike maudlin, self-glorifying guilt-tripping scenes -- and it seems to prevail in romance books -- but in this case, it was handled fairly realistically, and the cause was believable: Michael shouldered the blame for Gavin's death because he was the one who pulled strings to transfer Gavin to the unit that came under the heaviest fire. So, Gavin, long dead, plays a major role in this book, albeit a ghostly role. Literally. There are a handful of paranormal ghost scenes -- Gavin wants Michael to be happy. I liked the scenes with Gavin the ghost. I liked Gavin. EPILOGUE: I did NOT like the epilogue, because it was just another sex scene. Who cares? The sex scenes are well written in this book -- I could feel the heat -- but after the first time or two, I lose interest. This book had about four sex scenes. In the epilogue, I wanted to see the family settled safely, with scenes of prosperity and productivity. I wanted to see Michael doing what he was born to do -- breed horses. I wanted to see MORE of Robbie, recovering nicely from his grievous emotional and physical wounds. After all the hell these guys went through, I wanted to close the book with a satisfied feeling of healing and happiness. AUDIO: I listened to this book and also read it, switching between book and audio. The narrator is Keith Tracton. He could be superb, in terms of his ability to perform character roles. Good rendition of Annie, the heroine. Unlike some narrators, he didn't make his voice all squeaky and high pitched for her. His voice for the boy was good, too, as was his impression of the hero Michael, a Johnny Reb, even though I would rather he'd used his normal voice for Michael, with a Southern accent overlaid. His normal voice is pleasing on the ears, and has more depth, texture, and resonance than his character voice. At one point he had to sing -- a great little a cappella performance. However, when he is simply narrating, he sounds almost robotic. That is a real problem. Like a machine almost. So, narration gets 3 or 4 stars, I'd say. In the sequel, Terms of Engagement, Robbie (Dr. Robert Devlin) falls in love. In the third book, Terms of Temptation, Michael and Annie's daughter falls in love. Both sequels included Michael and Annie, according to the reviews. ToE sounds too grim for me, but I might try ToT.

Some funny scenes! Some sizzling sex! I liked Dageus -- a sympathetic and noble character. Chloe was likable, too, and funny in several scenes.  The plot was decent, even though the "hand of god" device was used to resolve things.

Good to see recurring secondary characters from book 4: Drustan and Gwen, Sylvan and Nell.

It would be 4 stars, but I don't like how Moning tells a story, for three reasons.

1) Too much repetition about physical appearance --  how ripped he is, how sexy he is, how hot all the Keltar men are, how thick and long his cock, etc.

2) Too much time spent inside the head(s). Thinking. Feeling. Regretting. Pondering. Questioning. Wishing. Fearing. Enough already!! I want more action or conversation.

3) Several times, Moning has a key character tell another character some important event that happened, rather than telling it to us when it happens. I want strong, vivid, descriptive language as the event occurs. Like, for only one example, at the end, when Dageus was killing people in the basement of the old building in London, we didn't see it happen, except for the opening bit.  About 10 pages later Dageus TOLD Chloe the "rest of the story"  (in spare, flat language).  He didn't even tell it all, leaving some unanswered questions.

Still, a fairly entertaining story, with likable characters, some good luvin' and some good laughs.

Adult content: Explicit sex -- several scenes. Violence and death -- pretty mild.  Swearing, with some F-bombs and too much  anti-religious profanity.

Loved it. A keeper. A joy. This is a subtle love story, not a bodice ripper, despite the cover art. Not a lot of action/adventure, but enough. I did read the second book in the series, telling Ramon's story. One Night Is Never Enough. There is no need to read the first book, Seven Secrets of Surrender. There really is little connection between books 1 and 3, hardly worth worrying about. Some reviewers feel the heroine was silly, not clever. I disagree. See my reasons in the spoiler at the bottom. Andreas is a BAD MAN who trusts no one but his brother and his old nanny. He is the ultimate overcomer, for he rose from the gutter -- where his father literally tossed his bleeding, broken body -- to become a wealthy, powerful casino owner and one of London's underworld kings. Feared by all, he mainly goes after slime. Because he has zillions of enemies, he will only eat food prepared by one or two trusted staff members, or by himself. For two decades, Andreas has been driven by a need for revenge. He plots to bring down daddy dearest. Along comes Phoebe, with that damn smile. That compelling, repelling smile! She needs him to help solve several problems involving her father and brother, but she grows quickly to adore him, seeing through his cold facade to a deeply loyal, passionate, and vulnerable loner. Phoebe sets his world on his ear, moving her family right into his casino to keep them safe. She bakes biscuits and other goodies for everyone, driving Andreas nuts with the smell of honey and vanilla. He tries to stay aloof, to scare her off, to ignore her, but every day he yields another inch, falls a bit further. Just delightful! First, she strategically wins desk space in Andrea's study. Once there, she sets out to win a smile from Andreas, then a chuckle, his trust, a kiss. The most revealing moment occurs when he eats her food. He will eat only her food, now. Talk about show not tell!! Mallory is brilliant! I was grinning from ear to ear through much of the book. Phoebe also helps him find perspective and balance on the vengeance plot. Towards the end, a tender fade-to-black love scene on the rug by the fire. Sigh. Loverly. Then another similar love scene, just as appealing. Nothing explicit here, but enough detail to fuel my dreams. Some reviewers wanted it more explicit, but not me. Not in this case. Oh what my imagination can do with the splendid cover art. Yummy, just yummy. One reviewer compared this with Barbara Cartland, simply because there was no explicit sex. I disagree. This was much too sophisticated, layered, and complex, and it actually offered more lovemaking than the old dame ever did. Cartland writes formulaic pap about vile wickedness attacking sweet innocence, with a superhero to the rescue. I heart Andreas. He was so afraid to believe that Phoebe could really love him, especially after what he did to .... Nope. That would be telling. I loved the ending too, describing their life 20 years later, but it was too short. I didn't want it to end. Flaw: Sometimes all the dialogue and internal reactions got a little boring. The pacing got a bit slow. Possible flaw: I would have liked Phoebe's POV sooner. Much as I loved hearing Andreas's thoughts, a sole focus on him made the story a bit difficult to follow. I was not sure about her motivations until about 1/3 or even 1/2 of the way into the story. But suspense ain't a bad thing, and too many romance authors reveal everything, including too much skin, much too soon. ;-) ========= Spoilers below ========== I disagree with reviewers who state that Phoebe was silly or stupid. She was shrewd and insightful. All the baking and cleaning was just a way to get close to Andreas and his staff, because she knew -- from his letters to her father, her first meeting with him, and her intuition -- that he knew something about her missing brother and/or the dirty scam. She gambled on Andreas being her best hope, and a trustworthy character, because of her meeting with his brother and Nanny. That meeting occurred before this story opens, but she alludes to it when pondering her plans. Phoebe expressed ALL these thoughts, beginning about 1/3 into the book. Situational awareness: Phoebe realized Andreas was at the theater(s), watching her. She also realized he was outside her home at night, guarding her. She knew he was following her through the streets of London, when she dressed as a man of business. More evidence of intelligence and intuition: Phoebe figured out that her brother went missing at the same time as the dirty scheme. She also determined early on that Andreas was motivated by something other than money, and eventually figured out it was revenge. She successfully impersonated her solicitor's fake brother. She reinvested the 20,000 pounds immediately. She had the sense to disguise her dad, when moving into the casino-- which WAS a safe choice of location. She had the foresight to gradually pack all their belongings in nondescript baggage, and moved them in a few bags at a time, knowing she might be watched. Realizing that the family business was vulnerable, with her father ill and her brother missing, she signed contingency control over to Andreas, should anything happen to the Pace family. She knew better than to trust Edward with such authority, because he knows only about farming, nor Henry, because he is easily controlled by his dad. She decided Andreas was her best option, especially since he already had a 30% share in the company. She figured out that Andreas only shot her brother to injure him, not kill him, and deduced that may have kept him from getting into more danger. She also allowed Andreas time to realize they belonged together (the month). So, in my view, Phoebe was a woman with a clear head on her shoulders. In addition to intelligence and intuition, she had her priorities straight. She would do anything for her family.

I read the entire series, and also listened to the superb audiobook performance by Simon Vance. This author held my attention enough to complete the series.  I'm glad I did and would recommend this series to readers who like recurring characters forming lasting relationships (friendships, loyalty, esprit de corps, and romance) and those who like fantasy that is somewhat light, or not entirely grim-dark.

Contents: No sex. Little or no swearing. Plenty of bloody gore, but it didn't (usually) feel too intense for me, and I'm squeamish.

Fantastical elements: Prophecies, mages, gods, demons, giants, elves, Orc-like creatures with multiple eyes and camouflaging scales, etc.

The series is named TRYSMOON for the three moons Trys, Duim, Minn. Each moon exudes different magical properties, but only to those who can work their magic. The moon TRYS is the most critical to the series. It's completely eclipsed at the beginning of book 1, as the cover illustration depicts. In addition to moon magic there is blood magic, forbidden by the powerful Church of the One.

There is romance in this series, with an irritating and bizarre love triangle. I like a little romance, but did not like the love triangle at all.

My quick response to the 4 Trysmoon books:

Book 1 ASCENSION: 4 stars (likable protagonists. A slow start, but gathers speed and ends well. Loved The Trials chapter and The Wedge chapter (after dinner, the evening the fat fianc first arrived in Mikmir. Too many typos brings it down a half-star.)

Book 2 DUTY:  4 stars (still quite engrossing, despite some vacillating characters and an emerging romantic entanglement I found boring)

Book 3 HUNTED: 3.5 or 4 stars (Love triangle becomes more intrusive, and I struggled to buy the character changes in Torbrand, Shadad Khairn)

Book 4 SACRIFICE:  2.5 stars (good beginning, gradually worsening due to absurd twists in the love triangle, various character breaches (our smart hero makes incredibly stupid decisions), several plot contrivances, unexplained emotional vacuums at illogical times, and a horrible epilogue)

Excellent narration by Simon Vance across the series.

A glossary or Wiki page would be helpful, because there are many places and people to remember, with odd spellings. Hard to remember, especially when listening to audiobook.

A jolly good story. Spy recovers in hospital, brought back to the light by the voice and touch of a woman he's never met before. Alpha male and strong heroine. Setting moves from Bethesda naval hospital to cozy cabin in Colorado. Not too much action, but just enough to keep the pages turning.

This book was more about relationship, less about spy games.

The sexual tension builds through most of the book, ultimately yielding to sizzling sex in the snow and elsewhere.

Fun read!!

The first book in this series. The author's first book, I believe. Outstanding! A paranormal romance,  historical, set in 1881 London. Some parts seemed like urban fantasy, especially where the girl is all tough, taking on all comers, not relying on her superhero hubby. SHE saves the day, while mentally castigating HIM for not telling her what was going on! ;-)

Miranda is a beautiful, loving, and loyal commoner who can mentally start fires. She is afraid of her power. She knows what it is to be different, to be rejected by a fianc,, and to feel guilt (for accidentally burning down a warehouse, etc). She loves her two sisters, Daisy and Poppy, who will probably appear in the sequels.

Lord Benjamin Archer is noble of heart and lineage -- a doctor who swallowed some cursed medicine. It changed him, physically and spiritually, making it necessary to wear a mask. He is lonely, rejected, tugged towards evil, yet striving to hold on to his humanity, even though his hope of a cure has been dashed multiple times.

Archer falls in love with Miranda, instantly. He marries her early on in the book, knowing he should not, but yet the marriage protects her from a nasty father and a life of crime. Slowly, so slowly, the newlyweds turn toward each other. The relationship grows and the sexual tension builds to a near-climax half-way through the book -- in an alley-- and a passionate yet poignant denouement that reveals ALL about 3/4 into the book. The denouement was a surprise.

The curse was original, based supposedly on old Egyptian legends. A new twist on paranormal fantasy.

Character development is not bad. We gradually discover more about Miranda, as she learns to accept her powers and her kick-ass temperament is gradually revealed. We also learn a lot more about Archer; we begin to see his noble and loyal heart. We also learn a bit more about his old friend Leland, his rival McKinnon, and even the housekeeper and butler. I loved the housekeeper.

As I said, they marry within the first three chapters. For the rest of the book, we find out more about the curse, the horrendous murders surrounding Archer, and Miranda's firepower. I began to suspect who the villain was fairly soon, but was not quite sure till much later, and so the suspense held fast. :-)

The final battle scenes? Vivid, believable, well-paced, tense, heart-rending.

The epilogue? Just okay.

Flaws: It could have been just a bit shorter -- some slow bits here and there. The flow or pacing at times felt the slightest bit  burdensome. Not sure what, exactly, but it could have been due to the language, yet unlike some reviewers, I did not see it as purple prose -- not precisely. The good news is the author did not subject her readers to endless pages where the characters are pondering, internalizing, ruminating on their guilt, etc. May others take a lesson from this rookie.

Also, a few times the author used religious swear words, which I find distracting and distressing.

Mixed feelings on this one. I read it on Kindle, after coming across it on several List-mania recommendations.

Just an okay read. Disappointing. Fairly boring and predictable.  I'd give it 3 stars if it were shorter, without all the filler scenes.

I liked the idea of a heroine (Laura) who struggles with aphasia due to a diving accident, limiting her speech, language and verbal memory. Kudos to the author for including such an interesting and unique lead character.

However, Anderson was inconsistent in her treatment of the aphasia issue. It's a challenge to write dialogue for a person with a language impairment, but having taken that challenge, it's important to do it right. Nonetheless, I appreciated the aphasia dynamic. It added a lot to the story!

I liked Laura and Isaiah. I was rooting for Laura, and happy to see her learn the ropes of a new job. I liked the setting, the veterinary clinic. I liked many of the coworkers at the clinic, and all the animals.

I liked Isaiah, too. Glad to see Isaiah get a home-cooked meal. For some reason, I am drawn to stories where hungry guys get a hearty meal.

But the story went on and on. At 432 pages, I expect a complex plot, an epic adventure, or a sweeping love story. Not so. This was a mundane plot. Should be only 300 pages, in my view. Predictable, too. No spoilers, but I predicted "who dun it" early on.

Liked the Coulter family, including the warm-hearted matriarch, Mary Coulter.

Did not appreciate dozens of religious expletives and exclamations, especially with the implied Christian upbringing (Mary). That type of language simply did not fit these characters. Plus, it is offensive to many readers, so why include it?

And, I'm sorry to say... the sex scenes were boring. They just did nothing for me. Not sure why, either.

Not worth all the hype, in my view, but some folks love it, apparently.
