None of the characters is simple.  No matter how flat or one-sided they may seem to be at any point in the film, each is given one or more moments to change unexpectedly and show additional facets to their personality.

Sandra Bullock's character is a perfect example.  If there was ever any doubt that Bullock could do "serious" work as well as she does screwball comedy, this film easily dispels it.  Bullock's character seems to fall too easily into the stereotype of the upper-class racist WASP, leveling prejudice at any minority who crosses her path. She is utterly dislikable; in fact, that is the point.  Bullock, along with Matt Dillon's character, are set up early to be the film's idealogical villains.  But as the narrative progresses, we see these characters in greater depth, with new contexts.  Just as the films "heroes" begin to show weaknesses and moral failings, the "villains" gain potentially noble traits.  By the time we get near the end of the film and witness Bullock clutching at her housekeeper and confessing her lonliness, we can feel the sadness of her limited life.  We don't have to like her, and most viewers probably won't but "liking" her or not again misses the point.  The point is that life isn't so easily divided into heroes and villains.

We all have blind spots and prejudices.  We all have the capacity for nobility, and for debasement.  We all struggle for connection and to be understood.  CRASH insists that every one of its characters be seen at their best and at their worst.  It doesn't solve anything, or even offer ideas for a solution; that's why CRASH isn't really a message film.  Rather it creates a world where characters aren't classifiable as "good" people or "bad" people.  A complicated world where people have to be met where they are at, by viewers who are forced to confront where they are at.  This sort of blatent honesty is uncomfortable for many, but it's important in the complicated, multifaceted world we live in.

This movie is definitely a low budget, indie film so if you're looking for Hollywood quality - prepare for a disappointment!  But what you are going to get from this movie is a fun romp from someone who clearly likes to make movies.  Effects are done on the cheap and there are some actually pretty good effects for what they're working with.  Also, the cast is clearly having fun and enjoying themselves - they are engaged and playing up their characters without camping it up too much.  Support independent artists who are working hard to create content to entertain you!

With the new adaptation of CARRIE in theatres, now is the perfect time to rediscover this amazing classic in all its forms, and this musical adaptation is quite good.  Although I love the original film version, Carrie White is shown to be little more than a victim; in the musical, similar to the new film version, Carrie is a much more complex character and the musical does a good job of highlighting the real issue at the core of King's original novel: the book/films/musical aren't really about a girl with telekinesis at all, but really are about bullying and the terrible pains that we humans are capable of inflicting on each other.  That the target of this bullying is gifted with special abilities is just what explodes the story into its terrible climax.  King was truly visionary in depicting the everyday horrors of high school and created a tragic hero in Carrie White who tests her new powers and imagines what revenge might feel and look like, finally taking that revenge when she is pushed too far at what should have been a special night.

The musical in particualr does a good job of creating the supporting cast: Chris, Sue, and Tommy all emerge as fully developed characters, and the ensemble numbers reveal the insecurities that all high schoolers feel, the desire to fit in and be accepted (or at least fly under the radar of those who would abuse them) causing them to make terrible choices and victimize others like Carrie White.

The music is strong throughout, but here are my favorite songs:
1. The World According To Chris - Chris is obviously the villain of this story, and her solo makes no apologies and doesn't try to explain away her behavior.  She's a mean girl, and she tells us exactly why. This song is honest and brutal, and helps set up the findamental differences between popular girls Chris and Sue.
2. Once You See - Sue finally begins to see that her actions have repercussions and she has a real growing up moment when she finally understands that you can't just do whatever you feel like doing and expect a simple "I'm sorry" to make everything right.
3. A Night We'll Never Forget - We all know how this story ends.  Hearing all of the students getting ready for the prom, singing about their future plans, their hopes and dreams, is just heart-breaking.

If you like CARRIE in any of its forms, I definitely recommend checking out this album.  The music is well done, the performances are excellent, and the whole album is a great experience.

To start, I am a huge Noel Coward fan and this is easily one of his best.  The wit is crackling and classic Coward, and features the tumultuous relationships among two exes and their new spouses.  The main characters, Eliot and Amanda, are a volatile pair, and their relationship is both passionate and deeply, deeply dysfunctional.  They have left each other and found new love with Sibyl and Victor, companions who are much quieter and much less exciting.  Sibyl and Victor and meant to represent traditional notions of femininity and masculinity respectively, and it's not surprising that they end up being terrible matches for the unconventional Eliot and Amanda.

The show is definitely a product of its time, and the violence in the show is played for laughs, but modern audiences should turn a critical eye to the very real issue that underlies this play.  At one point, after Amanda says that she always thought it was inexcusable for a man to hit a woman, Eliot replies "On the contrary, I think some women should be struck regularly, like gongs."  This sentiment is problematic, and though it becomes part of the over-the-top and very stylized violence that epitomizes the volcanic romance between Eliot and Amanda, it doesn't play the same way today as it may have in Coward's time.  Rather than relegate this piece to history as a relic, however, the play provides a terrific opening to talk about the issue of violence in intimate relationships in a more complex way; it's like Eminem's "Love the Way You Lie" for the 1930s crowd.

If you haven't read any Noel Coward, this is a great place to start as it showcases his wit and masterful construction beautifully (Blithe Spirit, Hay Fever, and Easy Virtue are also highly recommended).  If you are already a Coward fan but haven't read this particular work, you will not be disappointed.

Margaret Atwood is no stranger to dystopian novels (many fans discovered her with the 1985 publication of The Handmaid's Tale, another excellent dystopian imagining) and this one is no disappointment.  The world around us has degraded to such a degree that natural disasters are devastating and commonplace, and the rich have sequestered themselves behind the heavily secured walls of corporate compounds.  Quality of life is determined by one's ability to become (and remain) useful to these corporate havens; those outside the compounds live a miserable, and largely unelaborated, existence (unelaborated, that is, until Atwood released a sequel, The Year of the Flood, that largely takes place outside of the corporate compounds).

The story is narrated by Snowman, perhaps the only human survivor of a catastrophic plague that has reduced the world to darkened ruins of its former glory.  Through his reflections, you learn about how the world came to be the way it is, and about the two great loves of his life: Oryx and Crake.  Because above all else, this book is a love story (or rather, multiple love stories).  [Obligatory Warning: the rest of the review contains potential "spoilers"]

There is the love story between Oryx and Snowman, told in flashbacks and remembrances from Snowman's somewhat naive perspective.  It is a sweet love story with more than its share of tough moments (especially Snowman's obsession with Oryx's early life as a child prostitute) but it is not nearly as important as the deeply complicated platonic love between Snowman and his best friend, Crake.  It is Crake who orchestrates the plague that destroys human civilization, and it is Crake who ensures that Snowman will live through it.  His motivations are unclear.  Is it punishment, a sadistic torment from Crake's twisted psyche?  Or is it that in the end, even Crake can't get past his own fundamental "design flaw," his ability to feel love and compassion for his only true friend?  There is no easy answer, but the consequences of Crake's decision reverberate far into the future.

By the time the reader gets to the final confrontation between Snowman and Crake, and the unleashing of the plague, the climax almost feels, well, anti-climactic.  After all the buildup and walking with Snowman through the ruins of his childhood home, the flashbacks that reveal the beginning of the end have a hurried, "and then it happened" sort of feel.  The murder of Oryx especially feels rushed, even though it is a pivotal piece of Snowman's tortured memory.  It's not that it's bad, or poorly written, or even stretches the ability to believe; rather it just feels too brief, as though such momentous events deserve additional elaboration.

Overall, this is an excellent example of dystopian future fiction.  Fans of Atwood's Handmaid's Tale will not be disappointed by this offering, nor with its sequel The Year of the Flood.  And for any who feel that this view of the future is too bleak, I challenge you to read McCarthy's The Road as a follow-up.  Bleak, indeed.

Let me start by saying that there is nothing wrong with this figure per se. It's a nice sculpt of Wonder Woman in her Star Sapphire costume from the Blackest Night event. The features look good enough and the costume is true to the comic, though the lantern battery that comes with the figure is of a very different color than her costume and looks like a better match to the Atom's Indigo Lantern costume (another figure from this Blackest-Night-themed wave). The main problem with this figure is that its quality is clearly inferior to that of the Star Sapphire Wonder Woman figure that was part of the 6th series of Blackest Night figures from DC Direct (see below). DC Direct Blackest Night: Series 6: Star Sapphire Wonder Woman Action Figure The DC Direct figure is a much better option for collectors as the quality of the paint is better (unless you dislike the look of the metallic paint, which I feel enhances the figure), the sculpt is better (it looks more like a real body and less "toy-like"), and the price is comparable - in fact, you may even be able to find the DC Direct figure for less than this one. The main challenge for non-internet shoppers is that the DC Direct line is only to be found at comic and specialty shops while the DCU Classics figures are carried at just about any store that has a toy section including Walmart and Target. If we switch gears for a moment and look at the whole line of DC Direct Blackest Night figures versus this wave of DCU Classics, the DC Direct line also has the advantage of more figures overall and it offers the complete selection of "deputized" lanterns: Mera (Red), Lex Luthor (Orange), Scarecrow (Yellow), Hal Jordan (Green), Flash (Blue), Atom (Indigo), and Wonder Woman (Violet/Star Sapphire). The DCU Classics line doesn't have Mera, and instead of a Green Lantern figure it has Hal Jordan as a Black Lantern and in a variant figure as a White Lantern. If you are a Wonder Woman "superfan" and absolutely have to have every figure that comes out, then who am I to stop you? If you are buying this for a child to play with, this is actually probably a better choice than the DC Direct figure as it seems to have more/better articulation for play. But if you are buying this as a fan of Blackest Night or Green Lantern, or you only want to have one figure to commemorate Wonder Woman's brief stint as a Star Sapphire, then you might be better served to look into purchasing one of the DC Direct figures.

I love, love, LOVE Mark Montano's Big ___ Books...I have the whole series!  Every one of them has something new and different and creative that I just have to try!  As you might expect, this one is all about bling - jewelry and accessories that you can make yourself.

Here's what I love about this book (as well as the other books in the series):
- The wide range of projects.  No matter how long you've been crafting, there is always something new in his books for you to try.  The big treasure from this one for me was the chapter on the Fuseworks microwave kiln and fusible glass projects.  Who knew there was a way to melt and fuse glass in your kitchen??
- The wide range of styles.  Some people, like me, love weird and wacky and colorful and over the top!  Some people like things a little bit more understated, classic, and/or elegant.  Montano always provides projects for a variety of tastes so that if you want to get crazy, you can!  And if you want to keep it simple, you can do that too.
- The photographs are stunning, highly saturated, colorful and high resolution images.  Every page is super detailed and colorful.  The book is just as fun to look through for the presentation as it is for the projects themselves!
- Montano does a great job of writing instructions that people can actually read and follow!  I hate when I get into a craft book and I can't understand what they are trying to tell me to do.  Montano writes clearly and his illustrations (in full color!) provide a step by step process that is super easy to follow.

I recommend this book for anyone who is interested in making their own jewelry and accessories, and I recommend ANY of the Big ___ Books for the crafters in your lives!  They make amazing gifts, or buy them for yourself and have a crafting day!

For those who wonder what bisexuality is or what it's all "about," this book is a great place to begin.  It includes personal stories, reflections, and reminiscences of what it means to be and identify as bisexual.  Our culture not only privileges heterosexuality but also monosexuality, the idea that an individual can/should only be attracted to one gender.  The stories in this collection oppose that belief and provide a rich tapestry of experience to show how complex and beautiful intimate attraction can be.  Bisexuality is not just a simple matter of being attracted to "both sexes," though it is often understood that way and is at times accused of reinforcing binary thinking about gender and sexuality; rather, it is a "third space" that by its very existence calls the binary system into question.  As this collection deftly demostrates, there is no single way to "be" bisexual and by hearing all of the stories in this collection the reader is able to see how bisexuality can be understood as a space of potential, an openness to different manifestations of sexual and emotional attraction, and having this idea explored through personal stories and experiences can be just as effective, if not moreso, than through a weighty academic tome.

Definitely recommended for those who want a good place to start in exploring what bisexuality is and how people experience it.  Especially recommended for queer groups or individuals who are struggling with how to understand or be allies to their bi friends and group members.

This is one of my favorite of the Monster High doll collections.  She's a plant monster, similar in theme to Venus McFlytrap, with vine and floral accessories but her look is softer and more feminine.  This doll is not related to any of the movies that have been released on DVD, but I believe is part of the web series (I've never watched any of the web content, only the movies on Netflix so I'm not an expert with that!).  Like all the other MH dolls, her limbs are detachable for changing clothes and accessories and she has vivid blue/purple hair with a black flower detail.  These dolls are very articulated and flexible, so they are great for children who want to act out all kinds of different scenes, and are great for collectors who may want to display them as well.  The level of detail is always incredible, including fabrics that are printed in theme with the character's origin story.

I've heard to them referred to as the "anti-Barbie" and while I think they actually share a lot in common with Barbie (including oddly proportioned bodies and a preoccupation with fashion), I appreciate that they have tried to create a concept that celebrates people being different and enjoying their "freaky flaws" as opposed to Barbie's pink, plastic perfection.  I also appreciate that they have created such a diverse collection of dolls and characters - although some characters do get different outfits and styling, each collection has at least one new character and often 3 or more new characters to add to your child's playtime!

This version of songstress Catty Noir is absolutely adorable!  The whole Geek Shriek collection gives some of the ghouls makeovers with a geeky, retro, and almost rockabilly flair.  Catty's neon pink hair is popped up into a high ponytail and her white glasses against her black skintone is fangtastic!  Her pink and white dress has a great print featuring little cat faces - one of the best things about all of the MH dolls is how much detail they put into everything down to themed fabrics and accessories!

The Geek Shriek is the "value" line of dolls, but I think they are some of the cutest of the bunch and they feature a great selection of characters: Frankie Stein (of course), Howleen Wolf, Catty, Ghoulia Yelps, Gigi Grant, and Abbey Bominable. These dolls are a fun and inexpensive way to introduce a child or a collector to some of the different MH characters besides the 6 core collection dolls. It might have been nice to get a manster in this collection, as they are pretty rare to find outside of 2-packs and collections, but that's a minor gripe for a great collection of Monster High dolls!

users.query: There just are not enough books out there about this beautiful and talented lady.  Even though it was a novel, Ms. Washburn makes Carole Lombard come alive.

cands.text: I have read just about every book out there about Anne Morrow Lindbergh.  This book did not provide me with anything new or exciting.  I knew I would not pick it up to read again in the future, so I gave it to a local charity.

I would like to thank Donna Foley Mabry for taking the time to share her Grandmother's life with others. While reading it, it was almost as though I had stepped into the pages of this book, and I found myself relating to many of Maude's situations. Times change, but human nature and the ways of the heart do not. Maude found out what true love really felt like, and how empty and sad a marriage can be when you do not have that kind of love to share with someone. I also could relate to her mixed feelings about her children.  Most of us would feel too guilty to reveal those truths, and take those feelings with us to our graves.  However embarrassing or hard for her, she owned up to those feelings, and decided to share them with other women. I admire her strength of character tremendously. Because of her book, I now realize that there are some things in life that cannot be explained or fixed by a doctor or psychiatrist. It is "Just the way it is".

I am ignoring all the bashers of this book and giving Amber five stars for her honesty. It could not have been easy to write this book and rehash so much tragedy. She admits the stupidity on her part--many times in this book. Her decisions were often selfish and she acted many times on a "whim". How many times in our youth did we make mistakes like that?  Amber Frey just happened to get involved with a tall, dark and handsome psychopath. Scott Peterson possessed the most dangerous of all antisocial personality disorders because of the way psychopaths dissociate emotionally from their actions, regardless of how terrible those actions may be. If he would have been found "Not Guilty", I am sure he would have tired of her as well, and probably killed her, too. I am sure that Amber Frey was just as relieved with the outcome of the trial as we all were. And being that I haven't heard anything bad about her in the news since, I am sure she learned many life's lessons and went on to be a much better and stronger person. After everything she has been through, I wish her all the best in her life.  Like many others, I am a collector of true crime stories, and this one is definitely a keeper.

Thank you, Christina Croft for writing this book. I had always craved more knowledge about this third child of Queen Victoria and Prince Albert. She had so many shining attributes. When you read between the lines, you can see that she was far ahead of her time in her thinking and actions.  She also paid the price for "going against the grain" of what was considered "proper etiquette" in her time by breast feeding her own children.  Her mother slighted her by naming a cow after her. Queen Victoria also was resentful of Alice's asking for monetary help so she could come home to visit with her children.  However, the Queen knew that her future son-in-law, Louis, had little money.  She rubbed it in and made Alice feel guilty and ashamed.

Alice was always helping others. She nursed her father, her brother, Hesse's wounded soldiers, her mother, the Queen, as well as her own family. She was very solemn and pure of heart, facing the deaths of others with remarkable composure.  Alice, like her father, the Prince Consort, did not fear death.  When she lost her second child, May, it seems that she became aware of the fact that, she too, would follow her to a better place, free of pain and sorrow.

The saddest thing was that while she was alive, her mother gave Alice little praise or encouragement for all the good she did to help others. I think a few kind words would have gone a long way to lift Alice's spirits.  I am sure that the Queen realized this when this daughter died so young--on the 17th anniversary of Prince Albert's death, leaving behind a husband and five children.  I am sure Queen Victoria was haunted by the good things she could have said and done, but never did. She tried to make up for this by becoming actively involved in her orphaned Hesse grandchildren's lives, right up until her death in 1901.

I came away from reading this book feeling very happy that I am not rich or famous.  I cannot imagine that a child could have less value than a box full of jewelry or a mansion in Maine, but such was the case here.  I do not feel that Brooke Astor ever really wanted or loved her only child Anthony.  Being in the limelight was the thing she cared about most.  Sure, she did great things for charity and the fine arts.  But she could not give her son what he craved the most--a mother's love.  Brooke Astor did not even seem to try to get along with her son's wife, Charlene.  All she did was try to demean and embarrass her at every opportunity. I am not saying that what Anthony and Charlene did at the end of Brooke's life was right. But I can feel Anthony's need to get what he felt he deserved after a lifetime of trying to prove that he was good enough to be his mother's son.  Brooke Astor may have lived and died a rich woman, but her heart and soul were as poor as the tenants who lived in her late husbands slum buildings.

I have read most every book there is on the Romanov's and Queen Victoria and her entire family. I was skeptical about purchasing this book, wondering if the author would lean too much to the left or to the right of the story of the downfall of Tsar Nicholas of Russia and his entire family. Pierre Gillard spoke of his thirteen years with the family as HE saw them unfold.  And what a sad story to have to write about! This was no novel.  This was the cold, hard truth.  I would recommend this book to anyone who is a Russian history enthusiast.

I cannot get enough of reading about Queen Victoria and her ancestors. This book captured my attention (and my heart) reading about what those women were up against back in those very difficult times.  I found them to have an amazing amount of strength, conviction, and above all, resiliency.  Thank you Christina Croft for your time and efforts in bringing us this great reading experience.

I usually do not buy books that are fictional accounts of people's lives.  But as much as I love reading about the descendants of the British Royals, I thought I would give it a try. But, as soon as I read about Victoria of Hesse being knocked out of a tree by Liko of Battenberg, I knew this might be a little hard to get through. After all the fact-based information I have read, this just seemed highly impossible. So did a lot of other things the author "invented".  Sure, there here were a lot of facts mixed in with the fiction, which I realized as I read along.  But these facts were nothing that I had not already read about.  In 1930, Victoria's first born daughter, Alice, suffered a nervous breakdown, and was diagnosed as schizophrenic. This truth was skimmed over by the author, who only really addressed Alice's deafness as her major obstacle to overcome. In the following decade Victoria became the one who was mostly responsible for her grandson Philips's education and upbringing. This was during his parents' separation and his mother's institutionalization. Prince Philip loved his grandmother very much and remembers much of her involvement and impact on his life. There was very little said about that in this book.  I truly wish this could have been a book based on more of the actual truth about Victoria of Hesse and those closely involved in her life. There was too much that I could just not swallow as being things this particular woman would have done or said. Hopefully, someone will be interested enough to really bring her back to life for people to learn and read about in a future book.  I do give the author credit for trying. She probably could have pulled it off with anyone with less knowledge about Victoria of Hesse and her extended family. Fiction for me has always been disappointing and second-rate. There are too many real things that have happened to people in life to read about.  My problem is that I have pretty much read everything I could possibly read about Prince Albert and Queen Victoria and all their descendents.

I have read every book out there on Tammy Wynette and George Jones. If I was asked to compare the book Tammy's daughter Jackie Daly wrote to the one Georgette Jones wrote, I would have to say that I enjoyed Georgette's book considerably more. Although I feel that Tammy's death was surely tragic, Georgette brought her Mom "to life" in her book.  She shared many wonderful memories about Tammy, letting readers know that there was far more JOY in Tammy's life then most people think. "The Three of Us" was a wonderful, poignant read.  I could feel the love coming through Georgette's writing, and also the gripping angst she felt when things happened that were beyond her ability to control. I loved all the pictures and even felt a sort of longing to read more when I finished the book. If this talented woman decides to write any future books, I would definitely want to read them. Thanks for sharing your life with your Mom and Dad with us, Georgette!  It was a total reading pleasure.

I had always been under the impression that the Queen Mother was this little smiling, sweetheart of a woman.  She seemed like everyone's idea of the kind of woman who went around doing things for others and making everybody happy. NOT!  She was just the opposite of this persona. She clawed her way to the top and got rid of everyone who stood in her way. Although I admire her strength of character and strong desire to succeed, I have a problem with the way she went about it.  Her jealousy was like a fire that could not be extinguished.  She held grudges for a lifetime and never forgave or considered what it was like to walk in another person's shoes. The Queen Mother meddled in the lives of her two daughters, often making them feel that they were at their wit's end to know what to do about her. This book was an exceptionally enlightening read, giving its readers a whole new insight on this little woman, who was actually more like the "Tasmanian Devil" in disguise.

When it comes to history, I cannot get enough of interesting and well-written material. Some books I have read have been so disappointing.  Not this one!  I learned more about these four women then I ever have before.  Mr. Vovk succeeds at bringing the reader into their world. So much so, that you almost feel as though you have a personal relationship with them. This book is a definite keeper and I hope to find more books written by this author in the future.

I am fascinated by English history and this book by Marion Crawford was so well-written and genuine, that it made me feel like I had taken a trip back in time. Ms. Crawford's accounts were very personal, but never at any time did I feel that she crossed the line to where the book could have been considered offensive or insulting to the royal family. I am so very thankful that Marion decided to be true to herself. She ultimately decided to throw caution to the wind and write this book. Because of that, people like me now have a much clearer understanding of the very different paths these two little sisters walked in their lives and the driving forces behind them.

I have never seemed to be able to get enough of English history and think that I probably know enough now to teach a history class.  Victoria and Albert are my passion, but I have always been interested in their children, too.  I could never seem to find much on this fourth daughter.  When I ran across this book, I had to have it.  I could hardly put it down.  It was very well written and brought this special daughter to life.  What a remarkable woman she was!  Now, I am going to seek out books about her husband, Lorne, the Duke of Argyll, because I know I will be able to find some additional information about her there, as well. Thank you for such a wonderful book, Jehanne Wake!

I had been hard-pressed to find any books exclusively about this second daughter of Victoria and Albert's second son (Alfred) and his illustrious wife, the former Grand Duchess Marie of Russia. If you are not hooked on history, you will be after you are finished with this very informative, well-written book.

Wow!  So many of us girls would have wished ourselves to be Pattie Boyd back then.  I mean how lucky could you get to have one of the Beatles fall in love with you and want to marry you?  Or had two famous men write such beautiful songs that were specifically about them? Pattie was obviously a very beautiful and SPECIAL woman. But she ended up being just like so many other women of much less fame. Beauty alone is not going to keep your man true to you or home with you when you need him the most. After they sow their "Wild Oats', many men start realizing that they want to have children and leave an imprint of themselves and their lineage behind them before they die.  Sadly, I think that is how Pattie ended up losing both George and Eric. I think both realized that they wanted to be fathers, and Pattie could not (for whatever reason) provide either husband with the one thing that may have been the glue that bonded them together and prevented outcomes that were (in my opinion) tumultuous and forever life-altering.

This book is not just for those struggling to save a marriage. For anyone struggling to "find themselves", this is a uplifting and worthwhile read. I myself have let "Jesus Take The Wheel".  The relief I felt was as though a huge rock was lifted off my chest.  I can breathe again and never feel as alone as I did. Thank you Denise, for being humble enough to share such a personal journey. You are so right.  It IS "All About Him".
The book and the movie are timeless and so beautiful.  It is a love story unlike any other.  I recommend them both to all generations and can bet they will be read and watched long after I am gone.
This author knows how to draw her readers in, making each shared memory come alive once again.  The only thing I wish is that it was LONGER. Thank you for sharing your memories, Rita.
