It is easy to use by just screwing the lens onto the clip and adjusting over the lens on the phone or tablet. Ok with this is pro's and con's. Lets go with what I liked about it easy to use, can fit into my hand bag (AKA always with me), sturdy I'm not worried about it getting broke in my purse, and I have gotten some good pictures with it. What I did not care for about it I find it hard to get a clear picture without using a tri-pod this makes the pictures I can get a lot more restricted, when I use it on my iPhone 6s (my main device) the out side of the pictures are distorted. Overall for $20 this is a good lens and will get great pictures. I have no issues cropping out the outsides of the pictures with my phones editor, but it was disappointing before I knew I would have to crop because I never over shot the pictures. I have used this to get nature shots and sports shots both ways (action and still) have turned out better then I thought they would. I would recommend this lens for someone that is looking to get great pictures at a great price. I still stand behind the fact that I have had to crop every picture, but for $20 and the zoom that the lens gives I still give this a 4 star.
I check back often for questions, so please feel free to ask anything that I missed and your wondering about this product.
I received Paratron 10X Zoom Telephoto Lens Phone Focus Telescope Camera Lens Kit with Universal Clip for iPhone, Android and Other Smartphones at discount or for free for my honest and unbiased review. That has not swayed my review in any, way my review is 100% my own experience with this product.

Fun hat to add to our hat/dress-up box! It has soft fur, 2 padded horns, and a silky lining on the inside of the hat. My kids love to play dress-up and this hat is great because it fits all of us. Yes I play too with the kids. This hat was put made every well and looks like its defiantly going to be around for many years. The kids love playing how to train your dragon with this hat. I find it extremely cute the dogs AKA Dragons don't like it much. This hat looks good on my 2year old and my 12 year old. Honestly on me it is a little tight, but not uncomfortable. I don't feel like I have a large or small head just average. Overall we love this whimsical hat that adds allot of fun to our dress-up chest. It would be great for a costume as well. I recommend this hat for fun or a great touch to a costume. I received this product at a discount for my honest and unbiased review.

users.query: This is a wonderful collection, and is very valuable to any student of drama or writing.  Mr. Simon is a master at writing crisp, incisive dialogue. Studying his writing (as one would study a textbook), the reader should get a sense of how important it always is to start any play or film with a great script. Mr. Simon's writing is also worth studying as a reminder to actors how important it is to learn their lines completely and not deviate from the script.  His writing is so naturalistic and flows so well that it would be a real shame to alter a single word - even unintentionally. Very highly recommended.

cands.text: This is a terrific collection of scenes for actors, and will benefit experienced actors and newcomers alike. A tremendous amount of research has gone into this collection and the result is impressive. This book also works as an introduction to a wide range of playwrights and a starting point for further and deeper study of their work.

I'm a great fan of this book of quotes. It's well organized, and Mr. Fitzhenry over-delivers on content. This book is a valuable resource for writers and speakers. Mr. Fitzhenry has written a very thoughtful introduction to this edition, as well. A fine collection, and very highly recommended.

I've been curious about this series of books for a while and just picked up a copy. It's filled with wonderful suggestions writers can use to get themselves unstuck.  It's also beautifully designed and a pleasure to flip through for inspiration and ideas.  I think writers at all levels, novice and experienced, will find something in these pages to use right away. Very highly recommended.

I've been a great fan of Jack Canfield's work for a long time. All of Mr. Canfield's books are terrific, but I've always felt that this little volume is one of his best.  It's written in a clear, straightforward style and explains some very complex subjects in a manner that is logical and easy to digest (and apply). If you're new to self-help and LOA, this is a good place to start. The book is beautifully designed, as well.

This is an informative and enjoyable read, and will be very useful to anyone in the film and television industry. It's written in a lighthearted and entertaining style, and the author has a real knack for explaining how things work on a professional film set.  This is a solid tool for newcomers to the industry, but experienced cast and crew professionals will also enjoy this book and learn something new from the author's vast knowledge of film industry trivia. Highly recommended for all, as this author clearly knows his material and has a great sense of humor.

This is a terrific tool for actors, directors, and acting coaches. It's a very handy reference and will save people in the arts countless hours of research. This will be useful for both experienced pros and newcomers alike.

If you only read one book on acting ... please make it this one. This book is filled with practical, proven suggestions from the real-world acting trenches. I was fortunate enough to study acting personally with the author and saw firsthand how effective his approach can be in transforming actors' performances. In particular, his ideas on rehearsing with scene partners and preparing for professional level auditions with casting directors are extremely valuable.

Michael taught directly from his book, and it is filled with wonderful strategies to help get actors "out of their heads."  He was also an extremely witty and entertaining storyteller, and this comes across beautifully on the printed page.  More than three decades after its first publication,  Audition remains a fitting legacy for a truly brilliant and wildly creative man.

I used this as a supplementary text for a course I taught on film appreciation. It was extremely helpful, concise, and well organized.  The students enjoyed it very much. Authors do a fine job bringing foreign films into focus and introducing styles and themes in a manner that is readily accessible for beginning film students (or those just fulfilling distribution requirements).  I believe this is the type of book that many will keep and continue to enjoy long after their courses are over, as well. The photos are terrific and the book is beautifully designed.  I was also pleasantly surprised to see some of my all-time personal favorite films examined by the authors.  Many people tend to overlook these as being a little too obscure, so I definitely appreciate their inclusion in this volume.

This is a terrific small volume, very well written and organized, and easy to apply.
The author is very skilled at turning a phrase and presenting self- development and motivational material in a way that is unique, engaging, and easy to absorb and apply.  I also like the format a lot.  It's clean, crisp, easy to follow, and reminds me of Dr. Robert Anthony's early book "50 Ideas That Can Change Your Life."  I agree with one of the other reviewers who wrote that this is now one of his favorite motivational books, as well. There are a lot of good ones out there, but this one is a particular standout. Very highly recommended.

Absolutely incredible writing is Pirandello's legacy to the theater. Some of his work may be a little difficult for newcomers to the stage, but these plays deserve to be scrutinized as closely as a textbook. Pirandello blurs the line effectively between fantasy and reality with this collection, particularly in "Six Characters In Search of an Author."  At the same time, his works display touches of nihilism, especially when title character Henry IV declares openly how little he (and her own mother) care for his wife.  Also in "Henry IV," Belcredi delivers the chilling, pessimistic line "As soon as one is born, one starts dying."

Pirandello seems to enjoy playing a sort of cat and mouse game with his readers and audience, as well. After setting up impressive conflicts in both "Liola" and "It is So (If You Think So)," the author wraps up both plays just a little too neatly. The playwright seems to be telling us:"Don't look to me for answers."

Pirandello even lampoons himself. In "Six Characters ...", The Manager berates his company of actors with this tirade: "Is it my fault if France won't send us any more good comedies, and we are reduced to putting on Pirandello's works, where nobody understands anything, and where the author plays the fool with us all?"

There's some really strong material in this collection. These plays are well suited to creative theatrical companies that enjoy challenging themselves (and their audiences) with difficult, abstract material. It would be wonderful to see these plays performed more frequently today.

This is a terrific book, jam-packed with information and good old-fashioned common sense for actors. The author over-delivers on content throughout, and I particularly like his 7 chapter/ 7 Deadly Sin format, which offers up a creative and unique take on the actor's journey and day-to-day challenges.

I was a member of the author's organization, The Actors' Network, in Los Angeles for many years and participated in many of their workshops, seminars, and informational sessions. I can tell you that Kevn E. West pulls no punches and definitely knows his stuff. Very highly recommended.

The authors have put together a clear and concise guide intended to encourage readers to expand their vision, think bigger, and accomplish greater results both personally and professionally. Mr. Sullivan and Ms. Nomura write and teach in a direct and authentic style.  It's a powerful small volume, and I believe it can be particularly effective for people who consider themselves non-readers and may be intimidated by longer, more detailed and comprehensive personal development books. In this way, I think the authors perform a valuable service with this work and fill a definite need in people's lives.

I always enjoy reading entertainment industry autobiographies, and this one surely does not disappoint. Mr. Newhart's stories of his early days in stand-up comedy are extremely entertaining. They also shine a light on the process and training world-renowned performers go through to develop the skills that bring them their celebrity and renown. It's a very funny book, written in the easy-going, conversational style that we've all come to expect from Bob Newhart.  The author also includes complete  transcripts of comedy monologues he performed on stage in his early career and talks about how the material was written and developed. What I like most, though, are the stories of all the unusual part-time jobs he had during his lean years in show business. It's a great read and reminds me a lot of Charles Grodin's very funny account of his own early days in the industry.

This play has a couple of strong dramatic monologues for men. It also allows for just the right balance of intellect and emotion. Mr. Anderson builds his storyline expertly and takes readers on a wonderful ride in the process.
Terrific book, and Art Linkletter's foreword is absolutely wonderful.  It's well worth a read and makes a great gift for a favorite teacher.

This is a really solid collection of ten-minute plays. Ten-minute plays are a wonderful challenge for writers and are very popular with theaters all over the world. The editors of this collection, Eric Lane and Nina Shengold, have done a fine job assembling a diverse and eclectic group of comedies and dramas for this book, and also provide readers with lots of helpful background information on the history of the ten-minute genre.
If you haven't read ten-minute plays (or seen them performed in theaters), I think you'll be pleasantly surprised.  This collection has something for everyone  an excellent variety  and would be a good place to start. Particular standouts in the book, I believe, are the pieces by Christopher Durang, Warren Leight, Claire Reeve, Sean O'Connor, and Rich Orloff. Very highly recommended.

Steve Chandler's book is written in a friendly, conversational style and contains tons of useful ideas and information you can apply right away. Mr. Chandler is a unique voice in the personal development field and he offers wonderful real world stories to illustrate his points. His story about author Anthony Burgess is particularly inspiring.

This is a terrific read, and is written in a breezy, informal style. Roger Corman is generous and forthright in sharing stories of his early days, as well as the struggles and challenges of putting films together while paying attention to keeping the costs to a minimum. It will. be areal eye-opener for anyone interested in the way things work behind the scenes in Hollywood. Very entertaining and informative.  Highly recommended.

This book is truly a gem. It's filled with practical, useful advice from a bygone age.  Moreover, Ms. Brande writes so clearly that one can't shake the feeling that she is speaking directly to you.  The author's message holds up remarkably well eighty years after its first publication.  It's amazing how little the questions and challenges of writers have changed since then.
All of Larry Winget 's material is terrific, and it's nice to have him read this one himself on the audio version.  Very informative and extremely entertaining, as well.

This is one of my all-time favorite books.  Mr. Spielman did a fine job researching and documenting the exploits of one of history's most extraordinary figures, The Mighty Atom.  He also spent a great deal of time interviewing the world renowned strongman and getting to know him personally. I particularly like the author's use of reference materials to document many of Joseph Greenstein's mind-boggling feats of strength. It's as if the author knew skeptics would show up after publication. Most remarkable, I believe, are the newspaper clippings of the Atom holding back the airplane (twice) and the incredible story of being shot between the eyes with a .22 calibre bullet - and living to tell about it after the bullet flattened out against his skull.
I believe The Mighty Atom's son, Michael Greenstein, is now in his 90s and is a noted strongman in his own right.  He performs many of his famous father's legendary strongman feats. The Mighty Atom's protege, Slim "The Hammer Man" Farman, who is discussed in detail in the book, is still actively performing, as well. Very highly recommended.

I'm a great fan of Saul Bellow's work and I've always felt this was his most underrated novel. The focus is somewhat different, in that our title character is a gentile. Eugene Henderson is also on solid ground financially, unlike many of the author's protagonists.  His millions do little to quiet the chaos in his mind, although ultimately enabling him to depart for his African adventure. The African setting is exotic and unique in the author's work, as well.  Henderson's triumph in the wrestling match with the African chieftain is a powerful and dynamic event in the story's unfolding. Mr. Bellow crafts a wonderful "fish out of water" tale here, and this novel is well worth a read. Very highly recommended.
Great case at an excellent price. Fits perfectly and protects/ cushions well. Very satisfied with this case. I've also received many compliments on the design.

I've always enjoyed sports biographies and this is an especially good one.  Sugar Ray Leonard's book is extremely honest and forthright. The champ reveals a great deal of personal info about his family, his childhood, and his many personal struggles. He is especially candid about his infidelities and the all-too-familiar temptations available to world class athletes. Ray Leonard shows himself to be just as fearless with his readers as he was inside the ring. This book packs quite a heavy wallop. Like Sugar Ray Leonard himself, this autobiography is fearless, full of surprises, and will knock your socks off. Very highly recommended.

users.query: The trailer seemed to give away too much but it really didn't. Good acting from a fine cast and a great twist at the end.

cands.text: I rented this primarily due to my fondness for the lead actor and actress but not having ever heard of the film. It was actually much, much better than most of my recent rentals. The acting was very good and the ending providing some unexpected twists. Definitely worth watching if you enjoy seeing what deranged minds can do when they don't get what they want, and can have.
Interesting and complex plot that is well developed with good acting throughout.

I was skeptical that this was a Hunger Games rip-off but actually enjoyed it quite a bit. Just saw the movie which was quite well done but, as usual, didn't provide the depth of character and plot building found in the book. Clearly oriented to young adults/teens but enjoyed by a full grown adult, too.
switching back and forth by character perspective made this book feel choppy and it dragged in a number of areas, unlike the earlier books. terrible and surprising ending.

SO disappointed! Danielle Steel really bombed with this book as far as I am concerned. It was so boring and slow. I get she was trying to say someone that appeared to be perfect, really wasn't. But if she was poor and had things happen to her I may have bought it more.

Picked this up again after seeing the movie and having read it over 20 years ago. Interesting to remember that the book's version was a bit different from the movie in a few key elements although the major themes were consistent. A good reminder of the value of our somewhat flawed but complete human existence vs. the alternatives.
I was expecting more from Michael Connelly. This book leaves you hanging at the end. Certainly not one of his better works
An entertaining read with a good mix of intrigue, action and humor. The characters maintain a realistic balance of flaws and positive attributes. Another good entry in this series.
Filled with interesting twists and turns. It continues to focus on the talented and yet flawed personalities of a duo that takes on assignments for more than financial rewards. Another winner.
A fresh new character for what appears to be the first of a coming series. Well written with a good number of twists. Another winner for Baldacci.
Not bad but not one of Kevin Bacon's best. Going to a mild mannered investment exec to proficient killer is a bit of a stretch but keeps it interesting.
Not bad but not one of Kevin Bacon's best. Going to a mild mannered investment exec to proficient killer is a bit of a stretch but keeps it interesting.
Not bad but not one of Kevin Bacon's best. Going to a mild mannered investment exec to proficient killer is a bit of a stretch but keeps it interesting.

MH Sargent keeps the action going with his team in a new environment. It makes you wonder if some of these things could actually happen here. I like the fact that this is not an "everything works out well" approach to this genre of storytelling.
Solid and well made. Puts the cheaper hoses out there to shame. Reinforcement near the fittings is a nice touch. A quality hose that should last many years.

had never heard of MH Sargent and didn't expect much for a free book (#1 in the series) but was hooked on this series after reading the first book. well developed characters and enough twists within the plots to keep me interested throughout the books. nice to have decent reads for less than $4 each.
I was hooked on the MP-5 series after getting the first one free on my Kindle. Have not been dissappointed by any of them. Looking forward to #7.
Have read many of Coben's books, primarily the Bolitar series, and this book moves very very slowly by comparison. Ok storyline but certainly not one of his better books.
I've been a fan of the Jack Swyteck series for several years but found this particular one a bit slow going and got bogged down several times. Still a decent read, but not one of his best
good for the money. a bit inconsistent with repeated measurements but close enough if rough average of trigger pull tension is desired. not as accurate as digital versions but much less expensive.
Provides good lighting and adequate magnification. Adjustment knob on light is not the highest quality and easily stripped. Overall, a good value for the price.

Useful if you have a mil-mil scope but not very good if you have an moa version. I can see where they are a needed item before the advent of newer ballistic tools but feels a bit dated given today's available technology
Bought as a backup to our everyday coffee maker but was very surprised at the overall quality and features for the price. Shows you don't have to spend a $100 to make a good cup of coffee

Great size for larger guns and parts. Additional feature of storage for small parts and magnetic tray are very useful. Surface appears to repel small spills and wipes up easily. Excellent price for such a nice mat.

I love the quality and ease of slipping on/off these boots but I learned my lesson, as noted by other buyers, that these boots do tend to run significantly small. I normally wear 10.5 size shoes/sneakers and initially went with these in 11. They were quite tight around the toes so I reluctantly tried size 12 and they fit very well, although they look more like a big boot in that size than a well fitted version. But for what I will be using them for (slushing around in the snow and ice), a good comfortable fit is more important than a fashion statement.

users.query: I really liked Daphne and Joe but thought the mystery part kind of . . . off. It seemed like she randomly picked a previous character and made him the bad guy. It just fit weirdly. The intersection of her past and the bad guy was off, too; it never really seemed to mesh, especially since no explanation was given for his obsession with Daphne. The explanation didn't really cut it for believability. Otherwise, pretty good story if you just focus on Daphne and joe.

cands.text: I was enjoying this book until the ending. I thought it was completely ridiculous and out of left field. It felt like the author needed a quick ending and just decided to use what she had. There could have easily been a more plausible and better understood ending and reasoning behind the mystery. I just thought it was a let down.

I was intrigued by the blurb on the story -- rick preppy guy and MMA fighter's daughter. It started off ok although the dialogue was incredibly stilted and incredibly unrealistic. But then, the more into the story I got, the more I absolutely hated the main heroine. She is awful. She lets an ex-boyfriend bully her. His uncle is her business partner who she's known for years but does she go to him for help? No. Does she contact the police after he physically threatens her? No. Does her current boyfriend or business partner contact the police after seeing where the ex-boyfriend has chocked her? No -- it can be handled "in the ring". So stupid. Mind-numbingly stupid. But it gets better. Boyfriend is an investor in her business, ex-boyfriend calls and says boyfriend got her loan turned down. She IMMEDIATELY blames the boyfriend. Immediately. Doesn't even stop to consider that the ex-boyfriend, who is verbally abusive and has already physically threatened her, might be lying. Doesn't even stop to consider that she should trust the person she's just spent the last upteen weeks with. Nope, she immediately breaks up with him. At that point I just rolled my eyes. She has the mentality of a sixteen year old girl. It's worrisome that she is supposed to be twenty four and in charge of 62 businesses. But wait - there is more! She is in charge of these businesses and makes a point of saying she's the business person while her partner is the fighting person. But does she realize that ex-boyfriend is stealing millions of dollars from her business under a fake vendor account? Nope!!!!!! She doesn't.  Towards the end, she thinks that Jax, the boyfriend she broke up with, has moved on and is upset that she's so forgettable. If anything, I thought he should have moved on her crazy. It's worrisome to me that this is a character that is supposed to be likable. She is horrible and I hope that anyone reading this thinking that behavior or line of thinking is ok gets some help of their own.

I liked this book. It was creepy and suspenseful, even though I had guessed the baddie pretty quickly. I'm not totally sure why the author felt the need to add the romance -- it was so light and barely there and didn't totally add up. A good read, though.

I was liking the story until about halfway through, and then I kind of started to dislike Jenny. She was a major jerk to Jared and very judgmental. They both liked to party and have a good time, sleep around with no serious relationships, and she dragged him for that, even though he had a steady job, a steady paycheck, a steady group of friends, etc., and she was living in Paris, still in school, with no stability with a job or even her family, being so far away. It was a little frustrating having her treat him like he was a lesser being because of their SHARED qualities while not recognizing any of his positive ones, that definitely seemed to outweigh any of her positive characteristics. It was ok, though, because she "changed" but she rejected any of his changes. Just annoying.

I mostly skimmed the first book in this series. I just couldn't get into it, didn't really like the set up or the characters. This one was so much better, though. I really enjoyed both of the characters and the backstory with Vance and his family. I thought that their romance moved along nicely, even though it was a love at first sight thing. I also liked Baxter's story, too. The only part I didn't like was the ending -- it was a little off for me, but other than that, I really liked this a lot. I think that Vance's family should have been more proud of his Army service than they were, but other than that, I liked it a lot.

The story was ok. As I was reading, though, I felt like it was an episode of Bones. The main character was a little too close to Bones for my peace of mind, even though I really like the show. For some reason, it seems to be the new thing in romance books for one of the characters to be somewhat "Asberger's" or Autistic without really fleshing out the character. Despite how easy it seems, other people do not simply accept the main character's quirks without thinking them weird or rude in some way. Also, I felt like the main female character was simply really smart at the beginning of the story and stunted emotionally simply because her interactions were different but as the novel progressed, she became more Asbergers. And another thing, it seemed too easy at the end of the story for her to be done with the trial. If it was that easy, it seems like she could have done that years before, especially if she was keeping track of everything. There didn't seem to be any reason that the main villians couldn't have been arrested years before based on what she had uncovered, along with her being able to siphon the money off. I was also looking for some kind of view point of the major villians at the end, especially since we'd been given the viewpoint two previous times. What was the point of that? She knew they were still looking for her, and it added nothing to show the scene between Ilya and his dad if not some kind of conclusion from them. Overall, it was ok, and pretty typical of Nora Roberts' books, but it was no Montana Sky.

I was really enjoying this book and the two main characters. I liked how their relationship developed, and I liked that Amelia wasn't a weak woman, like most in the romance genre. However, the ending was a little disappointing. Without spoiling it too much, I didn't like the reasoning behind Houston's low self confidence and self hatred. She was setting it up to be something big involving the horrible father but then . . . it really wasn't. I thought that Dallas and Houston had more of a reason to be so distant but then . . . they didn't. It was like she was leading up to the big reveal but then couldn't figure out what she wanted the big reveal to be so she just put something in there. Other than that, great story.

I thought this book was really good and better than the first (I'm not counting the sisters' stories). The ending was a little predictable, which was somewhat frustrating, but overall, I really liked this book. I don't think that the characters had to have had the "fight" moment of the story where they're apart for a bit to realize they were both wrong, etc. Sometimes it seems like that doesn't really fit the characters we've been shown, and that's how I felt for this story. I like the how the secondary characters were used but I think the story about his job was a little much. It was really resolved in a good way since he was "late." Other than that, though, this was a great read. It's a keeper!

I find this series really hit or miss. I've enjoyed some of them -- especially Kelsey and Jonas's stories -- but find the rest just ok. This bordered on just ok. I really liked the stories with Kelsey and Jonas because they had background to them. Readers had met the characters in previous stories, instead of throwing up random characters that only connect through the Delphi Center. It's not enough of a connection for me, I guess. I was hoping that this story would be Elizabeth's or even Scott's but I guess we're going to have to wait for that. There wasn't anything wrong with these two characters - I liked them both together and separately, but Brian seemed to shoulder a lot of the responsibility for being low man on the todem pole. I thought the suspense part of it was a little lame and not really give enough background or detail. I guess this one just didn't really work for me but it was a fairly enjoyable read if not one I'll come back to. I'm hoping the next story isn't a miss . . .

I thought this book was excellent. The character development was really great -- there was character growth by both characters but without them acting psycho or wishy washy or super unrealistic. The dialogue and thought processes were some of the most natural that I've read- nothing sounded fake or stupid or unrealistic, which is amazing considering part of it includes bikers and Croatian mobsters. The writing was excellent as well -- at first I had a few problems because I thought the author could have put in the backstory sooner because I was confused about who was who because she didn't explain it for a while, and she could have used some proper nouns instead of pronouns a couple of times. I do agree with a previous reviewer that it probably could have been shorter because it almost started to drag, but other than that, a great first book. Looking forward to more if they're all going to be this good!

I mostly liked the book but . . . a couple of things. SPOILERS ahead. First of all, what I've always like about Linda Howard's books are her heroines. Her romantic suspense books normally have women who take no sh**. They stand up for themselves. And even though the timeframes of her books are short, I always feel like there is a good connection between hero and heroine. I think that's what's missing in this book. Jina is a take-no-bull heroine but the first half of the book is all her and her training. There is very little from Ace and very little to show their attraction. He is her boss and spends most of that half being a total jerk to her. And then he kisses her and she loves him. I don't like that. Like other reviewers, the title and blurb of the book is just one chapter in all of it. So after that chapter, she quits, they're together, and then there is this whole wrapping up of the villian, which doesn't really make sense and I mostly skimmed that part because I didn't remember it from the previous book at all and it was such a small part of this book it seemed superfluous. We already knew Jina was a bad-ss - we didn't need that last chapter to show us. And finally it showed that Ace did have a sense of humor . . .that very last chapter. I wish that her training had been a few less chapters, there had been more meaningful interactions between Jina and Ace, she got "left behind" and the second half of the book was them working it out.

I really miss old Linda Howard books and feel like these last three -- the one with the president's wife? I'm totally blanking, Troublemaker, and this one - are close to old Linda Howard but not quite there. They all seem to be missing something or things just don't tie together and make sense like they used it.

Definitely worth a read because the humor and kick butt heroine is there but not her best.

I thought this was a good book. Both main characters were fully fleshed out and very realistic, their "romance" happened very organically and the reader could see and feel the attraction instead of just the author telling us they were attracted and in love. I also liked the quippy dialogue between the two. The "mystery" wasn't really the best but it didn't overtake the story.

As a previous reviewer noted, it was kind of stupid to have d'Arcy and Lady Penelope actually take an interest in running the children's home- that part wasn't very realistic, but I didn't think that it overshadowed the rest of the story at all. Overall,  a very, very good read, better than I was expecting, honestly.

This was a very well written story. I thought it was excellent. The author presented the major obstacle for the characters and didn't add in a bunch of random conflicts just to create drama. I also liked how honest the characters were = no stupid misconceptions to mess everything up. Very realistic storytelling and great characterizations.

Hmmm. So I really liked the beginning of the book. I thought it had a lot of promise. I liked how the characters were with each other, how they started to have feelings for each other, etc. I even liked the premise. Where I started to dislike the story and started skimming was the big breakup. First of all, most of the reviews are putting the blame on James. But I really disliked Theo's character. She tells him to get out, leave, get on the ship and go. But when he does, she's mad that he didn't come back. He was only doing what she told him. Second, the seven years went by so quickly- it was mostly just the author telling what happened with the two, which is boring and doesn't really move the plot along. She could have stated that in less time- she spent quite a few pages telling what they'd been up to even though a few sentences would have worked- and more time with the characters together after James comes back. When he does come back, I liked how he was so upfront about his life, and how when she told him to get out, he did, etc. She acted like she was the victim but really, he was the one who was forced to leave his life because she wanted him gone- she got the estate and the life she was going to lead anyway- he had already told her she could be in charge of the finances, etc.

I wish that the original premise had stayed, the beginning chapters had stayed, even maybe him being gone, but once he was back, she should have taken more blame. I really wish that they had just stayed together and worked on the issue. I know he was gone for seven years so they could both mature but that's where the story got flat and uninteresting to me.

The blurb for this book was a little deceiving as it's less about the two "main" characters than it is about all of the previous characters of this series and the heroine's son. The romance seemed forced and rushed because so little of the book focused on it. Every couple of pages we'd get some character interaction and then it'd go back to the other previous characters or her son, who she never really followed up on.

It was an ok read, but it was just less about the characters on the back than I would have liked.

After the first few chapters, I just started skimming. It was stupid and boring at the same time. I think that it could have been a good story but . . . for one thing, the main characters decide that they love each other in about a minute. Granted, this is romantic suspense, but the main guy meets the girl, doesn't see her for a year, feels guilt about how he treated her, sees her again, loves her. Boom. Book over. There is no characterization to either main character. There is nothing except the mystery. He is rich and she is psychic. That's about it. The main lead has two brothers and a sister, I'm assuming to set up future books, but they're given so little time I have no interested in reading their stories. Second, it's supposed to be romantic suspense with this psychic edge. The psychic part doesn't bother me -- I think that her KGI book with the psychic girl and the army brother was my favorite book. This, however, was just ridiculous. There were so many things left out. The killer has a hold on the girl -- how? why? when? The backstory with her saving someone that he was killing and him stalking her from then on out . . . ok, he knows where she is at all times but doesn't physically come after her during that time? The one time he gets close enough she runs off. Literally, she is running. He has no car? But, she thinks he lets her go just to . . . play with her? GIve her a lead so he can mentally stalk her again? Ok, sure. Then, he's able to get into the mind of Caleb. Makes total sense, right? Keeping a hold on two different people at one time? Sure.

I don't know. I really used to enjoy Banks' KGI series but those have really gone downhill for me and now this as well. Either her writing style has changed or my reading habits are different, I don't know. I do know I'm not enjoying her books anymore.

This book was ok. It was a quick read, at least. I never felt that involved with the characters, though. I thought the ending to Tess's story was kind of stupid, too; Susan Elizabeth Phillips did that similar storyline MUCH BETTER in Breathing Room. I also thought the ending here wasn't that great, either. It just never felt that the characters had any real connection.

This book just seemed so short. I couldn't really get into the story. The whole storyline with the police was over the top and didn't really seem plausible. I think that it would have been better to have the reader SHOWN his progression from seeing the pictures and trying to deal with the mystery to the hostage situation, involving her from the beginning. The whole hostage situation seemed pointless, especially since he just let everyone involved go. It might have worked better to have him working from the mansion and her working as the hostage negotiator, figuring things out that way, since of going on the run and just looking at pictures on the phone. Also, wouldn't he only trust the justice dpt anyway? I don't know - it was ok. I wish all these characters who have their entire relationships evolve within two days wouldn't immediately rush into marriage at the end of the story. It just makes it that much more implausible.

There were quite a few things that I did not like about this book so spoilers ahead.

First of all, the characters' relationship. The entire reason they broke up in the first place is never really resolved. At the end, Jose just decides he thinks he could maybe want kids. Boom, they're together and happy. There was never any real discussion between the two. I felt like the heroine never tried to understand things from Jose's point of view, at all. She just kept badgering him about wanting a family, telling him they couldn't be together and then immediately sleeping with him, or being really selfish and stupid -- she never realized the danger she was in? She made some comment about not realizing how her job was similar to Jose's -- a Interpol agent doesn't realize her job is dangerous and has risks? Are you kidding me? It just struck me as really disingenuous. I liked Jose more and felt he had valid concerns - also he's onl 27!- and didn't like how his concerns were just brushed aside as if they were stupid. When the characters talked about their issues, nothing real was ever said or any resolution given - it was the same conversation five different times with nothing different, no compromise, nothing real about it.

Also, there is no real bad guy here. They are setting up this terrorist threat and this "traitor" whose family is being tortured and then . . . it's some random character we've never really met and nothing is resolved. His wife is dead and he's a traitor but he's caught! Story solved! Also, where is his family that these African terrorists can simply kidnap and torture them? Why was there no resolution for that? How did the student get involved with this? Again, nothing is there as explanation. It wasn't important enough to cover because the two leads had to have the same conversation five different times with no resolution.

And the last major part . . . her mom. Good lord, I hated this part of the book. Her mom is presumed dead for fifteen years, the main character has a lot of heartbreak about that, and she forgives her in about five minutes. um . . . ok. sure, that is absolutely how life works. Then, the mom realizes that after fifteen years, it's safe! She can come out now . . . again, whatever. This part of the story was just so, so dumb. She is an agent for the CIA but doesn't realize a teacher is selling kids off? Another agent is sent there as . . . protection? From what exactly? She's been dead for fifteen years! He also doesn't realize these kids are being sold to the warlords? Bright minds right there . . .

Overall, this book was really frustrating. It's getting harder and harder to remember why I liked this series in the first place and I think I'm about done.

I was really enjoying this story but it ends very, very abruptly. I felt like it was trucking along pretty good and then boom, it's over. It seems like right when she starts to get some good character development, she decides to immediately end the story. I think that the characters could have used a couple of more days together- either in the safe house or on the run- before deciding they were in love. First of all, I think it's completely out of character based on what we know of the characters. Second, nothing is mentioned about his previous girlfriend, the age difference, his family, what happens after with his job, etc., to sum up the story. It's simply, they're in love. Done. I think that the mystery part of it was pretty obvious but again, with a couple of more pages or chapters, it wouldn't have been so obvious. I just think that she starts something good but ends so abruptly and doesn't really give enough character development or tie up.

Ok, so I've had some problems with Banks's last few books. First of all,  this "super-elite" group never actually does anything that's elite and always seem to get caught in stupid ways or have something go wrong that was painfully obvious. They are also not a "secret" group because all the bad guys always seem to know where they live and their super "secure" place always seems to get broken into or someone gets kidnapped from there.

However, this book really took the cake. Donovan falls in love in about two seconds. He literally meets the main female character, sees she has a family, and falls in love. He knows this family for about a minute before telling the little girl she can call him daddy. Ok, that's not weird. Quite a bit was made about his age and how he really just wanted a family and then Eve was so young. And not young in the sense that a lot of things had happened to her and she seemed older. Nope, she seemed really young and he seemed way too old for her, like a father figure instead of a lover. It was weird. And then the culmination with the bad guy was just stupid. How dumb is this girl? How stupid was Donovan's plan? REALLY STUPID. I liked the KGI books, and Garrett's and Nathan's were my favorite, but I think she's been focusing so much on her erotica books she's letting these slide by. I kind of felt the same about her historical romances, too. The last couple of historical romances just weren't very good. I don't know. I guess I'm curious about Joe's story or maybe Swanny's but . . . Rusty seems way too young for Sean and I HATE her name so . . . we'll see.

I thought this book kind of started off slow. It seemed really contrived with the whole affair-finding out of the affair-carriage scene, etc. However, once the "hero" changed, the book got a lot better. It was nice that the "heroine" got her memory back in stages instead of all at one time, but it seemed a little ridiculous that she would have immediately thought herself in love with the other guy after all those weeks with David. I thought there should have been more conflict there with her wondering about her feelings for both, instead of her going to Andrew's house and then deciding she really did love David. It just seemed a little abrupt. I think more should have been given to his artistry and writing skills, too, and her to publishing house. It seemed like the author threw out these little tidbits about the characters without really giving total character development but overall, it was a good book. I read this before the other two in the series.

I'm not really sure how this book got so many positive reviews. I thought it was awful. First of all, the dialogue was horrible. Nothing the characters said sounded authentic in any way. It was so unbelievable. Second, Jake's character was pretty awful. He abandons his son, has no contact with him for 13 years, shows up, and assumes that Austin wants to see him and live with him? He basically said he thought he could stroll in and have Austin be happy about moving to New York. He takes the time to change and then decides, no, Austin should stay. Um, ok. Even though he ultimately sees the error in that- hello, quite obvious, I couldn't get over that he showed up, made Austin love him, told Austin they would live together, and then decide no. There was no character development until the very end and it was rushed and unrealistic. Again, not believable. What exactly is there to love about this person? Their "love" was forced and ridiculous, the dialogue was stupid, and even the setup was awful.

THe last book from Susan Andersen that I actually liked, loved really, was Just for Kicks, and I keep waiting for another one but I think I'm giving up on this author.

I was really looking forward to this story because I've always really liked Steele. However, it was missing a lot. First of all, Steele is the complete opposite compared to all the previous books. Although Maren remarks on it a couple of times, the explanation -- he's just so in love with her immediately and has always wanted her -- doesn't really ring true. That can be fine but his basic personality should stay the same because he doesn't even seem like the same character. The rest of the characters comment on how shocking his behavior with her is but it's just missing something. I wish she had kept him quiet and stoic. There just seemed to be a lot missing from their relationship -- they were immediately in love and boom, he's spouting all kinds of things. Neither of them ever held anything back, which let out a lot of suspense or even tension with the relationship, leading the main conflict with the bad guy the only tension. That conflict was really lacking although I was glad that Banks toned down the violence with this one; it was just way too much in the last novel. At the same time, the central conflict left a lot to be desired. It didn't make sense that the resident bad guy suddenly kidnapped her for no reason. Once she was out halfway through the story, he conveniently went crazy and became obsessed with her, although as a reader we saw none of that -- just word from Hancock. It made no sense. Obviously this man is not sane but the story really didn't add up. Granted, most of the time the conflicts in these books don't but because this one seemed really half-assed.

I really liked the series to start off but I'm kind of losing my interest. I really liked Nathan's story and was really looking forward to PJ and Cole but it was really violent, really fast and then those two characters spent the majority of their time apart and the book was lacking. This book was also lacking a lot and not what I expected, especially with Steele.

I would read it if you've read the rest in the series but it's certainly not the best or close to it. I was also disappointed with her latest historical romance, too. Maybe she's spending too much time doing too many different series and should focus on just one.

First of all, I did not read the first book in this series. It didn't get as good reviews and a couple of people mentioned this book was better, so I decided to skip it. After reading this book, I don't really want to go back and read the first one, either. It was obvious it was part of a series, though, because some things just didn't add up. I think the author would have been better served to have it be a separate timeline, or at least not include so many things from the first book. It just made the ending of the book feel weird and shoehorned in to fit something it wasn't meant to fit. It just didn't add up, plus the book's treatment of the two characters of the first book really didn't make me want to read the first, if that makes sense. I was reading this book for these characters, not the previous ones. She should have focused on this story only.

This story -- a couple of things I found interesting. I really liked Nicole's character but I felt she lost a little bit of herself as the story went. She flat out admitted she slept with all these guys for release. It was obvious the club had abandoned her and her brother, which Deke (Duke? can't remember right now!!!) mentions. I was kind of hoping she would get some sort of apology or at least recognition of that. I wanted everyone to see how badly they had treated her, especially considering all her dad apparently did for the club.

I guess I liked the book -- I felt like the writing got better as it went but then it veered too much in the storyline of the first in the series. I do think it would have been better as a stand alone so the characters could really come together on their own.

This review is for the "New" Square Wire (2014+) with Titanium Frame and Titanium Iridium Polarized lenses.

I've owned dozens of Oakleys over the last 20+ years, from Blades, Frogskins, Jackets and M-Frames to various wires. I have to say this is the most comfortable pair of sunglasses I've ever had. The frames are solid and sturdy, as well as insanely light, you will forget you are even wearing them. At first I was worried because the Ti Iridium polarized lenses appear so bright, I didn't think they would work well in bright sunlight, however they do work, and extremely well! These lenses are a 10-12% light transmission profile (about the darkest you can get), but because of the unique Ti Iridium tint and bronze lens base, they provide great contrast and everything appears bright, in nearly all light conditions.

The included hard case was an added bonus that I was not expecting, and is a great case, although it can be a bit tight if you don't place the glasses in it just right.

I would definitely recommend these to anyone looking for this style of sunglasses, and I hope Oakley keeps these around for a long time!

I have had this mouse for about 6 weeks.

From the beginning battery life was never stellar. Expect to plug in any time you're not using the mouse. After a full day of sitting on my desk with no use, the battery is usually warning it is low. Thankfully you can play while plugged in and charging - but as other reviewers have stated, the charging/usb cable is extremely stiff, and I find myself fighting for control of the mouse as the stiff cable wants to pull or push it in the wrong direction.

The configuration utility is decent enough, but it likes to randomly forget my key mappings, which is an issue, because what logitech doesn't tell you is that all but the standard buttons (left, right, middle, scroll wheel, back, and forward) buttons will NOT work with a game unless the game is specifically made to work with this device. Your only option is to bind alternate keys (e.g. ctrl+0) in the game to a function or action button, then use the configuration utility to map a mouse button to that key combination. For games like WoW, where you typically have multiple characters and use different key mappings, this is extremely annoying.

Now, after about 6 weeks of moderate use, a few of the smaller top/side buttons (G10 in particular) no longer have a "click" when pressed, making it hard to tell if it has been activated or not. I am now outside the amazon return window, so I will have to deal with logitech customer service and will update once the issue is addressed/resolved.

Overall, I wouldn't recommend this mouse. For the price, my $19 m510 was far superior, with battery life that measured in the months, and buttons that continue to work after years of use.

It really is a shame, for a premium ~$70 device from a respected company like logitech I really expected more. I would think they can address the battery life issues, and configuration utility concerns with a software/firmware update, but as this device was released some time ago, I'm not holding my breath.

Pros: Accuracy, Feel, Comfort, and Weight
Cons: Battery Life, Durability, Configuration utility, ease of setup, poorly designed charging / usb cable

I'm not sure I can say much about Slaughterhouse-Five that hasn't already been said by at least 50 other people.  Vonnegut embodies the concept of the modern American author, and Slaughterhouse-Five could quite easily be considered the book that does it best. By no means his best work, Slaughterhouse-Five seems fully American at its heart.  A retelling of the events of World War II, Vonnegut throws in his standard twist, namely, a character who seems to be completely insane...or completely sane, but appearing to be differently so because of extraordinary events.

So much could be discussed about whether Billy Pilgrim was ever abducted by aliens, or about what the Tramalfagorians (SP) represent.  But the real thing to recognize about this book is that it's just a ton of fun to read.  A quick read that makes you think as you're going through it.  It's pretty much the perfect example of what modern American literature should be about, and what Vonnegut was brilliant at.

If you've somehow managed to make it to adulthood without reading this one, you had better make it a high priority to do so now.

cands.text:
I read most of this book before I realized that I wasn't actually enjoying it. And it took me a long time to figure out why.
You see, I love Indiana Jones, and I loved learning more about the further exploits of the man...but the reality of reading about his adventures was a lot less exciting than watching them. I could only play the theme song in my head so many times before it got repetitive and useless towards building the tension necessary.
I actually own a few Indy comic books that I now realize this same bit about.
I think a portion of the issue, however, is that they often take on a much larger story than can be expressed within the confines of a standard comic model, meaning that often the action is suppressed, and the explanations are cut short.
There are some gems in here, but ultimately, just realize that Indy is one character that's just better on the screen.

I love graphic novels.  I've read tons of them over the decades I've been alive.  Very few, in my opinion, have been able to knock down the pantheon of great titles from my youth like Watchmen or Crisis on Infinite Earths.

This one does.

In fact, I might be willing to state that this is now my all time favorite graphic novel.  I mean...there are a ton of great ones out there, so I'm hesitant.

But simply put, we get to see Ralph Dibny, a character that is all too often overlooked for the much more flashy Plastic Man, and we get to see him in his full element.  Not only in the midst of a tragedy, but also in the midst of a mystery.

Beyond that, we also get to see the JLA second stringers and learn a bit more about what it is they are doing while the A squad are out kicking butt.  And those revelations are more than a little shocking/disturbing/should have been obvious.

This book reads more like a novel than a comic book.  It has twists, it has turns, it has gravitas.

And most importantly...it will cause you to look at things a little bit differently when you're done, which is always the sign of a great read.

Also...watching the Elongated Man literally melt as he copes with the loss of his wife is some of the best artwork I have ever seen.
Read this book.

I read this book as a kid and absolutely adored it...yet it's one of the few books that have made it onto my "favorite books" list that I've never read a second time...until now.
I was curious as to how much this book might hold up to the high esteem I had for it in my mind.
And it totally did!  This book is fantastic.  Lowry somehow manages to describe this world without color, without emotion, without pain, and then, even more amazingly, uses the people within that world to describe ours, to describe those exact things that they don't have.  Just in her description of things like sledding down a hill, one can't help but have a very specific image crafted in their mind, almost as if the reader is the receiver in training themselves.

But the true majesty in the story here is in the concept of hope, the dream of a brighter future, which pervades this text.  This world may share some similarities with many other dystopian novels (I can't help but think this is somehow held within the same world as Orwell's 1984), but the tale is one of hope, not of loss, of change, not of how the world is too big to make a difference.

And in that piece we find the item that keeps us wanting to root for Jonas, wanting to root for the plan, and hoping against hope that the end doesn't mean what it appears to mean.

Luckily there's more books in the series that should allow us to see where things move from there...books I have yet to read but will be reading very very soon.

I've long been a fan of the character of Peter Pan, whether it be through the movies, the musical, or its many iterations over the years.  However, until very recently, I had never read the novel.
What I think I find most interesting about the novel, over the other versions, is how absolutely poetic its prose is.  It's definitely the most difficult of the versions to ingest easily, but it's also the most beautiful.  We get to see deeper into the mythos of Peter himself, learn what makes him tick, learn more about where he comes from, and really, just get a better understanding of what Neverland is all about.
Spielberg's Hook hinted at a lot of the background laid out in this book, so it definitely deserves some credit there, but even those hints do the reality absolutely no justice.
The book might not be quite as fun of a read as other versions of Peter are to watch, but if you have any interest in the character at all, the tragic magic of Peter's history given in this version of the classic tale of Peter and Wendy is definitely something you should dig into.

I know I'm probably being a bit of a fuddy duddy by giving this book only 3 stars.  I also know that I probably should have read this book in high school instead of in my mid thirties.

But the truth of the matter is...I'm not sure about all the hype.

Is it a well-written book?  Sure.

Was it possibly a game changer of a piece of fiction when it was written?  I would guess so.

But I still can't help but wonder why....

I mean, I get it.  Early on in the book I started becoming more and more aware of the decadence in my own life, recognizing how much like the party-goers I really can be.  And as things progressed, I definitely saw a lot of Gatsby in myself.

And I recognize the even larger allusions and metaphors placed within the text (although the few I came across when looking up things like an Adams study seem quite forced).

But when it comes down to being an amazing novel, it seems to me that this book is much overhyped.

It's a fun book, and it's definitely worth the read, even if just for historical purposes.  But it gets lesser points just because of all the people who have told me it was the greatest book ever written.  If it weren't for those folks, I'd probably give it a four.

I know I'm probably being a bit of a fuddy duddy by giving this book only 3 stars.  I also know that I probably should have read this book in high school instead of in my mid thirties.

But the truth of the matter is...I'm not sure about all the hype.

Is it a well-written book?  Sure.

Was it possibly a game changer of a piece of fiction when it was written?  I would guess so.

But I still can't help but wonder why....

I mean, I get it.  Early on in the book I started becoming more and more aware of the decadence in my own life, recognizing how much like the party-goers I really can be.  And as things progressed, I definitely saw a lot of Gatsby in myself.

And I recognize the even larger allusions and metaphors placed within the text (although the few I came across when looking up things like an Adams study seem quite forced).

But when it comes down to being an amazing novel, it seems to me that this book is much overhyped.

It's a fun book, and it's definitely worth the read, even if just for historical purposes.  But it gets lesser points just because of all the people who have told me it was the greatest book ever written.  If it weren't for those folks, I'd probably give it a four.

Vonnegut is brilliant.  I'm not sure anything more important can be said about his writing than that.  However...that's a pretty boring review of a book that is anything but boring, so...
Breakfast of Champions is the epitome of amazing irreverence. Although the story to be told is, at times, quite deep, Vonnegut seems to have used this title to master his tone of tongue-in-cheek seriousness while also showcasing his true writing chops, specifically through moments like expressing Dwayne Hoovers ultimate disorientation during the moments of his mental breakdown.
I see this book was adapted into a movie.  That's a stupid idea.  There's nothing about this book that could be translated into film without losing the absolute joy of a read it is.  Nothing.
But you should read the book, because it's great.

Although one could very easily take issue right off the bat with the rather lame excuses Crichton uses to bring his favorite (as well as mine) character back from the dead, moving past that really brings the reader into a world much more special than that of the original novel. Being quite different than the movie, this book delves into exploring the history of the mysterious InGen corporation further, while also giving a great bit more detail into what all occurred that led to the creation of Jurassic Park.

I thoroughly enjoyed being able to learn more about the history behind the first book and, when it finally arrived, the action sequences in this book definitely build a great deal of suspense, although I feel that they no where near the quality and satisfaction of the original book. Crichton not only manages to bring in a few new species of dinosaur, but also manages to post conflicting ideas from the original book on things like how the T-Rex sees things, ensuring that such things comment on the original theory as well.

All in all, this book is definitely worth the read, especially if you enjoyed the first one (book or movie). It's sad to see that the film series departed from Crichton's vision so early in the process, I would have loved to see something much more in line with this book than the reality of The Lost World.
