users.query:
If you're not reader of historical romances, you probably won't notice the glaring errors of the era. Unmarried young ladies didn't dance three dances with the same man without being engaged. They also didn't wear "red" to Almack's, entertain "apothecaries,"  openly show an interest in science or read medical books. They certainly didn't publicly raise funds for medical institutions.

The story itself, is "OK," nothing special. I just found a lot of it to be unbelievable for that period in history. Charlotte is so unconventional, it's a wonder she's allowed in polite society. Her aunt and uncle want her to marry and she's determined not to. After one bad experience, she thinks all men are after her money, especially the poorer ones. She spends her time fund raising for medical equipment and ignoring the rules of London society. (And for some mysterious reason London society doesn't ostracize her.)

Edward's father wants him to marry and tells him not come home without a wife. Edward is determined not to marry a woman who's after his title and money so he pretends to be poor. I found it a little hard to believe that this very rich man, got everyone in London to believe he was suddenly poor. Naturally Edward decides he wants Charlotte and she doesn't want a "poor" man. He lies to her right from the start and continues to do so throughout the book. Then he's surprised when she finds out he's not poor and rejects him. What on earth did he think would happen?

Overall it's not a bad book, just not a great one.

cands.text: It's been awhile since I've read a good regency romance. The author did a great job developing the plot and portraying each of the characters.  Caroline is strong woman who takes care of her mother and siblings in less than ideal circumstances. Robert knows which woman he wants and doesn't waver. I enjoyed the book.

I really enjoyed this contemporary novel about a widow raising her two young sons who crosses paths with a wealthy, womanizer. When they first meet, he asks her to have dinner with him and she turns him down. She's still very much in love with her dead husband.  After finding out her husband wasn't the man she thought he was, she embarks on a way to get some revenge of her own by sleeping with someone else. Her plan pretty much backfires and the result is a great story about two exceptionally strong willed people. While the story is nothing "new," its very well written. I was hooked from the beginning to the end.  I will add a caveat that this book does contain some detailed sex so if that isn't your cup of tea, this might not be the book for you.

I did very much enjoy the book, although I wish the author had let Patrick make up his mind which girl to marry a little sooner. It seemed overly cruel for him to walk out when he did.  Also, given the time period, I found it a bit difficult to believe that any man would let his son go around kicking people. Even with those issues, I did still enjoy the book.

As with the first book of this series, the story is predictable but still worth reading. I appreciate the fact that the story isn't full of swear words or explicit sex scenes. I loved that Alexander stepped in to help the Queen and then hung in there even when things were hard. Some reviewers have commented on how Queen Christiana treated him. I think it was well written. She'd been through a lot prior to marrying him and I think her doubts and hesitations were appropriate for the circumstances.

This was a nice book, but there were a few plot holes in my opinion. When Emmy faints in her grooms arms, I didn't understand why he didn't just walk right out of the church with her. Since she recognized him, it would seem logical that he'd take her along to keep her from telling anyone who he was.  And while I absolutely detested Emmy's spoiled brat persona, I thought she changed way too fast. I also didn't care for the epilogue. I was expecting to read more bout the main characters and instead, I got to read about some people in another town that I didn't know. (Possibly these were people from book 1, but I haven't read that one.) There was a little info about Emmy and her groom via a letter but for me it wasn't a very satisfying epilogue.

This was a sweet, clean romance. It did get a little repetitive in places and the heroine's reason for refusing the hero's marriage proposals did get a bit tedious but overall I still enjoyed the book.

This book was "OK."  I would have enjoyed it a little more had the characters actually gotten to know one another before they fell madly in love.  A young penniless widow moves west to live with her well-to-do aunt. Along the way, she witnesses a murder.  After a couple of brief conversations with the marshal who's investigating the murder, the widow is in love.  He loves her too and all he knows about her is that she's a widow and she's pretty. To add a bit of "strife" to the love story, the widow's aunt is briefly arrested for murder. It would have been great if the hero and heroine would have spent a little more time getting to know one another before declaring their undying love but the overall story was interesting and well written.

For the most part I liked the book. That being said, however, I think the problems could have been resolved just a tad sooner. The story did seem to drag a bit towards the end and I got very tired of Olivia's stubbornness. The story is about three impoverished sisters trying to keep the roof over their heads, while also keeping their friends and neighbors from finding out how poor they've become. The two older sisters start robbing stage coaches for money and end up robbing the wrong coach.

This was an enjoyable book to read. As one reviewer commented, there is an 'attempted' rape about 30% of the way through the book. That was not "funny" or a "romp."  It wasn't meant to be. This is a very typical regency style romance in that you have a pair of sisters at the mercy of very evil guardians. (The attempted rape shows you how evil the guardians are.)  The humor comes into play with the addition of a family ghost and the way the sisters deal with their dire situation. Naturally as per any good regency romance, there's a handsome hero to help rescue them.

After Reagan's mother dies, her step-father and two cloddish step-brothers try to marry her off. When that doesn't work, they try to auction her off. Reagan is a very strong female and doesn't go down without a fight. Jackson, her would be hero, has issues of his own. He's accused of killing his brother. He can't remember what happened and is determined to find out.  Between the mystery, the romance and the trek through the west, there's a little something for everyone. I only had two problems with the book, first I think Reagan forgave her step-family way too easily for what they did to her. Second, the author decided to toss the "F" word into the story. Modern curse words have no place in historical romances. Granted it was only once but it still jerked me right out of the story's time frame.

As other reviewers have said, this book is pretty much sex from beginning to end, with a little story thrown in between. I skimmed many pages of detailed sex scenes looking for the actual story. This is supposedly historical fiction but the "F" word pops up throughout the book. Historical fiction should have language appropriate for the time period.

Spoiler Alert:
I found it a little hard to believe that Elizabeth would flee from her husband in London and travel several days to Scotland, only to end up working for the husband of her husband's deceased mistress. Of all the places she could have ended up, she ends up in the house of her husband's mistress? How likely is that? She doesn't even verify that there's a position available before she leaves her home. She just goes all that way assuming there's a job and she'll be hired. Then we have James who's deceased wife was unfaithful and he's sworn never to trust another woman. When Elizabeth faints due to illness,  he picks her up and immediately decides she's the most beautiful woman he's ever seen. Before she's even well, he's pretty much decided he can't live without her. He knows almost nothing about her except she's beautiful. Oh and another thing that bothered me was her illness. She was barely in town a couple hours and she became sick immediately but miraculously James was immune to the very same illness.

This wasn't the worst book I've ever read but definitely not the best one either.

This book is part of a series but can definitely be read as a stand alone book. (No cliffhangers)  I did like the book for the most part. Most of the "mail order bride" books that I've read are more about the story and the romance, without a lot of detailed sex scenes. While there's definitely a story, this book contains a lot of sex, more than I really felt was necessary.

I very much enjoyed reading this book. It was well written and kept my attention from beginning to end. While it is a novella and therefore short, the author does a great job at developing the characters. The book is about 3 sisters, 19, 17 and 15 years old, who lost their mother years earlier and are now responsible for working the family farm while their father is gone. (He left to earn money to pay the mortgage.)  The girls are strong women in a period when that was often not the case. My only complaint is that "romance" is part of the book's title and there isn't any romance in the story. Since it's obviously a prequel to a series, maybe there's more romance in the next book. This book is about how the sisters relate to each other and what they do to try and earn money to pay the mortgage after their father dies. The girls don't have an easy time of it but they do persevere.  Even without the romance, I did very much enjoy the book.

I very much enjoyed reading this book....until the author forgot what century she was writing about and tossed in the F word.  Nothing jerks me out of a good historical romance faster than the use of curse words that are inappropriate for the time period of the book. Fix the language and this would be a 5 star book.

I didn't care for this book at all. It felt like it was just a "piece" of a book.  Based on the description, I thought the book would be about Abigail writing for a mail order husband, their initial meeting and marriage. The book starts off with Abigail riding in the buggy with "a man." She tells the man that they need to go back to her cottage to live because it's free if she continues to give piano lessons to Florence once a week. (Who's Florence?)  He says they've just gotten married and maybe they should live somewhere else because of all the drama she's told him about. Really? The book title is "Abigail's Mail Order Husband," and they're already married on the very first page? There are no details whatsoever about them writing to each other, meeting each other, the wedding or how it came to be. She apparently married him the day she met him and she proclaims his "love" for her right from day one. How can she possibly "know" he loves her if they've just met?  They don't even know each other. Over the first several pages, other characters appear that are not explained. They're just there and we're supposed to know who they are, why they're there and what happened before they got there. It wasn't all that hard to piece together but this is definitely not a good stand-alone book.

Florence and Grace are so pathetic through most of the book, I wanted to slap them and tell them to grow up. Abigail's idea of being "better than the servants" and never having cooked her own meals is just sad.  Grace teaching Abigail to cook was ridiculous at best. She gave her the barest of instructions and somehow Abigail made a "wonderful" meal. Then there's the actual plot and yes there is one. It's very weak. All in all, this wasn't the worst book I've ever read, but it wasn't one of the better ones either. Needless to say, I won't be buying any of the other books in the series.

I very much enjoyed reading this book, even though I thought Georgia was a bit of whiner and way too indecisive. Thankfully all the other characters pulled it all together and made a great story. I especially loved Ian's little girl. I know most people would find her character to be a little unrealistic because she sounded so mature on occasion but I've taken care of several little girls just like her. They're rare but they really do exist and they say the darnedest things.

I would never call this a "sweet" romance. The author kills far too many people for this book to be labeled as "sweet."  In fact, at one point I thought I was reading a murder mystery. It seemed like every other page had someone being murdered.

As far as the romance goes, I didn't really care for Saffron's determination to marry Silas. The man basically ignored her and when he did talk to her, he treated her like dirt. Yet no matter how badly he treated her, she continued to believe they'd be married. She seemed to have this whole imaginary romance built up in her head that had no basis in reality. I felt like she hung on to Silas far longer than she should have.

I love a strong female heroine but Saffron being the only female on a hunt for a dangerous, rabid bear was a tad hard to believe. Then the author even threw in an Indian attack. It was just a bit over the top.

I have to admit, I'm truly puzzled by all the great reviews. As a romance novel, this one is sadly lacking in the romance department. The story started off great with Nikki and Mitch meeting as teenagers, while he was visiting his brother at summer camp. (Nikki was a swimming instructor at the camp.) After that one brief encounter, they each go their separate ways and don't meet up again until 10 years later. From that point on, the book pretty much went downhill for me. Now if this was an erotica book, then it would get a five star rating. It's sex, sex and more sex. If they're not thinking about having sex, they're having sex. There's page after page of explicit sexual encounters. No real romance, just a weak plot, "hot" hero and "gorgeous" heroine having sex, sex and more sex. The author described Mitch as "hot" and Nikki as "gorgeous" so many times I wanted to throw my Kindle out the window.

I know a lot of people thought this was a great book. Personally, I think the plot was very cliche and nothing special. The hero decides "he's" the best person to raise his orphan niece, a child he's never even seen before.  Even though he knows absolutely "nothing" about how to care for a baby, he still thinks "he'd" be a better choice as a guardian than the aunt who's been taking of the baby and loves her.  When he's discussing his need to have custody with the heroine, he thinks to himself that a will is just a "preference" and that the "courts" will decide who should have the baby, not the will. He's got loads of money so he can hire the best lawyers, therefore he'll get custody, regardless of what's in the will. Apparently he doesn't feel that the parents' wishes are important or he would wait for the will to be found and agree to abide by it. He's arrogant and judgmental and "always" thinks he knows best. He arrived on the heroine's doorstep believing she had low morals and stuck with that belief for far too long. He'd never even met her before he showed up to claim the baby. Granted in the beginning she deliberately misled him but he's supposed to be a smart, successful, international businessman and he misinterprets so many things it's unreal. He has money and yet doesn't do an ounce of investigating to find the "truth."  He only wants to dig up dirt so he can have custody of a baby he's never seen and doesn't know how to care for.  How is any of this, "Christian" behavior?

I did read the entire book and it ended exactly the way I knew it would from the very beginning. It's very predictable.

This book definitely had a lot of "cliche" moments, love at first glance, people willing to risk their lives for someone they didn't really know but immediately loved, she's kidnapped/he rides to the rescue, she's kidnapped again/he rescues her again and so on.  Having said that, the book was well written. There weren't a million spelling and grammar errors and there actually was a plot. It wasn't just two characters hopping from one bed to another.

The story follows a young white woman who was raised by Indians and is now scouting for a wagon train. She's hiding on the wagon train, hoping her Indian brother won't find her. (He's vowed to kill her for causing the death of his mother and sister.)  The wagon master has secrets of his own and while he's drawn to her, he doesn't want to be. While its unlikely any wagon train would have hired a female as a scout and certainly not one who's been raised by Indians, I still found the story interesting. There are several sub-plots along with the main one so there's a lot going on at any given point in the book. The characters are well developed. They have depth; flaws, hopes, dreams and regrets.  I very much enjoyed reading to see what would happen next and almost hated to see it end.

I was given a paperback copy of this book to read and therefore didn't see the reviews before I read the book. Thank heavens I didn't have to pay for it. Like so many others, after reading 496 'real' pages I was appalled to find out the story didn't end! If I want to know who the serial killer is, I have to find the next book in the series. Surely with almost 500 pages at her disposal, the author should have been able to figure out a way to actually "end" the story. I DETEST books like this. There should be a warning on the cover...."This book is incomplete."  Actually it's not even a "book" because books have a beginning, a middle, and an end. This book has no ending and is therefore only good for use as kindling in a fireplace.

I really didn't care for this book as much as everyone else did. There's no table of contents. (My Kindle font size is #3, so I had to scroll through about 16 pages to see the entire list.) The baskets are listed in alphabetical order, sort of. If you want to create a "detox" basket, you won't find it under "d" for detox. You'll find it under "n" for natural detox. Some of the basket ideas are similar, goat's milk soap basket & natural soap basket, cleaning basket and natural cleaning basket. (I'm not sure a basket full cleaning supplies would make my top 10 list of great gifts but someone might like it.) There aren't any photos of what any of the finished baskets might look like. (Even the cover shows an "empty" basket.) The book starts with an introduction and then just lists 101 ideas for various gift baskets. Each basket is numbered, has a title and gift ideas. I, personally, didn't find the ideas all that "fantastic."

Examples of a few gift baskets:

3. Aromatherapy: Reed diffuser, scented candles in pretty glass containers, potpourri, sachets, tea infuser with variety of fruit-flavored teas. (How about adding some essential oils to use with the reed diffuser.)

39. Goat's Milk Soap: Soaps, soap dishes, washcloths, dish towels, lotion

96. Wine: One or two bottles of wine, two glass or plastic wine glasses, small plates, cheese and crackers. (How about a corkscrew?)

I really enjoyed reading "Pieces of Ivy."  It's definitely a combination of mystery and horror, or maybe I should say it's a horrifying mystery. There's even a little paranormal thrown in. The story begins with FBI agent Vicki Starr having a terrible nightmare. When she arrives at work that morning, she feels compelled to work on a new case pertaining to a young woman who's been viciously murdered. After Vicki talks her boss into letting her have the case, she finds out he's assigned her a partner she doesn't know, one she takes an instant dislike to. Her new partner Hank Dashel, has issues of his own. He doesn't like his new partner either. They are, however, forced to work together to solve the young woman's murder. In the middle of the murder investigation, it appears that someone is trying to kill agent Starr. The twists and turns throughout the book keep you completely engaged from beginning to end. I didn't give it five stars because it aggravates me when books don't tie up all the loose ends. This one doesn't. The murder is solved so it's not a cliffhanger.

Somehow I missed the fact that this was book 2 of a series. It didn't matter. The story was great as a stand alone book. It starts out fast paced with Miriam getting mauled by a cougar and the action doesn't stop there. The adventure continues right up until the end of the book...no cliffhangers!  A very nice, clean, well written story.

users.query:
Awesome book!  So well written and such depth in the characters. Conner leaves the Marines after 10 years to raise his brothers and sisters after the tragic death of their parents and to repair the destruction of the house from a hurricane. He works as a mechanic and juggles the responsibilities of the kids. Beau is new in town to play hockey. He has blue hair and he stands out in a crowd. The brakes give out on his van and he is able to coast into the garage where Conner works. Beau ends up living in a trailer on Conners property while he helps with the reconstruction. Its heartwarming to watch the love evolve with the two guys and the four kids. The steamy parts are tastefully done with lots of dialogue between. This is the fourth or fifth book I have read from this author and they have all been outstanding while touching on delicate subjects with the veterans and abuse because they are gay.
I voluntarily read and reviewed an advanced reader copy of this book

Outstanding!!  10 STARS!!!  The bare bones of the sacrifices made by our service men and women.  They were portrayed honestly, gracefully and respectfully. It's the story of how a tragically injured Marine manages to live his life meaningfully by helping others and how he finally lets love give him happiness. You just need to read this book.

This was a pleasant lightweight read. Both characters have had painful pasts that are lightly explained. Because they are both from the same small town, they have a connection that can lead them to healing. Book is totally focused on the characters and not their environment.
I received a free copy of this book via Booksprout and am voluntarily leaving a review.

I really liked this book. The beginning is a little slow going while the background is developed. (Nice to know how the players are related). Cate is an interior designer who works for her overbearing and cruel mother. Jack is an accomplished attorney and Dylan is an inventive chef completing culinary school. Cate's grandfather, Sully, dies and leaves his Boston townhouse to the three of them. Sully was the kind of man to manipulate opportunities for deserving people.  Care used to visit during the summers and had a retreat from her vicious mother; Dylan was an aspiring cook who couldn't afford culinary school and Jack's family was poor due to his gambling father. These three basically grew up together from a young age. Misunderstood events lead to some pretty tenuous feelings. As they get back together, deep seated feelings surface and they begin to merge into a family. Nicely written. Worth the time to read!

This is the second book I have read in this series and liked it as much as the first. It doesnt have an intense plot, more sex than dialogue or super deep characters. This is lightweight love story that is very well written about Eleanor and Donald, long distance neighbors. There is some drama with an offensive cretin who wants an in to Eleanors family.  Its a great story to read when are in-between heavy duty books and your mind needs a rest.
I voluntarily read and reviewed an advanced reader copy of this book

This is the third book I have read in this series.  Although it is not written as hardcore BDSM, it was interesting and had enough steamy parts to keep you connected.  It had a well thought out and continuous plot line going.  The characters were portrayed as regular people; some with common deep seated emotional issues and how they were able to work through them. Not one of them was glorified as being perfect; not even the big bad Doms.  Nicely done.

While it may have had a few grammatical errors ( per another reviewer ), I was ecstatic that it was obviously proofed by someone older than 8 years old. I am not an English professor, but a voracious reader. It just galls me that a writer would release any kind of book without a spell and grammar check. Even MS Word can do that.  Do some of these erotica writers think their audience only gets off on the "juicy" parts and do not read the rest of the story?  Hey folks, we are not stupid and ignorant!!!

Ms Cox, thank you for a very enjoyable series!!  I look forward to reading the next book in the series.

I don't leave many 5 star reviews, this one was really good!  This book grabs you out of the gate and keeps you running the entire story. There is sassy, snarky, sad, hotish but not steamy, suspenseful, riveting and you just keep flipping pages to see what happens next, but you don't want it to end.
Anthony is a new hot detective on this Georgia county police force originally from New York. Shelby is fairly local and works at the battered women and childrens shelter is is a single mom to a two year old son, Lucca. They meet when Shelby comes to the station to make yet another complaint to the lazy, good ole boy police department. Took one look to render them speechless. Shelbys mother is vicious, hateful and neglectful junkie that sold her when she was 16 for a fix. She runs away and ends up with a man she thinks loves her only to eventually find out that he is dominating and physically abusive.  She runs again and is rescued by an angel, but leaves her looking over her shoulder waiting until the monster finds her again. In the meantime, Anthony has fallen in love with her and her son and is working very hard to be in her life, but she is afraid.
There are some really interesting supporting characters that round out this story. It is super well written and is worth the time to read it.
I voluntarily read and reviewed an advanced reader copy of this book

Nicely written. Good character development. This was a historical read; not my usual genre. The story is very focused on the characters rather than the events of the time period. It does point out how women were treated; from loving wives to property to be used and abused. Domestic violence is not a new concept during that time.
Story is about a kidnapping gone bad, depending on your point of view.  Insight to the nature of people.

Brianna and Michael meet when she puts her wedding experience up for sale. Michael decides he wants her too. He makes her an offer she can't refuse, be his for a year and be amply compensated.  It was nicely written and the characters backgrounds unravel as the story progresses.

A powerful story!  Read this book in one sitting on the edge of the chair. There is such a myriad of emotions, tragedy, betrayal, secrets, jealousy, mystery and happiness. Grabbed me from the very beginning. It is very well written and the characters develop as you read. Starts with two storylines that begin to weave together the lives of several sad people. Love Ann Major books!

This book was pretty intense. It hooked me from the beginning and I read it in one sitting. There were a lot of twists and turns so as soon as you would get a grip on the plot, it went in a different direction. It was a long book and I only got caught up with the POV a couple times. There were many facets.  The bdsm played the biggest role in Edens trust in Liam not so much in doing scenes. The psychological aspects of the characters was fascinating. Overall, I thought it was well written and good flow through the story. There was just enough suspense to keep you edgy.

This was a really funny and cute book. Her ex cheated and he is having unrequited love. They are neighbors. Her best friends cook up 10 dates in 10 days. Each one is more disastrous than the last including bodily injury. There are some laugh out loud parts too.

This book was well written for what it is. Turns out Cathy's husband Brett has had a fantasy to be a voyeur for his wife and another man. What a delightful book. I couldn't put it down. Yeah, yeah it's a fall in love, fear of commitment ,and HEA. It's not too angsty either. They have supportive families and some really crazy funny relatives. Well written.

A MILLION STARS!!  There just aren't enough words to convey how absolutely amazing this book is.  I was at such a loss for words when it came time to write this review; still am.  This was by far the very best book I have read in years, and I am old.  This book will just engage you from the start and rip your heart out along the way!  Theres unrequited love from the search and rescue veterinarian who is struck by her when she is given bad news about her husband. She has the most precocious and adorable almost five year old daughter. The underlying tragedy and trauma for her is coping with her rape 15 years earlier. This author has laid out on the table the horrors, nightmares and dysfunctional life of a surviving victim. Be warned, it is not sugarcoated. The book was longer than most but it was needed to tell this story.  It flowed so beautifully.  There is an endearing eclectic older gentleman (I just picture the KFC Colonel) who seems to appear and disappear after dispensing puzzling advice. There is even some snarky humor that snuck in there. Her life becomes a work in progress slowly coming to grips that she didn't cause the assault and is the victim. Little by little she is taking back her life. This was just an amazing story about love, support and healing.  Find a comfy chair, some tissues and prepare to read this straight through because you will not be able to put it down.  Wonderfully written!

users.query:
Is this a novel of repressed regrets inconveniently resurfacing, the challenge of reconciliation and the  ultimate acceptance of one's lot, the effect of unexpected life altering intrusions, learning from grief, or some other theme I can't quite figure out? McEwan explores all this while writing in the voice of the female protagonist, Fiona, a middle-aged comfortably well off and married Family Court judge. A case involving a young Jehovah Witness refusing life saving medical treatment creates the pivotal life altering event driving the narrative. Marital problems suddenly add to the flavor of a suddenly upended life that she had successfully shielded from outside challenges.

The court case is vividly described with all competing issues fully explored, making the verdict and subsequent impact all the more difficult to predict.

With McEwan, one can expect precise, vivid prose, neither flashy nor flabby. No exception here, and, as a result, the story flows both entertainingly and with fresh insights into the human condition. A joy to read.

cands.text:
This soft post apocalyptic novel features a population that has been subtly brainwashed into accepting life in a bleak society recovering from some long ago catastrophic event that they are lead to believe may or may not have occurred. Confusing? Yes, and the author deliberately teases out clues to past events in a world now bereft of any conflict or provocations, all enforced not by secret police or harsh laws, but by expectation that one will offer up an "I'm Sorry", whether appropriate or not. Music and art forms are dumbed down: pastel landscapes and sleep inducing music are the norm. Retention of souvenirs from long ago are frowned upon and kept hidden. There is a mysterious  higher authority monitoring all this, but again without any resort to door knocks and deportations in the middle of the night.

Of course, there is increasing inter-personal violence, and that is evident from the early pages, so no spoiler here. Into all of this the young male and female protagonists meet under unusual circumstances and eventually fall in love, maneuvering and adapting as best they can. . Could they have been chosen for some higher purpose by others trying to recreate a benign atmosphere? Read on.

A note about style. The conversations between the two - he's a maker of wooden candlesticks for the local gift shop and she creates decorative flowers - are inconsistent with those backgrounds and vocations. At first blush they do not strike one as espousers of heavy philosophical discourse. Yet, the author endows the two with dense literary exchanges that invite reflection and admiration for the author's literary chops. Heady stuff.

Needless to say, this is not your typical virus or World War III induced post apocalyptic novel. It also deficient in dramatic action. Still, an interesting take on the genre for those attracted to literary fiction.

Can dysfunctional families stay that way forever? Can external forces prompt reconciliation and growth?  Pulitzer prize winning author Strout probes these themes and suggests there are inherent, but buried, sibling ties that can blossom in the most unlikely circumstances.

The novel focuses on three siblings: a sister (Susan), who remains in a dying town in the dying state of Maine, and the two brothers of the title (Jim and Bob), who flee to New York City. Susan is divorced and coping with a sullen teenager (Zach), who commits a crime that is blown out of proportion by those with a political agenda or who refuse to accept an unintentional mistake in judgment. Jim, the oldest, is a hot shot defense lawyer with all the accompanying swagger and arrogance, but who is living with a horrible secret from his childhood. Bob is also also divorced and is drifting through life as a legal aid attorney writing appellant briefs. Zach's crime brings them home to Maine and everything unfolds from there. Supporting characters are no less nuanced or complex.

Strout masterfully portrays the racial dynamics at play. The town has experienced an influx of Somalis who can't or won't assimilate. In fact,they are ill-equipped to do by virtue of barriers presented by language and native customs. Many of the town citizens are unwelcoming when presented with the unfamiliar sights of an alien people plunked down into their insular world. Culture clash ensues, exacerbated by Zach's crime, and reconciliation is elusive even to the likes of the local Unitarian minister. Strout avoids any politically correct preaching, but as befits her literary chops, is balanced and sympathetic to both sides, including the hapless son when he becomes a political target.

As dormant Burgess family ties present an opportunity for healing, is there something intrinsic in the human community that also offers hope for eventual acceptance and understanding of our differences? You have to read the book!

Fascinating characters, including all the current and former spouses of the Burgess's, make this human drama a fast paced and ultimately thought provoking read.

The concept is simple, but masterfully and compellingly told by best selling author Atkinson. Namely, she explores how our lives pivot on what may appear to be happenstance or an insignificant moment that then is the proximate cause of a life altering or even fatal end. Think "It's a Wonderful Life." The life story of Ursula, the little bear, plays out in such a fashion as parallel stories focus on several scenarios where the common element is a single seemingly harmless act; eg. a stolen kiss in the garden. Ah, if that horrible boy hadn't been so bold! The author proceeds to tell you what happened in that case and many others, and a series of life resets are presented.

Ursula also possesses some sort of ability, not really all that clear to her, to forewarn herself of certain events that may befall others. Without knowing why, for example, she may sabotage someone's engagement so that person doesn't attend an event and be exposed to the deadly flu bug of 1919. In Atkinson's capable hands, what could have been a Stephen King wanabe knockoff, is avoided.

What resonates most strongly here is the heightened realization of how some combination of chance and opportunity (and preparation) lead inexorably to one's present status. Perhaps some resets, as were afforded Ursula, would be welcome.

The author is British and the book covers a wide swath of that country's history and its role in WWl and WWll. This could also be considered an historical novel.

The technique of relating different life stories of the same person occurring at the same time allows for the inclusion of Ursula's experience both in London during the blitz and in Berlin as the marauding and raping Russians approach. Both stories are told in depth and with harrowing intensity.

Some may say this book is too long, but that's not a valid criticism when the story is as fascinating as this.

Anne Tyler's family-centric tales are explored anew in this multi-generational saga of a Baltimore family. Settle in, if you must, to witness the family dynamics of disappointments, secret relationships, ambitions both smashed and fulfilled, heroic sacrifices, and plot enhancing revelations.  Her fans will recognize all this, but might be hard pressed to ferret out any deeper truths worth pondering.

Why? Grasping for reasons, I thought the characters, while interesting and quirky, were only just that. Were they, the family, not so much different than many other families? We have the black sheep son, the scion driven by an obsession, the guilt ridden and remorseful second generation father, the hardships associated with the great depression, and so on. We've seen this type of narrative before, although admittedly not in the hands of a gifted writer. Perhaps my expectations were too high; for whatever reason the book failed to resonate with me. Memorable characters were just not memorable enough.

So I plowed through this pleasantly plotted, non-challenging story, waiting for the pace to pick up. To no avail. A reader's guide is included. It seems a stretch to make much of it. The title of the book is considered a metaphor for something. Unraveling of family ties perhaps? Or something to add a bit of literary cred?

Anne Tyler fans will read and appreciate, but cross-over appeal will suffer. On the other hand, I was able to read this while watching a baseball game!

The author of the popular post-apocalyptic novel The Dog Stars switches to the here and now with a first person narrative of a person seeking to tame a simmering anger fueled by a tragic personal loss. In today's terms you might say he is attempting to achieve "life balance."

This theme is developed through two intertwined stories. In one, Jim, an accomplished and financially successful expressionistic painter and fly fisherman fanatic,  devotes himself to these pursuits in a remote region of New Mexico as therapy for his anger issues. In the other, suspense is provided by Jim's efforts to escape retribution from those who were a victim of said angry outbreaks - all triggered by his efforts to save a young horse from abuse. The story becomes a kill or be killed thriller with the criminal authorities sensing a yet unproven guilt. Can he outsmart them while still eluding his pursuers? Were his actions justifiable? Knowing this much  should not spoil the plot.

The ending is remarkable but seems appropriate in a natural law sense. I'll leave it at that.

If you enjoyed The Dog Stars, especially the exquisitely imagined nature scenes, you'll also enjoy with the versatility shown in this tale of a person seeking the always elusive life equilibrium.

Despite its outdated and stilted prose and often languorous pace, this post-apocalyptic novel (written in 1949) continues to offer a fresh perspective on life in a world ripped asunder by a swiftly acting yet unidentified disease of epic proportions. What differentiates this from most other such novels is the author's emphasis, especially in the first portion of the book, on the reason for the calamity. What prompted the outbreak in the first place? The author offers a scientific explanation, drawing analogies to other species that become vulnerable to diseases after reaching a stressful climax state caused by multiple factors such as lack of land, food, or too much tv. A few survivors remain to rebuild. With examples given, this all sounds very plausible.

The protagonist, Ish, short for Isherwood, narrates the story in the third person, and through his eyes we see up close the aftermath of the calamity as he wanders around the country and searches for someone of suitable stature to link up with. He initially finds a dog (or more accurately the dog finds him), and that companionship spurs him on to eventually find his human soul mate. Are these two the Adam and Eve of the new world.

Another significant difference is that the survivors, and of course there are survivors, have no desire to rebuild or create a more formal  replacement structure. Ish is frustrated in his attempts to instill some traditional values and incentives. HIs tribe of survivors, and increasingly their offspring, are content to live in a state of innocent ignorance, scavenging for the still abundant supplies and with no thought for the future. The original slackers. Is this because they're living in Berkeley, California?

How will they fare when all the expired can goods are finally eaten? The book answers this question on a somewhat optimistic note, but don't expect a flourishing of Renaissance ideals.

Yes, the earth does truly abide. It may take awhile, but its permanence  will prevail despite our best efforts to control and alter its inherent  nature.

As with the author's other works, the theme in this series of short stroies is suburban angst and anxiety presented in a gently satirical and nonjudgemental manner. The result? Engaging stories of ordinary middle class people whose so-called nomal lives are disrupted in life altering ways, but who then progress through all the usual redemtive stages - some more successfully than others.

The success of the book lies in the way the author creates a sense of intimacy and empathy with the characters. These people, disfuntional as they may be, are truly unique dispite their common backgrounds. Causes for optimism are displayed whether we take advantage of the opportunities or not.

As author Atkinson points out, this novel is not a sequel to Life After Life, but a companion piece covering the same time frame focusing on Ursula's beloved brother Teddy. In Life After Life, Ursula's life is rewound multiple times, a clever literary device that with dramatic effect points out how much our own can be altered by the most casual and inopportune events.  Here, the author drops that trope for the most part, content to tell Teddy's story and that of the other family members (even Ursula) in the more common non-lineal style. However, and without spoiling anything, she does indulge herself at one point with a "what if" alternative.

Teddy is a bomber pilot during the British night time raids over Germany that resulted in horrendous losses to crew and pilots, inflicted catastrophic civilian deaths (they started it!), and apparently did not do much strategic damage to German war industries. He survives, mentally scarred, but carries on withh his life in a steadfast, conscientious, British manner. He's presented as a good guy who now seeks comfort in the commonplace and simple pleasures of nature and his family. The plot has two elements:one, his interaction with various family members  and two, an accounting of his experience as an accomplished and well respected bomber pilot. Atkinson does a superb job in capturing the sheer terror of such missions.

As simply as I can state it, this is a good story well told. The interaction between the family members, who each get their own chapters, is complex and taut. Teddy has a profound impact on them all. And there's much to be admired in an author who can let the story dominate without abandoning the literary qualities of evocative imagery and insightful observations. This book is not a poor second to Life After Life.  If anything it fleshes out that book by focusing on a family member who has gone through hell and survivied at least in body.

This highly praised debut novel lives up to its billings as a southern based tale with all the usual rhythms and prototypes of rural tobacco country North Carolina. The novel is narrated through the voices of three people whose own backstories help explain how each, in turn, must deal with and ultimately reconcile themselves with the impact of a recent tragedy that dominates the main plot line. That story line includes a host of well drawn characters harboring inner demons, deep loss, festering frustrations, or some combination of all! The pace meanders as those stories are told and one wonders when we'll find out the circumstances surrounding the tragedy. As befits a southern novel, a corrupt, but charismatic snake handling Appalachian preacher takes advantage of these God fearing people in this bible belt setting and plays a key role in causing the lives of the three main narrators to  intertwine, the suspense to mount, and the story to successfully end on a note of muted optimism. Things can change for the better.

This acclaimed novel features dazzling writing, a complex, deeply layered plot, drama and suspense aplenty, and finely wrought characters. The two main protagonists, linked through murky circumstances and of dubious backgrounds and loyalties, seek monetary and emotional redemption while challenged by the unique political and cultural mores of post 9/11 Africa. It's fast paced. Actually, it's more than fast paced, featuring shifting and surprising plot turns that veer off into totally unexpected directions. . Describing the plot is a futile exercise; this reader was often lost the story thread, but hung on for the sheer enjoyment of the ride.

The main protagonist speaks in the first person or as an involved narrator. The writing is direct: "I ordered a martini. It tasted like one." One is swept along by the rhythm of the narration and the craftsmanship of the prose. This rises above the typical action/thriller category. And in  no way will you predict the ending!

What an entertainingly clever literary effort this is. Trace someone's life story as chapters in a faux self-help book promising ways to make it in a rising, but corrupt Asian country (probably India or Pakistan), all written in the second person. Meanwhile, insert generous but acerbic social commentary on the ill effects of globalization dished with abundant humor while also describing how the unnamed protagonist learns the life lessons that serve as chapter headings. So, for example, one, he leaves as a youth for the overcrowded unruly dangerous city, two, gets what passes for an education from an inept teacher, three, learns the distraction caused by falling in love, four, avoids idealists, and so on. An unrequited love interest hovers throughout, and we learn that she, aka "the pretty girl,"  has had an equally  eventful  arc of a life beginning  from impoverished roots. Will they ever get together?

The author provides keen insights into the cultural and conflicting societal issues present in an emerging economy where there are no real constraints on a winner take all capitalist system except those imposed by bribery and crime. And don't forget the environmental desecration
and inadequate infrastructure associated with unfettered and unregulated growth. No wonder someone from humble origins  entering these waters (no plot clue intended) requires the advice provided by this mock serious self-help book! No need to lecture or harangue on the plight of  and obstacles  to those attempting to succeed in this world when the story is infused with the author's highly original format,  humor, and perceptive observations. Could not put it down.

Lucy narrates her life story, focusing on an attempted reconciliation with her  estranged mother. All this is prompted by her unexpected visit to Lucy's hospital bed, where she is recovering from a long and unidentified illness. They reminisce and dredge up old gossip from a shared past, thereby lying the groundwork for ultimately achieving mutual understanding or, more optimistically, LOVE. In the meantime she tells her entire life story, from impoverished youth to making it in the Big Apple, with all the heart breaks and triumphs along the way.

This is a competently told story from a prize winning and best selling author. I enjoyed the Burgess Brothers more, a tale with more characters and interlacing story lines. Here, let's face it, Lucy's life is not all that interesting or unusual except perhaps her escape from poverty . Although the novel contains some of the literary insights one would expect from an author of this caliber; ultimately, it's all about Lucy working out her issues with Mom.

How does a heretofore seemingly tranquil suburb deal with the disruptive force of a church seeking to impose its rigidly uncompromising moralistic values on the populace?  To pull off this premise, the author must create some interesting archetypes. And he does.

In one corner, we find Ruth, a fiercely secular divorced mother of two teenagers who teaches a form of enlightened sex education, but who seethes when required to adopt an abstinence curriculum. Her best friends are gay. In the other corner, we spot Tim, also divorced, and father of one teenage girl. He's  in alcohol and drug addiction recovery thanks to his adoption of the hard core Christianity preached by the zealous pastor of said fundamentalist church. Oh, all the kids play soccer; after all, this is suburbia, and Tim is the soccer coach. Conflict ensues, principles erode, and you can probably can guess where this is all leading.

The book is four stars successful. Credit the author with prolonging what may appear inevitable by  an easygoing writing style, cleverly wrought character sketches, humor, and assorted plot twists. The author also "abstains" from mocking religion in general and even those church members with sincere beliefs, while showing how an overly doctrinaire approach to religion can have destructive consequences.

The ending, despite its inevitability, is ambiguous enough to avoid being pat, and you are left with an opportunity to speculate on how everyone's lives will proceed.

Radical twists and turns, startling reveals, moral ambiguities, brutal action written in stripped down pulsing third person narrative (when appropriate), and quirky and colorful characters all combine to produce a first rate thriller. And no run on sentences like the above!  You learn a lot about the publishing industry, which is the author's profession, as the plot revolves around the potential publication of a manuscript with disclosures so explosive that trained assassins are hired to prevent its release. And hence you have the plot outline: greedy and compromised people seek to reap the rewards from its publication in money, fame, or to rescue a career. The protagonist has other not immediately apparent goals. All are in danger as a de facto government agent who seeks to eliminate all who have access to the title. People are punished for their overreaching ambitions and other achieve some sort of moral clarity. An object lesson perhaps?

Worth mentioning as an added attraction are the author's keen social observations of the manners and mores of the socially striving millennnials who populate the book. After reading such passages I had to inwardly remark: "Yes, I know these people." In trying to self actualize in an individualistic way they are only achieving uniformity in thought and deed. Fascinating, as is the entire novel.

If you're considering this book you will probably have already read McCann's award winning Let the Great World Spin. You will not be disappointed, as he largely sticks with his winning formula of setting up several story lines with characters from each interacting with each other in surprising and enlightening ways in a nonchronological manner.

At its heart this is an historical novel of Ireland (of course) and US connections; hence the title. Duh! For example, there is a chapter on Frederick Douglass's visit to Ireland and another on the much more recent Irish peace accords negotiated by George Mitchell. There is also the story of a poor Irish emigrant girl's  hard fought success in this country as she and her progeny overcome all the usual barriers in becoming part of the melting pot. The more you read, the more the connections become apparent, and the more the pace quickens.

About the actual quote from near the end of the book. As in Let the Great World Spin, our worlds connect in unlikely ways not always obvious until events play out, but at some time, the author suggests, the world can at time allow the connections to mesh in an uplifting way. Now that's something to be optimistic about!

Did you enjoy Jess Walter's  alternatingly invigorating and poignantly written  Beautiful Ruins? I did, so I took a chance on this collection of his previously published short stories and was not disappointed.

Set in the Pacific Northwest, the book portrays with humor and empathy the lives of characters living on the edge, or who have actually having fallen off it, and who are driven to distraction or desperation for a variety of reasons. Why would one want to read stories featuring mainly sociopaths,drug and alcohol addicts, and other undesirables? For one, it's a change of scenery from the too frequent setting of Park Slope, Brooklyn or its equivalent. And also, you are both amused and intrigued by how these characters cope with issues we all share in common, but from the perspective of someone living in compromised circumstances.

As with all modern short stories, the tales aren't neatly wrapped up with clear resolutions, but force the reader to extrapolate the progression of the story and the point to be made. Some stories are a page or two and some much longer. All are entertaining, but don't expect happy transformations.

This description of the tone of the book may make it sound like a downer, but it most empathically is not due to Walter's engaging style and clever story telling.

This rambling arc of a story with multiple plot lines that sometimes fizzle out is set mostly in the deep woods of Montana with its colorful and sometimes creepy inhabitants. Antagonist Pete, a  family services social worker, lives a discordant life, demonstrating conscientious devotion to his young  charges while failing to control his irresolute personal life. The former sets him up for disappointment while the latter leads to, well, more drinking and guilt, mostly involving his daughter. Is he in need of a social worker?

After sifting through the multiple plot lines and wondering whether there is a unifying theme, the main thrust of the story finally arrives when a particular case leads to Pete's encounter with  a separatist, reclusive, conspiracy theorist, paranoid, apocalyptic preaching, right wing religious zealot with a violent streak. How that all plays out occupies the bulk of the book, although some earlier developed mini-plots reappear from time to time. This is not a tightly woven yarn.

An note about style, which suffers from an over reliance on too clever metaphors that a distract from  rather than  enhance  the prose.  These metaphors do not seamlessly flow but oft times draw too much attention to themselves.  And get out the dictionary! Yet, he is obviously a gifted writer.

The novel is enjoyable overall, especially the local color,  and one feels compelled to keep reading to learn how or if all the plot threads resolve themselves. I'd give it three and one-half stars if I could.

Hosseini plunges again into this troubled part of the world with empathy and a mlange of characters whose life stories are shaped by the continuous conflicts endemic to Afghanistan, whether wrought by kings, the Brits, the warlords, the Russians, and the Americans, all leading to the corrupt current regime. This is not an anti-war book per se, but one where the ever lurking turmoil causes a stew of fleshed out characters to adjust to and reconcile themselves with that reality as their lives intersect in unexpected, yet intriguing ways. How will they fare against the backdrop of a war torn Afghanistan?

Sometimes people's stories are wrapped up in summary fashion, but that device only tightens up the plot line as the significant interactions play out in full blown poignancy, especially the ending, which completes the circle of narration. Prepare to cry if you're so inclined.

I didn't know what to expect, having read the Kite Runner like everyone else in the world, and I wasn't particularly interested in his second effort. This one, though,sustains interest throughout  because of the author's ability to evoke the richness of the diverse characters. Hosseini offers just plain good old fashioned story telling. Is it possible to give it four and a half stars?

Lamott makes  prayer accessible and relevant, in a non doctrinal way, to the gamut of human concerns, worries, fears, and despairs. Simplifying the concept of prayer makes it no less powerful. This is a slim volume of about 100 pages, but what it lacks in length it makes up for with insightful and often humorous passages that one reads, ponders, reflects upon, rereads, and then rereads the next day.

When seeking help through prayer, it is most effective, she teaches, when we have exhausted our own ability to solve or overcome problems independently. Stoicism doesn't work anymore. An example makes her point. As she is writing this, she is dealing with an old dying cat, whose death she knows will have devastating consequences for her and her grandson. Praying for a miracle is not an option. Rather, consistent with the theme of this book, she prays for help in gaining strength to overcome her and her grandson's sorrow. By praying also for a pain free passing of her pet, she opens the door to giving thanks to the joy the cat gave and received.

She seems to be saying one should avoid "beggy" prayers and trust in and surrender to
a higher power, no matter who or what you call it. God works as an option! Her premise is easy to apply; after all, three one word prayers are about as basic as it gets.

By now everyone is aware of Kyle's remarkable career as an accomplished sniper and his untimely and almost ironic death. There is also the fascination with the Navy Seal program and its particular form of warrior mentality. Kyle certainly personified this breed of soldier, so it is worthwhile to examine the life of a person on whom we are dependent as a nation at war but also towards whom some are ambivalent. In other words, we cheer when they take out Bin Laden but choose not to contemplate the down and dirty work they do in the performance of their dangerous duties.

This book exposes all that. Here is a person driven by a love of country and an eagerness to engage in combat, the fiercer the better. To Kyle there are no gray areas, but only stark black and white choices, as he has no compunction in applying deadly force. He has no political or philosophical interest in the foreign policy reasons for the Iraq war or for the responsible politicians. Generals and commanding officers are viewed as obstacles to any effective strategy. His single minded purpose -and this is what I took away from his story - is to kill the enemy before they have a chance to kill one of his fellow soldiers.

No matter where you are on the pacifist to hawk continuum, this book is  a valuable testimony to the indispensable people to whom we don't give enough recognition for the unique skills they apply on a day to day basis.

replacement for the identical ball that somehow sprung a leak. Surprising since material is fairly thick. Good feature is the weighted bottom so doesn't roll around. This is used as a seating surface and works well in that regard.

Who started the horrendous deadly dance hall fire and explosion in a small, rural town in Missouri  in 1929? Investigated extensively at the time, the question of responsibility was left dangling. Was it an accident? The answer ultimately revealed provides a satisfying ending consistent with character development and other revelations. However, the pleasure derived from this novel is not so much from its "who or why or anyone", but in the author's skillful portrayal of interconnected lives and the impact of the disaster on those relationships.

The novel is told in the voices of the main characters in separate chapters in a non-lineal style. Interspersed with the main story line are separate chapters with brief life story vignettes of lives lost, many told with understated poignancy.

This is a short novel with the heft of one much longer. Passages are meaty, dense, efficient, and creatively structured. Innovative descriptions cause one to savor the author's depictions of time and place. One could and should reread this book to glean new pleasures from his mastery of language, especially as he conveys the motivations and mental states of the main characters. Why wasn't this considered one of the best books of 2013?

This is a novel of manners and mores that transitions into a morality tale ala a Greek tragedy. Claire, a young, attractive ambitious "working girl" gets caught up in the privileged world of the Hamptons with its beautiful lifestyles and lavish homes and entertainments. The men all went to Yale before assuming lucrative downtown NY careers and memberships in private clubs and prestigious boards. The women mostly "do lunch." Claire is obviously not a member of that class but is seduced by the lifestyle. She is also attracted to a happily married family man with the perfect wife. Indiscretion follows.

Because Indiscretion is written with some literary flair and through the parallel story of an involved narrator (think The Great Gatsby), we care about the characters and their ultimate fate. Suspense or at least curiosity is sustained. This is not some trashy soap opera.

Indiscretion is also thought provoking. Can one tempt and then cheat fate? Does the universe expect some kind of balance when morality is breached? Must a cosmic equilibrium be restored? What does the Old Testament say about this? A quote from the book is instructive. "We make so many right decisions in life, but it is the wrong ones that can never be forgiven." Yes, definitely Old Testament!

This is a first novel from an obviously talented writer. I'm glad I took a chance with a cheap download for my ereader.

I'd be happy with around 800!

Mark Tufo never fails to give his audience a real thrill ride! This is another great read! It has characters you can love and hate, and a story line mixed with humor and terror. If I was giving this a grade I would say A++++++ and if I was giving it points its 100 across the board. Sit back with a cup of coffee and enjoy this fast read from one of the best authors out there to date. One last piece of info-Mark Tufo writes like people want their lives to be like. We all have wanted to have special powers or to break the bad guy in two. We all want to face off against zombies and to be the hero against an unknown evil. Tufo gives us this ride in every book!!!

Cannot wait for the next book! Comedy is always present-which should be expected from Tufo at this point! But plenty of action and drama too. I have many questions and I cant wait to get the answers from the next books!! Awesome!
