This was a great ending to this series. Glad to hear the author is wanting to start up another series!! Can't wait to read it!! This book is about teenagers but anyone can read it and understand there feelings and the journey they take to become adults. Great apocalyptic thriller full of adventure and drama!! A+++++

This is a continuation of the White Flag of the Dead series. If anyone was wondering what happened to little baby Jake this is the book to read. Just a good as the rest of the series. Hope to get many more books in the future! A++++

So I was reading this book and getting involved with the characters. Some of them I like, some I hate. But I cannot wait for the next book to tell me what happens to my new friends. Traditional zombie story line...but a hot chick with a sword is a nice touch! Plus I like the newspaper man...I hope he lives. But the author has no problem killing off anyone at anytime. I thought surely she won't die..and she did. Brave author! But a really good flow to the story. Read this book in four hours! Couldnt put it down!
If you love action and zombies then this is the series for you! Hang on for a bumpy ride full of believeable characters, real life survivor scenerios, and lots of zombie gore!! Great book. A+++++
This show is good no matter what season or epidsode. It because the treasure they find are always different and the group has great dynamics! We really love this show!
I looked everywhere for floppy disks for a machine at our business. Walmart or Office Max neither had these. These were a good price and I got them fast.
Super cute gift! She loved it!! Totally would buy again!

users.query:
After hearing recently that Lois Duncan died, I found myself feeling nostalgic and decided to see if my library had any of her ebooks.  I know I read several of her books when I was a teen/tween, when I was looking for something a little darker than Nancy Drew.  Not sure if I'd read this one in the 80's, parts of it did seem familiar.

I understand updating books to make them more modern and palpable to today's audience (especially when they're written for younger readers), but I wish they wouldn't do it!  This book was originally written in 1966 and it would still be entirely readable unchanged.  They've (Duncan?  The publisher?) put in references to cell phones and texting, but it doesn't fit in with the dialogue and seems forced.  A teenage polio survivor who has a cell phone?

The story centers around five teens who are kidnapped by a substitute bus driver:  Marianne (stepfather issues, comes from a broken home), Jesse (loner, military family), Dexter (angry, polio survivor), Bruce (in the shadow of his older brother, probably grows up to become a highly successful CEO), and Glenn (future frat bro and probable serial rapist).

It's a pretty short book and I enjoyed reading it, but I found the ending a little too abrupt.  But it revived my Lois Duncan interest and I think I'll seek out a few more of her books.

cands.text:
T.R. Reagan is an auto-buy for me.  She's one of my favorite authors.  I loved both the Lizzy Gardner and Faith McMann books.  And Jessie Cole looks like the start of another great series.

There are several stories going on in the book:  Jessie is being investigated by the police for wounding someone she was tailing as a private investigator (I actually thought this storyline wrapped up a little too quickly), Jessie and Ben (newspaper reporter) are trying to find answers as to what happened to Jessie's sister who disappeared a decade prior, and the Heartless Killer, who is abducting people at random to torture and kill.

The Hearless Killer storyline was the most interesting to me.  It's pretty gruesome, but riveting at the same time.  No rhyme or reason to the people he picks to abduct, and he plays on their worst fears (that he uses social media to find).  Jessie is searching for a missing woman, Zee, who's connected to the case.  I really liked Zee, I'm kind of hoping she pops up again in future books.  Plus, she delivered some much needed levity in a dark story.

Jessie is the guardian of her 14 year old niece, and she's maybe dating a police officer named Colin (who is on the Heartless Killer case).  Colin seems like a good guy, but he wasn't in the book enough to get a good sense of him.

So, I liked the book, I look forward to reading more, but I can't quite bring myself to give it five stars.  Why?  It's all...a little familiar, there are a lot of parallels with the Lizzy Gardner series.  Hopefully, more time spent with the characters will make them shine on their own.

I have to say, for a first time indie author, this book was well written.  No grammar problems or typos.

I really liked the story.  Laney and Kyle were both 30-something adults who actually acted like adults!  Both scarred by their ugly breakup 12 years prior, they decided to act like mature people and talk things out, apologize and try to move on.  There was no unrealistic drama, just real-life problems and some skittishness on both sides.

Laney had a great career and I'm glad she held fast to that while at the same time trying to make a relationship work.  Kyle wasn't demanding and was really great at compromising for love.

I loved the small town setting and I look forward to reading more about Wardham in future books.

I borrowed this ebook from the library.

There wasn't a lot that happened in this book, but I liked it nonetheless.  At times I found Sydney a little frustrating, wanting her to stand up for herself, but then I remembered I was reading about a teenager, not an adult.  My teen years were long ago, sometimes it's a little hard to relate.

The Chathams were a lovely, quirky family, it was easy to see why Sydney wanted to be a part of that.  And Mac was a good guy, I liked that the friendship between them made the romance seem secondary.

Sydney's parents, especially her mother, were pretty unlikable people.  The fact that they think it's ok for Ames to be some sort of chaperone for Sydney was really bizarre.  Everyone else in Sydney's life could see he's a total creeper, but not her parents?

Having read quite a few Sarah Dessen book, I would rate this somewhere in the middle:  not my favorite, but it was good and I'm glad I read it.

I borrowed this ebook from the library.  In the last few months I've read all the Will Trent series (really good), one of the Grant county series (ok) and Pretty Girls (fantastic).  This book reminded me a bit of Criminal from the Will Trent series.  That book partly focused on Amanda when she was a young cop in the 1970's, this one focuses on Maggie, who comes from a cop family and been on the job for several years, and Kate, who we meet on her first day in 1974.

The sexism, homophobia and racism are hard to stomach, but not too hard to believe.  We've definitely made strides on those issues, but not enough.  Maggie and Kate are harassed on a regular basis simply because the men think "they don't belong", yet it's the only job in the city that pays women the same as men (even though a woman couldn't rent an apartment or open a bank account without a male relative's permission).  Maggie and Kate are both smart, strong, yet flawed women.  As with all the other Slaughter books I've read, Atlanta is another character.  I've never been there, yet somehow it feels familiar.

I didn't guess who the villain was until it was revealed at the end, so kudos to the author for keeping me guessing.

This was a fairly short book, I read it in a little over an hour.  It was entertaining, and it kept my interest, but it wasn't very believable.  So many times I kept thinking they should have been caught, but they managed to get away.  Also, the FBI were incredibly inept.  They didn't tap everyone's phone that knew Jason?

I definitely prefer the Lizzy Gardner and Faith McMann series from this author.  When it comes to this genre I like reading books that are a little darker and more intense.

This book has been sitting in my TBR file on my Kindle for two years.  I've been on a bit of an historical romance kick lately, so I sought this one out.  I enjoyed it quite a bit.

Radford was a complex character:  overprotective father, Civil War veteran with PTSD, lonely soul who finds an unexpected connection with this brother's fiancé.  Evelyn has been engaged to Kyle for four years.  He has been her BFF since she was a kid, but now he's so focused on his business that he has little time for any kind of meaningful relationship with Evelyn.

I'm not a fan of love triangles, but it worked in this book.  Radford and Evelyn's feelings for each other came about slowly, and both were equally torn up about hurting Kyle.  I enjoyed Evelyn's relationship with her father (a great supporting character), and with Radford's daughter Rebecca.  I found Radford's Civil War memories and the way they continued to affect him well-written and interesting.

It was hard to muster up a lot of sympathy for Kyle, he was such a hot-head and an unlikable character.  Especially after reading the first few chapters from Kyle's book that (MILD SPOILER) he'd been having a sexual relationship with the stepmother of an old friend the entire time he was engaged to Evelyn.  I think I'll skip his book.

After I read the first book, I drew some parallels to the Lizzy Gardner series, hoping that more time spent with these characters would make them shine on their own.  And they did.

As with the first book, there are several storylines going on at once.  The main one is about a man who lost his daughter to a medical condition where the insurance company wouldn't pay for experimental drugs.  He decides to take revenge on the CEO of the company.  The killer was a horrible man, yet I felt some sympathy.  Some of the conversations he had with Emily (the CEO's daughter who he kidnapped) were touching.  Emily went back and forth between empathy and anger, just like me.

Zee (the schizophrenic kidnapping victim from the first book) is back, working part time with Jessie, and I was so happy to see her character return.  She gives the story some levity, as well as being a hero in her own right.  She has her own method of doing things, which seems to involve chaos.

Jessie is also investigating a cold case about a newborn who was kidnapped from the hospital.  Though it's been seven years, the mother isn't giving up.  That storyline was a bit crazy!

My favorite parts of the book involved Ben, the reporter who helped Jessie find out what happened to her sister in the first book.  Ben is starting to have memory flashes of his life before the accident, and they are...disturbing.  He hires Jessie to really dig into his past, and I think he and Jessie should both be fearful of what she finds. Ben's story will continue into the next book.  I'm not sure how I feel about him, is he a good guy or not?

There was again not much of Colin, Jessie's sort-of boyfriend, I hope he gets a little more page time in the next book.  Can't wait for the next installment!

This was the only Kindle First pick that I was even mildly interested in, and I probably should have skipped it this month, but I clearly have trouble turning down a free book.

The book alternates chapters about three characters:  FBI agent Clarke (who has more chapters than the other two), kidnapping victim Bess, and the killer's childhood foster sister, Adelaide.  Honestly, I skimmed through a lot of Clarke's chapters.  She was unprofessional, unlikable and pretty stupid, especially at the end.  When everyone was telling her that it wasn't her fault, I was screaming YES IT WAS!  She just had way too many mental issues to be a competent FBI agent.  Truthfully, this book makes the whole FBI look incompetent.

The only thing that kept me reading were the Bess/Adelaide chapters.  Bess was pretty tough and she kept trying to be resourceful enough to improve her situation.  Adelaide's chapters gave insight to Simon, and what shaped him into the monster he became.  I suspected almost immediately what the connection was between Clarke and Adelaide, but I kept hoping I was wrong because it made the whole story totally unbelievable.  I wasn't wrong, and that whole reveal was one giant eye roll.

I borrowed this from the library, and I think I'll probably read more in the series, but I don't know if I'm up for 40+ books with these characters.

For a book that was written 20 years ago, there are plenty of timely themes here, particularly gun control and "family values".  I didn't love the whole set in the future thing, but it wasn't as distracting as I thought.

I was kind of torn about Roarke (who most reviewers seem to fawn over), he's a bit too heavy handed for me.  We will be having sex, whether you think you want to or not, comes across as creepy at best, rapey at worst.  And the fact that Eve (a smart, capable cop) turns to mush a lot when he's around made me roll my eyes more than once.  They do have some good moments, so it wasn't all bad.

My favorite quote from the book is this one:  Roarke clucked his tongue.  "All those women deciding for themselves if and when they want to conceive, how many children they want.  Whats the world coming to?  Obviously, someone has to bring them back to their senses."

I've read books from this author before, but they were all better than this one.  Honestly, I was bored.

Philip seems like he has a stick up his a** for almost the entire book, and Lucy is holding a (14 year old!!!!) grudge against him for something so stupid.  These people are 37 and 31 years old and yet they were acting like immature teens half the time.

The archeology/ghost hunting stuff had potential to be interesting, but it was a very minor subplot.

I borrowed this ebook from the library.

I liked this book, but I didn't love it like I do so many of King's books.  More than anything else, this is a nostalgic coming of age story.  Dev, in the present a man in his 60's, is looking back to his 21 year old self in the early 70's.  It's a little bit of a crime story and a little bit of a ghost story, but mostly it's just about Dev, his broken heart, and his summer amusement park job.

It's pretty short for a Stephen King book, and while it was an enjoyable read, it just doesn't pack the same kind of punch as some of his other books.  Still, a lesser Stephen King book is a lot better than most.

This was a good, albeit sad, YA book.  I liked the fact that most of the teenagers in the book were pretty normal.  No manwhores, no painfully awkward yet gorgeous girls, no excessively beautiful people who strike everyone around them mute by their beauty.  They seemed pretty relatable.

I liked that Harper had a shaky relationship with her dad, but was willing to work on it, and her dad was a major presence in her life.  She struggled with how to help Seth, but no matter what was always trying to help.

Seth was pretty frosty at first, but his attitude was pretty understandable.  Even though surrounded with people who cared about him, his feelings of helplessness felt believable.

This is the first book of two, so hopefully the questions I still have will be answered.

This is one of the better Kindle First picks I've read.  Make no mistake, there's no one to root for in this story.  It's dark and disturbing and I grew to hate almost every character in the book!  But, I found myself not wanting to put it down.

Laura is an absolute psychopath.  She works at a suicide hotline type place, and actively hopes that she'll get the call where she can persuade them to choose death.  The first part of the book is from Laura's POV, then it switches to Ryan's POV, whose wife Laura "nudged along".  And at first I was on Ryan's side, but as he and Laura got deeper in their cat-and-mouse thing, Ryan started becoming what he hated Laura for, and I found my sympathy for him withering away.

This book requires some suspension of belief (how on earth does Laura get away with so much?), but I was engrossed enough to overlook it.

The ending made me both elated and sad, elated that perhaps Laura will get what's coming to her, but sad that there's another psychopath in the making.

This is another book in the series that's pretty high on the gruesome scale, but it was really good anyway.

The book goes back and forth between present day and the mid 1970's, when Amanda and Evelyn are partnered on a case.  It was really strange to see steely Amanda acting so meek.  A case of missing girls that no one else seemed to care about jumpstarted Amanda and Evelyn's careers.  The sexism and racism is jaw dropping.  It shouldn't be that surprising, but it is.

Will's past is pretty much uncovered and it's even bleaker than I thought it would be.  But I'm glad he finally got some answers and some closure.  Not sure what to think about the bombshell Angie dropped at the end.  Hopefully, that whole situation gets addressed soon.

This book is divided into three parts.  Reading the first part, I thought this was going to be a five star book, I was glued to the page.  The POV was that of Jess, an almost 15 year old.  Nothing good happens to her or her two sisters, it goes from bad to worse.  Very disturbing, but I couldn't put it down.

Part two fasts forward 18 years and there's another teenage POV, Skylar.  Ugh.  Skylar is at best annoying and at worst TSTL, and I rolled my eyes through the entire second part.  She was the worst!

The third part goes back and forth between POV (Skylar and Jess).  It's more tense, but it's too much deja vu to be believable.

It's not a bad book, but for it to start so captivating and then fall into meh-ness was disappointing.

There was way too much of the secondary characters in this book, and I didn't particularly like any of them.  Nix and Scotland's story was fine, but too rushed and I was left with unanswered questions.

There was a lot of focus on Nix's Nana, who was described as an elderly lady with dementia.  But then we find out she was born in 1950, so that didn't make any sense.  I know I'm not the only reviewer who pointed that out, but things like that bug me and take me out of the story.

Clutch and Dray are Nix's BFF's and I didn't think they added much to the story.  Clutch was obsessed with a 17 year old high school senior (someone call "To Catch a Predator") and thus came across as a creeper.  Dray was mostly violent and immature.  What Cassie saw in him was beyond me.

I've read a few other books from Ms. Oliver, and liked them all better than this one.

I'm going to miss Monica and Jonathan, they've really entertained me over the course of this series.

I don't read tons of BDSM books, but I've read some, and this one (the entire series really) stands out among them.  In every other book I've read, the woman is suffering from some sort of trauma, or has some sort of dark twisted past.  The man always seems to steamroller her into everything, even when she voices concerns, because "he knows what she needs".  Usually it makes me angry, makes me roll my eyes, or grosses me out.  It doesn't happen that way in this series.  Monica is strong and smart and knows what she needs from Jonathan.  I, personally, may not "get it", but there is never a sense that Jonathan is pushing Monica in any direction she doesn't want to go.  They definitely compliment each other.

This book was less sad than "Sing", but there were moments of melancholy.  With a ten-year expiration date on Jonathan's heart, both he and Monica are wary of making life decisions.  Monica's career?  Pregnancy?  Fortunately, they handled everything together, like (mostly) rational adults.

I liked that everything ended on a hopeful note, but it wasn't completely unicorns and rainbows.  A very fitting end to the series.

I don't read much YA, but I loved her book "Attachments" and this was available at the library, so I took a chance.  I went in pretty much blind, and the story was a little darker than I expected, but that probably made me like it more.

Poor Eleanor, she is failed by her parents at every turn.  Her dad's a loser, her mom's been beaten down by life, her stepdad is a total creep.  Park is the one bright spot in her life.  As for Park, his life isn't as dismal as Eleanor's (in fact, his parents are pretty awesome), but he finally finds in her a kindred spirit.

Some of the reviews I read after the fact complain about the (non) ending, but that made me appreciate it more.  It's hard for me to believe in HEA endings in YA books.  I would love to read about these characters again, even if they're not together, just to see where they ended up in life.

I liked the concept of this book, it's different from anything else I've read.  Lisa was an interesting character:  brilliant, methodical, nearly emotionless.  She's 16, pregnant, just been kidnapped, but instead of freaking out she begins plotting revenge.  And some fairly brutal revenge that turns out to be.  It was pretty awesome watching her take that revenge, even decades later.

The bones of a really great story were all there, but it gets weighed down at times with tedious detail and occasional ramblings that made me want to scream, "Get back to the story!".  Lisa's POV chapters are interspersed with Roger's, an FBI agent assigned to find kidnapping victims.  With the exception to Roger's story about his brother, I didn't find his chapters all that illuminating.

The first 75% of this book was really strong, easily a 4-5 star book.  There's a lot going on, 10% in and there had already been sexual assault and murder.  Four inexperienced hikers with a "mountain-man" stalker on their trail made for some suspenseful reading.  The details of the hikers dealing with injuries, dehydration, hunger (and lack of cell phones, which was incredibly stupid) were riveting to me.  Almost every choice they made seemed reasonable at the time, but didn't always work out positively.

The reason I'm only giving this three stars is that I felt let down by the last 25% of the book.  Here's why:

1)  It dragged on just a bit too long, it lost the desperation.

2)  The "God will take care of everything" comments.  I rolled my eyes every time.

3)  The farcical "romance".  Sure he's a serial murderer and rapist, but he's not a bad guy!  Ugh.

4)  The end.  Way too abrupt (and more of the "God took care of everything" crap).  Could have left out some of the filler in the last 25% to expand on the "after" part.

After reading books 1,3 and 4 in this series, book 2 finally became available at the library.  I was especially curious about this book because after reading books 3 and 4, I wanted some answers about Angie.  But I really don't feel like any light got shed on that subject.  Maybe further down the line.

I have to say Karin Slaughter writes great prologues.  Every single prologue in this series has sucked me right in.  This one, especially when combined with the heartbreaking epilogue, is one of her best.

Will came across much more forcefully than I expected in this book.  He's much more...tepid? in books 3 and 4, and I liked him better here, I think.  He seemed more focused and in control.  There are more main characters to focus on in books 3/4, so maybe that's it.

As with the other books in the series, the pace is pretty frantic and I find myself not wanting to put it down.  This one isn't quite so gruesome compared to some of the other books, but that might be because there isn't a POV from the victim.

This series has quickly become an obsession, I'm not sure what I'll do with myself once I've read all the books.

This was an easy, quick read.

Eden takes a summer job as a companion to a depressed Finley (daughter to a rock god) and falls for her brother.  Eden quickly becomes BFFs with Finley and falls in love with Jude.  It was too much, too fast for me.  It would have made it a little more believable if things had slowed down some.  Jude was a little too hot-and-cold to believe she'd fall that quickly.

And I actually wanted to see more of Eden's independent side when she took the waitressing job.  I liked how she made the best of her situation and didn't wallow in pity.

I truly hated the last chapter, the fight was just silly and overly dramatic.  That could have been cut out all together.  I feel like there were some loose ends that could have been tied up a little better, and would have liked an epilogue.

These books keep getting better and more intense.  I can't wait for the final one (especially after that cliffhanger).

I was starting to really not like Jonathan at the beginning of the book.  He reminded me of Jesse in the This Man series (a character that I completely loathed), constantly using sex to keep Monica from learning more about him.  But he seemed to pull his head out of his butt by the end, opening up to Monica and letting her come to her own conclusions about him.  Monica is one tough chick, I just love her!

We get to learn a bit more about Jonathan's family in this one, and I hope we see more of them in the last book.  His sister/lawyer is awesome and I am intrigued by his father.

Can't wait until October!
I bought this for the occasional frozen pizza.  The crust always gets too dark before the middle is cooked thoroughly.  This solved the problem, and fit perfectly around the pizza.

users.query: If you're like me and just can't get enough of Edgar Allan Poe, then this volume is for you. All the classic tales are here, and they never, ever get old or stale. The writing alone is so gorgeous, it keeps you going and going.

cands.text: This is till one of the greatest and most eerie of all tales ever told--by Poe or anyone else. The opening line alone is worth the price of admission. Only Poe could write so formalistically and with such style.
I just couldn't get into the thrust of these stories and frankly could not understand the hype and raucously fine reviews this volume received from various reviewers. I was truly disappointed.

The great classic is still great after all these years. I read (and had read to me as a child) Pinocchio, and it's still magical, even as an adult. Well worth re-reading all these years later. My only regret is that the Kindle version doesn't have the wonderful full-color pictures that were part of the original volume.

After having read "A Tear in Time" and "Prisoner of Time" I was intrigued by Christopher Petersen's ability to take me to another time and place through his fiction. I just finished "The Tomb of Atlantis" and must say it was an odyssey through time and history that had me mesmerized. I enjoyed every page, and kept wondering what would happen next. No spoilers, so I won't talk about the plot, but you will be handsomely rewarded by reading this novel written by a talented writer. Kudos to Mr. Petersen.

I love novels that take me to places I've been, so I can relate easily to the scenery and the events. Cathi Stoler's "The Hard Way" does just that, and took me on an intriguing tour of New York and Las Vegas, filled with mystery and suspense. I finished this book in three sittings and enjoyed it immensely. Five well-deserved stars for a fine writer.

Mark Rubinstein

When Jon Land writes a novel it tends to be epic in proportion. He loves writing fiction about heroes/heroines who are on a quest. Often, his novels take on a mythic quality. Black Scorpion is no exception. If you want to read a book that has intriguing descriptions, a compelling narrative, and is deeply imagined, then this is the novel for you. And there's another quality about Jon Land's writing, one that suffuses all his books: he writes the best action-packed scenes on the planet. The absolute best. So, sit back, open the book (or turn on your Kindle) and get set for an epic-level ride through history and modernity, and you will come away from this novel understanding the price a true hero must pay in his quest to save civilization and in the process, come to terms with himself.

Mark Rubinstein

David Mamet is one of our most acclaimed writers. "3 War Stories" are connected by virtue of being related to wars. The striking thing about them is the language. Mamet is virtually a ventriloquist when it comes to narration and dialogue. The first novella, "Redwing," is the longest. It's a seafaring tale told in the style of Patrick O'Brian with a formalistic, English approach that sets it clearly in the 19th Century. "The second, Notes on Plain Warfare," is a disquisition on religion as told by a narrator involved in the American-Indian wars. The third, "The Handle and the Hold" is pure Mamet--dialogue driven with no real descriptive narration--between two Jewish tough guys smuggling arms into Palestine  just before the Israeli War of Independence. This one snaps, crackles and pops with Mamet-speak. On the whole, the three novellas demonstrate David Mamet's wide range of interests and his enormous talent. A solid five-star rating fromsomeone who enjoys the written word.

Mark Rubinstein
Author, Mad Dog House and Love Gone Mad

Before reading Christopher Petersen's novel, A Tear In Time, I stayed away from paranormal and sci-fi novels. But Mr. Petersen changed that.  He changed it because, for me, storytelling is everything. And he sure knows how to tell a richly conceived and gripping story. I've enjoyed every one of his books, and this one even more than the rest. This is a wonderful novel I finished in two sittings. Deeply imagined and a pleasure to sink my teeth into and get lost in. Five well-deserved stars. I look forward to more coming from this writer and will read everything he produces.

Mark Rubinstein

I'm a big John Rain fan and anticipated this novel with relish. I was not disappointed. I particularly enjoyed seeing the young John Rain; and it was great to see his development into what he became in later times (as explicated in earlier books). Character development and evolution are important to me, and Barry Eisler gave me exactly what I wanted and felt was important. Most crucial though is simply that  that the novel was suspenseful, multi-layered (complex) and dealt with the many issues the author enjoys touching upon: corruption; politics; sexual attraction; Japanese society; judo; violence; good food; coffee; booze; restaurants; and the descriptions of Tokyo and environs. But most of all, it was a great read.  Five well-deserved stars!

Mark Rubinstein
Author of Mad Dog House, Love Gone Mad & The Foot Soldier

Disjointed to the point of incoherence. I couldn't tolerate this novel. Lacking any discernible plot, it dragged on and on with myriad "characters" injected here and there, jumping from one time frame to another, with strangely capitalized words and others that were fused--as though they were typos, but they weren't; they were part of the author's pretentious "style." As for winning the Booker Prize; it seems to me that bloated prose in a "lyrical" and "literary" style outweighs coherent storytelling, characterization or paced plotting.

Philip Roth is one of our most prolific authors. I read this memoir only a few weeks before Mr. Roth announced his retirement. It's a poignant and compelling read using the author's formidable storytelling talents to depict his father's decline and death some years ago. It brought me close to tears on a few occasions and certainly cast Mr. Roth in a most human and compassionate light. The prose is impeccable, and I was profoundly affected by Mr. Roth's devotion to his father during his father's declining years and months. Anyone who has lost a parent can relate to the cocktail of feelings Mr. Roth so beautifully describes in this artistically told memoir. A well-deserved five stars.

Mark Rubinstein
Author, "Mad Dog House" and "Love Gone Mad"

This is the best "literary" suspense/crime novel written in the last many years. A real study in character, setting, and suspense. Bound to be considered a classic.

Mark Rubinstein

Many of Hemingway's earliest short stories are in this volume. Some are little more than a few pages and seem only anecdotal, while others are more full-bodied and robust. We see the early iteration of Nick Adams here. One story beautifully shows a war veteran with what today would be labeled PTSD. All in all, early Hemingway when he was gaining his sea legs.

Mark Rubinstein

I'm absolutely thrilled that the Coyote books are now a boxed set. Even though each one stands alone on its own, it's great to have them together in a boxed set. They're wonderful novels. I know...I've read every one of them.
Sean Chercover writes another fine novel with his use of the first person to put the reader right into the protagonist's thoughts and feelings. A solid read.

This is one of the most beautifully-written novels I've ever read and one of the very few I've re-read. In the 20 or so years since I first read it, the novel hasn't lost its luminous quality. Yes, some of the references, of course, seem a bit dated, but the deeper elements of the human condition remain as relevant and piercing as ever. One of the great novels of our time along with Roth's American Pastoral and Styron's Sophie's Choice.

Mark Rubinstein
Author of Mad Dog House and Love Gone Mad

Christopher David Petersen has never disappointed me. I've read every book he's written, from "A Tear in Time" through the entire Atlantis series. I just finished Volume 5, "Atlantis: The Sacred Orb." The author has a gift for taking the reader back and forth through time (this time, to ancient Greece, and back) and does so seamlessly. Reading his novels is like stepping into the magic of the rabbit hole. I get totally lost in them, completely forgetting I'm immersed in a fantasy world that doesn't exist. This is the sign of a gifted storyteller--one who can take you from your own time and place and transport to you an entirely different realm. Five well-deserved stars!

Mark Rubinstein
Author of Mad Dog Justice

Having read The Blue Coyote Motel, I had high expectations of Coyote in Provence. I wasn't disappointed. This is a finely-crafted and deeply imagined novel that not only held my interest, but I consumed it in two sittings. Other reviewers have synopsized the plot so I won't do that. Let me just say that Diane Harman knows how to write a compelling tale with characters about whom you care and with plot twists that will cause your stomach to clench. A well-deserved five-stars to a book from a writer who I know will keep them coming. I look forward to reading the next one...and the one after that.

Mark Rubinstein
Author of Mad Dog House and Love Gone Mad

Another Harlan Coben novel in which a person is missing and cannot be tracked down. I've always said Harlan Coben should be crowned "King of the Missing Persons" novels. Fine storytelling from a first person perspective. Very engaging, in typical Coben fashion. Enjoyed it greatly.

This is a wonderfully funny, sly and mysterious novel about friends, the nature of friendship and about how tenuous it all can be. It's much more than a "mystery" and I loved every word of it. The dialogue was spot on and the characters were people I cared about. Rosemary Harris has a great way of telling a story with a wonderful narrative arc that captured me from the very first paragraph. Five well-deserved stars for this diabolically clever novel.

"Murder at the Polo Club" is one of a number of books by Dianne Harman I've read. While I'm not ordinarily a fan of cozy mysteries, Ms. Harman's novels force me out of my comfort zone. Her books are well-written and like the best mysteries, are elaborate puzzles in need of solving. Pia Marshall sneaks behind the barn to grab a quick smoke. By the end of page 3, she's been murdered by someone who's placed a chloroform-filled gauze pad over her mouth and nose. The tension escalates and a number of suspects emerge. What do a pottery collection, a glass collection, an ex-husband who's a felon, a Mafioso lover, and a jealous friend all have in common? They figure into the mystery of who murdered Pia and why she was killed. As I said, a good mystery is a beguiling puzzle, and "Murder at the Polo Club" fills all the requirements of a top-notch puzzle. And Dianne Harman is a top-notch puzzle-master. Five well-deserved stars for yet another riveting read.

"Beat the Reaper" is the first novel written by a physician and fine writer. I won't go into the plot since it's been covered in other reviews. I'll simply say the novel has dialogue that snaps and crackles, and the author has a unique character in Dr. Brnwa, a former hit man for the mob and now a physician. The author provides loads of insight into hospital life and brings various medical issues into the novel in ways that fit and make the novel a rich read. Well done. Kudos. An exciting read that gets a well-deserved five stars!

Mark Rubinstein

After having read Daytona Dead by Karen Vaughan, I knew she had a sense of humor. But this was decidedly different from that novel. Dead Comic Standing was a delightful, five-star read. It was easy to slip into this novel about someone prowling the comedy clubs of Edmonton, killing comedians after they've performed their stand-up routines. Part of the enjoyment for me was reading the comedy elements. I also felt I got an inside view of the way comedy clubs are run. Part police procedural, part whodunit and part thriller, I breezed through this enjoyable novel. It was great fun. I truly enjoyed the killer's motive for doing what he did; it was unusual and humorous in an absurdist way. A wonderful way to spend some time.

Mark Rubinstein

Success has spoiled Stuart Woods. I read a few of his earlier Stone Barrington novels and they had some depth and told decent stories. In Paris Match, Stone Barrington lacks depth to an extraordinary degree. He's shallow, and there's not a scintilla of emotional depth or intellectual heft to the character. The novel's plot is quite boring and it's evident that Mr. Woods doesn't really care much anymore about his writing, or his readers. He seems to have very little respect for his readers. Mr. Woods bangs out four novels a year, and it's evident that this prodigious output occurs at quite a cost; that cost being a lack of good storytelling, a shallow protagonist about whom the reader cannot care or invest energy in, and the most prosaic writing  I've read in a long time. Ninety percent (or more) of the novel is written in pedestrian dialogue. The novel was a waste of time and Mr. Woods should retire to go sailing or fly his private jet. I feel generous in giving this effort even one star.

The grass seed arrived on time and was very clean, pure Zoysia. We prepared a 1,000 SF seed bed, buried a Railbird popup sprinkler system around the perimeter, broadcast a good fertilizer, broadcast the seed and then raked it in about an inch deep. One week later we have a good stand of one inch tall new Zoysia grass. We have the sprinkler system watering every six hours and that seems to work since we're also in a rainy period on the Big Island - Kona side, where we live. It is a small lawn in front of our bamboo home next to a koi pond and small Japanese garden. It should look great when it grows and thickens and will provide a green carpet of short grass for eating outside with a view of Kealakekua Bay and South Point. I will mow with a reel-type mower to keep the grass short. It seems to be the right solution in our situation for a small grass lawn.

I have both the 46" 650 and the 52" 650 sitting side by side and can make some comparisons.  The difference is far less than I originally thought and fixable. The 46" had what I thought was perfect color out of the box but now I think it might be a bit green in the White Balance G-Gain.

I found the 52" color on flesh tones and other things like carrots can be too magenta or green but there is something you can do about it.  The fix is NOT to adjust the Flesh Tones or the Colors Space but instead to adjust the White Balance.  The settings that I found to be the best are the R-Offset 24, R-Gain 23, B-Gain 23, G-Gain 26 (all the rest being default 25).  This took a lot of effort because I was originally adjusting Flesh Tones, Tint, and Color Space until I stumbled onto the idea that just the White Balance was the culprit. I guess it makes sense.  The white balance is the canvas all colors are painted on so it will change them all.  It could also be that the tv is new and the back light bulb hasn't had sufficient burn in time to produce it's expected kelvin color yet?

After making the minor color adjustments on the 52" I will be keeping it over the smaller 46".

One good difference between the two is the 46" needs to be set to a back  light of 7 (143 watts) to equal the 52" in brightness set to just 4 (166).  This makes the power difference of just 23 watts which I thinks is pretty good for the size difference.
