The book was published a few years back and I was curious to know what has happened to her.  SPOILER ALERT:  Things have not gone well for Nujood, now 15. The London Guardian reported on March 13, 2013, that the father and uncles have squandered the money received from the book.  Her father has acquired two new wives and now has 14 children. The publishers also bought the family a large house, but the father rented out the first floor to another family, moved a new wife into the second floor, and kicked Nujood out.  Nujood now lives with a brother.  It's unclear from the article whether she is in school. But perhaps saddest of all, the father has signed a contract to sell the younger daughter, Haifa, to a man twice her age.

Interesting book about a topic I knew little about: the interactions between the Japanese and Koreans living in Japan. Although a long book, it never seemed bloated with detail or unnecessary plot complications. Have tissues handy as parts are tearjerkers, but overall a testament to fortitude in the face of their life challenges.

This book provides just the right amount of historical background and context for the casual reader, like me, as we try to understand the problems in the region, without getting overwhelmed by detail.  Adding his personal story to the mix kept my interest level up.  If you're not a Middle East expert, and don't want to be, this is a fascinating read, well told.

I've traveled for years with Rick Steve's books and find them the most helpful out there.  This is the first time I've used a Kindle version of his guidebooks. Do yourself a huge favor and get the paperback, not the Kindle version.

As others have pointed out, it is frustrating and/or impossible to find information in the Kindle version.  Not only is there no index, but the Table of Contents is so "bare" as to be next to useless. The few internal links provided are to sidebars explaining something other than what you are probably looking for.  Sure you can search for things, but your search must be so generalized that you'll get pages of results and a difficult time figuring out which one is applicable. Your only real option for finding information in the guide is to flip through page after page until you stumble across it -- a painfully slow process on the Kindle.

In a nutshell, until they vastly improve the indexing features, stick to the hard copy-- where it is easy to find a nearby park or cafe to use your Kindle for reading a good novel. I love my Kindle, but it just isn't designed for reference works.
As others noted, too many syntax errors and basic grammar fails. Interesting way to present the story but ultimately the presentation was lackluster.

I agree with other reviewers that this is a wonderful book. But if typos drive you crazy like they do me, buy a print edition, not the Kindle version. It's apparent that the written text went through an OCR process to put it into electronic format, but no one bothered to proofread for common OCR typos, or even run spell check which would have caught many of these problems.  Some sections are fine, but others are ridiculous.  Exclamation points are turned into l's (oh myl), words are divided by periods (my good. ness), and other words are turned to mish-mash ("had afFrrmed-and he knew well" to quote an actual passage.) Don't get me started on the confused muddle of hyphens that should be dashes, and vice versa -- you get the idea. An error here or there can be expected, even in print editions, but this is beyond bad. If it was a free book, I'd get over it, but for $9.99 I expect a little effort in the production process.  Shame on the publisher of this e-edition.

Bought this for my home office that is carpeted with basic low pile carpet (the standard builder-grade stuff).  Works perfectly.  No problem with it slipping.  Had it for about a month without any signs of cracks or pits developing, unlike my last (really cheap) one that developed indentations where my chair wheels sat most of the time.  Can't say if it will hold up for the long haul, but it seems like it will continue to do the job. The price/quality ratio made sense for me, and I'm happy with the purchase.

Update:
At about the one-year mark, it started cracking.  I'm still using it, but will have to be replaced one of these days.
Good basic read on DNA tracing, but nothing much new here if you've read other Wells books or have watched the National Geographic programs on the Genome Project.

users.query: I've only had these for ten days but so far so good for fit and comfort. I bought half a size larger than normal as lately my toes have been pushing through all my shoes so I guess my feet have expanded. I was afraid I might be flopping around in them but not so. And my toes have plenty of room to spread out in the medium width. I only wear these for walking around town, not for running or on the trail. I like the colors. Only time will tell how well they hold up.

cands.text: These are really comfortable, sturdy shoes that I find myself wearing everywhere. The reason I'm giving them 4 instead of 5 stars is that it's been raining quite a bit and the soles are a tad slippery compared to my Asics Contend Gel 2. I can walk on the same surface in my 2s without any slipping at all whereas I have to be more careful wearing these. Having said that, these shoes are sturdier and give me the extra support I need.
I have this scarf in three colors (so far), pink, green and blue. I have a collection of scarves with patterns so the solid colors are very useful to wear with tops that already have a pattern.

This is a great product for the money. As I use them every day I need something very well made and sturdy, which these are. I only use stainless steel around food, not plastic, so these are perfect for me.
The perfect size for my needs. Seems to be pretty good quality, no complaints.

This black and white flowered scarf goes with everything so sometimes when I'm in a hurry I grab it as I don't have to worry if the colors match what I'm wearing. I wear a scarf even during the summer... This is lightweight so I don't overheat. And because it is scrunchy, I don't have to worry about wrinkles. It is what I consider a good "workhorse" scarf!

Vincent Van Gogh is pretty high on my top ten favorite artists list and who doesn't love his painting of irises? I feel very artistic when I wear this scarf. The fabric is described as being a heavier silk and that is true. It feels luxurious but it also makes the scarf a little bulky... but only compared to some of my other scarves made of thinner silk which are very lightweight. It depends on what your needs are. I wear scarves all year round for all occasions so sometimes I want a thinner fabric and sometimes thicker. I would not call this a winter scarf for a cold climate but for southern California it is just right for a cool evening. I've been wearing this for over six months. As with all my scarves, silk or otherwise, I soak them in warm water and iron very lightly.

I have been using these for nearly 5 months now and so far, so good. Last time I owned bamboo cutting boards I made the mistake of regularly putting them in the dishwasher and they fell apart after a year or so. So they must be hand washed only which is fine with me but they are easy to clean under the tap. Only time will tell so check back with me in another year

I can't tell you how many compliments I get on this stylish day pack. it's better than a purse. I fit all my camera equipment in here along with everything I need for a day out (including a hat). Two side pockets in which I carry water and an umbrella (if needed). I love the grey/green color. I'm happy!

I learned my lesson on a trip earlier this year when my older, non-TSA locks were cut on a domestic flight. A friend showed me her locks and how TSA can open them with a key. So I purchased these just for peace of mind. Not too much I can say about them except that if TSA wants to look in your bags, they will open your locks one way or another, so might as well have these.
UPDATE 07/01/2017: I am not changing my rating as I really don't know what happened but I now no longer use these locks, or any others, when I travel as there is no point. On my last trip my bags arrived without the locks! The only thing I can think is TSA either stole them, forgot to put them back on after opening, or didn't lock them securely. But as both locks went missing I can only guess. I mentioned this to other traveling friends who told me they no longer bother with using locks at all as nothing is secure. Don't pack anything you can't afford to lose. Make sure you have good travel insurance. That's the best you can do!
Always the best nature photos in this calendar. Whenever I see it on the wall I want to put on my hiking boots!

I originally bought this printer on the advice of a friend for printing out fine art photos in wide format. Unfortunately, I was very disappointed. The color range with only five cartridges just isn't there... my fault for not reading the reviews first. So I bought a Canon Pixma Pro 100 and I am very happy with that. I kept the iX6520 as I needed to print out non-photo images on different kinds of paper and card stock of various sizes. My old Epson printer stopped accepting anything except regular 8 1/2 x 11 copy paper. I can stack several sheets of cards in the printer and it happily prints away. I haven't tried wide format paper at this point because I haven't needed to. But it's nice to know the capability is there. The five color cartridges are very small so I don't know yet what the life span is. If I had bought this printer specifically for printing out posters, brochures, etc. I probably would have been ecstatic and rated it with five stars.
I am back to using the tried and true SanDisk memory cards after problems with another brand. The other brand started out fine but didn't last long. I never worry with SanDisk.
I use these all the time for freezing and re-heating. So far they seem to be as sturdy as the more expensive sets of Pyrex.
I use these all the time for freezing and re-heating. So far they seem to be as sturdy as the more expensive sets of Pyrex.
So many people have commented on these black cards. The black gives a whole new look to my photos.

There are so many opinions about what is healthy... in the end you have to pick what you feel is good for you and go with that. I found the book interesting. Some things I agree with, some things not. For me personally, I find I need good fats in my diet and very few simple carbs. If I stick to that, I am generally healthy.
I've been buying items for my Dickens Village for over ten years now. I am always delighted with the quality.
I printed out photos on this paper to make my Christmas cards. The color and detail was great. A good size for printing out photos.
I printed out photos on this paper to make my Christmas cards. The color and detail was great. A good size for printing out photos.
As a lifetime member of the Sierra Club I enjoy this calendar year after year.

Taking a class on the history of Islam and I found this book to be an invaluable and relatively easy read to cover all the gaps in the syllabus. I have a good understanding of the origins and later teachings and variations of the religion.

I'll keep it sweet and short. I didn't know too much (if anything) about the relationship of Hemingway and Gellhorn so this was an education. Gellhorn was an interesting character herself, competing in what at the time (and probably still is) a man's world of war correspondents. Kidman's portrayal is of a feisty woman who knows she is the equal of Hemingway and therein lies the attraction... and difficulty... for him. The film was also a lesson in what was going on in the world at that period of time. Might watch it again.

This headband arrived with what looked like a half-inch long ball point pen mark about one inch from the end. But as the mark sits behind my ear and is covered by hair I am not worried about it. The fabric is a little shinier than I would have liked but after all it is satin so what did I expect? It's a good width and stays in place even though there are no teeth. Also, it doesn't press on my head and give me a headache like some other bands I own. If you're looking for something blue, this is the ticket.

I don't like the idea of drinking hot water that has run through plastic parts. As I couldn't find a drip coffee maker made entirely of stainless steel I decided to settle for a percolator. At first I thought it was going to be a lot more work but now I have my system down it is easy. I started out using the same amount of water and coffee as I used in my drip machine but I have discovered it tastes better with just a little less coffee. I grind my beans every morning and now use three flat scoops of beans (33cc each or 2 1/4 tbsp) instead of heaped, to 24 oz (3 cups) water. I turn my gas stove to 4 for about seven minutes to boil the water, then turn down to just under 2 for five minutes. I leave the pot unopened for a couple of minutes to allow the water to completely drain through the basket. If I take the basket out immediately the coffee is still swimming around in water. Be sure to use an oven mitt when removing the top! I replaced the plastic knob with the Fitz-All Replacement Percolator Top, SMALL which is a perfect fit when installed as directed. I like that I can rinse everything under the tap or place in the dishwasher... no electrical parts to worry about.

users.query: First line drew me in. Good story overall. Ending seemed to set up a sequel.

cands.text: Excellent book with an ending that will keep me guessing for a  long time. Great style and overall an amazing story.
Story line held my interest but the backstory of the main character was a bit over played. Author writes well and could improve by having another editor take a crack at this book.
Story line held my interest but the backstory of the main character was a bit over played. Author writes well and could improve by having another editor take a crack at this book.

Very creative, well written and well formatted. The conversations between the main character and his wife were awful, annoying and utterly ridiculous, BUT they didn't take much away from the story. Ending was a slight let-down after an 80,000 word build up but, all in all I liked this book and may even read Rushed 2

I hate leaving bad reviews but this story was quite awful. Ended up skimming the last 20 pages in case something exciting or interesting happened.

The only good thing that happened was when the story was done.
Fantastic plot idea but the flatness of the characters made hr story very uninteresting. Needs some realism and life pumped into the dialogues.

First off, there are plenty of typos and errors in this story but not enough to distract or detract from the story itself.

The main characters are well developed and the authors ability to describe a scene and setting are powerfully honed.

I won't say this is the type of story I usually read but it certainly had enough of a grip to hold my scattered attention for the duration.

If the author had another editor take a look at the story and if he tightened up some loose story lines, it could earn five stars.

Like another reviewer stated it takes a while for this story to grab your interest. Once it does it doesn't let go. Characters are a bit lacking (I had no attachment to any of them) and the conversations were too manufacturerd. But the story itself was solid. At one point I really wondered if I needed to sleep with my lights on!

Book was fantastic at first but then lost its identity. I finished it only to satisfy my curiosity. Okay but could have been tremendous.
Same bad editing towards the end when a paralyzed man, who we are told cannot use one of his arms, is able to hold a gun in one hand and an object raised above his hand in the other.
Not good
Three books into the 7 (or 8) in the series and this one convinced me to keep reading. Excellent story.

Really liked the first book in this series but this one was tough to finish. Ended up skipping around 30 pages and wasn't lost when I started again.

Author is talented but this was just not his best effort.

Certainly a well written book and, if not for the slowness of the first 100 pages or so, it would have earned 5 stars, easily. The first half of the book creates great mystery and kept me wanting to read more, if for nothing else than to find out what "really" was going on in the story. The second half of the book is excellent. Faced paced and a true page turner.

This book has the traditional "false ending," but I wish the author ended it without adding the final bit of drama. It didn't add anything to the story and, in my opinion, was a bit of a waste.

As other reviewers pointed out, this is better than Mr Mercedes, which also was a solid book. I bought this on Audible and loved 99% of the story. Very good book with well developed characters. Ending was a bit predictable but excellent nonetheless. Looking forward to the third book in the series

Very few movies are as good as the book, and this movie is no exception. The characters are well played but the movie suffers the common "sequel" effect: It is not as good as the first Hunger Games movie
This was my first book from this author, but it won't be the last! Very engaging story and well written. Need to give my eyes a rest since I had some serious problems putting this book down!

Years ago, I used to read all of Koontz's novels, with Watchers being, by far, my favorite. But I stopped reading his books as it seemed like he was forcing stories. More precisely, his novels seemed to have "forced endings." Not the case with this book. The ending is long, detailed and finishes the story well.
What I really didn't like about this book is the interaction between the main characters. They were shallow and very unbelievable. Yes, this is a fiction book so doubt needs to be suspended, but not when it comes to characters and character interactions. Fiction or not, characters breathe life into a novel and these characters (except for the Chief of Police) had nothing in them but shallow sighs.

Bravo for telling a great story! Not sure what happened with the editing, but plenty of misplace periods. wrongly capitalized words and an assortment of erroneous punctuation marks that may have been the result of converting this to digital format.

I'm a bit conflicted with this review. For the most part, this short story was good. Very good, actually. The action was consistent and the plot was unique enough to stand out in a crowded genre. I'm not one to read "alien invasion" type stories, but the title and the tag line of this book caught my attention.

The things I didn't like about the short story were as follows:
1.) This is a sub 100 page story with no chapter breaks. There were a few logical places to stop reading but the story would have flowed much better had the author included chapters.
2.) This is written for those in the UK, meaning the language used and the references to areas/landmarks was completely lost on me. And I'm sure non UK readers would feel the same way.
3.) The main character thinks at one point in the story, why he is thinking about his father so much during the drama, but the author never picks up on the that possible storyline. Why bring it up if it's just left hanging there?
4.) There are several sentences that just don't flow well. Not sure if this is intended or missed by an editor, but it did cause me to be forced to re-read several sentences.

As I said, the alien invasion genre is crowded. However, this short novel (novella) presents a refreshing and very interesting twist to the genre. All in all, I give this four stars.

This was a bit of a challenge to get through. Certainly a long book that should have taken me a week to read took me nearly three.

I will read the rear of this series and believe they will be as good and hopefully a bit better than was this one.

I purchased this, the second in the Agenda 21 series due to my enjoyment of the first in the series. I quickly discovered that I had to re-read book one as this book demands an intimate understanding of book one.

The characters were a bit lifeless and predictable and the newly introduced characters were undeveloped.

I'm glad I read this but happier that I purchased it at a discounted price

I wish I could read this book again but since I couldn't finish it the first time, I highly doubt it will get another read. The content is excellent and the author's stories are applicable. The challenge is that the premise is based on an unrealistic idea that everyone can (and should) walk away to follow their dreams. As attractive as that concept is, I wonder how my wife and two kids would respond.

Probably a feel good book meant to inspire dreams.

Wished this book covered a lot more than just the proper use of commas. The content is well presented and (thankfully) well written. There are numerous examples that serve the reader well.

However, the reason it is not a 5 star book is that it doesn't cover enough topics. I get that there is a full version for purchase but, in my opinion, it would make more sense if this book provided an overview of several grammar topics rather than an in depth review of one

I could tell right away that this knife is well made and will be used for many years. It has a great weight and feel to it and the blade seems to be very well made. I've purchased a few other Gerber products: Some good and some not so good. This knife is a great value considering the price.
I haven't used it in a survival situation (thankfully) nor have I gave it a demanding test (yet). However, based on my initial thoughts and tests, this knife will be one of my go to knives when in the field

I always get a bit nervous when someone claims to be or is touted as being an "expert." But in Alison's case, the term is applicable and very well deserved.

Excellent book, well written and is a valuable resource for job hunters, regardless of the industry.

Case is well made and is well worth the price. The addition of the three back plates make this like having three cases in one. I'm not impressed with the color of the back plates, especially the gold and silver ones but, still, three cases in one.

Not sure about its durability as I just received it but the fit and build do suggest that a lot of attention was made in the manufacturing process

Great book for those who enjoy Paleo diets and need a healthy way to cool off during the warm summer months. I've tried several of these and while I can't say that I liked them all, many were very tast

users.query: Great bag and carrier! Absolutely love this set up! It has been through rain and snow and held up perfectly. I do use extra straps just for peace of mind but probably don't need them. Highly recommend.

cands.text: Bought this for my ezgo golf cart and I am very pleased with the purchase. I have a normal size roof and the rear flip seat. You can't have passengers in the back with this (and I knew that before buying) but it works perfectly for my application. It is well made and makes a huge difference in colder temperatures. Highly recommend.
Fanastic paired with a hitch haul carrier. Takes all the "wiggle" out of it and makes it rock solid. Highly recommend.
Great way to keep the four wheeler In a short bed pickup. Locked in place and was very secure. Highly recommend.
Really nice cover and a great price as well. Hard to beat. Really dresses up the spare. Highly recommend.
Very well made and a must have for any camper. Highly recommend.

Great addition to carts with the rear seat. I installed these on my club car ds and it worked perfectly. The only issue was that I need shock extenders if I wanted to use the factory rear shocks (which aren't really necessary with these springs).
Great replacement cover when your goes flying off while driving down the road. :-)
Very strong and well made zip ties. Time will tell on the UV effectiveness but these seem solid.
Fantastic weather proof cover for the blue sea systems toggle switch. Highly recommend!

Pretty good add on to any hunting cart. Like other reviewers have stated, it isn't rock solid. It concerned me at first but it has held up and it wasn't an issue other than me being worried about it breaking. So far so good and it is really nice to have a place to hold two guns. Used it with two shotguns and also two scopes rifles with no problems.
Great first aide kit! Has plenty of useful items and the case looks great and is waterfprrof. Highly recommend.
What a great addition to the boat! Love having this and highly recommend it.
Fanatic helmet and an unbelievable price. Fit great and looks awesome. Highly recommend.
Tires have been great. I have purchased 5 of these and they have held up great for over a year now with heavy use. Highly recommend.
Very comfortable and the perfect shoe to wear on the boat. Highly recommend.
What an amazing addition to the bog pod. I use this with my kids and it makes a world of difference. Highly recommend.
Great kit and exactly what I needed for my EZGO txt.
A very nice set. They don't stay in the holders as well as I would like but still a great set for the price.

The kit seems to be well made and makes a huge difference over the ugly stock look. Some directions could have saved me some time but I was able to figure it out on my own and this was my first time replacing something on a sport bike.
Exactly what I needed to keep the rear shocks on my club car ds after installing the HD rear springs.
Fantastic fit and finish and love how it feels on my hip. I highly recommend this holster with a good quality belt.
Installed this on my club car ds and what a difference it made. I highly recommend this inexpensive upgrade.
What a great device! Allows you to make any non Bluetooth device into one. Highly recommend.
Best speaker for the price and sound! This little dude is pretty impressive. Highly recommend.
Very nice 4-gauge wire and kit. Had everything I needed and was about half of the price at the local stores. Highly recommend.

users.query: Does what expected- holds a puck to keep it protected.

cands.text: Does what expected- holds a puck to keep it protected.

Awesome book for the hockey lover (or his/her offspring!) in the family. My son loves this book and now my daughter as well. Great introduction to some basic hockey greats and the alphabet as well! If there is a young hockey fan in the house, stop thinking and just add it to your cart!

My 3yo old had a blast playing with this. He didn't get the concept 100% but he would get really excited when he shot the balls up and they landed in different places. There is a small, plastic tab at the top of the part where the balls line up to be shot (I believe it's to keep the balls from rolling all over the place when you're not playing)- either way, it's supper small, plastic, and somewhat useless for my kids so I removed it- I try to keep small, ingestible items out of their hands while driving! Just something to note (and look for- I found it by chance when I was showing them how to play) if this will be played by younger children.
Perfect for the young hockey fan who is learning his/her numbers. My son loved this book (actually still does-he's 3.5yrs old).

I am new to the game of cribbage and my husband and I were using a pegging board app on the ipad- which got old quickly. This board is a great, simple board. I like that the scoring is continuous and that up to 3 players/teams can play instead of just 2. I also like the storage so we always have a deck of cards and a place to store the pegs. Some reviewers mentioned the magnet being too week to keep it closed- I do not find this to be the case- so far. My only complaint is that the markings on mine (start, finish, and scoring) are very faint in some areas- like they didn't get stamped on completely. This doesn't hinder usage at all as I didn't feel the markings were necessary- I almost just wish they weren't on there instead of being halfway there. Regardless, the board serves it's purpose and seems like it'll be one we can have around for years to come.

Gave this to my husband as a gift and I have never seen it again. Not sure if he's forgotten he has it or if he tried it once and didn't like it. My guess is the former- either way, it's a bummer because I thought it was a great gift.

One of my 2.5yr old daughter's favorite Christmas gifts. She measures everything now! It's easy for her (and my 14mo old) to pull out and carry around. They sometimes need help winding the tape back up. It's holding up great so far despite the contact pulling out and winding up. I'll update how it's holding up after we've had it longer.

My husband purchased this and was so happy with it. It holds its shape and because its got higher sides, it holds all the wood shavings and prevents a mess on my floor in front of the fireplace. Its easy to load and easy to carry.
This was a gift for my 5 yr old nephew. It was a big hit! I think it may be a bit advanced for him still, but that'll give him something to work on.
Locks and keys- not sure what else to say about it! They work well, easy to open.

Works great. My husband installed it in our garage underneath our can crusher so the cans and bottle caps fall into the same recycling bucket. Opens bottles with ease and is low profile/not tacky- I didn't want something that would draw attention to itself. However, it is nice enough to put where it'd be seen. My dad liked it when he came over so I gave the second one to him- he installed it as soon as he got home! It comes with everything needed to install both openers.

This is a beautiful journal. When it arrived I could t stop looking at the picture. It is well bound and the cover folds over to the back for when writing on the inside. The reason I deducted a star is because the top back of mine looks like it didn't get lined up correctly on the printer- the picture does not go all the way to the top. It was not a deal breaker since the picture on the front is so beautiful. I wish I had taken a picture of the back to better depict the flaw but I gave this as a gift (still gift worthy) and didn't think of taking the picture. Overall I am happy with the journal and would most likely buy it again.

Adorable onesie. Vibrant colors, soft to touch. Unfortunately the fit seems a little small (short) so it didn't last as long as I'd hope and I can't speak to how well it withstands multiple washings as we only got a few wears out of it. Overall a very cute onesie, I just wish I had gotten a size bigger.

I researched gliders until I was blue in the face. It's so hard to weed through the reviews and specifications and make that final decision. We went with this one for a few reasons- it got great reviews, with many reviewers remarking on the durability, it had two places for little feet so my tall 3.5yr old and shorter 2yr old can both be comfortable, it had coated chains, it's the same brand as the brackets we bought, and, of course, the price was right. Unfortunately, our problems started before we even hung it. My husband had a hard time getting it together and he could never get it completely straight. I didn't notice this until he hung it (he was hoping it would straighten up when he hung it). So he sat on one end and tried to swing to see if it went crooked while swinging- as soon as he picked his feet up the seat buckled underneath him (he is an average size- weighs maybe 165lbs). Needless to say this was quite frustrating and while we realized it wasn't meant for adults, so many reviewers mentioned it holding an adult and we've sat on a glider at another house that held us (separately) with no problem. I called Amazon and, as usual, their customer service representative was helpful and offered a full refund and free label to print to return the defective swing. It was a hassle to have to take the swing down and disassemble it, but when we spent that much money on a swing we were hoping for it to last. So we returned this swing and purchased  the back to back glider by creative playthings (also sold on Amazon) instead. Ultimately, this swing may have stood up to our young children swinging on it for years, but the thing that frustrated me most is the difficulty in getting a clear weight limit on the product in all of my research. Had the product clearly stated a weight limit, my husband wouldn't have sat on it, and all our trouble would've been avoided.

This was given as a gift, to Nana of course, so I don't have personal experience with it, but I have been told that she has used it daily since she got it and it is her favorite coffee mug. She hand washes every evening so it's ready for the next morning brew! Always nice to hear that a gift is so well loved!
We haven't quite tested its durability but I feel safe handing my iPad over to my 3yo son in the backseat when it's in this case. It's easy to slide the iPad into and doesn't interfere with use.
This was a present from my kids to their Papa. He wore it that day- looked great and fit as expected. He doesn't live near us so I can't speak to how it held up with washings.

My son loves this and it takes a beating (or a throwing onto hardwood floors)! He plays the games more than he uses the camera, but he's 4yrs old. My only complaint is the picture quality- most reviews I read when I bought it said it took great pictures, however I can barely get it to take a non-blurry picture. My kids all love it but if you want it for the pictures I think I'd look elsewhere.

This was given as a gift, to Papa of course, so I don't have personal experience with it, but I have been told that he has used it daily since he got it and it is his favorite coffee mug. He hand washes every evening so it's ready for the next morning brew! Always nice to hear that a gift is so well loved!

This is the second glider we purchased after the first one (from Eastern Jungle) crumpled under the weight of an average sized adult. I scoured reviews of gliders until I was cross-eyed and when I found this one, with great reviews and the lowest price I was so excited. Because of our previous experience I did call Creative Playthings before ordering to inquire about a weight limit since I could not find one online- I was told 160lbs (although I imagine this should be distributed throughout the swing, not all on one side/from one person). The glider arrived quickly and was easy to put together. My kids were so excited when we went to hang it on our swing set (the Kodiak from Swing N Slide). Only then did we discover that the chains were about 2 feet too short- I could barely get on it without being on my tiptoes. I went back to the product description and it did mention that it was for a 7ft swing bar- I admit that I didn't think much of this when I bought it because I assumed (big mistake) that most swing bars are a standard measurement. I called Creative Playthings again and customer service was very nice and offered to send chain extensions- unfortunately, they charged me for them, so I saved $20 buying this glider instead of the swing n slide glider and then had to pay $18 for chain extensions. With the extensions the glider works great, my kids (ages 2 and 3.5yrs) LOVE it and can get on/off and swing completely independently. Overall I'm happy with my purchase and it seems like it should last us for quite a while.

Not much to say about brackets- they are successfully holding our glider swing into the swing beam and I didn't hear too much moaning and groaning from my husband as he installed them. They are hefty brackets so I'm hopeful that means they will last us until our young children outgrow the set- I'll update if I have issues, but so far no issues after a couple of months.

Received these faster than expected. The bottom pot was cracked, but for the price, not worth returning. They are definitely small, but I'm using for a little girl's garden birthday party (planting herbs) so they are perfect for my use. They are pretty thin so I'll be anxious to see how they actually hold up- not sure I'd purchase them for home use, but for a fun party favor to grow a few herbs in they are colorful and perfect. The little tray is a definite plus!

My little one (9mos) loves this thing- as do her older siblings (2yo and 3yo). I followed other reviewers and put a little vinegar in when I filled it with water- it's been filled for two months now and no signs of cloudiness or mildew. The items are like vinyl clings so they do stick to each other, but with some work you can separate them out- or realize it does t really. After that much, I think she likes squishing the water around more than trying to go after the individual items inside. I took it to the beach with us and it was perfect because I emptied it for travel/packing, filled it while there, and then emptied it for trip home. And she could play with it in the sand and the outside wiped clean. Great toy, especially for the low price I paid.

I needed a box for 4x6 index cards and had no idea it'd be so hard to find. This fit the bill, although I didn't need one quite so rugged! My only complain is I wish it had a handle on top- I may be the only person who doesn't just keep it on a desk, I actually travel with mine as I use it to hold contact cards for my home based business. So it goes with me to many places. A handle would be nice. I don't use the lock so I can't speak to its durability or usefulness.

We love Robert McCloskey's stories and this is the perfect compilation of stories my husband remembered reading as a kid. My only concern is which of my three children to pass it down to when they start having kids!

users.query:
This book proves why the term "bestseller" should not be equated with the term "greatness." Bestseller just means that many people have heard about a book and decided to go take the chance and buy it.
If you take this book at pure fictional value, then it is a decent suspense. But, it hardly deserves the accolades and the attention it is getting. Controversial? Yes.
A masterfully crafted work of art? No. There are many "movie" type action sequences and convenient escapes by our protagonists; it becomes a bit cliched to the reader after a certain point.
 This, for the most part, was a slow read that was tough to get through because of its lack of depth. The only deep part of the book is the seemingly endless "facts" that are discussed about Da Vinci, the church, the Holy Grail and this  amazing code that has seemingly no end to it. The characters are constantly trying to solve the code, but the process of bringing these facts to play is absurd.  And these "facts" are really not real facts (only facts for the sake of the book).
Much of the dialogue, combined with stereotyped good guy/ bad guy situations,  make for a mediocre story. The protagonists manage to just get by the bumbling police, who manage to blow several key opportunities to get them. It would not have been surprising to hear the police captain scream "Don't blow this case" to a lowly, but eager rookie officer who wanted in on the chance to nab our heroes.  The characters are either evil and corrupt, or good and benevolent; it is as simple as black and white.
If there is an aspect that should be applauded it is Brown's ability to take many aspects of history (as factious as they are) and attempt to intertwine them into the plot of a story.  But, these attempts fail because they beg too many convenient coincidences, and the authenticity of the characters is seriously lacking as a result.
This book will probably end up being some major motion picture in a few years, with big stars and a big budget.
As far as being a unique work of fiction, this fails.

cands.text:
If there is one thing that is almost as good as a great book, it is a book about a great book or, in this case, great books. For those who love the classics, this is a fantastic and accessible resource.

This book is quite a handy source for anyone who is taking a literature course in college or handling the classics in high school English. While not a substitute for the actual reading of the classic, this book provides a great overview of many important novels and keys in on literary aspects within the novels. There are a wide range of classics included within the volume. Here are a few examples:  Aeneid, The Odyssey, Hamlet, Doctor Faustus, Crime and Punishment, Jane Eyre, Great Expectations, The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, Animal Farm, The Sun Also Rises, The Joy Luck Club, Death of a Salesman, The Bluest Eye. The novels and plays encompass many different eras and types.

For each work discussed, there are various points discussed and evaluated. Background information about the work is given, which is followed by a general summary for various sections of the book, where plot details are given. This is followed by a listing of key characters, with an explanation of their significance or role in the story. Themes central to the work are discussed, symbols are presented, and the author's style is chronicled. Finally, the book's context is put into perspective in a brief critical overview.

The book's structure makes for an easy source to pick up and reference. A struggling student could use this book as they read one of the classics, referring to it often after reading sections or chapters. While this guide does some thinking for the reader by presenting key ideas and concepts, a reader could use this knowledge to gain a better appreciation for reading a classic, and perhaps look for various plot devices, symbols, and themes on their own as they read another book. So, in this sense, it is not only a resource to help students understand a classic, but maybe a stepping stone for "thinking" about a book while reading.

Overrated, and overlong. I guess I should have know I wouldn't like this film since I didn't like the book either. I guess the film is better than the book in my estimation, mainly because we do not have to hear every single obnoxious blog entry from the main character. (Not sure why all the hype for either film or book, though, as they are both underwhelming.) This film is sort of standard Hollywood stuff: non-engaging, predictable, and weak dialogue, people going through motions. When you really could care less about a main character, then it really sort of kills the experience. It is one of those cases where the premise-- a man being stranded on Mars and having to figure out how to survive-- is so much better than the actual experience of the film. Very mediocre film, hard to believe it was one of the nominees for Best Picture. Was 2015 that watered down?

Personally, I'm a little befuddled with all the negative criticisms this movie has received. Although the movie lacks the appeal of a truly classic thriller, the cast is adequate and the premise, which is a commentary on the idea of possible corruption of the jury selection process and the ills of access to firearms, is truly what makes the film effective as a courtroom drama.

When a woman's husband is killed in a random office shooting, she sues the gun manufacturers and takes them to court. Dustin Hoffman does an excellent job in the role of the prosecuting lawyer who takes the case for this woman. He butts heads with Gene Hackman's character, and there is a gripping and poignant moment in which Hoffman delivers a great closing argument to the jury. Hackman, as usual, plays a scumbag who wants to pick the ultimate jury that will turn the case in the defense's favor. Hidden in a secret building, Hackman's team operates a system of tracking and following potential jurors using cameras and technology, playing a type of Big Brother of the jury system.

One of the "wildcard", or unpredictable jurors, is the one played by John Cusack. We follow the jury selection and case as it progresses, and there are a few more sneaky moves by Hackman's team to try to intimidate the other side. It gets a bit more complex when a woman who is working on the inside of the case comes into the picture.

The film really gets into the jury process and the corruption of this procedure, as well as the liability for manufacturers when disasters or tragedies strike. There is enough mystery in the film to keep the suspense going, and overall I felt that this was one of the best Grisham books made into a movie.

There is so much to say about this book. I recommend it so highly if you enjoy anything in the realm of psychological thrillers or mysteries that take place in a historical context. There is probably an element that any thriller/crime/mystery fan could take away from reading this book and enjoy. The book has a bit of a Sherlock Holmes-ian feel to it, and takes place in New York in the late 1800s with the origins of psychology beginning to take shape.

I think what makes this book quite amazing is that there is so much going on, both in terms of themes, criminology, and the mental aspects of crimes and nature. Some of the definitive questions that this book seemingly asks is: What makes someone evil? Is it nature? Is evil nature created, or part of a humans DNA? And, there are some very strong and quite fascinating characters as well. In many ways, bringing the CSI and forensics to the late 1800s New York was such a brilliant stroke of genius by Caleb Carr, well ahead of its time.

The Alienist, therefore, is as much concerned with the whys as the who with regard to the makeup of an individual. Dr. Lazlo, the alienist, takes up this cause in the hopes of not only solving the case and catching the perpetrator, but understanding the psychology of why someone could act in such a heinous manner. To find the killer, though, Lazlo and his associates must first get in the mind of the killer as they head into the nefarious and seedy areas of New York City.

As much as this is an intense thriller, The Alienist is also very character driven novel. I thought the characters were pretty strong and well developed, and all added dimension to the mystery through their various roles. Two of the more interesting and fascinating were Sarah Howard, an aspiring crime investigator, and the aforementioned Dr. Lazlo Kreizler, who has background in studying the psychological aspects of humans. The narrator, John Moore, has a sort of an everyman quality to his character. As far as the more minor characters that played a role, I thought the Isaacson brothers were interesting in helping with the case.

As some have mentioned, The Alienist is a very dark, disturbing and sometime quite graphic book in its content. Still, with that being said, I don't think Carr ever sensationalizes the graphicness to an absurd level; I believe he is creating more of a sense of realism for the basis of a very disturbing murder mystery at hand.

My edition also has a brilliant afterward from Carr, who reflects on the book and its origins and sheds light on his inspiration for wanting to write it.

There is a TNT miniseries currently airing and I look forward to catching up with that as soon as I can and then reading the sequel, The Angel of Darkness.

Definitely recommended for anyone with interests in crime or psychological thrillers.

Well, I think that thrillers often get a little overdone. Anyone who watches many movies will probably agree. I felt like this movie was one movie that stayed believable, yet still kept the audience enthralled in the storyline.
This movie started off kind of slow, which may irk some of the viewers who want to get into it. However, this movie had one of the best and unpredictable endings in a thriller I've ever seen. This alone made the movie worth it.
I thought the young actors, notably Reese Witherspoon, were admirable in their roles. There was not really any bad acting in this movie. The script was well founded, and I thought that this was an original and creative idea.
Many of the twists of the movie are explained through characters actions rather than overt telling of plot sequences. This is a movie that starts a bit of a ways in, then retraces its steps, and then continues on through the movie.
If you are a moviegoer that enjoys twists and unpredictable endings, then I think this is the movie to watch.

As other reviewers have attested to, this is a difficult novel to write a review about without giving away spoilers. Therefore, be forewarned that there are major spoilers in this review.

I was wavering on what exactly I thought of this book until I finished the third and final part, which sold me on the novel. Some reviewers didn't like the way the novel didn't have that "twist" or "wow factor" at the end, but I didn't think that was necessarily the point or important. When you come down it, the novel essentially questions what "being human" is, and the subsequent ethics of treating "clones" as less than human. Kathy's struggle with very human emotions as she witnesses the fates of those close to her, and finds out the information behind Hailsham.

Kathy's style of narration was distracting at first. She has a chatty, conversational tone, as if you are sipping tea with her as she speaks.  The problem with this is that she tends to throw these nuggets of information about significant future events at you, and then drifts off to describing something in the present, leaving you frustrated. The jumpy narrative is for a purpose, however, the picture of this world is slowly being revealed to us, just as it was to Kathy.

The first part of Never Let Me Go establishes the society Kathy and her classmates live under at Hailsham. Kathy meets two classmates, Ruth and Tommy, and develops a friendship with them.  Guardians oversee the students, and there is a push for the students to create art. One of the guardians, Miss Lucy , comes to Hailsham and seems a bit different than all the others. One day she reveals to Kathy and the others a bit about the real fate and nature of their existence and purpose, which puzzles them. From here, the second part focuses on Kathy, Tommy, and Ruth's lives at the cottages and the rivalries and friendships they build.  As Kathy has conflicts with Ruth over the relationship with Tommy, as well as their world, she begins to reflect on possibility of being a  carer. The nature of Kathy's position as a "carer",which she alludes to at the beginning, isn't completely revealed until the third part, and we see the significance of why she is telling us her story.  As a "carer", she has a job that requires sacrifice and the essentials that a "human being" must have to deal with pain and loss.

There's a certain level of bleakness within Never Let Me Go, but it is still a fascinating read, one that examines  a scary world clones are exploited for their organs, deemed not human and devoid of a soul. While there's certainly a backwardness about how the outside world relies on the vital organs of clones to subsist (irony in that, cruel as it is, it is deemed necessary and humane for the "human" world), I wouldn't exactly classify the novel as sheer dystopia. Never Let Me Go is presented in a quiet, reflective way, and, because of that and it's first person narrative, it's more poignant revelations are in the book's final pages, and makes one think about this society for some time.  Therefore, I don't think anyone should give up on the novel, as the final revelations make up for some confusion in early going. I know you can't judge a novel on simply one passage, but the final paragraph of this novel is quite moving and powerful, and pretty much puts into perspective the entire moral of this book.

While the premise of this book certainly sounded gripping and thrilling, none of it really panned out. In fact, this book was sort of a mess. The characters, the plot, the motives, and the explanations or detail of Fatale are as thinly developed as the book itself (weighing in at 93 pages). Cant understand the high praise for the book really. It really seemed a bit amateurish and a bit B-movieish (perhaps that was the intent). There are far better noirs, and probably far better noirs with dangerous or deadly female lead characters. It seems like the author is so enamored and obsessed with his dangerous female protagonist, Aimee, that he forgets there is some depth that needs to be covered. Basically Fatale reads more like a short story, and perhaps should have just been left as one. Perhaps the translation might have been an issue too, as some dialogue seemed a bit odd or awkward, and some plot description seemed uneven or forced.

Aside from that, there is a somewhat ridiculous plot (which , if you read the synopsis, seems like a doable and engaging storyline, but, alas, not to be), with characters that operate more like caricatures or stereotyped victims, ready to fall into a trap on a whim or playing the victim all too well. And, as far as characters, not really one to root for or identify with. There is this quasi-eat-the-rich or, better put, kill the rich theme that is rampant, but it seems false and manufactured, a way to make Aimee seem like some epic heroine or something I guess. Yet, it never really feels that way and everything seems all over the place.

Oh well, if you happen to despise the book, at least you can read it in a very short time, maybe like when you are waiting to have your wisdom teeth pulled or something.

Hearing so much about the movie and play, I decided to read the Gaston Leroux's novel. Leroux's story is a scattering of many different types fit together in a novel: it has romance, horror, suspense, mystery and is (loosely) historically based on events which took place at Paris' Majestic Opera House. The book is historically based on a tragic and mysterious death of an opera singer at Paris' Majestic Opera House. Leroux did some research in preparing to write this novel, and some tidbits of background into this event are in the book's introduction.
The novel's story has three central characters-Christine Daae, the beautiful opera singer, the Vicomte de Chagny (Raoul), who is in love with Christine from her childhood, and lastly, the Phantom (Erik), who is horribly disfigured and obsessed with music and Christine.
Reminiscent of a murder mystery, the novel's story is centered on the mystery of an Opera ghost that has caused havoc in one of the popular Paris Opera houses. After several murders, the Opera Ghost has ordered demands from the co-managers of the Opera House in the form of a letter, which many take to be a joke. However, after several more bizarre incidents, including an incident in which the chandelier falls on a guest during a show, many of those involved in the business of the house begin to suspect that something must be behind this. Eventually Erik, the Opera Ghost, becomes obsessed with Christine and imprisons her in many ways.
Leroux's writing is refreshing. It reminded me a bit of a work written in the tradition of Sherlock Holmes mysteries, yet there is a definite supernatural elements included to give it a dark, mysterious feel as well. Leroux is able to lay out the story, make the characters well rounded and believable, and then intertwine all the unusual events in a neat conclusion. This is a well written and, for the most part, overlooked work. Fortunately, eventually someone decided to make a movie about this book in the 1920s, and since that time, the book has been give at least a little of the recognition that it deserves.
Recommended also: The Hound of the Baskervilles

To Kill a Mockingbird, as other reviewers have noted, is probably not only one of the significant novels of our time, but also one of the most important movies. It is easy to see why this film resonates with the vast majority who see it, and why it consistently gets mentioned with being one of the 100 best films of all time. It is a rarity to have a film live up to a book, not only in its adaptation, but also how we visualize the story taking place. Producer (Alan J. Pakula) and director (Robert Mulligan) put together a perfect version of Harper Lee's novel, from the mood, music score, cinematography, and cast, who all personify the characters in the book. Gregory Peck was a perfect fit for Atticus Finch, as his taciturn manner, his stoic mood, and his unflinching attitude towards his principles is depicted with such precision. The young children cast as Scout and Jem also give fine performances.

The film itself explores the theme of racial injustice and conflict in the South, but also the essence of believing and doing something because it is the right thing to do, and sticking with it until the end. In this case, Atticus Finch is the lawyer who takes on the case of Tom Robinson, a black man charged with rape, knowing full well that it isn't the popular decision in the Maycomb community, and that ultimately, he and his children will have to pay for it through insults, gossip and general Southern "inhospitality". Still, Atticus sticks to his guns, and doesn't let this get the best of him, a lesson that Jem and Scout learn as the film progresses. Gossiping neighbors whisper, not approving of what Atticus is doing. Atticus Finch has several conflicts with Bob Ewell, a trashy member of the community whose prejudice is evidenced when he spits on Atticus, calls him a derogatory term, and then seeks revenge later. As a result of Atticus' strong principles, Jem, his son, and Scout, his daughter, see the world through realistic viewpoints (albeit the ugliness of society's views on race becomes apparent). The children endure taunts from classmates and even relatives about their father defending Tom Robinson and, as the trail unfolds, the ugliness of class and racial injustice surfaces. Jem and Scout experience a coming of age; their innocent world view is contradicted by these unsettling events. The subplot of To Kill a Mockingbird concerns Boo Radley, a recluse who lives nearby, but has not been seen in years. Rumors swirl about Boo, usually involving something to do with his apparent "craziness", but there is no real proof, and Jem and Scout are left to their own imaginings. However, a significant event changes their perception of him and the world; they are able, as Atticus puts, see things from another person's perspective.

This DVD is a wonderful tool also for any teacher who teaches the novel in high school, as the film is faithful to the book, including many essential scenes, so it is easy to read parts of the novel and then follow these with the film. Also included is a fantastic documentary which examines the making of the film, as well as interviews with several of the actors, such as Gregory Peck. All in all, this is one of the best films ever made, and a fantastic DVD to own.

I had bought this book awhile back, but had never really gotten around to reading it. Seeing many of the rave reviews, I guess my anticipations might have been high going into the read. After reading, I felt a little disappointed. While I have a strong appreciation for the authors' love of literature, reading, and bringing in a love story amid post World War II, details within the narrative seemed unessential and commonplace, and many letters seemed to be penned by gossipy hens with nothing better to do.

Written in epistolary form, this novel goes back and forth through character's lives as they experience the era of post World War II. The club that is formed is a secret way for these characters to communicate with one another, and Juliet, the author looking for a subject for her book, corresponds with many strangers and learns more about this society. While the book is written with a warm, loving feeling, it also has an air of naivety to it in many of the characters and moments.  The main protagonist, Juliet, comes off across as nave, childish, and silly; she might be the type that would roll her eyes at you at a literary club if you didn't agree with her literary tastes. The book is written in an overly sweet, genteel, chatty tone, which gets nauseating, as many of the characters prattle on about menial items like roasting a dead pig, girly crushes on suitors, and what to wear for dinner. The book's atmosphere just didn't stick with me, and, when there was a story with depth presented, it was given little a page or two of air time, and then a character would go on again about a dress or something else mundane. One of the focuses that could have been developed more was the story of Elizabeth; Juliet does end up doing some research on her eventually because she wants a subject, but this in the book's later stages. Another aspect that would have improved the book is just presenting more stories about the war, rather than forcing in war stories to give Juliet's love story a background.

While it was a less-than-satisfying read for me, I can still see how others might like it. With so many books thriving on shock material or trashy writing to entertain, Guernsey is one book that steers clear of this. The authors also clearly did their research going in, and for this I have a great appreciation for what they put together, even if I didn't like it the same way others did. And, being that Mary Ann Shaffer was experiencing an illness in the final stages of writing this book, it is an accomplishment that she was able to put together such a widely appreciated and loved book.  This seems like a book that Oprah would gobble up for her club, but the cutesiness and lack of real stories really made this a little ordinary and unimpressive in my estimation.

Hype sells: it is obvious. The marketing for this book has included not only local bookstores going out of their way to push this book on respective readers, but setting up a campaign for three blockbuster movies for the trilogy. This seems to beg the question: If we are told something is good enough times, do we actually start to believe it? Apparently so.

I guess I was like everyone else. I "had" to read this novel to see what all the fuss was. What I found wasn't unexpected, or anything out of the ordinary really: The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo is the poster child for bestsellers that are sometimes mediocre, clich, ho-hum, ordinary reads. I appreciate anyone who can write a novel with the best of them, and so it takes quite a bit for me to dislike a novel enough to give a negative review. The lowest review I've ever given has been The Da Vinci Code, which was 2 stars. The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo is pretty close to this in both its marketability and its style and publicity over substance, and there are times when the novel gets "all Da Vinci Code" on us (particularly toward the end). Still, I  thought it was slightly above this, which is slightly above mediocrity.

So, what makes a bestseller these days? Sleaze, gratuitous violence a la Hostel style torture chamber, incest, dysfunctional family secrets, and lots and lots of coffee. If that isn't enough, then add a good deal of hacker, computer lingo or some nifty corporate clich dialogue with some revenge thrown in.  If you aren't drinking vast amounts of coffee, sleeping casually with strangers (to give a "complex" angle to the story), hacking into others private information, exhibiting major revenge on someone who has in some way hurt you, or generally causing malicious harm to society (which may or may not include a torture dungeon that would have Hannibal Lecter licking his chops), then you probably aren't really with it, are you? Well, this is the world of The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo to many degrees. It seems to boast about its above the edge shockability (the back cover describes as it as"sexy"), but this doesn't mean it's memorable, especially when you get through the flat, uninspired writing. I understand that it could be translation, but the prose was just very mediocre.

Don't get me wrong. The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo, despite all my banter, does have some intrigue and mystery and interest attached to its plot. I was interested when the mystery unfolded, and I did care when Mikael Blomkvist took the case, at the urging of Henrik Vangar, of Harriet's disappearance. The problem was that it took a good deal of computer and technical lingo just to arrive to this point. Then we meet our female protagonist, Lisbeth Salander, who is this goth-alternative-hacker-antisocial type who helps Blomkvist along with the case. We are given some back story about her, and feel a certain amount of pity for her. She seems to have had a rough life, and we feel a genuine interest in her. Together they work on the case of Harriet's disappearance. We will learn that the story takes off into another direction though.

 However, while the story contains some amount of fascination, it is absorbed in protagonists who aren't really worthy of being protagonists,  a "twist" towards the conclusion that is aggravating on the nerves, and  a plot that finally spirals out control into some ludicrous ending that would satisfy Hollywood. Both "protagonists", while not as dirty as most characters, are hardly worthy to root for in this book, proving ultimately that looking out for oneself is the most important thing, as they essentially serve their own needs whatever way possible. Mikael sleeps around more than Austin Powers, and Lizbeth, for all problems in life, is just a stage below psychotic herself. The cute little "twist" that the author throws at us seems to be more publicity stunt than anything else; personally, I thought it was a cheesy ploy, and rendered much of the book "meaningless.". Not only that, but when we finally understand the antagonist's motives, it comes to us via Scooby Doo reasoning and plotting. Finally, the last part of the book (about the last one hundred pages) was the most unnerving, ingratiating, ludicrous, ill-logical, far-fetched tripe I've read. I literally wanted to throw the book against the wall. I couldn't decide whether to shout out protests, slam the book down in disgust, or just laugh at the lameness. It just seemed like everything fit so nicely into a little, convenient box. To me, this is where the book went really downhill, and pretty much solidified its place with the likes of overrated books such as The Da Vinci Code.

By the end of the six hundred and whatever pages, I was tired of the main characters and just wanted it done with. Does The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo have some intrigue? Sure, it does. But, many weaknesses in this book don't make up for that. It is just another "bestseller" type that is overrated, and builds itself on word of mouth, publicity, hype, Hollywood blockbuster films, and is designed to make the masses go gaga over it. It's not horrible--but very average--pretty much as good as anything you might randomly pick up in the mystery or fiction section at your local bookstore.

On a side note, I found out that that The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo actually translates in Sweden as "A refill of coffee, please." Honest. I researched it.

2  stars

I had tried once to get through the first chapter of A Confederacy of Dunces before putting the book down in utter frustration. I stuck it out and read the whole thing this time, but still didn't care for the book.  It seems the majority of the readers love this novel, but I really couldn't wait to be done with it. Virtually every character is unlikable and obnoxious to the umpteenth degree. The sheer obnoxiousness of this novel is difficult to bare. The author tries to make Ignatius as some sort of Don Quixote of 1960 New Orleans or antihero spouting his philosophies on Big Chief tablets, but it just doesn't work and comes across as rather sad and trite.

One issue was simply that these weren't characters; they were cartoons.  People commend the book for its dialogue, which they say is "real", but it felt more like a sitcom to me. And, much like an episode of Seinfeld, the dialogue and situations went in circles in A Confederacy of Dunces with little substance. Virtually every character behaves on the level of a maniac. Many of the other characters, seemingly caricatures, continually repeated the same cycle of badgering and belittling each other in the various episodes (Jones and the  bar owner, Mr. and Mrs. Levy, Mancuso and the sergeant, Ignatius and his mother, etc).

Yeah, I get it: it's a farce, comedy, satire, etc. Still, the ridiculousness of the subplots and the level of humor just made this novel feel cheap. The whining, yelling and general chaos was more of a chore to get through than entertainment. Sure, A Confederacy of Dunces might be mildly entertaining at points (I thought some of Ignatius' intelligent journal entries were humorous), but most of the humor is sophomoric. I vacillated between despising Ignatius and feeling genuine pity and sorrow at his pathetic, deranged existence.

In final, this is a novel that really irritates more than entertains, which is a pity, because I had high hopes.

One of the better sensationalist novels of the time, Lady Audley's Secret has all the various elements that make up this type of novel: a beautiful mysterious woman, investigations, intrigue, insanity, strange, odd experiences, blackmail, confessions, deception, and plot twists.

Some critics have said that Braddon's prose isn't anything special. I tend to disagree. Braddon has an uncanny ability in Lady Audley's Secret to take the narrative into characters thoughts and insights as if they were "thinking aloud", which gives a little variance to the novel and adds a dimension that you couldn't get in the ordinary third person narration. This way the character's motive is revealed in a short monologue, and then shifts back to regular dialogue with other characters present. We see this often with the principle characters of the book, Lady Audley and Robert Audley, as we hear their inner musings about the other.

Sensational novels put more emphasis on plot than on character, and this is evident in Lady Audley's Secret, but Braddon is able to do plenty with her major characters. One interesting quality is the way she takes the notion of the "blue eyed wax doll" female and turns it on its head. The funny angle to this is that Alicia Audley, Robert's cousin, who is disgusted and perhaps envious of Lady Audley's mannerisms, beauty and perfect charm constantly refers to her as this childish `doll', which is a bit of an irony. Robert Audley, the other central character, is quite reminiscent of the typical worthy protagonist, but who is not faultless. At times, he seems to brood a little too much about the negativity of the world and his task he must do, but still he is a great leading character as we move along in the mystery. Neither characters are very deep so to speak, but they are entertaining to keep track of as the plot moves along.

As other reviewers have mentioned, this is a tough book to review simply because giving plot details might spoil the read for others. I really enjoyed the amateur sleuth work of Robert Audley as he investigates the disappearance of his friend, George Talboys. This noble young man takes on the task of discovering what happened, but the puzzle gets more complicated the deeper he goes into his investigation, which is really Wilkie Collins"esque".

As the book gives away in its title, there is a secret that is to be shared that lends much to the story's conclusion. But, I don't think that the secret is the same one that we think it is, and I would venture to say that there are actually two secrets in this novel that are of critical importance.

A great novel, my first read of Mary Elizabeth Braddon, but I look forward to others!

4 1/2 stars

I can see why people wouldn't like this book and all. Really. I can. But, me, on the other hand, liked this book and all. It was a riot. A real riot....
People may not like this book because it obviously has very simple language at points and, as a reader, we are never given the point-of-view of other characters. However, I felt the simplicity of the novel gives it it's effect. Holden takes the world as being simple, yet there are many complex issues he must deal with. He is searching for his identity and the reason that most people are "phonies" is because he still hasn't completely figured out the world. Personally I felt as though the book couldn't have been written from any other point of view than 1st person and still achieved it's effect. I read the book rather quickly because it is as if someone is sitting there telling you their life story...well, in a way, Holden is. I recommend this book to anyone because it is original and definitely not boring. It is a book that many relate to, because it deals with the teenage world that we've all been a part of.
I still don't think this book is anything better than 3 stars because it is rather simplistic in nature. However, I can understand why people consider it a classic.

I wanted to give this novel a fair try, so I stuck it out into the end. However, in the end, I was a bit mystified and perplexed about the praise and glowing reviews this book gets. I give Follett credit for writing a lengthy book with a historical angle to it about 12th century England, but, as others who didn't like this book have noted, I think he was not the right author for it. I can't attest to other Follett novels, as I have not read any others, but this just felt like a generic, trashy type of novel that winds up on the bestseller lists. In short, the problems overwhelmed any positives. While the plot did have some sporadic intrigue, it quickly became diminished by repetitive over-the-top violence, gratuitous and ridiculously detailed sex scenes, inanely dumbed down dialogue on par with a modern reality show, and superficial and painstaking melodrama between Jack and Aliena, which encompasses a good two hundred pages of the later part of the novel.

The novel tries to have you believe that the core of its plot centers around the building of a cathedral, but this comes across as more of a guise for "depth." Other than Phillip, very few characters have any spiritual sense to them, or even care what the cathedral really means or symbolizes.

Characterization was one of the weakest points. Most of these characters are so dimwitted, superficial or so shallow that it's hard to care one way or another about them, as they are driven by their own gains, egos or wants.  For one, the main villain, William, is so blatantly and cartoonishly evil that he seems more caricature than character. His thirst for sadism knows no bounds, but Follett wants to drive that home to the infinite degree. Also, William cannot see a lass without going all gaga about her, and we have to read a three or four page description about what he imagines he might do with her. Can this guy be more insecure or inconsistent? He is terrified of Hell, yet his is repetitively doing mayhem (killing, raping, pillaging, etc). However, even the "good" characters are fairly artificial. We have that wonderful character Ellen, who is like a Medieval version of Hester Prynne with a dash of 60s rebellion thrown in. Part witch and part feminist, she lives in a forest, has a rendezvous with main character Tom Builder (great name, huh) and soon after Tom's wife dies, makes a bold (and blasphemous) statement by urinating on a sacred book (to which Tom witnesses and can't help thinking "What a woman!"...honestly!). Her atheist son, Jack, who despises the thought of being a monk and is indifferent to religion, of course takes up a cause to build a cathedral, even though he seems to be only building it because it will look neat. Richard and Aliena have this quest of fulfilling their papa's dying wish, which is to have Richard achieve earldom. We go through pages of this quest attempting to be accomplished--epic battles, politics, difficult journeys, people dying, more politics, building falling, then being rebuilt, then falling again, then they achieve it ...and then Aliena says "eh, I'll do what I want. I'm old enough." What? Unfortunate for the reader, we have the final parts of the novel shift to Jack and Aliena's story and their silly and head-scratching love affair. Perhaps Jack's motivation for life is stated best when he is speaking to his mom about his love, "I'm going to spend my life building Kingsbridge Cathedral and making babies with Aliena." Pretty much says it all. Aliena has to be the stupidest character of them all. She takes her child in tow from city to city looking for Jack, who she decided to reject in order to marry scumbag Alfred for no other reason than to give Richard his precious earldom. Able to overcome any odds, she sees Jack magically after years of journey, and they reunite. Her motivations and logic are off the charts when it comes to dimwittedness. We are "entertained" with the spats between the quarrelling lovers as Phillip, a much more interesting and important character, seems to disappear from the plot for awhile. In all, the characters, other than Phillip or Jonathan, had little to no redeeming value to the book, and are more like pawns or pieces in a board game, really, archetypes that fit into a nice little box, and without any soul or depth.

Another issue was the hokey 20th century dialogue. In some settings or times, it might work and be a creative way to write a book. Here, it just gives a flimsy quality to the story, and lessens any "epic" feel and replaces it with "beach read" feel. Follett seems to insult his readers by dumbing-down the dialogue.

Also, the book has too many repetitive plot elements. I mean, how many times is the cathedral going to be destroyed, only to be repaired? How many times is William going to consult with Waleran about his revenge plans? How many times is William going to come in and sack the town only to have it rebuilt? How many times do we have to read a two or three page play-by-play of William torturing, raping or killing someone? How many detailed descriptions of sex, body parts, etc do we have to have? Do these really add anything? Why couldn't the author spend as much time giving some context to the essential plot moments rather than focusing on the trivial?

Over all, Pillars might be a bestseller because the masses eat it up, but that doesn't mean it is memorable nor worthy of a second read. The only epic feel to this novel is its length, not its content or writing style. I saw the miniseries (last year) before reading the book, and thought that the miniseries treated the subject of the story a bit more seriously, which seems to go against the common maxim "the book is better than the movie." As far as Pillars goes, is has some moments, but wasn't worth the time slogging though.

 I say read it, and then wash your hands of it. Literally.
