users.query: This is pretty much a required text for a homeowner. It covers most, if not all, of the minor problems that can crop up in a house, from small holes in drywall to creaky chairs to troubleshooting appliances that are on the fritz. It covers all the fixable problems with decent diagrams and easy-to-follow steps, and also tells you what you shouldn't tackle by yourself, whether that involves calling a repairman or buying a replacement. A good companion to this is Home Maintenance For Dummies, which covers some of the more involved and costly jobs around the house. Armed with these two books, you can save a lot of money (I made the cost of both back with my first DIY fix) and keep your dwelling in tip-top shape.

cands.text: I'll be the first to admit I'm not a handyman, but I'm able to maintain my house on my own and make most minor repairs. As an academic exercise, I found this book to be an enjoyable read. I never really knew how an icemaker worked or what exactly those pipes leading from my bathroom up through the roof were for. Full-page diagrams with step-by-step walkthroughs will have the know the purpose of nearly everything in your home, and give you at least a general idea of how it accomplishes said purpose. If that was all this book was meant to be, I'd have given it five stars hands-down. However, I have to knock off half a star because the cover advertises the book as "a visual guide to understanding and maintaining your home." Most of the maintenance advice comes in the form of "Before Calling a Professional" all-text boxes (i.e. no pictures explaining the words). They are handy but simplistic, and I would have been alright with that if the cover had not lead me to believe I would see sections along the lines of what I saw in books like Home Maintenance For Dummies or How to Fix Everything For Dummies. Taken together, though, these three books will cover all your minor home improvement and maintenance needs. I also have to take a half-star off for some layout errors. For example, the direct-vent gas heater on page 84 actually has the description of the totally-unrelated ball-type faucet from page 16 attached to it. The mistakes are obvious and don't detract much from the experience, but are still there. All that considered though, if you buy this book with the intention of learning how your house works, you can't beat it - the diagrams are clear and explained in plain English. Just don't go into it expecting to learn how to rewire a junction box.

Let me start out by saying that while I'm decent at maintaining my house, I'm far from a contractor. So take this review in the light of someone who's not a handyman but tries to do things himself before calling in the pros. To say I'm impressed with the power this thing puts out is an understatement. I have a six-year-old corded Black & Decker that labors to make holes in the dense cement walls in my basement. The Bosch drills as easily through it as most drills go through dense wood. This power is all the more impressive when you consider it's cordless, which makes it infinitely easier to lug around. The fact that a spare battery comes packed in makes this even better (though one could argue that at a $440+ price point it should be expected). One thing I was disappointed to find out is that normal bits and shanks won't work in this, and no SDS-Plus bits are included, so you either have to buy the appropriate adapter to get your existing bits to work or run out and buy some new SDS-Plus bits, which are significantly more expensive than what I'm used to. A trip to the local Home Depot for a package that contained two small chisels and four masonry bits (5/32" up to 1/2") set me back over $30. But, man, after seeing this beast tear into my basement wall, it's money well spent. Other things I like about the drill include its relatively light weight and its balance (having the battery in the middle was a great idea). The mode selector knob is intuitive, and the speed is truly variable based on how you pull the trigger (not stepped like some other tools I've used - you can get this thing from barely spinning to Tasmanian Devil and anywhere in between). One place Bosch cut corners was in the battery charger. While it seems to charge at a decent speed, the indicator could use some work. The light is either on or blinking. Blinking means it's charging - okay, fair enough. But a solid light indicates either the battery is full, the battery is not connected, or the battery is defective. Would it have been so hard to incorporate a second LED or more than two states for the one LED so I can tell if my battery is good or not? All in all, besides some minor gripes about the charger and the sticker shock at the special bits it needs, I'm incredibly impressed with this tool.

I'm coming at this book from a somewhat unique perspective. I recently read the same author's Personal Finance in Your 20s For Dummies. In fact, Mr. Tyson has written a range of finance-related "For Dummies" books. I'm not saying this book is bad; far from it. It contains a plethora of pertinent, practical information. However, after finishing a read-through, it felt like I had already read about 75% of the information before. If you are looking into a book to make personal finance easier to grasp, this is it. However, if you have already read one of Tyson's other books, be forewarned that you will be treading over much of the same ground.

So I had bought the Shop-Vac 9650600 3.0-Peak HP Pro Series Wet or Dry Vacuum, 6-Gallon last year and really loved it. I was considering buying another to leave over my mother's house since I'm always over there doing projects for her, so when I got the opportunity to review the WORKSHOP Wet/Dry Vac I jumped on the chance. Long story short, I'll still be buying another Shop-Vac. Let me say what I like about the WORKSHOP vac first. The power cord is longer than the Shop-Vacs, and the plug has one of those clamps that will let you clamp it to the cord, making winding it easy. The vac is light, requires minimal assembly and cleaning, and rolls well on its casters. The attachments attach easily and securely (both on the suction side and the blower side) but still come off easily. That, unfortunately, is where my praise ends. The WORKSHOP only comes with two extender wands and a utility nozzle. The way the nozzle is constructed, however, makes it borderline useless. Rather than going the Shop-Vac route of "combing" the edges, the WORKSHOP nozzle simple extends the two short sides down somewhere around 3/16". This means that both long sides of the nozzle are not in contact with the surface you are using the vac on, resulting in a dramatic loss of suction. As a test I tried to pick up some crumbs on a commercial-grade carpet, and it took roughly ten passes over a single crumb to pick it up, even when going slowly. There's a precise angle you have to hold the wand at or you'll get no suction at all; nail that angle and you might get a third of the suction you'd get without the nozzle attached. Storage is also a HUGE issue with this vac because, with the exception of the power cord I mentioned earlier, there's nowhere to store anything on the vac. On the Shop-Vac there's attachment points where the various wands and nozzles can be stored on the machine. There's no such feature on the WORKSHOP, and nothing except the nozzle fits in the canister of the vac, so you'll either have to store the sizable hose and wands separately or leave them attached (which takes up a LOT of room). But the biggest sin of this Wet/Dry vac? The instruction manual says it's not designed to pick up wet stuff. No, I'm not making that up. You're not supposed to use the vac without a filter. That makes perfect sense because the filter is what stands between what you're sucking in and the vac's engine. According to the instruction manual WORKSHOP makes three kinds of filter for this vac. Two of those filters specifically mentioned that you should not pick up anything wet with them because moisture will ruin the filter, and the third says that picking up anything more than a minimal amount of moisture at any one time will degrade the filter. I should note that, not quite believing this, I went to the company website - which popped up as having security certificate issues in my mobile browser, by the way - and they do sell a wet filter that's advertised as fitting all WORKSHOP vacs, but it's over $20 (for comparison, the Shop-Vac 90585 Foam Sleeve is under $5 here on Amazon). So what the instruction manual (which was probably recently printed since this is apparently a new model) says contradicts what the website says. Between not knowing for sure whether or not this actually can pick up wet messes, a horrible storage situation, and a poorly-functioning utility nozzle, I can't really recommend this over the similarly-sized Shop-Vac.

I've read several very good books that do some critical analysis of comics and graphic novels - Watchmen and Philosophy: A Rorschach Test, for example - and as much as I thought I would like this book, I left disappointed. I suppose my biggest gripe with the book is just how *dry* it is. Comics are lively, colorful, engaging, but this book is full of unnecessary jargon (the terms might impress a professor, but not the reader), color panels are rendered in greyscale even though the text mentions the color in them (no, I don't notice the red line cutting through the entire page, because there are several lines and they are all grey), and paragraphs are spent discussing the smallest minutiae (did I really need to read a paragraph to tell me that the tail of a speech bubble points to the speaker?). Even the terms the author means to emphasize are dry - instead of being bolded or italicized, they're rendered in a different-but-still-visually-similar font, so they don't actually stand out. Don't get me wrong, the author makes some very good points. An example that sticks out to me is from very early in the book when Kukkonen walks through things we subconsciously absorb from comics and how authors can use those to communicate ideas to us, culminating in a very enjoyable section analyzing the first two pages from "V for Vendetta." Sections like this are the exception rather than the rule, however - immediately following this excellent section was a discussion of narration that made me almost fall asleep. The book continues in much the same way - you'll get a four- or five-page section that is really engaging (or at least mildly interesting) followed by ten pages of material that feels like a droning professor. I suppose part of the issue is that many comics most people are familiar with - Peanuts, X-Men, Calvin & Hobbes, and Batman, to name a few - are barely mentioned (especially in the beginning of the book, where you think they would be at least name-dropped to engage new readers), if at all. And single-panel comics - like "The Far Side" - are left at the door. There's also the issue of price and length - at almost $30 and clocking in under 200 pages (keep in mind that illustrations, pages dedicated to possible essay topics and class exercises, multiple reference pages per chapter, acknowledgements, etc. factor into that 190 pages the product description mentions), readers will be left with a very bad taste in their mouth. I'm not saying I didn't learn anything from this book, nor am I saying it was *all* bad, but I honestly can't recommend it if you have other options.

I took an Introduction to Sociology course that used both this and Jon Witt's The Big Picture: A Sociology Primer. While I found Witt's book to be engaging and informative to someone new to the field, I did not enoy Ritzer's book very much. Not to say he doesn't have good ideas, but I found the writing bland and, at times, overly technical. Ritzer argues that the fast-food priciples epitomized by McDonald's - efficiency, calculability, predictability and control - are permeating society as a whole. He takes examples from the mundane (food shopping) to the extravagent (climbing Mount Everest) to the horrifyingly extreme (the Holocaust) to illustrate his point. He also devotes time to detailing how one can "deMcDonaldize" society. He also has extensive endnotes for further reading. However, this book contains some very serious flaws. It is very obvious that Ritzer views this McDonaldization as a completely negative entity, glossing over the fact that, in non-extreme doses, some of those four priciples can be good things. His bias is so evident he goes as far to quote Weber and say that McDonaldization is leading us into a "polar night of icy darkness." I find it a little hard to take his text seriously when he uses such metaphors. He also devotes a chapter to "Globalization and McDonaldization," which starts out well enough but ends up being little more than a plug for another of Ritzer's books that made my head hurt with its liberal use of jargon and confusing syntax ("Although the grobalization of nothing is at odds with the glocalization of something,... the grobalization of nothing is also at odds with the grobalization of something... there is no conflict between the grobalization and the glocalization of nothing." - The whole chapter reads like that). And one more thing that bothered me - a pet peeve, I know, but still - was that the kerning (text spacing, or the space between the letters) is sometimes noticably different from page to page. As someone who has a passing knowledge of basic layout, this irked me. This text conveys some very interesting concepts, but it is executed in a less-than-stellar manner. I'd take this book a chapter at a time to minimize frustration.

"Build Your Own PC for Dummies," written by Mark Chambers, takes you through the entire process of building a PC from the ground up, from "Why would I build my own PC anyway?" to determining what kind of machine you should build to what components you will need to actual assembly to maintenance and upkeep.

The book is arranged sequentially, so by following it from beginning to end you will be led through each and every step, all with the trademark Dummies sense of humor and Chambers' vast insight. Each chapter is also self-contained, so if you only need help with, say, installing a new video card, you can skip right to that part (and if he references anything from another chapter, Chambers will tell you what chapter you should refer to).

As the book progresses, Chambers builds a top-of-the-line computer using the outlined steps, giving exact parts and the rationale behind why he chose them. A companion DVD to the book shows the actual assembly process for those who are more visual-oriented.

I was pleasantly surprised at the rather unbiased comparison of Linux, Vista and XP in the operating system chapter - rather than becoming a fanboy of either side, Chambers lists the strengths of all the systems and makes recommendations based on what you have in mind for your PC.

A handy section at the end of the guide is a collection of "Top Ten" lists, such as biggest assembly pitfalls and tips to maintain your hard drive.

This book is a fun read, conveys great information, is easy to digest and is generously illustrated. I give it my highest recommendation, and am using it to build a PC that will save me about 35% off retail and will last longer.

When I first got my Fire HD, I got leather case Amazon recommended on the product page. I loved how light it was, how it looked, and how functional it was. Its one shortcoming in my book was that there was no good way to stand it so that the screen was vertical, or to charge it while it was standing. So, when I had the opportunity to try the Timbuk2 out, I gave it a go. The Timbuk2 two solves my two issues. The piece that holds the tablet is velcro-backed, so you can disconnect it and flip 90 degrees (for vertical viewing) or 180 degrees (so the charging port is on top) then reattach it to the stand. That being said, the Timbuk2 performs less well in other instances. The material is less high-quality. The sleeve does not cover all of the Kindle's sides; in particular, two corners are exposed, which could lead to scuffing. If you don't have a screen protector, one of the velcro strips closes right over the screen, and looks like it might scratch it over time. I also found that I really missed the ability to close the cover and have the Fire automatically enter standby. I also found the price to be a little steep considering the material. If you had asked me to price this myself, I would have put it in the $25-35 range. $45 is just way too steep, in my opinion, even if the product does a decent job, which, to be fair, it does. I just expected more bang for the buck.

So I'm getting close to 30, and in the past few years I've bought a house, a car, and built up some savings. My family health history isn't that great. It hit me one day that I really need to start planning for my inevitable (though hopefully still far-off) demise. So when I had the opportunity to give Quicken's latest version of Willmaker a try, I took it.

The program itself takes up surprisingly little space - well under 100 MB, and that's after an 8 MB update it download when I started it for the first time - and was a completely painless install, even when I directed it to use a secondary hard drive (some programs freak out when they're not on the C: drive, but not this one).

There's lots of forms included, but right off the bat Willmaker presents you with five important ones you should fill out before the others. As someone with very little experience in the field, I appreciated that, as well as the interview-like way it walks you through completing each document.

The documents also save after each step, so you can bounce back and forth between them. For example, I started out with the Health Care Directive (aka "living will" - how I want my end-of-life medical care) and got to a section that gave me the option to reference a previously-completed document regarding my final arrangements. So, I paused filling out the Health Care Directive, completed the final arrangements document, then picked up where I left off with the Health Care Directive.

If you're ever confused during a step, you'll see at least three common questions on the right sidebar that you can expand for advice. Any question I ever had was addressed in the sidebar.

Once you complete the "interview" process, Willmaker takes your answers and formats them into legal documents that you can print out and sign (and, in many cases, have witnesses sign and get notarized).

All this being said, I should also note I have a very uncomplicated setup when it comes to my estate. If you have an overly complicated setup (for example, if there are conditions that have to be met for multiple people's inheritances or you have dual residency in multiple states) you will probably want to sit down with an estate lawyer. But for straightforward situations like mine, this software will get you to do all the necessary paperwork at a fraction of the cost.

I've used the TP-LINK TL-PA511, a similar product, in the past, and enjoyed the functionality it gave me, using it to hook up some older video game consoles that were in rroms far away from the router. On the surface, this competing NetGear product makes a sacrifice in top speed (200 Mbps vs. 500 Mbps on the TP-Link) to add some nifty features, with an increase in price of about 50%. The most noticeable of these features is a pass-through outlet, which means you're not losing a socket when you use this (although it does make the other socket in the outlet a tight fit for a three-prong plug). It also includes a USB port in addition to the Ethernet port, meaning you'll be able to hook up any USB widget to your network (printers and hard drives come to mind as obvious choices). The Netgear also comes with a cable that will allow you to hook up speakers with RCA plugs (the red/white ones) or a 3.5mm cable (a "headphone cable"). And, of course, USB speakers will work. Finally, the device is Airplay-compatible. Now, that's all well and good, but this requires it to work, and since I have an older, pre-WWII house, this becomes an issue. Most of the outlets in my house were originally the old two-prong outlets, with only the laundry room and kitchen having true grounded outlets. For the rest of the outlets, they're either still two-prong (meaning the Netgear won't plug in at all), have three-prong outlets that simply aren't grounded, or have been retrofitted by me using GFCI outlets like this one. I've discovered that the Netgear extender does not seem to want to connect to the base Netgear when plugged into GFCI. That being said, when plugged into any other outlet, included the non-grounded three-prong, the Netgear connects without any issue, even through a surge protector (which the TP-Link won't do). While on the topic, I should mention that Netgear advises you to not plug this kit into a power strip (which the pass-through makes a moot point, anyway, since you can just go outlet-Netgear-strip instead of outlet-strip-Netgear). The slower max speed isn't noticeable under most circumstances (since most ISP connections are still well below 100 Mbps, so only intra-network transfer speeds hit the max), so unless you're going for a lot of data transfer within your home network or have an older home like me, this Netgear is a better choice than the TP-Link.

If you have a recently-constructed house, you can ignore this review. But if you house is older and/or has non-standard (i.e. 1 3/4" thick) doors, like mine, keep reading.

I suppose I'll get the good stuff out of the way first - the hooks are sturdy, large, and have rubber caps on them, so they can handle large loads while also preventing them from slipping off. There's also rubber that covers every point of contact with the door to avoid scratches.

Now the bad news. My house is older and still has most of the original wooden doors, which are 1 3/8" wide instead of the modern standard 1 3/4" and have some decorative recessed panels. This combination plays havoc with the rack.

The rack has two springy arms on the hooks (if you look at the picture you can just barely see the one on the left hook). These are 1 3/8" away from the back of the hook, and can be bent to accommodate a door up to 2" thick. However, since my doors are the 1 3/8", when I install the rack there's no spring tension to keep it in place. What's worse, since the rack's horizontal portion actually fits inside one of the recesses, the whole rack sits at a slight angle. This in turn causes top to angle up, which prevents the door from closing. Since the top of the hook wasn't meant to contact anything, it's not rubber-coated and scratches the door frame.

I moved the rack to a door that does not have the recesses, but since the door is still the bare minimum size this rack can accommodate, it still does not hold securely.

While the rack itself is good, and works well when you get it on the right door, OXO really needs to specify what thicknesses this will work well on rather than making a blanket statement that this will fit all doors without damage. Make sure your doors are at least 1 1/2" thick, and no more than 2" thick.

This review can really be divided into two halves: terrible battery installation and pretty good performance.

Let me get the bad out of the way first: getting the (not included) batteries in is way more work than it should be. Instead of a battery door, you have to basically disassemble the light to get them in. To make matters worse, it requires one of those tiny Phillips screwdrivers that you usually only find in glasses repair kits or specialized electronics toolkits.

Once you have the batteries in, though, the light performs admirably. The magnet is strong enough to hold it securely but still not make it a chore to take off, the button is responsive, and the lights do a good job of illuminating my full-size (12"x16"x72") locker.

Given the chore that getting the batteries in is, I would recommend you use this in an area you don't access often but will need a light when you do need to access. I'm using it in the tiny basement closet where I keep my holiday decorations, for example.

So, I love XCOM: Enemy Unknown. I think it's the best turn-based strategy to come out in the past decade. I pre-ordered both the game and the guide. Two-day shipping being what it is, I actually downloaded and beat the game before getting the guide, which was no big issue for me since I tend not to use a guide until the second playthrough anyway. But having seen what the game has to offer already, I can tell you this guide is lacking in many respects. It also needed someone to read through this and fix some glaring errors before this went to press and did not get it. Let me tackle that first. A good editor will make sure there are no spelling/grammar errors and that information is correct. However, I ran into several instances of both (grammar/spelling example: "Any weapons you Research, younumber of researchers and labs to make the time investment worth the payoff."). The spelling/grammar ones I can tolerate, but often the book gives conflicting information, sometimes within the same paragraph, like when in the Support class's section it talks about suppression. The first sentence claims that its suppression imposes "a 30 penalty to aim" (which is identical to the Heavy's suppression) but then says in the second sentence that it imposes a penalty of 10 instead of the Heavy's 20. The book is laid out well and contains a fairly exhaustive section of tables detailing armor, weapons and other things you can build. All of this information is available in-game, but the tables themselves are handy for a quick reference. As you probably know, the game is divided between strategic and tactical sections. The strategic layer gets a *very* thorough walkthrough, divided neatly into "phases" bookended by the priority missions you get in-game. The book provides a timetable of what you should research when, and about what in-game time you should be at at the conclusion of the phases. As good as the strategic walkthrough is, the tactical wakthrough is not very extensive. Part of this is due to the random nature of most of the missions in XCOM. In fact, only the final mission gets a detailed walkthrough, and the guide gives tactical suggestions on dealing with the "boss" (I use the term loosely) characters in two other missions. There's also a walkthrough of the tutorial mission, but since you have no choices in that mission and are just clicking where you are told, I don't count it, though the "walkthrough" does a good job of explaining the game's concepts along the way. While I wasn't expecting a complete walkthrough, or even a section with layouts of all the possible single-player maps (there are over 80, last I heard), the guide hardly touches the tactical layer outside of what I mentioned above. A cursory explaination of how to build a decent squad at least would have been appreciated. There's some hints buried in the soldiers' upgrade tree descriptions, but that's about it. Multiplayer gets about 30 pages after the single-player section. It does a very good job of breaking down the units and suggesting squads for the 10,000-point default matches (though I found the lack of any sort of Archangel Sniper build - which the developers almost always used in pre-release multiplayer showings and are even pictured in the guide - curious). The three-paragraph descriptions are very bare-bones, however. There's also another 30 pages of concept art at the end. It's good enough for a flip through but given that this is almost a sixth of the book, it feels like padding and I can't help but wonder if at least some of that space had been used for more tactical advice that the guide as a whole would have been better. If you're wandering into the world of strategy game guides for the first time, this is a decent guide. If you've played a strategy game before, though, buy this book only if you want the in-game information in a more-readble format of if you need a walkthrough for the final mission. After reading the guide, the only information I learned that I didn't pick up from my in-game experience was that there was some research I missed, and that was only because I beat the game so quickly (in in-game time) that the most powerful UFOs hadn't appeared yet. I'm not saying that at the price (just under $13) that I didn't get my money's worth, but this guide had a lot of potential and didn't meet it. Pros: +Detailed walkthrough of the final mission +Detailed outline of how to play the game on the strategic level +Well-laid out with useful tables and breakouts Cons -Numerous typos and errors -Glaring lack of tactical advice -Almost all the information given in the book is available word-for-word in the game PS: Please don't take my so-so review of the guide as a commentary on the actual game. I love the game and would recommend it to almost everyone.

Larry Tye's history of the Man of Steel is a thoroughly enjoyable and educational read. Most books I have encountered that discuss comics/graphic novels are either novelizations or texts relating the subject matter to the real world (like the very good Watchmen and Philosophy: A Rorschach Test). This book is unique in that it investigates the history of the character Superman and by extension his creators, his handlers and his on-screen personas. Tye does cover the major events in the Superman mythology, like his Kryptonian origins, his lack of direct involvement in World War II, the multiple reboots, his on-again-off-again marriages, and his death & resurrection in the early 1990s. However, these take a backseat to the behind-the-scenes history of his creation, his explosion in popularity, and the ownership issues that continue to play out in court until this very day in 2012. The fact that Tye is not a rabid Superman fan - in fact, prior to writing this book, he had never heard of the show "Smallville" - lends the tome some credibility, backed up by almost 100 pages of notes and sources for a 300-page work. Tye also thanks an extensive list of researchers in his afterword that aided him. This also gives a fresh perspective to the traditional legend that Superman's creators were muscled out of the business by greedy moneymakers, showing you a totally different side of the story that, while not exonerating either side, doesn't place the blame either. Comic purists may be riled up, but I appreciated an unbiased overview, including excerpts from letters written at the time. Tye, who had previously written a biogaphy of the Negro League pitcher Satchel Paige, posits the premise of the book as such: "There's no better way to understand modern-day heroes than to look at Superman, the superhero who tapped into the American psyche more effectively than anyone else and, as a result, has lasted longer than all of them." On that count, Tye succeeded impressively, crafting an informative and fun read that has me itching to go watch those old Christopher Reeve movies again. Note: Vine reviewers get an advanced uncorrected proof of the book. I noticed several *very* minor factual errors in this book, but I writing this review according to Vine guidelines, specifically with the assumption these errors are fixed in the final, edited version.

I've used several Goal Zero products in the past - namely the Nomad 7 panel and the Guide 10 battery pack - and have had pretty decent success using them to charge devices in the mid-Atlantic region (I could probably have gotten away with just the charger if I lived in, say, Arizona, but here in Pennsylvania the sun didn't give enough juice for the panel to charge medium- to high-draw devices). I was incredibly impressed with the build quality though, so when I had the opportunity to take this larger panel for a spin I hopped on it. First, the quality of materials used here are just as good as my Nomad. You can tell they didn't cut any corners in the construction, from the panels (which are actually gridded and not simply cheap panes as in, say, the Sunforce 50012 this replaced for me), the cables (which come with a variety of adapters to accommodate your particular need), and the casing (which has durable attachment points and suction cups). One thing I love about this panel, especially when compared to the Sunforce, is that it has an in-line charge regulator. Besides preventing overcharge, it also prevents discharge (a.k.a. current flowing from the battery to the panel, draining the battery and potentially damaging the panel). Practically, this means I can leave the panel plugged into my car's 12V socket indefinitely and not have to remove it every time I start my engine, which was both annoying and eventually damaging to the Sunforce's plug. The regulator also has a small, unobtrusive blue light to let you know when the panel is getting enough sun to charge the battery. And in the ultimate in efficiency, the panel powers this light itself and it will go on even if not connected to the battery. Unlike some cheaper battery maintainers, which will only put out 2 Watts or less to prevent battery discharge, this panel is rated to put out 10 Watts, which means that it will (slowly, granted) actually *charge* a battery. I'm not sure I would trust it with charging one that was dead, but as long as the battery has some juice this panel will build it back up. All this is well and good, but does it actually work? A resounding yes. I just so happened to have a car battery that was pretty low. The car would start but almost immediately the low battery warning would pop up. Every time, until I put this charger on. I plugged it in and left it for five hours, and when I started the vehicle, no battery warning (then or since). I am sold. At $100 you might be tempted to go for the cheaper "maintainer" panels, but trust me, you get what you pay for in a very good way here.

I've been using Great Stuff for years now and swear by it. This new 20-oz size is ideal for larger projects; I wish I had had this when I was sealing the gaps in my mother's crawlspace because one 16-oz can was not enough but two was overkill.

If you've never used Great Stuff before, it's fairly simple in theory: you spray the foam into the gap, and it expands to fill, insulate, and seal it. Sometimes it can be a bit tricky to judge how much to fill larger gaps (there's a special kind of Great Stuff for widths greater than 1 inch) but I tend to err on the side of filling it too much and then just trimming the excess later after it has expanded and hardened.

Two pieces of advice. One, make sure you do not get any on your clothes. It will be stained permanently, and you'll have pieces of sealant on there for many, many washes to come. Two, if you don't use the entire can and want to save the rest for later, make sure you thoroughly clean out the applicator right after; otherwise, the sealant hardens inside the applicator and makes it useless.

If your goal is to keep your HDMI devices a significant distance from your television, or you abhor the idea of a wire going to your TV, this is a decent option. However, several shortcomings in design have kept me from really liking this product.

1) The remote. It's tiny. As in, smaller than my credit card, very easy to lose on the couch or even in a basket small. It also only seems to work for me maybe half the time. The worst part, though, is that it only has three buttons - up, down, and OK. So all you can do with it is select an input. There is no option to turn the adapter off, which might not have been such a big deal if the blue power indicator lights weren't *always* on and were bright enough to illuminate the entire room in the dark sometimes.

2) With such a spare remote, you would think there would be easily-accessible buttons on the device itself, but they are all located on the back of the device, so you would physically have to pick up the device and turn it over - perhaps pulling out some cables - to see them.

3) I would have loved to see a little more imagination in the options I get for naming the inputs. For example, if I have multiple video game systems hooked up to the adapter, I can only name them "Game." I would have *really* loved an option where I could input a custom name.

4) Finally, there's no detection function on the adapter, so you have to manually select which input you want, even if only one is on. Since some 4-port wired HDMI adapters have this and cost less than $20, this is a big shortcoming.

Does it do it's job? Yes. The range is great, the signal strength is consistently high, and the remote control IR blaster is ingenious. But there's so many nagging omissions here I can't recommend it.

This product review really has to be split into two parts: the cable itself, and evaluating your need for said cable.

The cable itself is great - well-made, reliable connection. The snagless molding protects the connector, but makes it impractical for constant plugging/unplugging (to be fair, this is the same for *all* snagless connectors, so if you'll be constantly removing the cable get one without the molding). This is the ideal plug to use for a PC whose router is on the same desk: plug it in once and forget about it for a while.

Now, the question is, do you *need* a CAT6 cable as opposed to the standard CAT5e? Probably not. Yes, a CAT6 cable is capable of a faster data transfer speed than CAT5e, but remember that connections your network will run at the speed of the slowest part. In many cases, it'll be the router's connection to the Internet, which usually fall in the 15-75mbps range - well below CAT5e's threshold, and obviously well below the CAT6's. The only time you'll notice a difference is if every single part of you network is gigabit or faster - which either means you have a heavy-duty, industrial-strength Internet connection, or you're simply connecting devices via a gigabit-speed LAN with no concern for Internet speed.

Think of it as comparing the speed of a Ford Taurus and that of the sportier Ford Taurus SHO in everyday driving: yes, the SHO can top out 30-50mph faster, but realistically you'll never utilize that because both cars are easily capable of going the speed limit on your average highway. The only time you'd really be able to tell the difference is if you took them to the racetrack or the Autobahn, which is simply not a situation 99.9% of people will run into.

There's also talk of using this cable as "future-proofing." That's hogwash, in my opinion. I could see if you were buying a length of cable to wire your home so you won't have to tear the wires out in 10-15 years, but this is a patch cable and may wear out before you'd even need it.

The "Death of Superman" and "Return of Superman" story arcs are classics almost by default simply because they are so integral to the Superman mythos, whatever your feelings on the quality of those particular works aside. "World Without a Superman" (called "Funeral for a Friend" when it was originally published) bridges the gap between those two arcs, picking up right where the former left off (the first few panels are Lois still holding the dead Superman and Guardian trying to revive him) and leads us right up to the next arc, teasing us with the possibility of Superman's return.

Plotwise, WWAS covers the weeks following the Man of Steel's death, including a memorable funeral that features a procession of nearly all the DC heroes and a speech by then-President Bill Clinton. Metropolis's crime problem did not die with Superman, and everyone from kids to other heroes attempting to fill the void. A number of subplots are included, like an attempt to clone Superman from his dead body and medical drama in the Kent family.

The artwork in WWAS is very similar to the other two parts of the trilogy, and for the most part has no real weak points (with the notable exception of one of the Cadmus Project sections, which is simply horrendous, but it was originally published as a supplement to the "Funeral for a Friend" arc rather than a true chapter, so I'll forgive it). The story is also very moving in how human it is - all of us have lost a loved one and tried to fill the void, and this story simply extrapolates that to a global figure we all related to. One of the most touching points of the book is early on, as all the newscasts are reporting Superman's death, when someone asks "Jeez, did anything else happen in the world today?" to which another replies "If it did, it doesn't matter."

My only complaint is that the story drags at times, especially when read immediately in order as part of the trilogy. After the frantic pace of "Death of Superman" and the mind-boggling plot of "Return of Superman," the slow, human story of WWAS is not so much a break to catch your breath as it is a "race to the red light, slam on your breaks, watch the people on the street while you wait thirty seconds for the light to change, then floor it when the light turns green" - you appreciate what's going on, but you really want to get a move on to the next part. This is easily solved by spacing out your readings, however, and is one of the only weak points of an otherwise excellent graphic novel.

Before I get into the meat of my review, I must acknowledge that this album was one of several that distanced the "hardcore" Metallica fans from the band. Many felt betrayed by the band, which they had seen as moving away from their thrasher metal roots. This is indeed true; the album is very radio-friendly. That said, the album on its own is very solid, whatever your opinion of how it compares to the band's previous work.

From the distinctive opening noted of "Enter Sandman" all the way to the end notes of "The Struggle Within," there is not a bad song on this album. Several Metallica staples, including "The Unforgiven," "Sad But True" and "Nothing Else Matters" also make appearances on the album.

I know the above-mentioned "hardcore" fans find a positive review of this album a heresy, but for many who have never sampled metal before - myself included - this acts as a gateway album for getting into Metallica. An avid fan myself now, I would have never delved into "Ride the Lightning" or "Master of Puppets" if I hadn't heard "the black album" first.

I'm going to start out by saying I don't have much experience with cleavers. So a professional opinion this is not.

The first thing that struck me about the cleaver is that it is a full tang (i.e. the cleaver is made from a single piece of metal, with that metal extending the full length of the handle). I've seen too many piece of cutlery that were not full-tang snap off at the top of the handle to trust something I'll be hacking with unless it is full-tang.

The handle itself is wood and seems sturdy to me, but it's not particularly ergonomic for my (admittedly larger) hands. The grip gets a little uncomfortable after a few swings. And this might just be my inexperience talking, but the weight distribution feels a little off to me, and I keep getting the sensation that I'm losing control of the swing even when I'm not.

Speaking of swings, that's what this "Heavy Duty Cleaver" is for: you're not going to be slicing, you're going to be hacking. It does the hacking well, but if you try to do fine cutting with this you'll quickly find even a serrated steak knife is probably better-suited to the task. Stick to hacking, though, and this cleaver acquits itself well. The blade is sharp but not so sharp that it quickly dulls, gets stuck in the cutting board, or is particularly challenging to keep an edge on.

And it's a small touch, but I like how the hanging hold is a little larger than normal, making it a cinch to quickly store on a hook.

All in all, this is a good entry-level cleaver. I'm not sure that it would hold up well to constant use, but for the occasional uses I utilize it for it's pretty good.

The bass fitting is well made and highly polished. i was disappointed because the top of the pole tapers dramatically and the suggested Flagpole Rotating Rings do not fit. The swivels are for the bottom at 1-1/4" the top is much narrower. The product  photos are misleading. Now I know they are showing two (2) bottom poles that are both untapered.

I am keeping the flag poles but, unfortunately, wasted over $16 on the Flagpole Rotating Rings

Small box that expands into a large chair. The instruction say it takes a week to fully expand but it was 95% by the next day. I did help it along by fluffing it, punching it, and rolling it around. Very comfortable. Fabric cover is smooth and feels good. It also seems to be durable.
Easy to install, Good pressure, and seems sturdy enough to last
What can you say about a plastic cover? It works. It arrived unbroken and fit as expected
Love it. It is in my car all the time. I like the red glow around the edge. the dual outlet is great when people get in the car.
piece of junk that broke very quickly. Handle snapped on the first weekend use
I little flimsy but can get the job done. The hook does not fold smoothly into the handle.

Cheesy but great. Good graphics. The string ties on the side are good but will not withstand much pulling. Good size. I am over 6 feet tall and the bottom of the pizza slice was about a foot below my belt
Fits the Olympus TG-4 perfectly with space for extra memory cards and a cable.
Works just fine. I am still evaluating it and i am trying to see if it makes a difference in my plant growth. I have it on a timer every night for 6 hours to supplement the diminished winter sun.

I received this package quickly. The item was well packaged and could not have been damaged. It was easy to assemble and is still working well. As a reminder, the wall color is key to this clock. A dark wall will make the hands seem to disappear, a lighter color wall is better.

The disks are great and the quality seems fine. I woudl have liked if the packaging remained the same through out the seasons. I purchased the first seven season in the full pack version, thin pak was not available, and then purchased the last two season in thinpak. Its an aesthetic thing but it bugs me.

users.query: The case fits perfect and was inexpensive. It was well worth the purchase. Only reason for not giving it 5 stars is I could have done with out the imprinted X on the back of it.

cands.text: It has a nice fit but quality seems questionable. Time will tell how well it holds up. Was priced much cheaper here than at big box sporting goods stores.

OtterBox used to be my preferred brand for phone cases.  Not anymore.  Product quality is not as good as it used to be.  Item received appeared to have a defect whereas the soft rubber insert was unevenly shaped and not molded to properly form the contour of the phone.  Hard outer plastic cover is too slippery and feels slightly different, cheaper like, than past ones I've owned.

It's an okay bumper case with some flaws.  Bumper is nicely machined aluminum but it is a bit bulky.  Port holes are too small.  Some headphones and many charging cords will not fit while using this.  With some improvements this could really be a nice product.

This cover fits the Jenn Air 720-0337 perfectly.  The screened section allows just enough air to move through under windy conditions to help prevent the cover from tearing or getting blown off.  This is the second cover I've owned with my first one lasting nearly 5 years under full sun conditions.  It is a tad pricey and I wish the material was a bit thicker, but all in all a very good grill cover.

The 4.8" bag works very well for me holding an iPhone 6s in its slim hard case. It's a nice fit in my opinion; not too sloppy with too much room or to tight to manage getting it in and out.  In addition to a cellphone, the bag has enough room to easily hold your wallet, keys, and some essentials.  The Velcro straps work with holding it to the bike frame, but it does have some play.
This keyboard has some awesome features and looks great. Nice clicking too!!
This is an exact replacement and very easy to install.

It's a nice tri-fold wallet but not very slim.  RFID blocking works well, and the leather material is somewhat rigid and will break in nicely over time.  I wish it had the spare key holder slot, but most wallets seem to not have that feature anymore.

This table is beautiful.  It looks better in person than online.  Be aware to check the table's size before ordering as it is small, but is perfect for my application.  It pairs nicely with Leick's matching oval coffee table.  The quality is very good too.  The packaging is rather poor so inspect immediately upon arrival.  Luckily mine was fine even though the box didn't appear so.  It does ship in its originally box.
These work great for a tight fit but that's the way I like it.
These sunglasses look awesome online, however once received they looked and felt really cheap.  Quality is nothing like previous models.  A must return for me.
Good price compared to retail and Mopar's version.  Fits and functions perfectly.

These are by far the best Bluetooth headphones I've tried for the price range.  They fit better than anything else I've tried and I've tried several other brands/types.  They stay put quite well during physical activity and are comfortable.  For example during my 20 mile mountain biking ride I did not have to adjust them once.  And when I took them out, my ears did not feel sore at all.  As for sound quality they are descent, not perfect, but very good for the purpose; highs are good, mids are ok, lows are fair.

Great looking durable belt for all around casual wear  The reversible sides goes well with just about any men's pants or shorts.  The leather is thicker than many similar belts, and is also rather stiff.  Time will allow it to break in nicely but mine has not gotten too soft or out of shape in the 12 months that I have had it. In all fairness to other reviews,  I only wear this particular belt on average 4 days per week.

These replacement lenses are amazingly great quality for the price.  Only downside Ive experienced is with the Titanium Mirror Shield Coating, which for me started to flake from the lens.  Not sure if they were defective.  However in all fairness, I have had problems with mirrored coated lenses before including OEM and other brands, in the environment in which I wear them which is close to the ocean.  Rest assured though as Revant replaced them hassle free, and sent me a set of smoke instead.  Their customer service is awesome.

This table is beautiful.  It looks better in person than online.  Be aware it is a smaller than average coffee table but is perfect for my application.  It pairs nicely with Leick's matching end tables.  The quality is very good too.  The packaging is rather poor so inspect immediately upon arrival.  Luckily mine was fine even though the box didn't appear so.  It does ship in its originally box.
This cross/crucifix looks great.  The quality appears to be top notch.
Beware this is not compatible with the Elite controllers. Battery door is different. Bad decision by MS to change the controllers basic battery layout.

I should have returned the item when I had a chance, instead I figured I'd give it a try to see if I could get used to it. So 2 weeks later I do not like it. It is too big and doesn't fold proportionally across where it should. It has lots of slots for cards but if you use even half of them the wallet will be so thick it's uncomfortable to carry around in a back pocket. It has many layers in between slots and compartments. The leather material is really soft if you like that. I prefer more rigid leather that breaks in over time. On the upside the RFID blocking works well. The size is about 4 1/2" long when folded by 3 5/8" wide and just over 1 1/2" thick (when filled at half capacity). Also there are no spare key slots, which seems to have been discontinued on most wallets these days for some odd reason.
Great all around ball & bat bag for a reasonable price. Quality is good too.
Great tow strap for the price.  Several vehicles and a few tree stumps later it's still going strong.  I did notice some slight stretch in length but this is very typical of these types of straps.

This Wi-Fi plug could be so much better.  The user interface, IOS phone app, is poorly developed. It can not hold mutiple programmed schedules.  Also unit does not always respond days, or hours later. More time spent offline and or not responding than it's worth. There's better alternatives out there.

They look great and appear to be of very good quality.  Just wish it came in a larger size.  This set pairs nicely with www.amazon.com/dp/B00SFU9ZDU/ref=cm_cr_ryp_prd_ttl_sol_7?th=1 (ASIN: B00SFU9ZDU)

Stay away from these unless you want problems.

Mcgard claims "Every McGard wheel lock is fully machined from restricted chemistry steel made specifically for McGard and through-hardened for its unsurpassed level of security".  Well the unsurpassed level of security is true for the wheel lug lock, but not so for the lug key.

I HAD these on a Dodge Ram 1500 and the lug key broke while changing out a flat- not once, but on 3 different subsequent occasions.  Luckily for me the first one that came with my truck brand new broke after I put the spare tire on while tightening the wheel lug lock back on.  I figure no big deal, it could have been worst.  At least Im no stranded somewhere in inclement weather.  So I had to go through McGard's customer service department to order a replacement lug key at approximately $15 (plus shipping if you want it expedited).  After 2 weeks go by, it finally arrived.  I never really inspected it when the replacement one arrived; rather I just tossed it in my glove box.  About 2 months later, when I needed it for the first time, the replacement lug key also snapped.  Except this time I had a leaking tire that would not hold air for more than a day, which I was attempting to take off.  Well once again I was on the phone with McGard customer service, ordering a new lug key.  They refused to replace the one they sent me at no cost, so I was stuck paying another $15 for a second replacement lug key.  Again, I waited about 2 weeks for it to arrive because I was not about to spend another $30 for them to overnight it to me.  After 2 weeks it arrived, and I was able to remove the leaking tire.  I then go to remove another wheel, which was the temporary spare from a couple months ago, and this second replacement key snapped.  I couldn't believe it.  Three keys breaking like this in about as many months with the last 2 being ordered back-to-back.  The third time was it for me.  No more McGard!!!  I decided not to order another one at cost and wait another unreasonable amount of time for shipping since there was no guarantee it wouldnt happen again.  Besides McGards customer service seemed to care less about the issue altogether.

I decided to break the lug locks off manually without a key.  See my very basic instructions at the end of this review if you are interested.  It is a bit of work but can be done if you are in a situation where you cannot or do not want to wait.  With the proper tools, patience and muscle I was able to remove all 3 (the 1st one came off with the 3rd lug key before it broke) in about an hour with no damage to my wheels or the studs.  Costs to me were about $15 for 2 deep well 12-point sockets which became ruined in the process, plus my time.  The net-net here is no more dealing with McGard, and risking being stuck in a bad situation.

Now some may say the lug locks must have been put on too tight, however that was not the case.  I tighten all my lug nuts and lug locks by hand with a torque wrench.  In this particular application, specs call for 135 ft-lbs per lug nut, however with the lug locks I go much less at 90 ft-lbs (as a precautionary measure).

My conclusion is the metal they are using for these lug keys are of cheap grade, and too malleable for its purpose.  They quite possibly have a quality control issue in their production machine shop and or the manufacturing of these for it to be a repetitive problem as I experienced.  My advice, if you must have lug locks, I highly recommend you go with the spline type.

Here are some basic instructions if you break your key or lost it and want to remove the lug locks yourself.  Be advised this may not work on all vehicles, and or may cause damage.

1. The McGard lug locks have an outer cylindrical band that spins on them so you cannot simply grab onto the outside perimeter of the lug lock to loosen them.  For instance bolt extractors or specialty wrenches will not work.  For this reason you will first need to remove this outer metal band.  Take a thin flat head screw driver or similar flat tool like a small chisel and hammer in between this outer metal band and the lug lock inner nut.  If you look closely the outside edge of the lug lock has a bit of a raised lip, but with some persistence and a steady hand you can get it in there by tapping with a hammer.  Once in, keep hitting lightly while trying to pry it apart.
2. Once the metal band breaks apart, and you can easily remove it by hand or with needle nose pliers
3. Now take a deep well 12-point socket, sized smaller than the diameter of the lug lock, and hammer it on with a sledge hammer.  Make sure it mashes down enough on top of the lug lock that it bites into the outer edge lip that I mentioned in step 1.
4. Take your breaker bar, attached to the socket mashed onto the lug lock and now attempt to break it loose.
5. If the socket spins, without biting into the lug lock nut, then you will either need to beat the socket on further so it covers the portion of the lug lock where it raises back out (becomes wider) just past where the outer metal band was removed.  Or alternatively, you will need to remove the socket and replace with the next size down and repeat from step 3 until it bites into the lug lock bolt enough so it can be loosened from the bolt studs.

My Xbox unit is 30+ feet away from the screen and Kinect unit, and this cable works very well for my home entertainment layout.  Only reason for not rating 5 stars is the attached ferrite core is rather large which presented some challenges with pulling it through an AV wall plate/gang box, and upon start up of the Xbox, there is slight delay with initiating the Kinect unit.  However this clears up and does not hinder performance thereafter.  I've tried many different other cables and wiring solutions and this by far has been the best.

users.query: I saw this when it originally came out but my wife didn't, so after years she has finally agreed to watch it. I think this is the best TV series ever made with the best finale that's ever been conceived. I think she's coming on board with me.

cands.text: It took me a bit to get into this as I was waiting for a story to break out. But once the plot got going it held my interest until the very end which was quite contrived...a lot like one of those TV dramas where they lead you to believe the threat has ended and then try to surprise you with one more peril. In this case, it was one peril too many. But I enjoyed the read so I'll give it a "not great" but certainly good enough.

Okay, I'm going to ignore the ending for a moment (which is so quick that the book ends before the reader even knows what's up). This is a really terrific legal thriller. Great characters, a really good protagonist, and a plot that will keep you going. At times it's funny. It's always interesting with just enough twists to keep you guessing. I'm going to read more in the series. It's that good. However...that ending!!! I can say "wow I didn't expect that." However that doesn't refer to "whodunnit." It refers to resolution so quick as to knock your socks off. When I taught journalism I always taught that the ending is the hardest part of the story. Many stories just STOP. I always sought what I referred to as a "cigarette" moment...you know, the moment after "you know what" when you're completely satisfied. This book stopped, and abruptly. However, 99% of it was so good that I'm giving the ending a pass. You'll like this one.

I really enjoyed this one. It moves quickly, the plot is interesting and Stephen Carpenter makes you care about the characters. It has that hard-nosed detective feel to the narrative, and the chapters are short and quick. I really liked it.

My theory is life's too short to continue reading a bad book. And this one was bad. I have read every book in this series, but I quit this one about a third in. Way too complicated and difficult to follow. The only scenes I like were the prison scenes, and they could not carry my interest. I guess I'm done with Liz Salander.

Haven't finished it yet, but I've read her other two novels, and they were great. This is an open invitation for Gillian Flynn to have coffee with me. I must find out what's behind her "sick" mind (and I mean that in the best possible way). She is one helluva writer.

I love legal thrillers, and this was a great one. Lots of twists and turns, and about 75% in when I thought I had it figured out... I didn't. It kept me turning the pages, and even better, thinking about the story when I wasn't even reading. William Myers really knows how to spin a great legal yarn. And as soon as I finished it, I bought his second book.

I'm a big Seinfeld fan, so I read this specifically to learn about the behind-the-scenes goings on. Some reviewers complained there was too much emphasis on the writers, but that's what I found so compelling about this book. It's well written, well researched and a must read if you were a fan of the show. Wish it were longer - I could have read a lot more.

I really loved this book. I found the plot very interesting and the characters engaging. I had not read a Quinn novel previously, but now I think I'm hooked and I intend to spend a lot more time with Quinn. You'll like this a lot. I sure did.

This is so well done, it's hard to believe it's a first novel. I think Jeff Miller is going to be a very productive novelist. His main character, Dagny Gray,is very likeable with a good back story and a heroine's demeanor. His writing style is fast-paced and propels you to the next page, next chapter, etc. And though the ending was a little too predictable (and I still don't really understand the motive of the "bad guy"), it was satisfying enough that I hope Miller is working on the next Dagny Gray novel. Bottom line is, you'll enjoy this read a lot.

I once heard a story about a writer who couldn't come up with a satisfactory ending for his book so he wrote the following: "Suddenly, a truck came over the hill and killed everyone." The Conviction reminds me of that. A decent story relatively well told until the end where several events come together to miraculously solve the puzzle. Also, does no one edit e-books? There are more mistakes and typos in this book than in any I have read in recent memory. As for the book, it was a decent read until the final couple of chapters, which kind of spoiled the entire read for me.

I'm a big fan of 60 Minutes, so this was a wonderful opportunity for me to get a look behind the scenes of this magnificent program. I thought there was a good bit of repetition of information and it could have probably used a better editor. But for anyone who has enjoyed this iconic program over the years, this book is well worth reading.

Katy Tur did such a fabulous job with this. I'm a retired TV journalist and even though I never covered a national campaign, her stories ring true from what I've both witnessed and heard about. I always like her reporting, but this book increased my respect for Katy and all the journalist who went through hell to report on the Trump campaign. I bow to Katy's talent. Great read
I read 10 chapters of this. Couldn't' get into it, so I quit. Cannot recommend. The story did not go anywhere. Boring to the max.

This is my second Sheldon Siegel book, and it's another winner. I love Siegel's "voice," how he interjects his character's thoughts just ahead of the dialogue. Daley and Fernandez are excellent characters, and the plots are interesting enough to keep you wanting to move forward in the story. I expect to read all the Mike Daley books. I feel as if I've found "my" novelist. I bet you'll love them as much as I do.
One of the best books I've ever read.  Can't believe I waited so many years to read it. Love it.

So many legal thrillers are compared to Grisham novels and fail to meet that gold standard. This one meets it. It has it all. A good plot with interesting twists that are not telegraphed. A likeable hero who's not "godlike." A narrative that keeps you turning pages. I could go on and on, but you don't need that from me. Just know that this is a really good read that is definitely worth your time and attention. I'm now an official Scott Pratt fan, and I'll be reading more of his work.

I'm about halfway through this book. I like to read mysteries and thrillers, and I find this book is "quieter" than many of the suspense books I read. But in this case, that's a good thing. Lashner's characters are interesting and well described, and the plot of this one slowly thickens. As I say, I'm halfway through, and I think I know "who dunnit" but that usually means I'm 100% wrong. The other thing is I almost never drink hard liquor. But Lashner's descriptions of bar drinks and how they are made by a pro has me thinking I may ask for a drink next time I'm in a nice restaurant. (Nah, probably not. I'm too cheap to spend $12 or so on a drink). But he has me desiring them. Anyway, this is a good and gentle read, and I recommend it.

This is the second Jack Rhodes mystery I read. Like the first one (Killer), it grabbed my attention and held it. Rhodes is a great character and one I hope to follow as Stephen Carpenter, hopefully, continues the series. We're not talking about great literature here. We are talking about good, strong characters, strong plotting, and a narrative that sweeps you along to a satisfying conclusion. You'll like this book a lot.

This book was great. It's a page turner even though the 2 main characters sit and watch their intended victim for page after page. Mr. Seymour is a skilled writer to be able to pull this off and sustain suspense when there's a lot of non-action going on. You really get to know these two characters, who could not be more un-alike. I loved it.
Hang on for a great read. Just the kind of thriller that grabs you at the top and keeps you immersed in the story. Now I'm going to have to read more Murray McDonald novels. Loved it.
I had not read Dugoni before, but I found this book very compelling and interesting. It kept me turning the pages. I intend to read more of his novels.

This is my second Tyler Dilts book although I read them out of order. I'm not on my third. Dilts hero, Det. Danny Beckett is very believable and likeable. To Dilts' credit, he refrains from making Beckett a cartoon hero with almost super powers. Instead, this is a hard-working homicide dective who's more than willing to do the laborious work it takes to find a killer. The plots feel as if they've been taken from a local newspaper, meaning they're real. The only flaw in this book is Dilts' math when he writes about some of the dates in the victim's history early in the book. I'm no math major, but by my calculations, he's off by about ten years. The victim would have had to been born 10-years earlier for the math to work out. So Dilts is no math major, but he is a heck of a writer. I'm reading the third book in this series now and hoping the fourth is not far off. You'll love this series and this book too.

I really like Michael Buble, but not so much this time.  I like the standard Christmas songs to be done like standards.  On some songs, that's how he interpreted them and that's why I gave it three stars.  But jazzy renditions of some of these songs turn me off.  I should have listened more closely before I bought this.  It's near the bottom of my Christmas music collection.
I had read a review of this book that said it was terrific and the reviewer is spot on.  Great read.

users.query: Humans are not necessarily going to be the winners in this series.  However, the aliens are not necessarily going to be evil.  Also, the most unlikely and happy things can continue to be the winners of this series. When this story is complete, the humans have yet to be the winners of this series and the different types of  enemies are not necessarily going to be  winners.

cands.text: Amazingly imaginative in the creation of a righteous philosophy of the aliens. You will be unfulfilled if you don't continue reading the series. As most stories go, the humans are always going to be the winners in the final chapters. However, in this series, the humans are not necessarily going to be the winners.

The humans are possibly going to be beaten by the most horrible enemy Overlord and lose the future of mankind. The aliens have been able to be an extremely difficult challenge and deadly. The. SYSTEM OVERLORD has been able to set up traps that can totally destroy the entire human fleet. The only question is if the humans are going to avoid the traps.

So many extremely unexpected twists and turns throughout this story are doubled in this the final book of this series. The aliens have been more than willing to totally destroy entire species in their campaign to totally dominate the galaxy. The time has come for the attack on the earth and the defenses do NOT look like they are going to be enough.

Corruption and deadly enemies abound in this story with aliens and corrupt politicians. In other words, nothing seems to be different from many ways of the present day except for the aliens invading. The humans are not necessarily going to be the winners unless they were very very lucky and the aliens are not necessarily going to be the winners. The humans are not different from many of today's norm; the political leaders are what you expect, and the different types of military are very normal in this story. However, as this story progresses, several people are presented as very different from the standard. These are the surprise twists that continue to happen in this story and the different ways that things happen. Surprises continue all the time and add to the excellence of this story.

When you think about it, we are not necessarily going to be the winners in the future of mankind. We are not the most important thing in the future of mankind. We are fighting against our own natural instincts to achieve the most and be the winners. Unfortunately, the enemy forces in this series is not imagined. The worst thing is that they are us! We can only pray for guidance.

I would love to see this series made into another science fiction T.V.series. There are more than a few surprises in this story. The aliens have been able to get the most unlikely and horrible things planned for their attack on the Earth. The humans have been able to get together with many extremely unexpected twists and deadly serious plans. The final battle between the two will be disastrous for one of them.

The aliens have been able to attack the humans and meme and all the different types of aliens that were not Scourge but they have now been beaten repeatedly. The humans must now expect them to attack in a larger version of its all-out destroy-all and eat everything plan. The humans are not willing to be destroyed by the enemy, so they must find a way to defeat the enemy completely. They should take the fight to the enemy leadership.

Unique twists and turns in the most unlikely ways to achieve the decidedly different and intriguing story. The aliens have been more than ready to totally eliminate all the humans .... or so it seems. The main hero of this story is not comfortable in his role and constantly questions himself. But the majority of his decisions work out in his favor. Then, the humans are put into what could possibly be the "final battle"for the decision on whether or not the entire remaining human population is to survive or be destroyed.

How does anyone have any time to be the most unlikely and interesting subject of a very different story. The aliens are not necessarily going to be the strange experience of a righteous person. The humans are possibly going to be the strange experience of the aliens. Some weapons will always be the mind of the most unlikely and horrible things that can happen. Words cannot be expected to achieve the same as a very different weapon of alien construct. However, you don't have to fight the most unlikely and horrible things that can happen in this series.

The aliens have been more aggressively moving forward to the distruction of the humans. The humans have been more aggressively fighting against the aliens and have been building more ships. The aliens have been moving forward and attacking more planets. The beginning of the end is almost in sight, and the view is NOT so good.

As the saga continues, a new enemy and a possible new ally arrive in this new system that they have just taken from the aliens. The new threat and possible help are in their own conflict and may not be able to find the best results for the humans. However, the best results against failure often can be used by the most unlikely and bizarre actions of well meaning but naive people. Only time will tell.

The humans are not willing to be the most horrible curse of all the different ways that things could possibly be wrong with the most unlikely war against aliens that are not really aliens. The Hok armies turn out to be humans that have been changed by the enemy to be the most horrible things that you can imagine. The real enemies abound in this series and the different types of aliens are constantly being used by the "good guys" . The octopus looking alien is not the easiest to like as they think very differently than the humans. However, they are very good guys and provide many extremely unexpected ways to achieve the best results against the real enemies.

Nobody has a clue about almost everything involved in the most unlikely hero of this story. The humans have been able to get together with many extremely unexpected twists before arriving at the most horrible and deadly war against the aliens who had destroyed the humans and enslaved them. However,the war against the aliens was not necessarily going to have the results that they were expecting. The secret weapon that the humans have discovered was not necessarily going to be as good as they hoped.

Although most people are not necessarily going to have an interest in how an enemy disposed of their captives, the humans are definitely not willing to be captured alive.  The aliens are not willing to stop fighting against the humans as they think in totally different ways from most humans.

Although the most unlikely and horrible things that continue to happen are mostly against the lizards, Skippy and crew have been able to survive mostly without losing any of their own. The aliens have been able to prevent some of the worst things that were planned against them, but they have been consistently lacking in successfully preventing the humans from many different types of disasters that the humans had set up against the aliens. The humans have been able to get most of their goals completed without the aliens finding out that humans have been able to get into space. That secret is the most important one in this series.

I am certain that Nick Webb spent many hours or days on parts of this story. The humans and aliens are certainly well described as they think in this series. The story itself is very different from most of the science fiction stories that I have read over the past sixty years or so. I really enjoyed this series and the surprise twists and the surprise ending.  I am not necessarily surprised that the humans in this series are not different from what they are today; especially the political leaders.

More information about almost everything involved with the most unlikely and hopeful series about a possible future. This series is not the easiest way to make sure that you would like to be able to find out the newest enemy of mankind is not the only way to be able to get into the next new and improved world. However, the aliens have been able to get the job done by the most horrible curse of all time and the different ways that things could possibly change the humans have been more aggressively applied than the humans have been able to fight. Many of the most important things that can happen to anyone in this series have been able to find out what constitutes an extremely unexpected twist of fate. The aliens have not yet lost the battle to achieve their goals and deadly intent.
How long  will the aliens bleed the humans? How long can the humans fight back before they totally give up?  Will any of the original few last long enough to see the end of the war ?

War continues to evolve into the most horrible disasters this world has ever seen. The aliens have been able to counter every new tactic against them and find more deadly ways to continue the attacks on humans and all their resources. Things keep going from bad to worse.

A battle in space against the aliens would have been lost in seconds if the aliens had been more alert and cooperative with each other. And the humans would have lost badly. As usual, they were notr necessarily going to get together with many others. The aliens have now been warned of the most important information about the humans.

Very believable tale set in the times of Jack the Ripper but not involving the Ripper. Some people were infinately worse than Jack the Ripper. Lives of common people were of little value to those of the Upper Class .

Two very young kids who have been at each other whenever they could are forced to help each other to try to survive and save themselves and their own parents when their spaceship is attacked by pirates. The story is very good and the most unlikely facts about everything involved are easily accepted as they are well written and thoroughly explained. Altogether, a very different and intriguing story with many extremely deadly possible endings.

How does anyone become a killer or a drug addict? If you have the right kind of friends or the wrong kind, they can make it really easy. If you are really lucky, you might possibly get away with the murder and get your life straightened out. Then again, the past can haunt you endlessly until it catches up with you.

The honor of the leaders of the Alliance is never in doubt. The lack of honor of the  Jung from the lowest to the leaders remains to be consistent. A new tactic of the Jung involving nanites is going to be a major problem for the Alliance. I would love to see this series as a TV show or even better, as a series of movies.
