Only 3 calories!  I purchased a number of different kinds of training treats, including these, when I recently brought home a rescue dog.  Besides his former owner house training him, the boy knew nothing.  In the 3 weeks between his first vet visit and his booster shot, I put 10# on him.  While he carries it well, it was not my intention to plump him up, and he's now on a weight-reduction plan.  These treats are perfect, though.  They are not sticky, will not melt in your hand or pocket, and they will not pack on the pounds.  The cats, who have been rolling over on command for years, like them too.  This is a staple on my Amazon Wish List.

The antler appeared to have been sterilized and polished and clipped on one end.  This chew was extremely skinny.  It was a little over 1 inch in diameter at its widest clipped end and tapered to what I considered a dangerously sharp point at the other end.  What I allowed my 50# shepherd mix to have lasted less than a full 24 hours after being given to him.  I took away the last 3 inches to avoid having the pointed end swallowed whole.  He still has 4 inches of a wider antler purchased 5 months ago (no longer in stock at the time of this order). To be fair, the previous one was twice the price, not on sale and not Prime, but, nevertheless, a value by comparison.

My review should reflect a verified purchase for which I received no remuneration.

The herd has taste tested no fewer than a dozen different kinds of cat food, with varying results. Each of the 3 has his/her own preferences for their own reasons. The bully will eat anything so we won't dwell on his preferences. The formerly feral female is sometimes a little more choosy than you would expect, and the "Felix" (from The Odd Couple) cat is the most challenging. This kibble is about the size and slightly concave shape of a pencil eraser. Felix (not his real name) has finally learned how to bite kibble as a result instead of swallowing it whole and often choking on it - a completely counter-intuitive effect.  They love the taste.  They are eating less due to the protein content.  Their waste is reduced and less smelly.  They're drinking more water.  Their coats are soft and their eyes are shiny.  They're more playful.  There has been no post-meal vomiting. THIS is IT.

I have returned to upgrade this to 4 stars because, despite the picture of what this product supposedly looks like in the bowls as compared to the package picture, my cats are still healthy, have had no digestive problems, and are much peppier and more playful than they had been before switching to this kibble, and they love it. I will be reordering.
-------------
This was purchased from Amazon since my grocery store has never carried this variety.  It is a mixture of mostly tan and reddish-brown crunchy kibble with VERY FEW teeny, tiny, itsy, bitsy pieces of those "meaty tender morsels" of chicken that you will need a magnifying glass and plenty of time to locate. No resemblance whatsoever to the photo.  Pfft.  Since cat-boy had a really bad digestive reaction to Purina's turkey kibble, and dog-boy got a severe yeast infection from their turkey morsel kibble (potatoes high on the ingredient list), I thought it best to stick to the chicken.  Please send your best wishes our way.

The first large (extra?) Lambchop I purchased came from Amazon, and my destructo-dog loved it.  He seems to have a preference for toys with squeekers.  It is about half his own size, so he has some difficulty getting a grip to tear things off because it is so plush. While I am a little frustrated by the squeeker moving around in the belly of the beast, the search occupies him.  Then I purchased the smaller one (twice) from the grocery store aisle - one to play with while the other is in the wash.  He knows there are squeekers in the paws, but hasn't been able to "work" them and focuses on the belly squeeker.  The top seam on one of the small ones did come apart even though it was in a laundry bag and is awaiting my repair. I have found them to be worth the expense.  Other toys have not survived his concentrated efforts to dismantle, puncture, shred, or eat them.

Spraying up-wind of this stuff has become a priority, as is closing the windows before going outside.  I have enjoyed my flowering hostas and my ferns enormously this year, and the deer haven't.  Had a live urban red fox for a while that rid my yard of the rabbits and squirrels, but someone must have called Wildlife Mgmt. or it found a more habitable location because they both returned.  Whatever is in this formula works very well, and the smell really only lasts (for humans) for a short time.  The pump sprayer works very well and is adjustable for a wide mist or a straight stream and any number of middle settings. There's a feature that locks it in the open position for ergonomic reasons, I suppose, that frustrated me for a moment because I couldn't turn off the flow until I figured it out. I've used it multiple times over the season and have not experienced any leakage.  Good purchase.  When they develop a squirrel repellent, I'll be first in line.

Shark products have the most amazing suction!  It almost vacs up stains!  I've been collecting huge amounts of cat litter dust and dust from any number of other sources since switching from a Hoover.  I bought an extra set of foam and felt filters so there is always one clean and dry and ready to use.

The model has a few shortcomings.  The vacuum head is rather narrow, which is okay when going between dining chair legs without moving them, but which requires more strokes for open areas.  There is no place to attach an extension rod -- it has to be fetched from wherever the attachment bag is located -- for vacuuming those pesky spider webs in high places, and the "stretchy" extension part is not very stretchy at all.  The unit is top-heavy and often falls over when using that part unless it is positioned just so.  The lift-away container likes to hold onto that very fine dust, which makes wiping it out a frequent necessity.  I have had to place a trash can in the garage because it does not empty cleanly and spews this same very fine dust back into the room.

Again, the suction is remarkable; it gets the cat's very fine fur as well as the dog's double-coated fine and stiff fur and all the dust I mentioned before.  It is lightweight and easy to maneuver.  Love the way tilting the handle changes the direction of the stroke.  Nice long cord, sadly, not retractable.

I do like it a lot and feel I can breathe better since switching.

This turned out to be perfect for pre-treating the wooden (forgot the type) shower seat I recently purchased. The water beads up exactly as I had intended. Applying it to the individual slats and base of the stool took about an hour. I allowed it 24 or so hours to be absorbed before using it in the shower. Obviously, since it's the equivalent of "food grade," I have no qualms about placing my butt on it. I did not purchase the applicator that is advertised on the same page, and sort of wish I had, although it may have been too thick to fit between the slats effectively.  Instead, I used a Scotch-Brite scrubber. You'd have to have an awful lot of salad bowls to be able to use up the contents, so I found the amount (and accordingly, the price) was more than I would have preferred.  I feel certain that I will find other uses for the remainder, including refreshing the shower seat, but it may take awhile.

UPDATE (March 24th):  Have added the fifth star because, six weeks after receiving them and almost immediately after posting the original review, my big boy decided the small tunnel was a nice, snug fit after all. That's where I find him most of the time now, and, of course, it's their job to make liars of us.

(March 13th): The little formerly feral female particularly likes the long tunnel with the peep hole and has made it her own. It captures the blown heat from the vent where I placed it, and she can see what dangers lurk nearby. The smaller one is too small for the easy-going male, and he had no interest in it beyond an occasional swipe at the jingle ball from outside the tunnel. Ultimately, I cut that off and tied a knot at the end of the string so he could swing it around, which he much prefers. My rating is generous from a cat-likeability perspective, but the tunnels are well made, with sturdy fabric, and the krinkle factor (of the smaller one) *should* have been more attractive to one or both of them based upon hosting a lot of cats over a lot of years.

This is a very lightweight, fragile basket which you will not want to use for any item(s) heavier than a loaf of bread. As another reviewer stated, the color shown online is much lighter than what was received. Due to poor packaging which included a substantially heavier item, one of two received was damaged in transit.  Both were returned and credited promptly.

My television has a power saving feature that turns off the picture if it is on hold (YouTube, Netflix, etc.) too long, so I thought a little light to guide me back to the remote in an otherwise dark room would be a good thing. My really old house has very few outlets not in use, so the battery option was mandatory especially since Im not sure where I want to place it. Because I have a vindictive cat (and they always have some kinda gripe), I stuck a few tiny drawer bumpers left over from some project onto the slippery plastic base to help keep it in place. Theres nothing elegant about it but it fits in with my decor, does the job, and the price was right.  It lost two stars when the specially purchased AAA batteries turned out to be too small. I have NO use for them so it drove up the price considerably.

Bought the XL for my medium size rescue dog, with issues, referred to elsewhere as Destruct-O-Boy.  Seven wks ago, it was offered to him as a 10" chew with 3 good size points and a root(?).  Today, it has been reduced to a 6" length missing all its points, BUT, he has eliminated long braided rawhide chews within the hour.  He has yet to start working on the root, or whatever it's called.  He uses it to de-stress and/or fill his time indoors. There is no mess left behind when he moves on to other activities; it did not splinter or cause any ill effects.  It has been worth the money for the length of time it has survived. This has qualified as a staple.

I used this again today.  It has a smooth operation; still no unwanted drippy stream from any of its joints.  If something could be improved upon, it would be the ability to lock it open.  I think the picture here shows it, but I couldn't find it.

users.query:
Great full-bodied English Breakfast tea.  No discernible bitterness.  Full-bodied with good medium malty flavor and an earthy finish.  Not as malty as the Assam, but darker and slightly more tannic.  Not as full-bodied as the Irish Breakfast.

My recommendation for brewing (I like my tea strong and full-bodied with a bit of sweetener and milk, Indian or English style):  1 level teaspoon per 8 fl oz of filtered water that has been brought JUST to the boil.  Put into a large brewing vessel like the Teavana Perfect Tea Maker http://www.amazon.com/Teavana-PerfecTea-Tea-Maker-16oz/dp/B004X7DIHI/

Steep no longer than 3 minutes and dispense into a big mug that has been warmed.  Add milk and sweetener to taste - a great way to start any day!  :-)

Some people like to use less tea and brew for a longer time, but this will make fore a much more bitter and less flavorful cup of tea

cands.text:
If you are an English or Irish Breakfast Tea drinker and enjoy the heavier/maltier side of the tea spectrum, this may be a nice choice for you.  The is particularly true if you drink your English Breakfast tea in bags or pouches (you owe it to yourself to get a good infuser like this one: http://www.amazon.com/Adagio-Teas-ingenuiTEA-Bottom-Dispensing-Teapot/dp/B000FPN8TK

Some reviewers have complained that this tea comes as mostly dust and fannings, but I did not find that to be the case with my package.  It definitely contained more dust/fannings than some of the finer grade Assam I buy from a local tea shop, but I'd attribute that more to the fact that it is being mail-ordered in small quantities and not being graded again after receipt.  (see photo for the character of my batch at the bottom of the bag once I'd consumed most of the tea in the bag).

As to the flavor profile and character, I should first say that my taste preference is on the extreme side of earthy/malty with as little astringency (tannin) as possible.  I drink my tea with milk and agave syrup as a general rule.  My typical favorites are certain Assam teas (which I typically brew heavy but short) and Irish or Scottish Breakfast blends.  I also generally enjoy good quality Keemun and Dianhong teas.

My general reaction to this particular tea blend is that it stands up well to a heavier brew (the way I like) but it is very sensitive to over-brewing.  The directions say 3-5 minutes, but I found that a 3 minute brew at 195 to be just at the edge of my preference for astringency, but having a great full body, malty character, and more exotic/floral notes than a typical Assam or Breakfast blend.  The smell of the dried leaves almost seems like there is some bergamot (what gives Earl Grey its distinct flavor) but there is no mention of any additives to this tea blend, so I have to assume that it is coming from one of the more exotic varieties of tea used in this blend.  Speaking of additives, I've poked through the leaf mix and there is nothing in this blend besides tea leaves, so please ignore reviewers that mention bits of citrus or other additives - this looks to be a pure tea blend (and this is also stated by the producer).

In summary, if you like a good hearty cup of tea and are looking for something with a bit more complexity and a different flavor profile, but still with the maltiness and caffeine kick of a good Breakfast tea, give this one a try.  But do yourself a favor and throw away that "ball" type infuser and get a full-cup infuser like the one I linked to above!

Forget those useless little "tea balls" - they simply don't allow enough "breathing room" for your loose leaf tea to steep properly.  if you enjoy a good cup of tea (especially a nice dark Assam or English Breakfast) then you owe it to yourself to bring one of these on your next trip rather than relying on awful bagged tea at your destination!

I gave two stars because this COULD be such a great product.  Perfect for my family, where my wife and I both drink different brew each day.  Also perfect for camping.  A great idea that could so easily be a four or five star product.

Unfortunately, despite repeated attempts, I could not get these mugs to brew coarse ground coffee without having an unacceptable amount of grinds floating around in the brew.  I tried different water levels, different grinds of coffee, different temperatures of water, and different speeds of plunging (the last and final was done so excruciatingly slowly that even if it had resulted in a mug of coffee without grinds I probably would still be returning the mugs.)

I've been drinking French Press coffee at home for many years, so I am accustomed to the inescapable bits of coffee bean you get in your cup.  This unit delivers very poor results.  Let me put it this way: if you don't mind sucking your coffee through your teeth, then spitting out the grinds before your next sip, then this mug could be the ticket.  Even the best result of the four or five attempts I made resulted in about 1-1/2 teaspoons grinds in the strainer I used to test the results.  (1. Brew coffee according to directions, 2. push plunger down, 3. pour results through fine strainer.)

I'm going to return this item and keep looking for the perfect insulated single-serving French Press.  Bummer.

Worked well for intermittent use for the first few years. I recently switched completely to drinking tea every morning and after about 2 months of daily use it stopped shutting off automatically when boiling.  Then after another 6 months the electrical contacts in the base wore out so that it won't reliably heat water.

For $30 I suppose that's about what can expect in terms of lifespan.  Now that I'm a daily user, I'll probably replace it with something that is higher end and will hopefully last longer.

After spending a month researching options for pod coffee makers, I settled on the SimpleHuman.  The big draws for me were the sleek looks, small footprint, and reputation of the company for good customer service.  (I always believe that deserves to be rewarded).

My wife drinks decaf and I drink regular - usually one cup each.  Making two cups a day from our Krups thermal carafe was getting to be a real hassle, not to mention grinding beans, etc.  I was spending 20 minutes every morning just making two cups of coffee!

For me this was more of a convenience item - little did I know how impressed I would be with the quality of the coffee this little blue and steel machine makes!  The Molto coffees that it ships with are great (don't hesitate to order extra when you order the machine, especially the Sumatra Mandheling if you like a really rich, flavorful cup of coffee)

Note that this is NOT an espresso machine - I would compare it to  a fresh cup of drip coffee that you would get at a gourmet coffee house, perhaps a little better since it never splashes into an urn and then squirts out into a paper cup, but is dispensed straight from the beans a few inches into your waiting mug.

The design allows you to leave the water tank in place and simply fill it with a pitcher (something I cannot do with my Melitta One:One pod machine) and holds enough for about 5 full sized cups of coffee.

The brew temperature is very consistent at about 185-187 degrees measured at the stream coming from the spout (this is measured without a coffee pod) and consistently delivers just over 8 fl oz for the large size and about 6 oz for the small size (even though it says 5 oz).

I highly recommend this coffee machine if you are the kind of person that gets up and just wants that one really good cup of coffee to get going in the morning, and then maybe another one an hour or so later after a walk or workout, etc.  With this machine (or any other pod brewer) you don't have coffee sitting around getting stale in a thermal carafe or urn - it is brewed fresh every time.

In my opinion the only drawback of the Simplehuman is the lack of an ability to make larger than an 8 oz cup.  With the regular 9 gram coffee pods, this is not a problem, since the coffee is just right with 8 oz, but companies like Baronet are starting to make 12 gram pods and it would be nice to be able to make a 10 oz cup of coffe for a travel mug or larger "to go" coffee.

Some will complain about the immovable spout, but I find that by removing the grate and drip tray I can easily fit most of my stainless steel travel mugs except for the very tall narrow ones.

I bought a mini instant pot for my senior mom because she loves to cook, but I wanted something easy for her to make quick nutritious meals.  She's very innovative, and rarely uses cookbooks, but the "technology" in the instant pot throws her off a bit.  This cookbook is the perfect accompaniment to the gift, in that it takes easy recipes (that she can riff on) and explains step-by-step how to program the machine for each recipe, including which release method to use.

If you're a gourmet cook, you'll find the recipes very simplistic, but you can use them as a starting point for other innovations.  For those just starting out with an Instant Pot, its a great way to dive into the various cooking methods available with the machine.

Taste is a very subjective thing, so take this review along with others and form your own opinions.  I'll review this on three axes - Taste/quality, packaging, and Sourcing.

Sourcing
 You may not know this, but a LOT of chocolate produced in the world is made under circumstances that would horrify all but the most jaded people. Cacao production involves a lot unskilled labor in countries notorious for human rights abuses, and the economics of the chocolate industry create an environment ripe for human exploitation.  In much the same way as "fair trade coffee" has been gaining ground in recent years, UTZ certification is gaining ground in the chocolate industry.  UTZ certification purports to ensure that no forced/child labor is used in the production of the cacao, and that sustainable practices are used.  This of course means that the chocolate ultimately produced is more expensive, but personally I'd rather go without chocolate than know I'm eating something that literally could have been produced by a child stolen from his parents in some far off third world country (I'm not making this up - Google it yourself).  With UTZ certification, this chocolate can be "guilt-free" at least in that respect.

Packaging
The bar itself is thin - about 4mm or so thick, and I think it originally had "scoring" along its length to allow you to snap off a piece at a time.  Unfortunately with all the warm weather we've been having in Southern California, my bar had obviously melted during shipping and while still relatively flat, was misshapen and had basically "glued" itself to the foil wrapper and was no longer completely flat.  Peeling it apart was quite a chore.  Think about this when ordering - if you live in a hot climate, or it is a warm season, you may want to reconsider, unless you're just using it to cook with.  Speaking of which, the flavor and appearance of the chocolate itself did not seem to be negatively affected by melting.  There was no graininess, blotchy discoloration, or other typical problems associated with melting and re-hardening of chocolate.  The outside packaging is just as shown in the listing on Amazon, with what I'd call a "gift-grade" printed paper box enclosing the foil-wrapped chocolate.

Taste
Well... you either like dark chocolate or you don't (and I do).  If you are into dark chocolate, and your tastes run to the extreme, then you may really like this chocolate.  At room temperature (about 75F) the bar is firm enough to snap off pieces, but melts quickly in the mouth, giving a thick, buttery richness and a smooth, clean mouthfeel.  The sweetness level is relatively low - what many would consider "semi-sweet" but the flavor is not over-powered by bitterness - there is a really good balance between sweet and bitter. (Many lesser grade chocolates will mask bitterness with excessive sugar).  Also, unlike many chocolates in this category, astringency is very mild (no strong "pucker" or mouth drying).  Despite being a very intense dark chocolate, the balance between bitterness, sweetness, and astringency is really nice. (FWIW, if you prefer milk chocolate, you will probably really dislike this chocolate!).

Bottom line, this is a fun gift to give someone who really likes "serious" chocolate and wants a special treat to nibble on, or if you're doing a chocolate tasting, its a good option to complement others from regions like South America.

Oh, one final note - this particular chocolate seemed to go quite well with a late harvest Zinfandel!

NOTE:  Despite being a separate listing, this product is the same listed at http://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B014UAGKRW
I didn't realize this and ordered both, but it is good enough that I don't mind having extra!  :-)

The ability of this mug to keep drinks hot or cold is as good or better than any similar product I've used.  I also own several RTIC coolers and have been BLOWN AWAY by the dominating superiority of those coolers as compared to any other hard sided cooler.  However there is one glaring problem with the RTIC mugs I own (both 20oz and 30 oz) - the inside has a finish that seems to attract coffee/tea stains like there is a chemical bond even when it is hand-washed every single day.  The contour of the inside and the narrowness of the bottom make it impossible to reach in there with a scrubbing sponge to get it thoroughly clean and so it just builds up over time into a dark brown layer that cannot be removed (I use a bottle brush with dish soap but it does not cut through this chemical bond).  I finally just broke down and went at it with a round-ended metal scraper and scraped out all the crud, yielding about 1/2 a teaspoon of what looked like fine coffee grounds!

I think this problem could be solved with a smoother finish on the inside of the mug - my other stainless drinking cups and mugs don't have this problem.

Fix this one problem and I'd rate this mug 4.5 stars (I like a completely spill-proof mug, and the lid that comes with this mug has permanent holes that cannot be closed - if you knock it over, liquid WILL spill out.

Compared to its primary competitors, the Camelbak Chute performs well in terms of its ability to keep hot stuff hot and cold stuff cold.  I was able to put 212 water in at night before going to bed, and then 10 hours later the water was a respectable 126 - hot enough to feel like you are drinking a hot beverage even after 10 hours (ambient temp was around 66).  Similarly 43 water measured about 50 6 hours later after being carried around in the car with an ambient temp of about 72.

The down-side of the Camelbak Chute is that the lid assembly is way overcomplicated.  There are three separate parts (or maybe 4 depending on how you count) and it cannot be opened or used single-handedly.  It actually requires not only two hands, but also your knees or a steady surface on which to place it while you fiddle with the cap; first unscrewing it and then trying to tuck it under the carry handle.  Camelbak seems quite proud of this feature - there is a sticker on top of the cap and a mention of it in the listing here on Amazon.  But I have to be honest - it works horribly.  The lid does not tuck neatly into the carry strap without a lot of pushing and fiddling and even then it has a tendency to pop back out after about 20 seconds.  I cannot understand for the life of me why they made it so complicated.  If you don't manage to tuck it into the carry handle, then you have to use your hand to bend the cap back and out of the way while you drink (or just let it hit you on the nose while drinking).

Given that the Chute is about the same price as other competitors such as Hydroflask, it does not represent a particularly good or bad value. - it is on par with its competitors.  However it is easier to drink from than a Hydro Flask (once you finally get the lid/cap assembly dealt with).  I found that drinking out of it while walking or driving had a much lower chance of pouring water down the front of my shirt than my wide-mouthed Hydro Flask tends to do.  But it is a lot less convenient to open than a Hydro Flask.  If you unscrew the complete top assembly (such as for cleaning or to add ice cubes) it is very easy to cross-thread.

The grippy texture on the bottom 2/3's of the flask is nice - a bit grippier than a Hydro Flask, and it will stand up squarely on a flat surface without a risk of falling over.  It also fits in a standard car cupholder (a 2015 Ford F150 in my case), which is an important feature for a lot of people.

Bottom line, this could be a great drinking flask based on its performance, bit the lid/cap assembly is just too complicated and inconvenient.  If they come up with a different cap retention system, this could easily be a 4 or 5 star product.

Easy, and makes great coffee - very easy to program and flexible enough to make good strong coffee for people who want it.  Bottom line, any Keurig based maching is going to be very dependent upon two things - the quality of the K-cups you use and your ability to customize the brew strength and brew temp.  This machine has all the adjustability you need, so as long as you get good K-cups, you'll be happy.

And a side note on the adjustability - I bought this as a Christmas gift for my 75-year old Mom who lives alone.  She LOVES how easy it is to use, and can even adjust the cup size settings on her own.  That is a good testament to how easy it is to use.  The only thing I have to remind her about is to change the little charcoal filter pod, but that is also incredibly easy to do and very fool-proof.

A final bonus is that it also will dispense hot water for people like me that want to brew a cup of tea and not use K-cups (I have not had a K-cup tea that I thought was any good).  A quick push of the "rinse" button, then hit the "hot water" button for a pre-programmed amount of hot water.  Super easy and the perfect temp (I keep it set at 195)

Great, compact and totally self-contained unit for producing a hot shower (or flowing hot water) anywhere you want.  The unit itself is lightweight and easy to carry and set up for just about anyone (the hardest part will be carrying the 5 gal bag of water).  The best part is that there is NOTHING else you have to do or buy in order to have a nice hot shower (except for the propane).  Most other systems are piecemeal and either rely on flowing water from a hose or a separate pump that you have to rig. This puppy is self-contained!

Setting it up involves the following simple steps:
1. Charge the battery

2.  Assemble the shower head to the discharge hose, then plug it onto the quick-disconnect discharge outlet on the main unit

3. Attach the pump assembly (which is part of the intake hose) to the full container of water, and plug the other end into the intake quick-disconnect on the main unit.

4. Screw on a canister of propane

5. Flip on the power switch, then turn the dial to the pilot position, hold down while the ignitor ticks a few times and lights the pilot, wait for it to warm up, then release.

6. Adjust the heat to the desired temp.

The whole process took me maybe 10 minutes from unboxing, and that was because I was carefully reading the instructions.  Normally I think it will take less than 2 minutes to go from packed away to "flowing hot shower" (not including filling the water bag).

The unit lit instantly on the first try and maintained an even temperature during my entire testing period. I found a setting about 2/3 of the way to be comfortably warm for showering.  The flow is enough to shower, but I don't think it would be sufficient for bathing a dog with a thick coat.

This thing is so easy to carry and set up that I plan to use it on my boat for post-dive warm ups and to shower off after surfing or diving sessions on multi-day trips.  It all packs away much smaller than anything I've used in the past (or seen on other's boats like the Zodi systems).

Negatives:
This unit only comes with a 12v car charger.  Luckily I had a 12v wall charger with the same plug dimensions laying around the house so I was able to charge it at home (I didn't want to have to drive around in circles for a couple hours to charge it for the first test!)

Markings on the main unit for charging connection, pump connection, inlet and discharge hoses are NOT well marked.  They are cast into the molded plastic case, but there is no shading or coloring to make them stand out.  Depending on the lighting (and your eyes) it may be quite difficult to tell which is what.

System can only be used with the included 5 gal water jug because the threads on the pump assembly are designed to screw onto the mouth of the 5 gal water jug (and are NOT regular hose thread).  This means that if you want to use a larger (or different ) water container, you're going to be making at least one trip to a plumbing supply house for some adapters.

The single biggest negative (and this is a BIG negative) is the inability to shut the water off while showering.  The heater and pump work together, so when you turn on the unit to light it, it immediately begins pumping water.  While the unit does light very quickly, this seems counter-intuitive and will end up wasting water.  It should have been easy enough for coleman to have integrated a water shutoff valve that also put the water heater into "pilot" mode while the water is not flowing (so as not to burn out the heating unit).  The end result is that you will consume more water than strictly necessary.  The normal "navy shower" routine of (1) turn on water and rinse (2) turn off water and soap up (3) turn on water and rinse off soap is not possible with this unit.

There are some clever work-arounds using a "diverter valve" that routes water back into the tank, and I think I will probably do this at some point, but it will add an additional hose and a bulky valve to the system.

I have two sets of fishing boots - the Viking VW24 boots and these Xtratuf boots.  Both are sized about right, assuming you wear hiking type socks (i.e. I normally wear a size 11 shoe, but I can fit into the size 10 XTRATUF or Viking boots with thin socks).

Either pair of boots are great for wearing all day on a boat, but there are some subtle differences that might make one better for you than the other.  The main differences are as follows:

Sole construction
The sole on the Viking is built like a pair of old school Keds shoes - with a separate sole piece and a thick welt bonded around the outside.  The XTRATUF boots seem like they are all molded from a single piece of rubber and then have a reinforcement around the outside edge.  The result is that the sole flexes more with the boot on the XTRATUF than it does on the VIKING.  Also the tread pattern on the XTRATUF is aggressive and much better suited to "working" (e.g. standing in fish guts or other crud) than the Viking boots, which have a 'top sider" type slit pattern that will gum up with anything other than water.

Flexibility and comfort
Both boots are comfortable enough to wear all day long (though because they are rubber, your feet will get sweaty and stinky no matter what you do!)  I wear thick wool socks (SmartWool brand) and use a corn starch and tea tree oil powder to keep my toes comfy.  The XTRATUF boots are definitely more supple and flexible than the Viking boots, which remind me of a short pair of "Wellies" or Hunter type rain boots.  You can see in the product image the way the tops will roll down on the XTRATUF boots - this isn't possible on the Viking boots.

Interior lining on both pairs of boots is similar - a thin layer of lycra type material that is stretchy and slippery so that the boots come off easily.

Bottom line, if you're looking for something to wear on a commercial boat or for serious fishing while you're likely to be standing in fish guts and slime, the XTRATUF boot is the way to go.  If you're looking for something to wear in foul weather for yachting or sailing then the Viking boots might be a better option do to their "yachting" type sole and spiffy looks.

Like a lot of hunters and shooters, I've never owned a high-end (>$1,000)  scope or optic (I just have a hard time spending 3x or 4x on the optic that I spent on the rifle, which I know is silly).  I am also not a "bench shooter" other than to sight in rifles and practice handling of various configurations.  Everything my son and I do is focused on preparing for "the one shot that counts" in a hunting scenario.

I mounted this on a Ruger Gunsite Scout .308, which is not really the best application for it, but I don't currently own a more typical (longer, more  traditional) rifle.  It required me to remove the pic rail in order to clear the front bell, but I was able to use the factory-supplied Ruger rings to mount it.  I will probably use it in this configuration for the upcoming season to give it some field time.  One key advantage with respect to the Ruger GSR is that without glass, it is a ~6 lb rifle - my goal for this rifle is something very lightweight and handy for use in tromping around looking for wild pigs (and mule deer).  I did not want a scope that would add excess weight, and the Bushnell Elite seems light weight for its level of performance.

After lapping the rings and leveling the scope in the rings, I quickly laser bore-sighted from about 20 yards away, then went to the range the next day.  I was on paper in about 3 shots at 50 yards, then went out to 100 yards and re-zero'd with almost no effort.  As others have mentioned, the knobs under the turret covers make it VERY easy to make field adjustments, and sighting it in was very simple and without any problems at all.  I did not validate the 1/4" per click, but looking at groups and then counting 1" marks across the targets, then calculating the # of clicks required seemed to work every time in both windage and elevation adjustments.

As others have mentioned, the eye relief is a pretty narrow band, so you want to make sure you pay attention to your cheek weld when setting this up.  I also found on the Ruger GSR using the factory rings that I need a cheek pad to get my eye up at the proper level. (this is more of an issue with the rifle and its fit to me than the scope).

The sight picture through this scope is clear and bright, and having a 2.5x at the low end is very nice for typical hunting applications.  As others have mentioned the reticle is NOT illuminated, nor does it have any markings whatsoever (no mil dot, BDC, or anything).  It is a very plain-Jane "duplex" type reticle with very fine lines.  I prefer a wide duplex simply because of my older eyes, but this one gets the job done.

The zoom ring has grooves cut into it that make it easy to distinguish from the scope body if making adjustments without removing your eye from the scope, and a small knob gives an idea of the relative zoom ratio with a quick touch (is it at 9 o'clock, noon, 3, etc).  It has just the right amount of resistance to keep from being moved inadvertently, but still smooth and easy to dial in while sighting through it.  The diopter adjustment is very similar, and worked well to get a crystal-clear focus for my eye.

After about 50 rounds through the rifle, there does not seem to be any change in zero, and no adjustments necessary.

I'll post an update once I've spent some time in the field with the scope, but for now, I'm giving it 5 stars for its combination of build quality, ease of adjustment, optical clarity, and weight for the price.

I'm a pretty die-hard "foodie" and I love to read books about food and travel (see some of my other reviews).  This book was recommended to me by a friend, and I have to say I was skeptical at first because of the lack of "adventure" I assumed it would have.  (How "adventurous was a book by the editor at the NY Times likely to be, after all...).  And, I was right - if you compare this book to something by Anthony Bourdain or Bill Buford it does lack "adventure".  But what it does have (and what I really enjoyed) was wonderfully-written observations on human nature; how we respond to one another based on our perceptions.  There were sections that made me laugh out loud because of the ridiculous scenarios Ms. Reichl found herself in at times, and other sections that were heartwarming and familial.  The book is really more of a memoir, and unlike most memoirs, I enjoyed it immensely.

Yes, there are wonderful descriptions of food, and of the meals Ms. Reichl was fortunate enough to enjoy during her tenure at the NYT.  She reveals a very interesting and new insight into not only the life of a food critic (and the inevitable "food politics" involved) but also the day-to-day workings of the "front of house" in many of New York's most famous restaurants.

Bottom line, I don't think you have to be a foodie to enjoy this book.  Ms. Reichl has a smooth and engaging style, and a perceptive ability to capture many nuances of human interaction that are missed by most other authors in this subject area.  A great book for a long train, plane, or boat ride, or a weekend getaway.

I got hooked on these chiles while in Sicily and Calabria a few years ago, and only occasionally see them on menus of Italian restaurants.  One of my favorite things to do with them is to smash them with anchovies, garlic, and parmesan with olive oil to make a spicy/savory spread for fresh bread.  OMG so good!  Also great on sandwiches or slice them onto a pizza.

Once the chiles are all gone, don't throw away the oil!  Its great to drizzle over salads, sandwiches, or anything you want to add a bit of punch to.

On a spicy scale, I'd say these are equivalent to the dried Chile flakes you see at most pizza joints, but with a MUCH richer flavor

As a devout "foodie" and world traveler myself, I relish the vicarious enjoyment I get from reading other peoples' travel journals - especially when they focus on food! The best of these, in my opinion, are "A Cook's Tour: Global Adventures in Extreme Cuisines" by Anthony Bourdain and Heat: An Amateur's Adventures as Kitchen Slave, Line Cook, Pasta-Maker, and Apprentice to a Dante-Quoting Butcher in Tuscany (Vintage) by Bill Buford. Both have a wonderful level of detail and nuance that really paint a vivid picture of the places visited, the people there, and the foods they enjoy. After reading an excerpt of the book in an airline magazine, I was excited to read the book and hoped it would give me the same depth of experience as these other favorites. Majumdar's "Eat My Globe" is a fun and easy romp around the world with a guy with a great level of passion for food, an interesting back-story, and a good gift for story-telling. But Eat My Globe lacks the detailed stories, texture, and emotion of my favorite books in this genre. The book is arranged in chapters that roughly relate to countries visited. The formula is repeated more or less throughout the book, and starts to get a bit predictable after about five or six chapters. My biggest complaint about this particular book is that as each chapter develops and becomes interesting, there is a brief culminating story about a meal and then the reader is whisked off to a rapid and sometimes perfunctory close in order to advance to the next chapter. Perhaps Majumdar was trying to finish the book (and cover all his countries) within a number of pages limited by his publisher (this is how it seems at times). I could not help thinking that if Majumdar had spent a bit *more* time with each chapter and covered fewer places (or made the book longer) I would have found it more rewarding. There are moments of comic brilliance that had me laughing out loud, and Majumdar nicely captures the human intimacy and friendship that goes so well with the enjoyment of food (both the simplest to the most refined). But he doesn't linger long enough on these areas to make the reader feel as if he is able to enjoy them as fully as possible. Given the chance to read this book again (having not read it before) I would do it again - it is a good read, fun, and full of interesting vignettes of his life traveling around the world, including some of the hardships. For many readers, the lack of depth might be seen as an advantage - it keeps the reading light and breezy, and makes starting and stopping the book (with perhaps weeks in between readings) very easy to do. For me, however, the lack of character and "back story" development was a flaw in an otherwise competent and fun-to-read book.

If you are looking for a pair of durable headphones that you can wear on your runs or cycle rides, the Jabras are probably the best I've found in terms of durability, fit, and comfort.  They are however lacking in the sound quality department.  My wife is an avid runner, and for years has tried all sorts of headhones with her iPods and never found anything she liked.  In-ear units "gave her a headache" and over-ear or "on-ear" (like Apple ear buds) would not stay on during runs.  For a brief period she had a pair of Phillips in-ear buds that came with really squishy ear pieces and she found them comfortable and really liked them, but after a couple weeks of running with them, the sweat and environmental moisture killed them.  She is thrilled with the Jabras, because they stay put, they are comfortable, and after several months of running (even in the rain) they are still going strong.  I use them on cycle rides and have also found them to be quite comfortable, even under my bike helmet.  No, the sound is not as good as my Bose or other higher-end headphones, but none of my other headphones will stand up to the punishment that these units seem to be able to take.  Another plus is that the cords are made from a thick rubbery material that doesn't make weird noises when it rubs against your clothing or itself, and it also seems incredibly durable.  The two-part construction is a nice touch as well, so that if you are the type to clip your Nano on your shirt collar, you don't have 3' of cord dangling all over the place, but if you want to put your phone in your Camelbak on a long ride, you can attach the cord extension and reach all the way back there with no problem.  The adjustability of the earphones is also very good - there is an almost confusing array of options for different ways to set up the headphones with the various ear gels and loops.  In fact the instructions are pretty weak about this, but they do provide some basic diagrams that would otherwise make fitting the various earpieces much trickier.  Bottom line, if you are an athlete, frequent runner, or cyclist, these are probably the best headphones out there, particularly at this price point.  Unless you can afford to replace better-sounding headphhones once a month, your best option may be the Jabra Sport units.

I bought one of these from Smith & Hawken about 10 years ago (remember when they used to have retail stores in malls...?) and I have to say that it is without a doubt the handiest garden tool we own.  Originally, I bought it for my wife as part of a gardening "gift basket" but I constantly use it, too, for things like:

Scooping charcoal briquettes out of the BBQ
Digging out sprinklers that need to be repaired
Lifting dead, eviscerated small mammals that our cat has left on the doorstep
Clearing the rain gutters
Banging on bike parts
Cleaning between the bricks on our patio
Prying out dandelion weeds from the lawn

Heck, I even use it for gardening once in a while!

The makers of this device really perfected the right combination of sharp tip, curvature, and scoop volume to make it extremely handy for all kinds of things.  When I am working on a project that requires me to poke, pry, lift, or dig, the most common question to my wife on the weekends is "Honey, have you seen the soil scoop..??"

The premise of this book fascinated me and led me to choose it.  The idea that someone who is now a very accomplished writer and successful member of society could have been so whacked out on drugs that they literally had to conduct an investigative journalism exercise to rediscover their past is fascinating to me.  And I will say that after reading the book, I was not disappointed.

I had my fears, though... So many books/movies of this genre tend to be preachy. The authors tend to vary between the "my pitiful life, feel sorry for me" perspective and the "look how strong I am now; you can do it too!" exhortations that can become so tiresome.  Carr is not only a great story teller, but he writes about himself with such detachment that it almost feels like you are learning about his past alongside him, with the same sense of wonderment (and shame) that he is experiencing.

This book is far more than just a narrative of "one man's struggle against addiction" (I would not have made it all the way through it that had been the case!).  Carr's self-deprecating humor, his knack for highlighting the unique (and uniquely flawed) characteristics in himself and the people around him, and his style of writing make you forget that you are reading what is essentially an autobiography.

There are scenes that will horrify you (especially if you are a parent), and scenes that will make you laugh out loud.  But mostly, this book is a study of human character flaws and the relationships that people create that help them deal with those flaws.

I'm not usually much of a biography (or autobiography) reader, but I found this book very enjoyable, well-paced, and insightful.  One of my measures of a "good book" is that I can learn from it, or there are elements that linger with me into life; Night of the Gun definitely did that for me.  In fact, I am planning to look for more work by David Carr.

Kudos to Carr for no only picking himself up finally to create this work, but also his honesty and the straightforward tale he tells of his life for us to enjoy!

My youthful memories of Christmas are rekindled by this masterpiece written directly for television. And amazingly, in a very short span of time. As a child of the 50s & 60s, "Amahl and the Night Visitors" will always stay in my heart. This was a huge part of my childhood Christmas tradition year after year.

I couldn't quite give this recording any higher rating than four stars though, due to the reproductive quality of the old mono sound. But I would still recommend it for the most part. Probably not the program I grew up on, since this is the original from the very early 50s; I was born in 1955. But the power of this story and the superb music written as an opera, probably the best ever composed for television, will delight anyone familiar with this work. And I'm sure many others will be won over as new listeners.

There are said to be many local stage productions of this classic annually, but I've only had the pleasure of seeing it once live on stage, and that was the early 70s, put on by my high school drama and music departments. There was even a newer production shot in Israel in the late 70s, but I didn't enjoy that much higher budgeted effort anywhere near as much as the earlier version I remember, or this recording from the original cast done back in 1952. The newer version just didn't have the same emotion or magic. So much for location scenery.

At this time, I await with great anticipation, the black-and-white DVD offered here on Amazon that I recently ordered. They also offer the newer 70s version, but I wasn't interested. Be forewarned though, the very dramatic ending will bring many to tears, especially from "All That Gold" to "Oh, Woman, You Can Keep The Gold." A television classic.

cands.text: An idea I first thought was a bit irreverant, turned to complete joy after listening to my brother's copy. A fresh new take on one of the musical masterpieces of all-time. Now a joyous part of the holiday season, or any season for that matter. A fabulous gathering of some of America's top African-American musical talents, will win you over after giving it a listen.

For that need something to get you in the real spirit of Christmas, this ranks amongst the very best. Karen's extremely smooth and near flawless vocals are greatly missed, but the superb brother and sister team have left one of the all-time gems for the holiday season in "Christmas Portrait." My wife and I had this CD in the car stereo all the way from home to work today. She stopped it after dropping me off. We'll resume play when she picks me up this evening. Neither one of us wants to miss a single track. I can count my very favorite Christmas albums on one hand, and this is definitely one of them!

One of the last great musicals Hollywood has given us. Topol shines brightly in this Norman Jewison directed marvel. Visually and musically stunning, a perfect film to make one laugh, cry, sing-along and think. Why don't we get many others like it today? One of my very favorite musicals. Favorite films for that matter. Cast to perfection.

Like "The Passion of the Christ" Hollywood has probably overlooked what could be another box office sleeper. A beautifully filmed version of the Old Testament Book of Esther. And when recent months have seen huge drops in movie theater revenue, the motion picture industry should take note, that it doesn't always take $100,000,000 plus budgets to put a finished product up on the big screen that really looks convincing. Made on a budget of somewhere around $20,000,000, "One Night With The King" is evidence of that. This looks and feels like so much more. A story of hope and faith for both Jews and Christians, somehow it seems Hollywood just doesn't get that there is an extremely large audience just waiting for more. But with 20th Century-Fox making recent announcement of producing more faith-based films, there could be another Cecil B. DeMille just waiting in the wings. Well worth the price of admission for this long-time movie buff.

I saw the stage production at Hollywood's famous Pantages Theater some years ago, and was quite impressed. I then purchased the CD, which has been in my CD player many times. But I somehow feel the original Movie soundtrack was a bit more superior. Especially the powerful film opening of 'Circle of Life.' I just feel the strong African male vocals delivered much more impact. And not to sound sexist, but Rafiki was also better portrayed as a male, than the female actresses seen in the stage productions. But still an extremely enjoyable listening experience.

A bit of nostalgia, some of the best recordings ever made. My children were totally speechless(unusually quiet)when I popped this CD into the car stereo on a long drive home from, ironicly, Las Vegas. The rich orchestral sounds accompanying Sinatra's smooth vocals, were a style they had never heard before. After our trip to Nevada, it somehow seemed the appropriate music at the time.

I saw this movie in the theater 11 times; more than any other movie. In 1967 this movie totally captivated me. I even fell in love with the little Indian girl at the end of the film. And after purchasing this DVD, I'm still crazy about it 40 years later. Some of the catchiest tunes ever, and way ahead-of-its-time animation. Everyone in the family will love this Kipling and Disney classic.

And after purchasing this DVD, I'm still crazy about it 40 years later. Some of the catchiest tunes ever, and way ahead-of-its-time animation. Everyone in the family will love this Kipling and Disney classic.

This is the fourth recording of "The Planets" I've purchased, and I am extremely pleased. The Los Angeles Philharmonic was at its best here, and much of that was owed to the genius of its then director Zubin Mehta. Crisp arrangements, and a full orchestral sound is how you achieve the full effect of "The Planets." Other conductors should take note. Not my favorite, that honor still goes to the Los Angeles Philharmonic, under the leadership of Leopold Stokowski. But you definitely can't go wrong with this one.

A good time with mostly christian standards, from down home southern to traditional choir. I waited to review this new Take 6 release, only after having several listens. And unlike one previous reviewer, I'm far from getting bored with it. Quite frankly, owning most every album they've released since 1988 I consider this comparable to most anything else they've done. Their vocals and arrangements haven't skipped a beat. This release also marks the farewell of longtime band member Dr. Cedric Dent (baritone), and the arrival of Khristian Dentley. Mr. Dentley had been filling in for Dent over the last few years, during various concert dates the good Professor was unable to make. The transition is almost seamless.

But what about 'One'? The tracks in short:

1. Down Here I've Done My Best: A great opening number. Inspiration for preparation of that final rest that awaits the faithful. Upbeat and smooth.

2. One: A celebration of the ONE and only name under heaven whereby we can be saved. The title track. An extremely fun listen.

3. Can't Imagine Love Without You (Feat. Stevie Wonder): This was originally recorded on Mr. Wonders 2005 'A Time To Love' Gold certified album. And is probably my least favorite hear. Not to knock two of my all-time favorite recording groups and vocalist. But I prefer the original. The vocals are almost too syrupy sweet on this one. Stevie's harmonica playing is all that keeps this from being totally acapella.

4. What A Friend We Have In Jesus: This classic hymn is given new life, and for me personally this is where the CD rolls over into a whole new level of Joy. The listening experience takes another turn as the beat starts to move you from here...into track #5. See if you can keep from bobbing your head up-and-down; Reverently of course--

5. In My Heart: --Feel the beat? Smooth transition wasn't it? You wouldn't even know the songs were changing until you started to hear the familiar words of this next track. Can hardly sit still can you? This is Take 6 at their very best!

6. Noah: Story telling--or should I say preaching at its finest? If you liked 'David' from their 1988 platinum certified 'Take 6' you'll really love this one. uptempo, astounding vocals. It then takes on a Brazilian sort of vibe that is out-of-this world. Ever wonder why they are the most Grammy nominated vocal group ever? Just listen to track #6. And we're not just talking gospel; that includes all genres.

7. Allelula: Who but Take 6 would even attempt this standard without a full mega choir host of sopranos, altos, tenors, baritones, and bass behind them? I'm talking Mormon Tabernacle calibre!. I even had the experience of tackling it as a tenor in our high school chorale of some 75+, under the direction of Don Fontana. Former director of Robert H. Schuller's Garden Grove Community Church/Crystal Cathedral(Hour of Power)Choir from 1974-1981. I still hear and remember some of those high tenor parts near the end. Outstanding.

8. Glorious Day: This gospel standard is given its due in the very capable hands of Take 6. Powerful vocal solos are a standout on this energized recording. Have you ever heard the gossip that "Take 6 don't really sing with the Spirit?" "They can't really get down with true gospel?" Just take a listen, then get back to me once you stop "Havin' church" brothers and sistas.

9. You're Gonna Need Him: Southern Gospel Done Well!!!

10. Farther Along: Southern Gospel Done Well!!!

11. Noah Reprise: in case you didn't get enough of that Brazilian thing going on... Love those raindrops!

And just a heads-up; this is not really an acapella effort. Most tracks do include either drumbeats, tambourine, guitar; and in the case of 'Can't Imagine Love Without You' Stevie Wonder's beautiful harmonica playing. Noah and Allelula being the only true acapella offerings. But with music this good, who cares?!

This was my introduction to Anointed, and I've bought everything else they've put out! I still like "The Call" best. What a talented group of singers. This album carries your soul to new heights. A beautiful  Christian witness.

Still the most compelling program ever aired on televion. I bought this set so my children could experience a bit of their history. Great transfer to DVD, and still packs a powerful blow to racism. The cast is one of the best ensembles ever assembled for any project. A great adaptation of Mr. Haley's years of research.

Whether from the '30s, or more recent years, average and serious movie buffs alike will always find most anything they're looking for here. I purchase a copy about every other year, and have been extremely pleased with the huge volume of entries. I even underline every film I can remember ever having seen in my lifetime. Just a hobby. I find the larger edition somewhat easier to read, and makes for much better underlining.

Do you want Mariah at her very best? Do you want a Christmas CD that makes you feel warm and fuzzy inside? This is the one. Not only a top R&B and Pop singer, but with the strong vocals Mariah so powerfully let's loose on this one, she easily could be the top Gospel artist as well, had she chosen that route. I believe she gives her strongest recorded performance here, especially track #3 "O Holy Night". She's that good.

How can anyone have something against "The Lion King?" The opening is dynamic, the story powerful, no matter what the source, and some of the best Disney Songs ever written. My children were very young when they saw it, but seemed to handle the tragic moments quite well. I heard many more little ones crying during the screening of "The March of the Penguins." And yes, the story is reminiscent of Shakespear's "Hamlet" like "West Side Story" used his "Romeo and Juliet." The Box Office numbers didn't lie as to how popular this film was to the general public. Rates amongst Disney's very best.

A day in the life from dawn till dusk, reminiscent of Holst's "The Planets." This sounds like a classic film score, and could very well have been adapted as such. Some of the best rock to come out of the '60s, and surprisingly not ranked amongst the greatest ever recorded if my memory serves me right. An often overlooked masterpiece of composing and pure listening pleasure. Puts one at peace with one's self. "Nights In White Satin" is the finale of all rock finales, with the exception of few.

The Los Angeles based women's Gospel group Futrel, were as good as they get. And had they received better fan support would still be recording. Still one of my Gospel favorites, I was fortunate enough to have my CD signed by one of the ladies, after being informed by a friend that she worked in our  building. After one listen to "Declarations" any fan of contemporary Gospel will be hooked as well.

Since my Junior High School years, I've been an avid fan of Oscar night, and the whole history of the Academy Awards and its winners. I guess I'll always love movies, and the allure of Hollywood, having lived in L.A. all my life, and being an aspiring actor in my younger years. In High School as a hobby, I and my best friend and fellow drama student, use to bet who could pick the most winners from each category every year. There is something about Oscar night, and all the glamour that goes with it, that keeps me glued to the set every year; first to hear the nominations, then the big ceremomy to announce the winners. And this book is up-to-date; from the very first winners of 1927, to 2005 and the surprise of "Crash" taking Best Picture honors (my personal favorite). If you enjoy films, and specificly The Academy Awards as much as I do, then you'll love this book.

I relate each years winners and nominees, to historic events and lifestyles of the times. Sort of an insight into what was going on then.

My first real appreciation of this sound was from watching the film "Slaughterhouse Five" in the theater, back in the '70s. That soundtrack was just a taste of what you get with this recording. My family pops this CD in the car stereo on long trips, and glide down the highway to some original smooth grooves. Helps the miles pass swiftly. Music for the soul.

They don't make too many love stories like this anymore. One of the most heartwarming films on enduring love, the entire cast is to be commended. Especially James Garner and Gena Rowlands. Proof that we can't just push aside our aging performers. Their is much to be learned from the elderly, and real lifetime commitments. Beautiful cinematography, a film that will even have the average man shedding a few tears in the end. I did.

Starts off somewhat poorly , then picks-up as a cleverly written thrill-ride. But hardly the threat to Christianity or creationism it purports to be. And despite the National Geographic consistently harping that Darwin could not have possibly been wrong, it still stands that all he ever really proved was that when isolated, as was the case with wildlife in the Galapagos chain, there is much evidence of adaptation, not evolution; some iguanas became more adapted to marine life but remain iguanas, tortoises developed different shapes to their shells, an adaptation for the purpose of feeding but remained tortoises, etc. But more then a theory? No. And throughout the years since Darwin and his 1872 "The Origen of Species", evolutionist have consistently hit a brick wall when it comes to certain things like the lack of pre-Cambrian fossil finds, radiohalos and even the rediscovery of the thought to be extinct Coelacanth; showing not an extinct fish with unusual fins that other land creatures supposedly evolved from, but a very much still existent contemporary, though very unique species. And how often has the faked "missing links" just been glossed over by evolutionary theorists? Yes the old Piltdown Man hoax, and how about that lesser known American favorite Nebraska Man? Supposedly a missing link based on a tooth that in reality belonged to a peccary(pig)! But we could go on and on with arguments from both sides of the fence.

In conclusion, Mr. Hartley is an extremely talented writer who is very familiar with the places he writes about, having visited and lived there. And though I in no way found "On The Fifth Day" a crushing blow to my Christian faith, it did stir a desire to visit the many back drops to the story; especially Pompei and Mt. Vesuvius.

Even though I liked the Telefilm, and thought Halle Berry was the obvious choice to play Miss Dandridge (both were born in Cleveland), I was somewhat disappointed with it, after having read this book first. Dorothy's many trials and heartaches were only lightly touched upon in the film version. This book reads like a well written novel, starting from her early years as a child performer. The physical, verbal, and sexual abuse at the hands of her mother's lesbian lover. The failed marriages, and financial ruin. And most heartbreaking of all, the birth of her extremely mentally challenged daughter. But there are the triumphs also. Like making the cover of Life magazine, and receiving a Best Actress Academy Award nomination for the 1954 film "Carmen Jones." A first for an African-American actress. Unfortunately, the making of this film marked the beginning of an affair with the director Otto Preminger, that would end on a very sour note. Something she apparently never fully recovered from. Even being verbally abused by the same director during the making of "Porgy and Bess."

Another great aspect of this book, is the social background of Black Los Angeles and Hollywood during the '30s, '40s and '50s. And who could ever imagine, Dorothy riding the streets of L.A. with her good friend Louis Armstrong, and him puffing on a marijuana joint? A must read for those interested in the history of Black Hollywood and Tinseltown in general.

For years a classic true story from Australia, of one woman's search for truth. It wasn't the Watchtower(Jehovah's Witness) movement she belonged to. Very revealing Bible truths no matter what your background. Good easy reading.

The moving story of a single mom who's beauty left her long ago, trying to cope with keeping her four children united while dealing with being hugely over weight. Johnny Depp in the title role, is the glue that keeps everyone together as the elder brother. Especially true with his mentally challenged younger brother Arnie, magnificently played to the fullest ability by a very young Leonardo DiCaprio. Before viewing this film years ago, I had never heard of Mr. DiCaprio, and reasoned they surely must have found some talented kid that actually suffered from some mental handicap. His performance is that believable. And Johnny Depp's Gilbert is so likable, one can't help but pull for the fate of the entire family. Thought provoking and heartwarming throughout, but can also be heartbreaking at times.

Cute and adorable, but this film opens a window to the real world of daily penguin life. That world can be filled with love and dedication, from seeing the hatching of an egg through to fruition, to the improper transfer of that egg from parent-to-parent, and its hasty demise in the bitterly freezing temperature of the Antarctic. Or the ability of parents to recognize their own young, amongst thousands of others simply by recognizing each others vocal cries. As good as documentaries get, this film rivals the best of National Geographic. Though it may bring your little ones to tears, as I witnessed in the theater. The English version of this French produced film, is fortunate to have the sensitive narration of Morgan Freeman. Now a permanent part of our family DVD collection.
