Epic story of the author's family, beginning with her grandparents on both sides who lived in Eastern Europe. The stories commence at the beginning of the 20th Century and go into the period of the rise of the Nazi's and the Holocaust.
You follow each member of her family and their stories as to what they went through. Even though only a few of her aunts and uncles were in concentration camps, the things each had to do in order to survive, and how the fear of capture permeated their very existence, is a horror in itself. The author herself was a young girl whose parents feigned that they were Christian and she had to make believe with them that her new name was always her name, even when questioned by SS officers.
As an adult, she writes of how she interviewed her surviving aunts and uncles who were scattered in different countries; she writes of the death of both her father and then her mother and the unanswered questions that she wishes she asked them when they were alive. Upon her return to Poland with her grown daughter, she meets the priest in the village where she and her parents concealed their religion from everyone, only to find out from him that everyone knew, but no one in their village chose to denounce them.
It's hard hitting when you read of the atrocities that so many Jews had to endure from their supposed neighbors and friends.
Just for the breadth of experiences, and how each member of her family survived or succumbed, this book is a vital history of that time period that everyone should read.

Very enjoyable writing style and interesting story which takes place towards the end of WWII, beginning in the U.S..
A wealthy group of people, who were prone to pranks, were friends for years. There were two men, Ellis and Hank, and one woman, Madeline. The men appeared to be very irresponsible as they never had to work for the money they spent. They also were considered to be "society". The woman also came from money, but her grandfather, her mother's father, was considered a "robber Baron". Ellis and "Maddie" had eloped, as there was a stigma regarding Maddie's mother, apart from not being from "society". She was in a loveless marriage and had run off with another man, but was forced to return because of societal pressures. Because of her situation, she ended up ending her own life. That may have been the cause of Maddie's rebellious streak, and she fit in with Hank and Ellis, though for a different reason.
Ellis' father, a Colonel, had gone to Scotland many years before to get proof of the Loch Ness Monster. Besides being suspected of fabricating a photo that he got, he had a horrible reputation of going after the young girls that were in the village.
Ellis was treated poorly by his father, first because of his choice of wife, and secondly, because he wasn't serving in the armed forces and doing his duty. Ellis' excuse was that it was discovered that he was color blind, and was a 4F. His friend, Hank, also escaped the army because he was flat footed.
In order to redeem himself in his father's eyes, Ellis arranged for himself, Hank and Maddie to go to Scotland and get proof of the monster, as he was in danger of being cut off financially.
They were able to get a boat that was part of an armada going to England, and, when one of the ships was torpedoed by a "U" boat, the survivors were taken aboard the other boats, including the one that the trio were on. It was there that the true differences in the character of each of them started to come out. Where Ellis and Hank were indifferent to the suffering of those injured, Maddie was truly affected.
When they arrived to the area outside of Loch Ness, they found a simple inn, that appeared to be without electricity and basic amenities that are taken for granted. Though the men keep their spoiled boy attitude, Maddie becomes helpful, but she also discovers a sinister side to her husband that she never realized and almost loses her life with the discovery.
Kept my interest throughout.

Extremely interesting story and very well told. In 2004, (the present time of the story), an 83 year old man who is a Holocaust survivor, confronts another man of about the same age who is Jewish, and pulls out a German luger and presses it to to his head. The 83 year old accuses the other of being a non Jewish Nazi who took on the role of being a Jew in order to escape persecution. In addition, the money he came to the United States with in order to build up his weath (he is now a billionaire) came from moneys he stole from Jews, including large amounts of money and precious items from the 83 year old's family.
From there, the 83 year old locates an attorney who is going through her own issues, and she reluctantly hears his story of his life during the war years in order to determine if there is a case against the billionaire.
Although this is fiction, it appears to be based on experiences of what people went through during those war years. Extremely powerful and a book that you can't put down until you finish it.

-All great elements for a great story and executed very well.
-You start with a driven female reporter who is having issues because of a miscarriage, and mix in a horrific murder scene where a whole family was killed with a samurai sword; a clandestine military plot; a rogue elite soldier; a Chinese martial art club along with a mysterious "suicide", and excellent writing, and this makes for a great read.
-Gabriela Giovanni, a reporter for a local newspaper in San Francisco receives a call to meet a woman at her apartment. The information the woman wants to give her is too sensitive to give over the phone. When Gabriela shows up, the door to the apartment is slightly open, and when she pushes on it, there's slight resistance from something behind the door. As she enters, she sees what looks like a little doll, but it's a little child who is sitting in the middle of dead bodies that have been cut up, with blood throughout the rooms. Gabriela is shocked when she sees this, and removes the child but becomes totally protective over the little girl.
-She now has to back track to discover what it was that the mother was trying to tell her. Through the grandmother of the child, she discovers that the child's father is dangerous and a soldier who is capable of this type of carnage. He's supposed to be in Iraq, and according to all information coming from the military, he still there, but, when Gabriela goes to the apartment on her own to search it for clues, she's attacked and barely escaped with her life by someone that she swears looks just like the child's father.
-Because of her issues with her miscarriage, and her fixation with the welfare of this baby that she found, everyone around her thinks she has become delusional. She is so driven, and so persistent, that she secretly continues to research the case even though her superiors at the newspaper insist she back off from covering the case and her boyfriend feels he has to leave her because she's become a different person. The fate of this child becomes all consuming for her, as she discovers that the baby will be given over to the father who is supposedly coming back from Iraq shortly, but it's a father who Gabriela believes will end up killing the child.
-Even as Gabriela digs deeper, so many questions still remain, but the beauty is, as the book progresses towards the end and the loose ends are tied together, everything makes sense.
-Very good, suspenseful and satisfying story.

-Very absorbing book of a group of Jews who were hidden away within Berlin during the time of the Holocaust. The author does a tremendous job in keeping the stories of these survivors, who were just a few of many thousands, very clear and she was able to convey the fear, the hunger as well as those isolated happier times that these survivors experienced.
-Where there are many stories of Jews who survived the concentration camps, there were also many who hid under the noses of SS within Germany itself. The courage of the German citizens, and the self sacrifice they exhibited in the face of Nazi threats against anyone found harboring Jews, is nothing short of heroic.
-The author follows the family of Dr. Arthur Arndt, a well liked family doctor who treated both Jew and Gentile alike. Because of his giving nature, his patients were appalled from what he was going to have to endure when Jews were being sent to the camps. He faked his death and went into hiding along with his wife, Lina, and two grown children, Erich and Ruth. Eric's girlfriend, Ellen Lewinsky and her mother Charlotte, along with Eric's friend Bruno, made up what ended out to be 7 in the group. Besides being looked after with the help of over 100 kind people, they also did what they could to help each other.
-The resilience of this group, and also so many others that survived under these conditions is something that must be marveled at. In addition, the number of people who both actively helped at the risk of their lives, and those that helped in other ways, by leaving extra food for the group, shows that German citizenry did act against the Nazis, and that those that joined the Nazis in their oppressive acts, had no excuse.
-The fact that all of the seven not only survived, but were able to have families and stayed close to one another, was a feel good ending.

-Fictional portrayal of the society of North Korea, where anything the leader says becomes fact. Events are twisted so that he will look the hero; through fear, the people are forced to turn their backs on reality; they know that what is true today may not be so tomorrow.
-Pak Jun Do is introduced to us as a young boy living in an orphanage. Beautiful women, as was his mother, are pulled by the authorities to be mistresses to the important members of society. His father, the head of the orphanage (The Orphan Master), raised Jun Do with cruelty, because of the anger and humiliation that ran through him because of the abduction of his wife. He also would not acknowledge Jun Do as his son, as that would make his embarrassment public.
-Orphaned children are given one of 114 martyrs names and Jun Do, carrying a name from that group, was always mistaken for being an orphan. We follow his life as he seems to rise up in society and it seems like both a comedy, but is also jarring because of the acts that he must carry out.
-Jun Do has an innocence about him that allows him to be successful. Because of talents that he picked up as his experiences multiply, he is better able to handle himself later on, and develops an inner sense of right and wrong that can't be thwarted by turns of events.
-As a young man, one of his duties was to be the radio man aboard a Korean fishing boat who listens for communications that may show the whereabouts of "the enemy". All men on the boat have been assigned wives and as a rule, they Tatoo the image of their wife on their chest. Jun Do is neither a real fisherman, nor is he married, and so, to make him pass for a real fisherman, he is told that he must have a Tatoo. He decides on the image of a famous actress, Sun Moon, and her image is now part of him.
-Events proceed, and because of his knowledge of English and acts on board the ship, he is mistakenly thought to be a hero and is assigned to join a group going on an initial political trip to the United States. Because of his Tatoo, he is believed by the Americans to be Commander Ga, a very high ranking official under the Korean leader, who is the husband of Sun Moon.
-Because of the perceived failure of the mission, he is imprisoned, but manages to meet up with the real Commander Ga and kills him.
-What follows at times seems impossible and yet, because of the controlled mindset of the society which has to obey the whims of their leader, Jun Do is in a position to not only think independently, but he shows acts of courage at the risk of great torture. You read his story from two vantage points, as a prisoner who is being tortured to give up information in the current time, and as what could be called the hero of the story, in the events which led up to his current situation, where he touches on the lives of the people around him, and because of his goodness, they believe in him and are themselves transformed. You wait to see if his sacrifice will result in others being saved, or if all will be lost.
-It's an amazingly written story, and you feel the conflicting emotions of the people as they try to comply with the demands that are placed on them, but realize that a wrong move could also destroy them.
-The story envelops you.

-It's an unusual novel, because it starts out examining the actions of individuals who are hurting inside, but we don't immediately see why. It then morphs into a "road" novel with comedic overtones and then, keeping the light mood, goes back to the characters dealing with and accepting their hurt and finding themselves.
-In Paris, in our current time, we're introduced to Jean Perdu. He lives alone in a building, where he is aware of the other people living there, but has no real interaction with them. He's about 50 years old and his parents are divorced. His mother was from a sophisticated family while his father was from a working class family. Jean's routine is to go to his mother on Saturday, and hear her complaints about his father and then on to his father on Sunday, and hear the reverse.
-A woman moves in on his floor and she has recently gotten divorced from a man with whom she had struggled to keep up a marriage, but he found someone else. He was well to do, and controlled everything, but when he wanted to divorce, he merely packed his wife's things and left them outside of the door of their former apartment, which he vacated. She had to fend for herself.
-Jean has an unusual talent. He owns a bookstore which is on a houseboat. He doesn't just sell you a book but he sits with his customers and can sense from the way they reply what type of book would most suit the hurt in their soul. He is right with just about everyone, but he has no recommendation to repair himself.
-When he hears of the plight of the woman who moved in, he goes to her and senses books that would help her and he wants to give them to her. She has very little in her apartment, and he eyes a table that he's had for years, which is sitting in his own apartment. He decides to give her this as well.
-When the woman, Catherine, does take the table and books, she notices that there is a drawer in the table, which has been painted over. She manages to open the drawer and discovers a letter, unopened, that is addressed to Jean. She calls on him to let him know about it, but he reacts strongly and says he doesn't want to see it. She opens it and then calls on Jean and tells him he has to read it.
-Catherine invites Jean over and you could see that these are two individuals who are both carrying their hurt, but Catherine is able to speak about hers. Something about Catherine revives something in Jean, and the two are attracted to each other, but the demons that afflict each of them get in the way.
-The letter is opened, and it's from a woman by the name of Manon who sent it to Jean 21 years before. They had been lovers, but after some time, she got married and moved to the south of France, but still kept coming to Paris to be with Jean for years afterward. It was a little before he received the letter that Manon walked out suddenly and never came back. The letter, which he expected to be Manon telling him that even though she loved their relationship, their relationship had to end, was something completely different.
-Manon wrote to tell him that she could no longer come to him, but she wanted him to come to her. It was cancer, and the cancer was eating away at her body. She wanted to see him before the end.
-It was devastating to Jean. He hated himself for not having the courage to read what she wrote, for by now, he knew she was long gone.
-He decides to go to where she passed on and see her husband. He knows that he has to do this, even though he knows that there are beginnings with his relationship with Catherine. A young writer, Max, who was very successful with his first book but has had writer's block since then, joins him. A third person also joins and they ride on the houseboat to the south of France in search of themselves.
-Although the adventures become silly, at the end, the characters all learn to deal with the weights that are pushing them down. Satisfying but the change in the tone from the beginning of the book to the middle and then back again to the end left me left me unsure of the type of book I was reading. The writing is good though, and the ending is one that seems real, with a life lesson that is practical.

-Very powerful endeavor by the the author to determine if her grandfather was complicit in the killing of Jews and others during World War II in his native Lithuania. It's an especially jarring project because of the fact that, while her mother was a Catholic from that country, her father was a Jew.
-Where normally, the tales of survivors are of those who were in the camps, Ms. Gabis' research takes her to those who mainly suffered through the war outside the camps. We follow the first hand accounts of many of these survivors as their humanity was slowly taken away from them. They were shuttled from one ghetto to another. Sometimes, they just missed being transferred to a location where their relatives were, only to find out that every single person who had gone to that other location was killed.
-We follow the young teenagers and adults, who helped organize a resistance, all the while with the fear that even another Jew may reveal to the authorities of what they doing.
-Within Lithuania was the infamous Poligny, where Jews were rounded up and the Germans, who only set the process going and merely watched, were aided in their bloodthirsty plans by the willing hands of the local population. Local Lithuanians were the ones who coldly shot and killed thousands of Jews, whose bodies tumbled in open pits in the forest. After, the shooters would have a meal and the name of the book is taken from that situation. Was the author's grandfather responsible for the atrocities, especially as he was the head of the security police under the Gestapo? And was he a witness to or even an organizer of the mass killing?
-The author repeatedly goes back to Lithuania, to Poland, to Israel. She interviews many people, both subjects of the killings and those that risked their lives to save others, and it's painful to read of what people in that country went through. There was a hierarchy in the country because Lithuania was once independent, then the Russians took over and killed; then the local people thought the Germans would save them from the Russians, but they were worse; then the Russians came back, and it was worse still.
-You read of the torture that was inflicted. The author's grandmother, after surviving the Germans, was taken by the Russians and tortured, the skin on her arms being ripped out with pliers. Others, young Jews, were tortured horribly to reveal their plans of resistance, but the Jews withstood their suffering so that others would be saved, even though the torture included being buried alive.
-It's a difficult book to read, because it consists of stories of never ending cruelty. Through it all, the author keeps trying to find records that would reveal secrets of her grandfather that would show his innocence, but all the evidence  she uncovers shows just the opposite.
-It's a must read book to give you a picture of the suffering that people went through, a suffering whose effects never left them throughout not only their lives, but the lives of the next generation.

Very well written suspense story. A young girl who had a boyfriend that turned out to be violent has been trying to make a new life for herself. The ex boyfriend was sent to prison in Philadelphia and she heard he was recently released on parole. The girl, Jayne, is a photographer and by chance took photos of celebrities that were sold to a tabloid. The editor of that newspaper hires her to take photos of a sculptor whom no one else has photos of and he sends her to a small town in Maine where his information says the sculptor is living.
There she meets an ex policeman who had lost his wife to a murderer several years back and who, for a while, was thought to be her killer.
There were two young men who disappeared from that area, and Jayne becomes a potential 3rd victim, but manages to fight her way out and escape, but her abductor doesn't give up.
The suspense is kept up through the very end of the book.
Well written and the type of book you don't want to put down.

-A young woman in her 30's goes to a doctor who is famous for discerning the causes of unusual ailments. He examines her and finds nothing physically wrong yet she feels that death is very close by. He advises that her problems are caused, not by physical maladies, but by mental.
-He is intrigued by her manner and unusual complexion. When he sends a servant to follow her, he discovers she is the Countess Narona, and is a person who is followed by scandal. She is due to be married soon, and she reveals that her betrothed had been engaged to another woman and broke that engagement to be with her, which leaves the Countess guilt ridden. She explained that when she tried to break off the engagement, her fianc, Lord Montbarry, threatened to give credence to other false accusations about her, where it was said that her brother, the Baron, was actually her lover. She had to go ahead with the wedding.
-The Countess had met Agnes Lockwood, the scorned fianc, and found her to be kind and forgiving, but a terror of Agnes took hold of the Countess and she foretold a time that they would meet again under very bad circumstances. Because of the intensity of the Countess, fear rose up in Agnes as well.
-The married couple took a short honeymoon and their incompatibility was apparent. Another trip was made, this time to Venice, where the Baron joined the couple. A large residence was rented, and the Lord became ill. His cold worsened and doctors were called in, but his condition worsened until he was declared dead by two prominent attending physicians.
-Because of legal stipulations, the Countess could not inherit anything of the Lord, but a 10,000 life insurance policy was taken out on the Lord before the trip. This was paid out to the Countess as no impropriety could be found.
-The Countess returns and says she was drawn to London and to Agnes, despite her terror of Agnes. The Countess predicts that they will meet again, because they must. It will be either here or even in Venice. The Countess departs for the US with her brother, the Baron.
-The brother of the Lord, Henry, had invested in the construction of a new hotel in Venice, which was to be the modification of the very building in which his brother died. After the hotel opens, he happens to be given the room in which his brother died, and strange feelings envelop him. His sister, too, was given that room and she ran from the room in fear. All the family follow to the hotel to celebrate its opening because of Henry's investment.
-It's here that the haunting of that room reaches its climax. Fear grips the characters and discoveries are made, along with admissions by the Countess, that bring the secrets behind the mysteries to light.
-Written extremely well. Very good and recommended.

Well done in describing the angst felt by the main character as his need to return a piece of artwork clashes against his fear of what punishment will be meted out to him for taking it.
The side characters are developed so that you can empathize with the feelings of the main character as he interacts with them. Throughout his life, which appears to go from bad to worse, his choices in life continue to plague him and despite the fact that he doesn't find happiness, he's able to get to a point where he gets a clean slate from the repercussions of his actions.
The problems that have been not of his choice stay with him, but you feel he has a chance at finally having a life.

-Unusual coming of age story about a young Jewish man whose parents had been divorced for some years. His father was a Polish Jew, but always scheming to make the dollar, and always seemed to be scrambling. That life was too much for his mother, and she divorced her husband and married again.
-Izzy and his sister Becca had lived in NY City with their parents, but after the divorce, their mother took them to Long Island, where she met her current husband, an accountant. Though Becca excelled, Izzy kept falling into bad crowds and was constantly doing drugs. His mother and stepfather's move to New Mexico didn't improve the situation and he was expelled from college.
-A postcard arrives to the house, from someone who claimed to be an associate of his father, saying that Izzy's father, Alojzy, was dead. Despite his mother's wishes for Izzy to stay with her and not go to New York, Izzy leaves, and meets up with the person who sent the postcard, only to discover that it was sent on the chance that Alojzy's debts would be paid. Izzy questions whether his father is even dead, and starts to trace back to people who knew him in order to find out for himself.
-Alojzy, it turns out, was a street corner bookseller but there was also something more that Izzy soon discovers. There were some underworld Russian Jews that his father was connected to, as well as others. A sketchbook that his father kept had pictures drawn of a number of people and Izzy soon took over his father's book selling business in order to search those people out.
-A young girl who he sees on the street has a remarkable resemblance to an image that his father drew in his sketchbook, and the girl turns out to be a runaway. Izzy befriends her, and the story gets very interesting at this point, as she has a religious background and seems to be hiding from some type of abuse that she experienced.
-Izzy now finds himself involved in intrigues with a religious Hasidic sect, and the Russian underworld. Things start to get traumatic, and Izzy quickly becomes his father's son, as he deals with the situations he finds himself in, as his father would have, with force.
-Very good at the end, as Izzy learns to be a survivor.

-Memoir by the author, of her journey from being a Christian to her conversion to Judaism, which was the religion of her paternal grandparents. As a young girl, she was told by a Jewish friend that her father was a Jew. She didn't believe it, but didn't learn the full story of her family history until later on.
-Her paternal grandparents were from Czechoslovakia and experienced the oppression against the Jews in the early years of WWII. They were to leave with her grandmother's parents, but left first in 1941 and made it to Canada. Her great grandparents, though, never made it out.
-When her grandparents arrived, they wanted to avoid the oppressive attitude they had felt that was directed against Jews, and they wanted their future children not to have to worry about being accepted in society. As a result, they turned their back on Judaism and converted. Their son, Thomas, who was Alison's father, married a Christian, and it was as a Christian that Alison was raised.
-When she became an adult, Judaism always had a fascination for her. She became engaged to a young man, Degan, and he encouraged her to pursue her interest. She was conflicted, as her father was ambivalent about the religion; she herself wasn't sure if that was what she wanted; she also wasn't sure if her fiance would go along with this, as he didn't seem to want to convert as well.
-As she got more involved with the conversion process and classes, she was told by the female Rabbi who was guiding her, that without Degan converting with her, Alison's conversion request would not be granted, which added another layer of tension to her relationship.
-Ultimately,  through Reform rabbis, she was accepted, but for me the ending is bittersweet. As much as she seems committed to the religion, she is not considered a Jew by anyone other than the Reform movement. This can create more confusion going down the road, as the Judaism of the Reform movement, which states that the Bible was not written by G-d, but was divinely inspired, along with other disavowals, is not a universal belief among Jews. It's an interesting book, and well written but the premise of the book is not to my taste. Her successful conversion raises more issues and is not what I consider to be a happy ending.
-A very interesting and important point was raised in the book. In Alison's meetings with a psychologist to help her through her decision, the widespread belief was brought out that, because so many Ashkenazi Jews lost family members in the Holocaust, their descendants equate Judaism with that horror. It was when Alison realized that both were distinct that the therapist said that Alison reached a major breakthrough. A friend of mine, who belongs to the Reform movement, was speaking with his son and his son said he knows why marrying someone Jewish was so important. It was only because his grandma lost so much of her family in the Holocaust and it was important for her to see her grandchildren marry Jews. Because of his son's lack of feeling for Judaism other than as an expression of support for the grandmother's resistance against the Holocaust, once the grandmother was not going to be around, there would be no reason to prevent him from marrying out of his faith, which is what his son also expressed.

-Thought provoking short but deep novel, that explores events that shape a person's faults and strengths through the thoughts that go through a young woman's mind as she lays in a hospital bed.
-Lucy Barton is that young woman. She's in the hospital for an extended period of time with what may be a life threatening disease. The background of her life slowly opens up. Her mother comes to visit her in the hospital and stays with her five days, but it's a mother who has not seen her daughter for nine years. Lucy's parents struggled heavily when she was growing up, and her siblings, a brother and a sister, have never climbed out of that downtrodden mindset. Lucy had dreams of more and she pushed herself to be a writer, but she, too, was battling inner demons.
-Lucy recalls being made fun of in her early years at school and being a pariah family because of the lack of money. Because of their troubles, her father could be cruel and her mother cold. When Lucy married, it was to a man whose mother was from the Midwest but whose father was a German prisoner of war, brought to the United States to serve his time. Though Lucy's father in law was said to have denounced the German ideology once in the US, Lucy's father looked at her husband as one of the Germans that killed members of his family who served in the armed forces and refused to acknowledge him or his daughter. With the arrival of her mother to the hospital, despite the coldness that Lucy experienced in her youth, all Lucy wanted was to hear her mother's voice with a very deep need.
-Lucy had befriended a woman who is an accomplished writer and she went to the woman's writing workshop. Lucy was told to write of characters with all of their faults and not to gloss over them. Only then would she be successful. In doing so in this story, the author, who writes in Lucy's words, displays Lucy's faults that destroy her life in one way but brings her success in others.
-In a most poignant scene, her youngest daughter tells Lucy that when she writes a novel, she can re-write it any number of times, but when raising a family, you have only one chance to do it right.
-It's a book that digs deep into fears that are basic, as well as prejudices. It shows how frail people are and how, even if they're considered to be strong, it's only because they're trying to conceal a weakness inside, that, to them, is glaring.
-Recommended.

What starts out as an investigation to a crime which is grisly evolves into a complex scheme.
Dr. Temperance Brennan is called in to evaluate the bones of a just born child who is left to die. There is a woman who had gone to the hospital complaining of vaginal bleeding and, according to the doctor, appeared to have recently given birth. It appears that this woman had a child and after its birth, wrapped it up and left it to die. Slowly, the identity of the woman is revealed, and, at the crime scene, Dr. Brennan discovers more child bodies.
A hunt is on to locate this woman who is found to have left 4 babies to die.
The trail leads to western Canada, and the Dr. is asked to continue with the investigation and is joined by Detective Ryan as well as a Sergeant in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. As they delve deeper, other characters surface. What appears to have started as a homicide investigation, morphs first into a drug turf battle and continues its evolution into so much more.
Using her forensic knowledge, as well as bringing together other scientific facts, Dr. Brennan uncovers a plot that was years in the making, and through her investigation, it starts unraveling, putting her in danger for her life.
Very good and involved plot with the pieces coming together in the end.

Very illuminating book on a period in American history, when children in the east coast were shipped by the thousands to families in the mid west during the 1920's. These children were unwanted and were either orphans or given up by parents who couldn't afford to keep them, or who simply didn't want them. The homes they went to, more often than not, were only desirous of workers, and many of these children suffered all forms of abuse.
This book gives a fictional story of one of those children, but it begins in the current time, by telling the story of a child whose father had died and whose mother was a no good drug addict. The girl, Molly, is forced by the "system" to go to several different foster homes. She has a rebellious streak to her and keeps to herself. She turns gothic in her appearance and dress to demonstrate her toughness. Getting into trouble by disrespecting authority is something she's grown used to, as she hasn't experienced people who are interested in what she wants, only what they want of her.
Molly is currently living with a couple, Ralph and Dina. Ralph has hopes that Molly will turn around, but Dina and Molly clash tremendously. A boy in school, Jack, has seen through Molly's hard exterior and befriends her.
Because Molly is very intelligent and devours classic books, one day, when Molly is in the school library, she has an urge to own one of those books. She selects a book whose title she loves, that is old and worn out, and then tries to sneak out of the library with it. She's caught and is now forced to do community service work for 50 hours as a punishment.
The punishment now involves assisting a 90 year old woman, Vivian Daly, in cleaning out her attic. Vivian owned a department store with her husband, that was very successful and when they sold it, she moved to Maine and bought a large home near the water. Molly's boyfriend, Jack, had arranged it, as Jack's mom works for Vivian, and he thought it would be an easier type of endeavor for Molly to complete.
Despite Molly's rebellious nature, she is a naturally very organized person, and she meets Vivian. As each day passes, they slowly go through the contents of the attic, barely throwing anything out, but Molly begins to get the story of Vivian's life, a life that has been much more tortuous than anything that Molly has been through. Molly realizes that this "rich woman" who seemingly is very far removed from understanding Molly's hardships, experienced them with even greater force.
The story of Vivian's life flows out, and things that were buried in Vivian's life that had stayed hidden for years, pour out. In a twist, Molly then becomes the one to help Vivian trace back to her history, helping Vivian locate and unite with her family who she never even dreamed existed.
Very touching story and shed's light on events that very few people are aware of.

-Interesting way of telling a story, by jumping from the point of view of one character to the next as the story progresses. We start out with Lev Meyer, a young boy whose mother had passed away recently. Lev has an older sister, Samara, and their father is a professor by the name of David Meyer. David was religious at one point, but lost his feeling for religion, and was studying Kabbalah as a secular subject. His feeling for religion, rather than one of apathy, was one of repulsion. We learned that both he and his wife were religious at one point, but he turned away, while his wife still embraced the religion. When David decided to completely separate himself from religion and shaved his beard, his wife went deeper into Judaism, but died soon after, when she was struck by a car.
-We see Lev's sister now secretly taking Bat Mitzvah lessons without her father's knowledge and when several young girls are called on to read in front of a large crowd in a mass Bat Mitzvah ceremony, Samara was sitting in the audience. All of a sudden she rose and walked to the remaining empty seat on the stage and surprised and angered her father, by reading a section of the Torah in the ceremony. Because of her father's reaction, she wanted nothing else to do with Judaism.
-Years later, we follow David Meyer, who has been secretly dating a string of his students in the university where he teaches. Even though David was no longer religious, he was obsessed with delving into Kabbalah, but only as a secular enterprise. His son Lev is now, to David's dismay, a yeshiva student, while Samara is attending university on a full scholarship and is in a secret lesbian relationship.
-David's attraction to Kabbalah and the explanations of it, are something akin to what Madonna was probably exposed to. It is sorely lacking in practice, and is spoken about as a search for the Tree of Knowledge, with the ten Sfirot as a ladder that, once climbed, will enable a person to reach mental perfection. In the 3rd and 4th part of the book, Samara has elevated her mind to the highest level of the Sfirot and is in danger of losing her mind. Again, this would have been much better if they only tried to attain those levels instead of appearing to have actually been able to have done so.
-As a book covering a subject which is divorced from what Judaism really teaches about mysticism, it's very interesting and the story is told in an unusual way, but the fact that the Kabbalah of the story is so distorted from actual Kabbalah, it leaves me with a feeling that I've read science fiction, where the science portrayed has no relationship to any of the scientific laws that we accept.
-It's because of this that I would have to give the book a mediocre rating, although others, who have no clue what Judaism and Kabbalah actually are, may like it.

-Maisie Dobbs is called upon to investigate the death of an artist, Nick Bassington-Hope, by the artist's sister. Inspector Stratton of Scotland Yard, had been on duty at the time of the death, and he felt that there was no mystery about it. The artist was preparing for an exhibition of his pieces, and was alone on a scaffold, and working late at night in the art gallery. When the caretaker came in early the next morning, he found Nick lying on the hard floor, with a broken neck, and the scaffold railing had been broken. To all appearances, it seemed that the artist had leaned against the scaffold railing, which broke, and he fell to his death.
-Georgina Bassington-Hope, Nick's sister, felt, in her heart, that something was wrong. There was no evidence of foul play, and her whole family felt she was wrong. There was something in how Georgina described her inner feeling, the same type of inner feeling that guides Maisie, that made Maisie take the case.
-Maisie's process of discovery involved trying to understand the dead man fully, from his likes and dislikes; how he lived; who his friends were; and the source of the emotions that were directed into the paintings that he produced, especially his final painting, which was supposed to have been his piece de resistance, but which remained hidden away in a place only the dead man knew.
-Nick's brother, Harry, is the bad apple of the family, and is always in trouble because of gambling debts. Maisie overhears Georgina giving Harry money, which is promptly taken from him by underworld thugs when he leaves the house. As Maisie continues to probe, she develops a case map, a graphic representation of what she has discovered so far, along with numerous notes. Her office, though, is completely ransacked, and the case map stolen, so that Maisie fears that violence may be directed at her own person.
-Billy Beale, her assistant, is going through his own turmoil, as his eldest daughter, Lizzie is struck down by a disease, and she keeps getting worse. When Maisie finally goes to Billy's home, she realizes that it's diphtheria, and she rushes with the young girl to the hospital, where Billy and his wife Doreen stage a constant vigil.
-The case is a difficult one, as Maisie doesn't know who is telling her the truth and who is not, and it's only when small clues show up, that Maisie begins to piece together what happened on the night that Nick was found dead.
-This is another fine and interesting mystery, as Maisie, though seemingly so in control, still must battle her own insecurities along the way.

-Rick Dockery is a quarterback in the NFL but has had a very lackluster career. Over the course of 6 years, he has been traded to 8 different teams. He's been a third string starter, but, even though he'd shown great potential outside of actual games, his performance during play has been detrimental to his teams.
-We come across Rick while he's lying in a hospital bed, after a brutal collision in a playoff game. He's earned the enmity of everyone in Cleveland, the home town of his team, after three of his passes were caught by the opposing team in the last 11 minutes of the game, turning what should have been an easy win for Cleveland, into a loss.
-His agent, Arnie, has been told that Rick has now been sacked from the team, and no team in the NFL would even consider hiring him. It appears that his career is over, especially as the press, particularly a reporter by the name of Charlie Cray for the Cleveland Post, has a field day with attacks on Rick's performance.
-There appears to be no one in the country who would be willing to hire Rick, but Arnie, his agent, is contacted by a team that is outside of the country. In Italy, it turns out, there is a league for teams playing American football, and one of those teams, the Parma Panthers, want Rick. It's several steps down, especially as his pay would only be 4,000 Euros a month, while the local players play on a volunteer basis, but Arnie convinces Rick that it's still something and RIck goes. It will be a commitment for only 5 months and it's during the spring, so Arnie hopes that people will forget the embarrassment of those 11 minutes of the playoff game.
-Over the course of those months, Rick is introduced to Italian culture and comes into his own as a player. He has his ups and downs, but he gets his life back. Despite having a chance to be hired in the US only having just started in Italy, he remains loyal to this group of men who are struggling to win their own Italian Super Bowl. The arrival to Italy of the vicious Cleveland Post reporter who continues to write scathing critiques of Rick's abilities, by severely twisting actual events, does shake up Rick but he learns to deal with it and he eventually leads his team to victory.
-It's an uplifting story that also shows the tension as they prepare for each game, while at the same time, we watch RIck's personal life rise as well. Good story.

users.query: Repaired my favorite lounge chair with this cord after the original stuff deteriorated from the sun.  Back in action!

cands.text: Bought this for a pendant necklace I (foolishly?) bought here on Amazon.  Their chain broke immediately, this one is significantly stronger.  I gave it a tug just to be sure.  Seems solid!

Bought this from a different website and have since returned it.  I'm not sure if there was a defective materials batch or what the case was, but this thing rusted in just a few days.  There were other things I didn't like, but compared to the rust, they aren't even worth a mention.  A lot of 5 star ratings for something that rusts this readily.  Not enough chromium in this stainless steel. Junk.

This is the watch I just recently replaced.  I purchased it elsewhere, but I figured I should write a review.

When I first received the watch, I absolutely loved it.  Appearance was excellent, craftsmanship appeared solid, nothing was out of place-- I was feeling pretty good about my purchase!  I wore it all the time.  Well, it appears I got a bad one.  The water resistance on mine was nonexistent.  I was washing lettuce of all things, dunked my hands in the water, and that was pretty much the end.  A little water got inside, I figured I could just lay it in a bag of rice and let it dry out--nope.  It dried, and it died.  The watch was under warranty, but they required $28 for return shipping, after I pay to ship the watch to them in the first place.  That's approaching 42 dollars from where I'm located.  For a watch that's under 50 dollars in the first place, I'd rather not go weeks without a watch to save a few dollars resurrecting a watch that I'd be afraid to ever get wet again.  After reading some of these reviews of the horror stories of sending it in, I do believe I dodged a bullet.

Anyway, I went with a different brand this time.  I don't know much about the Invicta brand, but after that little fiasco, I'll try someone else.

I don't know who started the trend of having ridiculous over-the-top luxury style packaging for basic cables and things, but these guys do it too.  A bag, a tear away pouch, then another plastic sleeve around the perfectly-wrapped little cable.  Good grief, it's a cable, not a Rolex.  But if you love opening fancy packages, this one's for you!  Super silly, but I'm not going to subtract a star over it.

Fits both my iPad 2 (with a folio style case attached) and my iPhone 4S (with a bumper style case attached).  Yeah, yeah, I'm not exactly cutting edge here with my old Apple stuff, but it still works great.  It charges both devices with no warning message.  Seems like a sturdy enough cable, I will update this review if I have any problems.
Works great, fiance's other similar case self destructed, this one seem far better built.  Odor wasn't too oppressive out of the packaging, either.

Our local vacuum shop closed down.  Good to see I can still get filters for my Filter Queen Princess III.  My parents bought the vacuum when I was a child.  They eventually wanted an upright vacuum and replaced it over a decade ago, I told them I would gladly take it.  I'm now 33, have my own family, and we've been using the vacuum for 9 years in our own house.  Excellent vacuum, will use it as long as I can find filters.  And since they all seem to take the same filter, that should be for a good long time.

So, hmm.  Is there a point to update a review on such an old product?  Sure, why not!  You can read the review below, as it was 100% accurate up to a couple months ago.  Freezing, poor compatibility, crashing apps...  Now, finally, they seem to have nailed it down.  I haven't had an app crash since the update.  Everything is silky smooth, perfect compatibility with popular websites (youtube, facebook, etc).  I'm glad this tablet has new life, as the Amazon Underground service is fantastic.  And oddly enough as the new hardware is all budget-based, the old HDX tablets are the best Kindles to utilize the Underground stuff.

I've only rated my Kindle 3 stars, and that's mainly due to reliability.  Not reliability as in durability, just overall functionality when I need it.  For me, a tablet needs to be at the ready to browse the internet or whatever task I have at hand for it.  The Kindle, well, it just doesn't always work.  Or things are more difficult than they need to be.  I don't have any games or excess apps on mine.  It's basically an internet machine.  I typically watch YouTube or Amazon Prime or some other video streaming service in the morning as I eat breakfast.  It's definitely gotten better through updates, but it still struggles.  It still freezes.  It still has me frustrated to the point of going to my PC to finish the task on occasion.  And I mention YouTube, but of course, being an Amazon device, it doesn't actually have the official YouTube app.  You have to browse to YouTube on the internet.

That's the problem.  With a Tablet PC, that doesn't happen.  With an iPad, that doesn't happen.  For the price, it's an okay machine.  That's why it's 3 stars.  It doesn't blow me away.  It works most of the time.  It works for most of the tasks I want it for.  But whenever I visit any of my friends with iPads, there's really no comparison.  Even little stuff, like "sometimes" making a noise when you plug the charger in, but not always.  Why?  Or when I'm browsing the internet, then push the power button to put it to sleep....and it comes back on 3 seconds later for no apparent reason.  Why?  Or repeatedly telling me "I'm in fullscreen mode" for the internet app or any other app I've used hundreds of times.  It just lacks polish.  They've tried very hard to create this Amazon silk atmosphere, but you can tell it's just a shell of an operating system that just isn't that solid.  Oh well.  I won't be replacing it.  It's good enough for what I need it for, but it's absolutely not a TabletPC or iPad replacement.  Not even close.

Update:  I received an e-mail after complaining to Amazon that Fire OS 5 will be released to this tablet.  Will this cure its maladies?  We'll see.  Second update, that e-mail was retracted as it wasn't factual.  OS 5 never came and never will, after I received a second apology e-mail.  Classy.

Absolutely fantastic.  My CP1215's ability to print in color decayed long ago.  New OEM cartridges did not fix it.  Magenta was all over the place, cyan and yellow were never aligned no matter how many tries. Really didn't want to sink $260 into HP toner AGAIN to "see" if that would fix it.

So I have been using this printer as black and white only for over a year.  But since it still printed black, that means the fuser works...right?  When the black toner ran out, I purchased this set since it came with 2 blacks and all the colors for less than the cost of just the black HP toner.  I figured at worst, the color still wouldn't work and I'd have two black carts on hand.

Put bluntly, these fixed everything!  Perfectly aligned, I have color again!  Beautiful, streak free color!  I am impressed.  These things come packaged very nicely with proper seals and drum covers to keep them safe.  I couldn't be happier, and will most definitely be back for more when the time comes.

I also own a Brother HL-3170CDW and I see that Toner Kingdom makes replacement cartridges for that printer as well.  I'll see how they hold up, but so far I am impressed.  If anything changes, I'll adjust my review.

I love Amazon, but Kindle accessories are priced even worse than Apple accessories.  This charger should have been the one in the box with the HDX models, especially since the component cost difference is pennies.  I mean, I get it.  The tablet was a bargain.  It truly was.  But between this and the OEM Kindle HDX case's absolutely ludicrous price, I can't justify spending the money on either right now.  Cut both in half and it'd be a done deal.  Again, I LOVE the tablet.  Not a single complaint.  But these accessories, come on guys.

Anyway, it's a 1.8A charger.  You likely have at least a 1.5A 5v charger in a drawer somewhere from an old cell phone.  Until this price comes way down, use that.

**Updated Star rating from 1 to 5 for the printer.  Customer service is still very, very unimpressive however.**

First of all, stupid me for waiting.  I bought this in November 2016, didn't install it until after the holidays.  AKA, after the return period.  Didn't work immediately.  The printer fails to fuse the toner to the paper reliably.  All 4 toner colors completely fade or disappear.

Ok, sure.  Defective unit.  Fine.  I have been battling with Brother since December to get this resolved.  It's now April 20th, still no resolution.  I have been bounced around from escalations to senior specialists.  The latest dagger was being told that they would send a refurbished printer for me to exchange my model with, and that it would arrive in 2-3 business days.  Gave them my credit card info, all that standard stuff.  But finally!  A resolution!  ...That was 15 days ago.

I'm at my wits end.  I already own a Brother HL-2140 and love it.  I've run reams and reams of paper through that little printer and it continues to serve me well.  But after this?  I can't recommend Brother brand anything to anyone.

I called again for the umpteenth time to ask what the status was on the exchange printer that was being sent to me was?  They had no record of that ever happening.  Blood pressure rising.

Anyway, after a total of 5 months, I was finally able to get Brother to swap my defective unit with one of theirs.  From then on out, we've had zero problems.  Prints are beautiful and have not had a single print issue since.  I haven't had any jamming issues ever, so it really does seem to be a decent printer marred by a horrible experience in customer service.

But upon reading reviews of just about any home/small business grade color laser printer, they're all riddled with 1 star reviews.  So it seems it's just luck of the draw.  There doesn't seem to be a clear choice.

For us, there was a lot of strife, but in the end, we do love the printer.  It works great from our computers, and even if we need to quickly print something from our smartphones using the appropriate plug-in.  It's really a nice machine.  After using it, it enters sleep and eventually a deep sleep state where it rests and doesn't make a noise until you call upon it again.

This will be my last year of this magazine.  It's not a bad magazine, but the company behind it is the most lowdown, dirty, stereotypical "used car salesman" style company I have ever dealt with. And that's unfair to the car salesman.

Get prepared to make some phone calls.  They've sent me two books, then aggressively tried to charge me for them each time.  Problem is, I didn't order either one.  I didn't use a credit card, but I wouldn't put it past them to make unauthorized charges, so be careful.  Enough verbal threatening over the phone will eventually get them off your case, and they'll just tell you to keep the books.  Believe me, not worth it.

And lastly, I'm no longer getting my money's worth.  The price per issue has gotten far too high, and keep in mind each issue is only approx 30 pages.  Pair that with only 6 issues per year, and you're not getting much for your money.  Their equipment reviews are nice, their product comparisons are nice, but the recipes are hit or miss. Far too many tend to focus more on how pretty they look rather than how they taste.  But overall, it just isn't worth the hassle any longer.  Not to mention you'll get inundated with junk mail.

Warm up your cross-cut shredder, you're going to need it.  I'm here today because I got a warning that my subscription was about to expire, even though I swore I just extended it a few months ago.  Since there are only 6 issues, they pretty much bombard you with renewal requests right out of the gate.  Annoying, to say the least.

If anyone at Cook's Illustrated monitors these reviews, let it be known that your PRACTICES are why I will not be renewing, not your content.  Impossible to recommend until they change their ways.

All in all, I would buy this controller again.  There are a few annoyances, one being that it requires 3 AAA batteries.  I read one review here about the R2 and L2 buttons getting stuck, I tried it, and the commenter is correct.  If you squeeze down hard on them they can slide up a bit and get stuck in the controller housing.  It's easily popped back out, and I honestly have never done that while playing.  My other gripe is the analog sticks have a rubber coating, but they're quite slippery.  Those points aside, it's still a great controller that has been completely reliable and the analogs have been perfectly accurate for me (that's always risky with 3rd party stuff, licensed or not.) Also, the buttons are a lot more tactile than the Dualshock 2, that controller's buttons were rather mushy.  One last aspect worth mentioning is that the controller has a sort of coating on it that makes it nice to the touch and prevents it from becoming slippery.  Between this controller and Logitech's wireless controller, it's a bit of a tossup.  I like and dislike certain aspects about each one.

It pains me to write this review, as I did enjoy this pencil immensely.  But I would just like to warn people that despite its stout feel, it's quite fragile.  I used this pencil at work on a low height desk.  I accidentally swiped it onto the floor, about a 3.5 foot drop onto a carpeted floor.  Shockingly, that little drop was enough to render this pencil useless.  The integrity of the pencil depends on that colored plastic sleeve that the nose cone threads onto, which sheared right off.  Someone dropped the ball designing this pencil.  To build the rest of the pencil out of rugged materials, only to hold it all together with a piece of fine-threaded plastic?  Why would anyone do this?  Needs an immediate redesign.  Such an integral part should be far more durable.  Color-anodized stainless steel would have been beautiful.  Color-anodized aluminum would have sufficed.
Absolutely love it, plenty of grippy lines that do the job well.

Excellent!  Had an old 3 way splitter that was resulting in a couple channels being too weak.  Put this little gem in and now we get channels we didn't even have before.  Full marks!  You'll need an additional coax cable to run to the AC adapter.  It uses a COAX cable as the power cord.  Odd, but functional.

These were pretty good shoes.  My first pair of shoes that weren't $25 at a department store.  Very, very comfortable shoe, however, I will give a list of things I noticed over the year I wore them.
1.) You're going to need replacement insoles in about 6 months.  They start off extremely comfortable and supportive, but after 6 months mine were flat as a pancake (175lb male)  A couple bucks for a cheapo insole was all it took to make them feel like new again.

2.)  There are several circle shaped details on the tread.  These circles trap snow and mud like no other shoe I've worn, and immediately let go when you walk indoors somewhere.  A small detail, but one that annoyed me to no end (and caused me to pick a different Merrell shoe this time around).

3.)  The Vibram soles showed wear extremely fast.  I do a lot of hiking on dirt trails, but expected far better from Vibram branded material.  If you look on the heel end of the sole, there are 4 circles.  Within 6 months those lugs were worn flat, the circles were gone.  I don't drag my feet while I hike and have never had a sole wear flat like that.  Very odd.  But even with the flattened lugs, they still gripped very well.  Perhaps it's planned to wear there?  I don't know.

I'm still giving the shoes 5 stars, as I did love them and bought another pair of Merrells.  I don't expect a daily-wear shoe's materials to last over 12 months.  It just isn't going to happen.  And for the comfort and support these shoes give, well worth 5 stars and a recommendation.  They're amazingly comfortable.

It seems to be a perfectly decent product.  Looks great, repels water as you'd expect.  I did my wife's new Rogue with the Wolfgang, and my 2013 Elantra GT with a widely available synthetic wax that's well under half the cost.  Both need to be applied every 8 weeks, just as all waxes and sealants do.  Some waxes will claim 6 months or what have you, but if it's left outside or you're driving it daily, that really isn't realistic.

So, does it give good results?  Sure does!  But I can't say it's superior to anything else I've tried.  Loses 1 star for value, but other than that it's a perfectly capable sealant.

Very well-made strap, here.  It runs a little long, but my wrists are fairly small at 6.5 inches.  I ended up running the tail through both loops, then back around and through the first loop again.  It has yet to ever slip out.  I actually ordered it based on specifications of a watch that claimed to be 20 mm, turned out my watch is 22 mm.  Figures!  I will not be returning the strap, however.  I have another watch it will look great on.

I wasn't sure what to expect buying a strap sight-unseen over the internet, but I'm glad I did.  They put some effort into this thing.  The strap is tightly woven and well cut, no fraying what-so-ever.  Highly polished closure and rings, wrapped in plastic and it even came in quite a fancy box.  Whoever was in charge of presentation sure hit the mark.  I am ordering a second as soon as I am finished writing this review, so there's your real proof.  Excellent item, highly recommended.

After wearing these in over a few miles, I took them to Las Vegas.  Averaging 35,000 steps a day, these felt great.  No foot issues what-so-ever.  They do run large, at least the pair I got.  I typically wear 12's, these I'm wearing 11s and they're still on the roomy side.

We'll see how they hold up.  The sole is made up of tall pillars of foam rubber, so at the very least it should take a while for them to wear down completely.  No visible wear after pounding pavement all day for 4 days in Vegas.  I hope they hold up well because they're incredibly comfortable shoes.  Weren't for the first mile or so, but after a short wear in period they've been fantastic.

After burning out a cheap pair of foam-tread shoes in about a month back in the day, I swore them off for years.  Now I'm giving them another shot, so far so good?  All they have to make is 6 months for me to be happy.

I'm always shocked when I go to local stores and still see this radio on the shelves.  There's a reason for that.  I bought mine well over 5 years ago and it's still the absolute best portable radio I've ever used.  Digital tuning with presets, a surprisingly effective AM antenna, great sound, weather band, a battery indicator, it's really well-equipped.  Over all these years, there's only one feature it lacks that would make me buy another:  A light.  If you're using it at night, it can be a bit tricky to see the display.

Honestly, that's the only complaint I've had over all these years.  Anything else is common of all portable radios, such as minor interference near computers, etc.

A true 5 our of 5 product, it may seem a bit pricey, as cheap radios can be obtained at dollar stores, but it's worth it.  Well worth it.

There's also the Sangean DS-200X which is a decent option.  The user interface drove me nuts, but it may not bother you as much, especially if you don't switch stations often.

Let me share with you how Amazon tablets work.  Okay?  I bought a Fire HDX 7 in late October, 2014.  Beginning of 2015?  End of support.
No bug fixes, no OS updates.  That new OS that came out, Fire OS 5?  Comes with these tablets, that have slower processors, less RAM and lower resolution screens.  But not for our $200-400 HDXs from 1 year ago.  Sound absurd?  It is.

That's what you're signing up for.  1 year of use, then it will become obsolete, bugs will not be fixed, programs will not be supported,  things won't work, and you're out of luck.  $200, down the toilet a year later.  Their answer?  Buy a new one.

Want advice?  Save for an iPad Mini or iPad.  Even the iPad 2 from 2011 is still supported and runs the latest iOS 9.2.  That's how you support your customers.  What Amazon is offering is a disposable tablet, yet continues to make direct product comparisons to the iPad and iPad Mini line throughout their advertisements.  They're not iPad competitors.  They're far closer to those $30 Generic Android tablets you find at discount stores.

Don't fall for it like I did.  These are a waste of money.  You WILL regret it.

I have had this Thermostat for a few months now and it works great!

I had lost the directions for installation and Programming but was able to find them in PDF format after I Googled it.

Installation was a breeze. It was 4 wires, 2 red, 2 black. Took 5-10 minutes.

Programming it took about 10 minutes and it has worked great ever since.

I use it on a forced air electric heater and it's WAY more accurate than my old dial mercury switch. Well worth the $$. Dropped the electric bill by almost 40%.

I have it programmed to turn on 10 minutes before I wake up in the morning and turn off when I leave. I have it programmed to turn on anytime in the evening if the temperature drops below 65 degrees after 6pm until 10pm. It's awesome!

I would highly recommend it.
