This is a wonderful idea for a book, and it provides a great deal of information, but I never quite could figure out what the purpose of the book is. It's sort of a collection of essays about bad clowns.

Radford starts off with a bit of history, and he puts together in the clown category some aspects I would not have thought of, but that make sense. The Punch and Judy puppet shows of course feature Punch's gratuitous violence to all and sundry, but I would not have seen a connection with the figure of Harlequin in commedia del'arte or the ancient business of kings having fools and jesters who can get away with criticism by dint of their defined role. Then there's the British clown Joseph Grimaldi (1778-1837) whose troubled life apparently is reflected in his memoirs, edited by one Charles Dickens, and Dickens seems to have much to do with the development of the bad clown trope (I must have missed those novels).

Other chapters address many related topics. Chapter 4 discusses irrational fear of clowns. Chapter 5 examines bad clowns in ink, largely comics. I had never heard of comics specializing in bad clowns and evil clown characters. Based on Radford's reporting, I'd say it is an acquired taste. Chapter 6 looks at "bad clowns of the screen" including film but also television (and now one assumes in social media), including The Simpsons. Chapter 7 discusses bad clowns in music--apparently bad clowns show up in contemporary music of the sort older adults like me are blissfully unaware of. Chapter 8 discusses clown porn--discusses, with no examples or illustrations, thankfully.

Chapter 9 covers creepy clowns and killer clowns, including some real killers. Chapter 10 covers activist clowns, clowns who use their humr and techniques for partisan views, which must hearken back to court jesters. Chapter 11 covers dip clowns, persons in clown costume suspended above a water tank; these insult passersby to the point they buy several baseball tosses to dunk the clown. Chapter 12 which is brief, looks at phantom clowns. These seem to be a few furtive individuals lurking in some form of clown costume and just plain phantoms existing in the minds and perceptions of people. Chapter 13 discusses trolls and the future of bad clowns--internet trolling is an interesting connection to make with clowns.

cands.text: I've reread this book ,and my impression is the same: this is a fun, fast and fairly informative read. The "Diabolical" and "Wicked" in the title are accurate only in the sense of irony. Stewart has wit and at times the book is really, really, funny. This is not really a bug book or about entomology, it's a vehicle for Stewart's wit, a hodgepodge of the odd, and the gross. The illustrations are black and white and have the effect of woodcuts.

This is a fun book but also substantive in research and quite well written. From the title, I had expected essentially a listing of the outrageous. Judging from the description of an upcoming book, it will incorporate this material and extend the length of history covered. The focus of this book is primarily Britain, and while it goes back to Tudor times and has some elements before that (clean-shaven Romans in skirts vs hairy Britons in trousers, for irony). After the cod-pieces the focus is mostly on women's fashions, save for wigs. There's an appendix of eclectic odd information she found in doing the research, including sumptuary law, recipes for make up (some of it rather dangerous) and more. The illustrations are excellent and there are a good many of them.

Chapter 2 concerns Medieval fashion, Chapter 3a the Tudors. In the 1400s lady's hats got tall, up to four feet. Men's shoes for a time had long toes, sometimes two feel past the toes, and some clergy thought the Plague was God's anger about men's shoes. Codpieces appear to have at origin been for modesty but for half a century emphasized men's genitals, often with color, even with ribbons--there's a nice portrait of Henry VIII wearing one. Her chapter titles are rather witty, such as Chapter 6 "Gorgeous Georges" on the Georgian era, a pun some readers may not get. Chapter 4 looks at ruffs, and has a good discussion of how they were made and worn. Chapter 5 covers the Stuarts and such things as lace-making. Chapter 6 covers wigs.

Among other intriguing chapters is 8, "Death by Crinoline," dangerous because of the extreme width of the dress (the illustrations give a wonderful sense of this) a woman could catch on fire without being aware of it. The corset and the emphasis on tiny waists was far more dangerous, resulting in deformity in some women.  Chapter 9 examines bustles, which really did, at least in one illustration, make women look like they had the rear of a horse attached. Chapter 10 is roughly the Edwardian era and has some excellent illustrations. Chapter 12 looks at fashions in World War 2, and is best on the rationing of clothing--perhaps oddly the war freed women from the worse concoctions of fashion. There are a couple of very short chapters after, but the meat of the book stops with the war.

This is one of the most interestingly infuriating books I have ever read. I recommend it but find it difficult to explain why. Foster's writing is excellent, but sometimes self-indulgent. The beast in the book is the human named Charles Foster, and the book is a study in extreme eccentricity. I don't think anyone but an Englishman could have written it. In the US he'd probably have been arrested for child abuse--hanging out with a son in a den dug  in the ground, eating worms and trying to understand badger-ness would probably have been great fun for his son. His six children were included in some of his attempts to understand these animals (not all the children on all the adventures). What stories they have!. Foster seems to be one of those writers whose writing and venturesome-ness merge. The result can be great reading or self-righteous sections not so palatable for a reader.

Foster writes "This book is an attempt to see the world from the height of a naked Welsh badger, London foxes, Exmoor otters, Oxford swifts and Scottish and West Country red deer..." Those locations, other than London, are likely to mean nothing to an American reader, and some of the detail is explicitly British (a centuries old badger sett, for example). Those assorted British-isms are minor, though. He does try to see world from their height, whether inches form the ground or in water, feel life in a den, taste their food, whether grubs or dumpster fare. It's matter of fact in the book but does have a sort of "ugh!" factor, perhaps deliberate. He sets up a chase (of himself) by hounds to see what it might feel like. He sniffs in the grass, sleeps in a den, defecates in the woods.

The chapters vary a good deal. The one on red deer is partly an account of and reflection on his hunting of red deer, although he gets into the habitat and tried to understand a deer's view, as he does with the others (well, not so much the swifts). The chapter on otters is not so good as the others, although it has some intriguing information. The chapter on foxes is mostly on the urban foxes. The best two chapters are the introductory chapter, "Becoming a Beast," and the following chapter on being a badger.

In another sense the book is less about understanding these animals' lives than an attempt to come to terms with otherness, whether with other humans or other species. It's a failure, he says, perhaps as any such attempt must be, but it was a long, lively and interesting adventure.

Every so often, I am pleasantly ambushed by a book I had not expected much of. I expected a discussion of how we use tropes based on personal understandings of the American Revolution, but this book is superb. The author is a professional historian, but this is not academic prose. He intentionally chose first-person narrative to foreground the historian's craft, and it works. I highly recommend this book; it needs to be read by people on all sides of our current political spectrum. In addition, it has a quite excellent annotated bibliography for any reader wishing to pursue these topics. Not everyone will like this book: while he is objective and surprisingly positive about the Tea Party, he is still opposed to some of their views.

Key in the book is that he breaks down views into two opposites: essentialists and organicists. Briefly, the essentialist position admires the Revolution and the documents such as the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution, but frames the view that these are the basics and should not be interpreted--we should seek the original intent of the Founding Fathers and measure our status as Americans by them. The organicist position sees the Revolution and its documents as continually evolving and never finished, continually creating a more perfect union. Shocket defines the Revolutionary era as running from the 1765 Stamp Act to the ratification of the Constitution in 1788.

He considers different delivery systems, as it were, and how they present the concepts based on the Revolution. The chapters could be read individually for people researching, for example, the presentation of the Revolution in film and on television.

In Chapter 1, he analyzes the rhetoric used in recent decades by presidential candidates--he notes, as one example, that Republicans use "Founding Fathers" and Democrats use "Founders" minus the Father part.

Chapter 2 looks at books, both popular and some academic (he portrays a volatile academic fight between two of the most prominent historians, among other things). He describes how a kind of Revolutionary chic has emerged, which tends to have strong essentialist views.

Chapter 3 is amusingly titled "We the Tourists" and describes the presentation of sites such as Colonial Williamsburg (he went to college in Williamsburg and worked there in the mid 1990s); he visited many of the sites, and his analysis is excellent. He notes that these present a simplified view, partly because most are non-profit and cannot afford to alienate sponsors or limit visitors. Most avoid preventing much about the vexing question of slavery in a recital about the triumph of liberty. Shocket calls some of the views "white fantasy slavery lite."

Chapter 4 is titled  "Give Me Liberty's Kids," and examines several films and television series such as "Liberty's Kids" and Mel Gibson in "The Patriot." This discussion of a historical theme in visual media is quite simply the best and most nuanced I have ever read.

Chapter 5 is titled "Originalism, the Tea Party and Reenactors." This is the most opinionated section of the book, because Schocket openly discusses his "organicist" views and finds the Tea Party a bit simplistic. Yet, his discussion of them is rather sympathetic, if slightly ironic, and he discusses how outraged citizens acting politically and engaging in political theater is as common as apple pie throughout the entirety of American history. The irony is that the original tea party in Boston harbor was an organized radical mob destroying private property belonging to a corporation. His discussion of Revolutionary era reenactors is fascinating--he observes that while they are most often conservative, they are also concerned with authenticity of uniforms, arms and more, and have a more complete understanding than most, and that they differentiate themselves from Civil War reenactors who sometimes  shade over into racism. He discusses the serious issue of "originalism" that has established itself in our court system, with Justice Scalia as exhibit number one, a view that excoriates judicial activism but is itself activist, and one that relies on original intent, an intent that Schocket describes as anything but uniform, with the political landscape and interpretations differing as wildly as they do today.

His last section describes how he sees the historian's craft and that our increasingly polarized political climate remains selective in how partisans choose to interpret founders and documents.

An entertaining, somewhat repetitive read. Each scoundrel or rogue has six or seven pages and some sort of photo. The style is sometimes a bit melodramatic. The sections are on the whole, rather good.

What bothers me are the selections. Ed Gein and the Harpe Brothers were clearly monsters and killers. But Hetty Green? She was a supremely difficult personality, and must have been hell to work for or be related to, but I don't see how she qualifies as a villain, scoundrel or rogue.

There's also a sort of moralizing tone in many of the portrayals, as in this-guy-was-evil and-it's-still-going-on tone. The fact that people are nasty, mean, murderous and sometimes monstrous is just that, an apparent fact of human existence, and this one aspect is my main gripe. But the characters are colorful and even readers allergic to American history will get some solid historical context in reading about them.

This is a lively and well-researched account of dealing and not dealing with filth, as defined by the Victorians. I found it a good read, However, some readers might want to know that some chapters go into considerable detail on policy debates, organizational conflicts and local government, which may not interest everyone as much as it did me.

The basic fact is that London went from a million people in 1800 to six million in 1900, and keeping the city clean was a challenge, and by today's standards, not possible. Houses cooked and kept warm by fires, mostly coal. Horses in their tens of thousands contributed huge amounts of dung and urine to city streets. Infrastructure was not particularly extensive, and dire--really, really dire--poverty was widespread. Access to water was spotty, people bathed perhaps once a week to once a year, sewage was a huge problem, disposal of refuse, washing clothes, even simply walking in the street were problems.

Chapter 1 deals with dust, which included cinders and dust from coal fires, as well as what we Americans would call trash. The details of recycling are amazing. Suffice to say that for a portion of the 1800s, trash collectors paid for the privilege of collecting. Chapter 2 concerns mud, a mixture of dirt, soil, water, horse urine and horse dung, and this chapter has to be read because description does not tell a potential reader much. Chapter 3 concerns night soil, that is human excreta, and the details on cesspools, primitive toilet facilities is fascinating--and London must have stunk.

Chapter 4 is "removable causes" and think slum clearance, because poor people can be removed, though there is more than that. Chapter 5 considers "vile bodies," that is corpses. Burial traditions were colorful and the smell of decaying bodies must have contributed to the city's odor. This chapter discusses changing practices and is intriguing if slightly macabre. Chapter 6 considers "The Great Unwashed," that is the mass of people, particularly poor people. And imagine trying to keep clothes clean with a lack of water, constant dirt and the miserable technology of the day--it's likely that a woman from mid 1800s London if transported to today would see Laundromats as the peak of civilization.

Chapter 7 discusses public toilets and some of the practices of the day--men seem to have urinated whenever they felt the need. Chapter 8 discusses housing and slums, and some of the attempts to improve conditions. Conditions were absolutely horrible in some areas. Chapter 9 discusses soot (a word we don't hear much of these days) and airborne pollution. People were aware that it had ill effects, but the struggle to improve it did not achieve much. This chapter also discusses chimney sweeps, with some sad detail on the children used (cancer, joint malformation, lung disease, beatings), but at least this was successfully dealt with.

The chapters can be read individually; for example if you are interested in fireplaces, chimneys and chimney sweeps. I personally found the chapters on dust, vile bodies and soot to be the most interesting.

This is an excellent book, but the title is somewhat misleading. The book has a lot of circus history, but it is by no means complete. You'll pick up a lot of circus-related information. George Washington was a repeat customer of the first American circus in 1793. Picasso's first lover was a trick rider and his first art dealer, a former clown. Alexander Calder (inventor of the mobile) made toy circus figures and then on his hands and knees would manipulate them as a performance--audiences loved it.

Simon breaks down the circus into 10 chapters that includes the development of circuses like Ringling and Barnum Bailey, but the strength of the book is looking at the kinds of acts that go into a circus, and these chapters include some remarkable stories of iconic and not so famous performers. These include Chapter 4, Cavalcades, on the era of circus parades. Chapter 5, Without a Net, looks at rope acts, high wire acts and related, including such artists as Blondin.. Chapter 6, Beasts, is on animal acts, particularly big cats and "lion tamers." Chapter 7 Clowns, looks at how clowns developed and at some of the major artists such as Oleg Popov and Emmett Kelley. Chapter 8 Feats, looks at strong men (and women), acrobats, contortionists, jugglers and others. Chapter 9, Prodigies, looks at sideshow elements such as the bearded lady and three legged boys, and may be the best chapter in the book--apparently, the circus provided a sense of acceptance and larger family for people who'd not have done so well elsewhere. The book is nicely illustrated.

The other chapters are less focused. Chapter 10 "Transformations," looks ate the present and evolving future of the circus and while brief, the rise of shows like the Cirque du Soleil. Chapter 1 lays out a circus history and Chapter 2 "Cirques Intimes" looks mostly at French and British shows ancestral to and variations on the usual idea of the circus, but these tended to be repeated shows in a dedicated venue rather than the traveling circus that is the usual circus stereotype.

If you review ratings of this book, you will find that most reviewers like it, but there is a scattering of gripes. Part of the concerns seem to be that Gilmour is not a historian and skips all over the place. If you are expecting a dour, chronological history, Gilmour is not your man. The book is partly his personal exploration of Italy. He tells the one story of Italy as a collection of interlocking regional histories, most significantly, of course, the division between north and south. He is rather negative about the House of Savoy (the Piedmont/ Sardinia rulers who provided the kings of united Italy). To an extent, he sees Italians as victims of their government (his discussion of the Berlusconi era is long, passionate and highly negative, justifiably so, I think).

The book does deliver a look at the various regions of Italy and their peoples. It's worth remembering that several of the larger European countries had a welter of dialects and regions, often at each other's throats. A majority of the people in France being able to speak French is an achievement only a bit more than a century old, for example. Italy is similar, and regional dialects apparently retain lots of differences. To be Italian, therefore, represents a number of variations. This would include regional cuisine, dialect, attitude toward the Church, preferences of saints, local power structure and the rest. Some areas of Italy remain largely devoted to the Church other areas have a multi-generational tendency to Communism.

Italian history is equally complex (and of course is the origin of some of the regional differences). Latins, Romans, Greeks, various Goths, Byzantines, Normans, French, Arabs, Aragonese and others are culpable in this history. Gilmour covers all this. He has sections on the mafia and mafia-like groups, perhaps the most depressing segment of the book: they remain powerful and are becoming more efficient and up to date. Gilmour sees a variety of structural elements retarding reform. His discussion of the Facist  era is good.

He is particularly good on the creation of the legend of unification, the regional dialects, and the persistent problems in the south. He notes that there is something approaching racism in the northern view of the south, commonly expressed as "Africa starts at Naples."

The book is not a fast read because of the welter of detail. It is witty, sometimes wry and often opinionated. It's a good read, though.

Gilmour more or less sees Italy as a failed state. A mystery exists, in a sense; Italy doesn't work so well as a nation, but a large portion of Italians live lives in health and prosperity. Is this because of or despite the historical and social constraints Gilmour explores?

This is a superb book, but before you buy it, realize that it is long, there are several dozen major characters and many more minor ones, so keeping track may get in the way of enjoying the book. The title and subtitle suggest a sort of sensationalist approach, but this is a serious work of history for a general audience (that is, not an academic study or textbook). There is plenty of violence and murder, rebellion, and executions and repression are important elements.

De Lisle knows her material exceptionally well, and manages to make even the infighting among court favorites to be compelling reading. Her description of many of the women in the greater Tudor family shows them to be, convincingly, formidable and interesting characters rather than the limp accepters-of-fate many accounts describe them as, A good example is Queen Mary, Elizabeth's sister, sometimes remembered as Bloody Mary, who emerges in de Lisle's account as a powerful, smart and adept political operator. Perhaps surviving to adulthood required that one develop such skills--women went to the scaffold as well as men (and sometimes were more dangerous). Henry VIII's wife Isabella of Aragon emerges as a formidable queen who could run a war in her husband's absence, not just Henry's first wife. And so go her descriptions of women, such as Lady Jane Grey, executed at 16 (by Bloody Mary) or Mary, Queen of Scots.

In particular, Mary Beaufort emerges as a power in the realm (mother of Henry VII). De Lisle makes plain a lot of history I had wondered about (such as where and how did the Tudors emerge out of Wales?). I had always been bored with tedious accounts--not this account!

I was surprised at the raw violence. Queen Mary had more than 200 Protestants burned at the stake. Elizabeth had 800 to 900 people hanged for a 1559 rebellion in the north of England, and in another incident, she ordered that conspirators be caused the maximum pain as they were executed, "for more terror" to deter others. The story is more than all the violence and conspiracy, the  murder of kings and all. De Lisle's character sketches are always good and sometimes superb. There are plenty of love matches, perhaps the most poignant being the love of Elizabeth's life who she could not marry.

If the book has any defects, I think it is in the story of the last dozen years of Elizabeth's reign, which seem a little hasty, as if de Lisle was near the end and her editors wanted to release the book.

I somehow missed this book when it came out. It has a great deal about jaguars, a great deal about Alan Rabinowitz and a lot about the problems of working with government and international conservation bodies.

The book is in a sense inspirational. Rabinowitz overcame what he says was a debilitating stutter and perhaps a not so happy family through discovering his specialty in science. Anyone looking for testimony that work in nature can heal humans should note this book. It is not a natural history of jaguars, at least not in the usual sense. It contains a great deal of information about jaguar evolution and for me the most interesting part, about jaguars in Amerindian cultures (such as the Olmec and Maya). There's some interesting material on how the jaguar kills its prey, differently than other big cats. A short but intriguing section is on jaguars in the USA; likely the ones seen are wanderers, and sealing the border may have eliminated that. Another section discusses how jaguars repopulated some areas where they had been extirpated by pre-Columbian Americans--the idea that the population crash in the Americas (losses of perhaps 95% and some estimates are ten to a hundred million people)  allowed forests to reestablish and animals to revive is an uncomfortable one. Note that by implication, jaguars might survive another big human population crash, perhaps one coming up soon?

Rabinowitz recounts his career, without intending to; his personal journey to more completely understand jaguars parallels the jaguar's journey. The "journey" isn't too specific, but from the old to the new world, and how jaguar "corridors" can link more jaguar-rich areas. Some of what he discusses is sad stuff. Jackie Kennedy sparked a huge uptick in killing of spotted cats, because of a fur she wore. Laws protecting jaguars are often ignored and the future is not assured, although discovering that it is one species rather than several subspecies is something Rabinowitz lauds. The jaguar is likely in better shape for survival than tigers and lions. Somehow the book ends on a positive note.

This is an excellent book about books. I found the writing crisp and witty. Another review notes several historical errors, but so far as I can tell, any are incidental and unrelated to the main theme. The book will interest book lovers and people interested in printing, collecting books and in illustrations. Readers without those interests may find it tedious.

the book is broken into four thematic sections (each of which is largely chronological). The page, that is what a book is made from, papyrus, parchment and paper. The second section looks at text, including writing, the development of printing, then on to typesetting and printing. Part three examines illustrations, that is woodcuts, copperplate, lithography to modern printing. The last section looks at the form of books, from papyrus scrolls to the codex and book binding. All the sections contain good detail, some of it fascinating and some only a true book lover would appreciate.

Among the things I found interesting are the following (you may of course have a different selection, the point being lots and lots of detail). In 1855 the USA used 405 million pounds of rags for making paper, which would be 200,000 tons or so--I know it was very high but I'd like to see more sourcing on that figure. The legend that US papermakers used mummy for making paper appears to be true, in the one instance of a New England paper maker. Between 1454 and 1500 some 12.6 million items were printed, and from 1750-1800 western Europe alone published 600 million books. That's an information revolution. Possibly the most entertaining fact is that the Book of Durrow (written between 650 and 700 CE) was rescued in the 1600s from a farmer who used it "like a sacred teabag" to produce holy water for his ailing cattle.

I found several discussions to be particularly good. The explanation of acid and acid free paper is the best I've read anywhere. The story of Gutenberg is quite entertaining. The section on inks and inking is fascinating, but some of it was over my head. The detail on the papyrus scroll is excellent.

The book itself is nicely produced. The illustrations are unusually well printed.

This book is not a guide to weird dinosaurs. It's a highly readable and entertaining account of some of the stranger dinosaurs discovered in the last decade or so. It's more about contemporary paleontology and paleontologists than anything else. It's a kind of science journalism, in which Pickrell travels to various places (including some actual sites) and interviews lots of people. Some of the stories are remarkable, such as the historic one of Franz Baron Nopcsa von Felso-Szilvas; Nopsca was a paleontologist (and adventurer and possible spy) from the Transylvania part of the old Austrian empire, whose speculations were borne out decades later, and who shot himself and his lover in 1933 when Hitler came to power--a script for an adventure movie.

There's been an explosion of knowledge about dinosaurs in the last couple of decades. In 2006 there were thought to be about 527 dinosaur genera, and that estimate was up to 1,100 genera in 2016. There must be tens of thousands of dinosaur species with more being recognized every year. The book's chapters cover fossils and expeditions in Alberta, Egypt, Romania, Mongolia, Australia, Argentina's Patagonia, Madagascar, and both the Arctic and Antarctic. The latter are fascinating--even with a temperate rather that polar climate (in today's terms of "polar") the animals still had to deal with several months of near-darkness, and appear to have adapted well.

Among the surprises the book discusses are the extreme range of sizes, dinosaurs the size of a rabbit to 70 tons of animal more than a hundred feet long. My favorite from the book is named Yi Qi (pronounced ee-chee) one of the remarkable fossils recently discovered in China, a bat-like glider. I was unaware that dinosaurs on islands could evolve into miniature forms (the way elephants became pygmy elephants on some islands).

Pickrell also brings in other aspects. Some places are simply too dangerous for scientists to visit (Algeria, Libya) and others have little or no local community that supports paleontological research (most of South America except for Argentina), so large areas are simply not well-known in terms of fossils, and future expeditions are likely to bring many more surprises. Then there's the business of fossil poachers, people who find fossils and sell them to dealers, the market apparently being large and unusual fossils of quality bring large prices, but they are usually lost to science and the circumstances of their discovery unrecorded.

For me, the most interesting portions were looking for fossils in Antarctica, and fossils discovered in the opal-mining region of Australia. Opals are a semi-precious gemstone, and opalization can occur in fossils.

I'm giving the book five stars because of originality, but I had to juggle 4 and 5 stars. This is a good read, but a good chunk of the book is peripheral to cannibalism, covering mad-cow disease and transmissible spongiform brain damages--he covers the New Guinea research which discovered a form of that disease in a people who engaged in ritual cannibalism of their dead. This is serious stuff and he makes a case that we my face something of an epidemic in the future, but that's really a second book.

The book does cover cannibalism in some interesting ways. He does a brief survey of cannibalism in nature, such as a study showing that herring gulls cannibalize about a quarter of chicks and eggs, and the in utero cannibalism of the sand tiger shark, and female cannibalism of the male preying mantis during mating. He notes that reports of polar bear cannibalism go back a century, so it is not simply a function of shrinking Artic ice.

Whether cannibalism has actually occurred outside of survival and ritual contexts is a contentious academic debate, but Schutt seems to say yes, it has occurred. He has some interesting categories.  Epicurean cannibalism is eating humans because they taste good, apparently known at times in Asia. Survival cannibalism is more common, with examples in Leningrad during the German siege and during famines such as the vast famine in China during the Great Leap Forward (when upwards of 30 million may have starved to death). Perhaps the most interesting category is medicinal cannibalism, an example of which is the long time belief that the blood of freshly executed criminals has therapeutic value, or the use of body parts from such a criminal's body (in potions, plasters, drinks and such). Another example of it would be the craze for mummy in the 1800s, literally from mummies imported from Egypt. Mumia was sold at a pharmacy in Germany as late as 1908 at 17.5 marks the kilo.

There's a lot, maybe a little too much, on the famous Donner party, but it's an interesting section.

This is a small book about an obscure topic. but one that's worth reading about. It contains examples (from the Getty collection) of beasts from Medieval illuminated manuscripts. The illustrations were generally small, and often in the margins of the text. Books produced and illustrated by hand must have been tedious sometimes, but these graphics show lively and fertile imaginations.

As in the title, some were fantasies and some factual, insofar as factual had an image. It's not clear which are original in the Getty materials, or whether they might have n]been copied or re-imagined, but they are delightful. Seems to me that they offer a kind of communication with the manuscript illuminators; people with imaginations so vivid would be worth meeting.

With so many reviews already available, I can't add much. I read the book because of the topic. I wasn't expecting much, but found it to be a serious book with a great deal of information. It's written in a sort of tabloid manner, which I don't much care for, but again, the research seems solid and the conclusions seem sound.

The book begins with an overview of drug manufacturers in Germany--because of the country's primacy in chemistry, perhaps it was natural that firms manufacturing drugs are notable in Germany, from the later 1800s. Chapter 1 is largely focused on a very popular drug called Pervitin, which according to the book, was a form of methamphetamine. The drug became very popular in the German armed forces, and Ohler argues that some of the achievements of German arms was achieved by forces kept alert and functioning by the drug. It's a bit ironic given the Nazi's harsh views of drug addiction (often mandatory cold-turkey or a concentration camp).

The book also details Hitler's growing drug use (it didn't start out as drugs in a sense, but rather injections of chemicals for health--the story of his "personal doctor" who kept Hitler injected full of chemicals and drugs throughout the war, is really the main focus. Hitler's and Goering's drug use account for the miracle of Dunkirk, says Ohler.

If Ohler is correct, Hitler's health, mental acuity, strategic vision and general physical health went down in a drug-drenched spiral, leaving him a wreck by war's end. One wonders how Germany managed to conduct the war so well for so long, under such a leader.

I don't know how solid Ohler's conclusions are, but the Hitler he describes is an interesting one.

I thought this was going to be one of those collections of offbeat and interesting information. It isn't. This is a wonderfully written, quite serious account of how we look at and think about heads. Larson is an anthropologist by training, and this book is thoroughly researched, but she has a sure and wry touch. This is important because while the book starts with the three-century career of Oliver Cromwell's head, some of the book details what could be excruciatingly boring material, the Victorian academic vogue for collecting skulls, but manages to make it fascinating.

The book is full of surprises. She considers the shrunken heads at the Pitt Rivers Museum (British) where she's worked. Several aren't human, but the ones that are may be items of commerce, heads of people murdered and shrunken for a lively trade in the jungles, a head for  a gun. The practice of shrinking was originally connected to religious practice, but proved adaptable to the market.

Chapter 2 is on trophy heads, and rather wide-ranging. American soldiers took enemy heads in several Asian wars. One photograph shows the crew of MTB 341 grinning while a member of the crew puts a cigarette in the jaws of a Japanese skull, the boat's mascot. This can get sobering, because of an undercurrent of vicious racism--they didn't take German heads. There's a photo, which was a Life Magazine photo of the week in 1944, of a GI's girlfriend peering at a Japanese skull her boyfriend had sent her. More amazing trivia--for more than 300 years there was a Keeper of the Heads who lived in the gatehouse on London Bridge, whose job was to arrange heads and body parts to maximum advantage (the body parts from executed prisoners).

There's a chapter on deposed heads, of aristocrats via guillotine and other contexts. There was a large market for guillotine portraits, sketched just after decapitation and sold, apparently something like broadsides. A fascination for executions and  other such macabre things was characteristic; she writes that the Paris morgue was among the main attractions of the city, drawing a million visits a year. Larson discusses Madame Tussaud, who had connections so she was able to make death masks just after execution of Louis XVI and Marie Antionette.

Chapter 5 is on potent heads, largely those of saints, relics of sanctity. Chapter 6 concerns bone heads, that is skulls, and this is the chapter detailing the amazing Victorian vogue for collecting skulls, many many collections (most of which currently reside in museums), and largely for the study of racial differences--the "science" was closely connected with phrenology (which largely was concerned with living heads, judging character by shape and bump). Chapter 8 considers living heads. This is of two kinds, the decapitation and freezing of living heads in the hope of becoming alive again at some point in the future, and of what fleeting consciousness is there in heads just decapitated.

You don't have to read the book straight through as I did. The chapters can be read separately. I think that the most interesting are the first chapter with Cromwell's head, and Chapter 2, on trophy heads.

I had been meaning to read this book for several years, and finally got a copy in my local library. It's in an Oxford UP series, and anything in the series is going to be a good read, as well as thoroughly researched.

This is NOT a campaign history. It covers that and does so well, but it goes deeper. Jackson probes the difficult French/ British alliance and discusses problems (the Belgians were also an issue) of cooperation and mistrust. Jackson offers much context in terms of the French politics of the 1930s, and does not conclude as some historians have, that the 1940 defeat was caused by political rot at the core of the Republic.

His version of this immense event is that it was a close-run thing. The French had equipment as good as and in some cases better than the German. They were not outnumbered and really, not outfought. They were simply outgeneraled. German tactical training was superb and allowed much more flexibility at the point of battle, and that, Jackson seems to say, is why things turned out the way they did. The French did not counter in any effective way the German thrust through the Ardennes and that was the whole ballgame. The legend of the unstoppable power of the German blitzkrieg appears to be just that, an after-the-fact legend.

The troubled alliance is described in detail, and one must remember that the Allies had several linked commands and the Germans had the advantage on only one (and only one language of command).

There's more detail in the book than this, but that's the heart of Jackson's book. I find it entirely convincing. The writing is very good, although it does drag in some spots. The research is impressive and the bibliography (now dated a bit) is excellent. Some readers may find this overly academic, and be forewarned it is a narrative with not much of the dramatic personal story that characterizes recent history on the subject. It is not an easy or fast read, but I found it compelling and informative.

This is potentially a riveting story, and the book does make the suspense build, but it's a mediocre book. The writing is often clumsy.

The odd dynamic is that this serial killer is tracked down by normal police methods in the context of an anything but normal police state. There is the usual period before authorities connect the dots and identify common elements and that they have a serial killer on their hands, then false leads, and then narrowing the possibilities until they identify the suspect. The suspect starts with harassment, the gradually escalates to violence and then murder, following a classic pattern. He is not particularly malevolent, more of a banal figure, with some native wiliness, able to use his position of small authority to facilitate his crimes.

He's caught, confronted with evidence, finally confesses and is executed. And in an interestingly macabre detail, his wife was billed for wear and tear on the guillotine used to execute him.

This isn't a chilling story, it's a bit mundane to follow. The dramatic tension is that a serial killer commits his crimes and is tracked, and found guilty and executed by the rule of law--all in a regime characterized by huge mass murders and utter contempt for the meaning of human life. That's the real story here.

Tim Flach's photography is utterly amazing. The various animals come across as individuals, and you will inevitably find yourself thinking that this picture reminds me of someone, but who? My only reservation about the book is that the brief text sections are overly pessimistic--there's a difference between pessimism and despair, and the text tends toward despair. Certainly in certain parts of Africa the combination of the bush meat trade and actual war merits the despair, for the human inhabitants too. Otherwise, the short texts are very well done.

The photos I found most compelling may not be what other readers find exceptional. I was fascinated by particular photos. The olm, the axiolotl, the mandrill, the Philippine eagle, the military macaw, the Egyptian vulture, the snow leopard and the saiga antelope.

This would make a good gift for lovers of wildlife. I can't say enough about the compelling-ness of these images. It's not just good photography, its treating these animals with respect and sees them as individuals like ourselves.

This is an entertaining book, well written and engaging. My quibble is that the various characters populating the book and the historical background seems a little arbitrary. I didn't see much system in the book, and at times it seemed like I was reading a Sunday supplement society page. Other readers may find that more to their liking.

The characters are of course real, and they are an amazing bunch, musicians, dancers, fashionistas (not sure what else to call them), painters, sculptors, composers, poets, writers, society mavens (and whatever a male maven is) and talented or simply rich hangers-on. Toss in the auto makes Citroen and Renault (with an intense rivalry), and, fascinatingly, Charles de Gaulle, and the mix is intriguing. There's a background of French politics (the author really likes Clemenceau) and enough context to make this era in Paris bright against a developing darkness.

The characters are gradually introduced and then intermixed, almost year by year. There are many Americans--the number of American expatriates in Paris, she says, jumped from 8,000 in 1920 to 32,000 in 1923 (helped by a weak franc against the dollar). Among them all are Proust, Clemenceau, Coty, Milhaud, Renoir (the filmmaker), Cocteau, Dagheliev (and a bunch of Russian dancers and composers), Dos Passos, Hemingway, Le Corbusier, William Carlos Williams, Josephine Baker, Cole Porter, Ravel, Kiki, Man Ray, various Dadaists and Surrealists, Gertrude Stein, and lots more. Intermixed are stories of their creativity, love affairs, a few scandals, more than a few sadnesses, sexual exploration and promiscuity, and a great deal of creativity of all sorts.

The book ends more or less wistfully, and fairly suddenly.

This is an excellent book, with one qualification: some chapters are heavy on the science, particularly chapter 3, which gets rather arcane in discussing the chemistry. The authors are an anthropologist and a molecular biologist. The writing is consistently good, sometimes rather charming, and largely accessible even with the fairly difficult science sections. It's short enough to read in an afternoon, and if you read it through you'll know a lot more about wine.

The first two chapters set up the history of wine--it seems to have started in the South Caucasus about 6,000 years ago, and the authors think in the area of Armenia. There's some interesting history: in pre-dynastic Egypt the king Scorpion 1 was entombed with 700 jars of wine, equivalent to about 4,000 liters, so one hopes he has a had a happy afterlife. A 5th century BCE Greek shipwreck has yielded 10,000 amphorae which is equivalent to 300,000 modern bottles of wine, so it's been a sizable scale trade for a very long time.

Chapter 3 is largely the chemistry of wine. Chapter 4 is largely about molecular tracking of various grape cultivars, and is to me the dullest chapter. Chapter 5 is on yeast, and while some of it is technical, I had no idea of the complexities. No yeast, no fermentation. Yeast occurs naturally, and newly colonizes vineyards each spring, and spends the off season so to speak, it the intestines of a wasp; its life cycle is amazing. Chapter 6 overlaps with chapter 5, and discusses interactions, that is the ecology. This should interest anyone interested in ecology, it's far more complex than just grapes growing and then harvested and trampled by barefoot peasants. Chapter 7 looks at the story of phylloxera, and shows it to be a danger still, even to California vineyards.

Chapter 8 is perhaps the most interesting, on terroir, the impact of soils and local conditions on wine, which some people think does not exist and others pontificate on. Chapter 9 discusses wine and the human senses, in the matters of wine color, smell and taste, and is interesting in several ways--the science of the eye and tongue discussed here is quite accessible. Chapter 10 discusses wine and inebriation, again a bit on the scientific side but quite readable.  Chapter 11 is brief, considering technology and wine. Chapter 12 looks at climate change and "frankenwines." Apparently GMO wines will be dicey given the market depending on matters taste and reputation, but climate change may be a very serious matter.

There are a number of helpful figures and graphics.

I didn't get to this book when it just came out. I will echo the sentiments of some of the other readers--this is an excellent resource on the Great Lakes. That word "resource" makes it sound academic; the information is indeed solid but Grady is a fine, engaging writer. He's Canadian, as is the publisher (Greystone) which to me means a somewhat different perspective than we Americans might give the book. Maybe I'm wrong, but I think that on average, Canadians appreciate nature more than we Yankees do.

It is well-illustrated, and the illustrations fit nicely into the text. They are also excellent in themselves as an exhibit of the Lakes. Chapters survey such topics as geology, human history, alien species (no irony intended as I write this sentence, it is accidental), and more.

I think that the book establishes the magnificence of the Lakes and that exploitation that endangers the Lakes is a sacrilege. That's the feeling a reader is likely to take away after reading.

This is a good introduction, a sort of overview of global chocolate. It is slightly more political than most of the many books in the "edible" series, Moss seeing a large gap between the producers and the far more prosperous consumers. This doesn't go very far, but it's similar to many views on the negative impact of commodities in world trade. This is a very small part of the book.

The book describes some of the history of how chocolate developed from a New World curiosity to a sizable range  of commodities, largely but not all in Europe. The chocolate consumed in 1650 Holland and 1950 New York are not the same. Early on it had a sense of being a drug. For me, the most interesting part is the early marketing that created both demand for products and created specific products, such as the beginnings of today's iconic chocolate firms, hot cocoa as a comfort foods, and so on.

This is a quite short and easy read, yet still with informative content. You will learn a bit more about chocolate that you knew. This is not a recipe book, or a cookbook. It does have some recipes, sort of.

To an American like me, the term "Levant" is obscure; I would guess that 19 out of 20 American readers would not know the term well enough to place it on a map. Better perhaps to describe the book as a cultural, social and political history of three cities--most literate American readers should have at least heard of Beirut, Alexandria and Smyrna.

This book has lousy maps and the photos are so-so. It is carried by a very good writer who tells many stories, some so-so, some utterly fascinating. The main emphasis in on those three cities from about 1600. They were of wildly mixed religious and ethnic composition, European, Jewish, Christians of many sects, Muslims, and a variety of minor sects. There is a kind of undercurrent of how Europeans maltreated the natives. Mansell seems a little nostalgic, somehow. Among the intriguing aspects are families based originally in these places that over generations bridge centuries and continents. Mansell ends by saying that with globalization,  "We are all Levantines now."

This is a book that should be read just for the unusual and intriguing approach. That approach I would describe as we humans are just another member of the animal gang. By that, what I mean is that animal health and human health are not so vastly different. The book isn't about how illness transfers from animal to human, but what kinds of illness we share. Part of that is looking at conditions in animals for insight on the evolution of human health and illness.

For example, human eating disorders seem to relate to evolutionary stress, and heart attacks to sudden shock such as experienced by a prey animal suddenly seized by a predator. An adrenaline shock seems to be related to the huge surge in energy by animals attempting to escape--costly in energy terms but worth it in possibly preventing death. Capture myopathy (some animals handled by humans, for example, suddenly  die) may be related to fainting. There are  STDs in animals (koalas are an example cited), self-mutilation, various manifestations of fear.

If you do not credit the idea of evolution, don't bother with the book. Otherwise, I think it a refreshingly novel look at what humans and animals have in common.

So why do I hate this book? Its like buying a book of visiting the National parks and getting detailed descriptions of only the out houses going so far to climb down into the pit. Cowboys and fans of that lifestyle are so for specific reasons and its the wide open spaces; the film captures this, LM does not! He fails to discuss the issues with them, the feel of the wood, the report, the reasons for choices, the smell of gun powder, what it feels like to be shot.

Cities are not described. A character is simply in Dodge or San Antonio. LM fails to paint any picture of the environment

Conversely LM will go into horrifying detail of the brutalities. The blood the gore, the sheer brutality is repetitive and one can only surmise LM is delighting in it or suffering from some unspeakable obsession with the ugliness of life.

The people are stereo typical and mean for the most part. There is no denying Gus is a one of the more interesting character to come out of American books but he becomes cartoonish after a while. Once again Duvall masterfully fleshes out Gus McRae as do most of the actors of the film.

If you are looking to expand on the film note youll only get more brutality and gore. The film captures the west of most of our imaginations. This book as I said is trip in the sewer and where it belongs.

If you saw the film that should be enough. This book just fills it out with ugliness and brutality.

I come from a geology/physical science background and understand the basics of biology and this was a stretch for me to grasp all the authors had to offer; but I feel I learned much.

I also come from a "creationist" background (not to be confused with a young earth creationist) in that I am Catholic; I believe in a Creator who used the methods (or similar or at least I can surmise based on scientific evidence) suggested in this book. Many.....no, MOST books of this nature attempt to bludgeon those who hold beliefs science can not prove or disprove. For the most part the authors have side stepped the debate to their credit. I'm not saying they softened the facts but wisely chose not to argue.

That said this is an excellent book for those like me who hold beliefs and are scientists (I have an MS in geoscience). It stays with the science.

It's not to say it's perfect or more to point that I understand it all. It does tend to drill down into some advanced areas of biology and neglect deeper analysis of more basic science. It does not shy away from present hard science though and will challenge the average reader if not spark further study and enthusiasm.

I feel it's the best of the earth history books by far!

It's one thing to have a great idea and lots of data but an entirely different to present it in a way it can be understood.

This book had no such editor.

There is maybe ONE illustration, ZERO photos.

It gets one star because it is so poorly organized and as I said goes around and around to get to the point to make it unreadable for me.

users.query: The Books of Elsewhere have characters and plot lines that don't play down to children. I think that's why my grands like them.. cands.text: Any book that gets the kids reading is a great book to me. But 'The Marvelous Effect' was a fun read for me, too. I had heard the comparisons to Harry Potter, but found the story to be original and interesting. The main characters are kids, and there are good and bad guys, but that's where the similarities end. The basic concept is that two young boys (Louis Proof and his friend, Brandon) and Louis's little cousin, Lacey, have this great adventure against the bad guys from another dimension. I found the characters adorable but not icky where the boys wouldn't want to read the book. They are a little street at times, which I think makes the books kool for the kidz! 4 out of 4 liked it, aged 11, 12 and 13.

This book does exactly what it was meant to do, introduce children to history in a way that made it beautiful in spite of the subject. The writing is perfect for small children. The cadence of the prose draws them in. The pictures are so detailed and amazing. Children know everything is not always peachy-keen. They can deal with that if we show them and let them. For those who thought not enough time was spent on each woman, I hear you. And I would love to have a book that did just that. But that would be a book for an older child and this book is perfect the way it is. I once read it to a kindergarten class and didn't have to ask them one time to listen or settle down.
