The scale is tiny but works extremely well. We used some small weights to calibrate it and found it was perfectly calibrated when we received it. I think for the price that this is an excellent small scale that is perfect for young students.

First off let me say I think this book is wonderful and should be read by every Christian or anyone seeking to further their understanding of the Jewish Feasts. I first heard of this book when taking a Beth Moore Bible study where it was referenced, and I looked for it in several bookstores before breaking down and ordering it from Amazon. I grew up going to church weekly (Protestant denominations), attending Sunday school, and going to Bible studies. Yet this book managed to make my jaw drop more than once. The authors explain the Jewish Feasts in painfully easy-to-understand fashion and include lots of charts and illustrations. In the past, when I would read the New Testament and see a reference to a Jewish Feast, I never really gave it much thought except to possibly date the events being described. I had no idea that by not understanding the referenced Feast I could be missing the point of the entire episode. The book charts the Feasts in terms of their being a calendar of the Kingdom of God, and the explanations make crystal clear sense. Now when I read about Jesus attending the Feast of Tabernacles and referring to Himself as the Living Water and the Light of the World, I actually have context in which to understand how an audience of first century Hebrews might have understood Him. I'm finding myself looking underneath the surface of Bible stories I thought I understood and ascertaining new and beautiful meanings, all pointing to God's wondrous love! I shared this book with my Sunday school class and several friends, all of whom say it has given them new perspective on scripture. I can't recommend this book highly enough to anyone who might be interested in learning about the Jewish Feasts and what they have to teach us today.

I've always enjoyed reading about the ancient Greek world, and when I picked up this book I couldn't put it down. I have an interest in the subject but am no expert on it, yet I found this book so skillfully worded and explained that I had no trouble following it. Waterfield seemlessly presents a complex story brimful of fascinating characters and events and ties it all together to paint a vivid portrait of the political environmnet in which Socrates' execution took place. For the modern reader without much background knowledge of this world, Socrates' death has always been so puzzling. How can this greatest of philosophers and much-admired man have been found guilty of corrupting youth and then executed? Waterfield's book seeks to answer that question. Chapter by chapter he depicts the characters and events which are pertinent to the story, building his case beautifully. This book would probably appeal to people who don't know much about Socrates already, but it would also appeal to people like me who have read a lot about Socrates but still need an expert to help us put the whole story in context.

I'm a schoolteacher and also volunteer often as a Sunday school/VBS teacher at my church. So all of my life I have been using trimmers like this to cut paper for lessons, art projects, etc. I have never thought about getting one for home use until I saw this one available through the Vine program. Now I'm kicking myself for not getting one years ago. This particular trimmer is for smaller jobs and is therefore nice to have at home. I have always known I could go to the workroom at school or church to use their trimmers, but it's great to now have one at home for my own convenience. I got this one just in time to use for this summer's VBS, and I've used it a lot just in the last two weeks. Its blade is nice and sharp, and the motion of the handle is very smooth. The blade locks down so that with the handle, I have been able to take it with me and have in my classroom to use on the spot. It's so convenient to have one of these at home to use whenever I want and be able to take with me. The base being made of recycled plastic is nice, too. Overall, I'll say that this is a great, inexpensive trimmer that is super-useful to have at home. It's not large or sturdy enough for heavy use, but for personal use, I recommend it.

These things are pretty neat! I'm not the greatest gardener, but I've grown veggies, flowers, and various shrubs and herbs my whole life. Whenever I needed to tie up a vine or "leggy " plant, my trick has always been to use old pantyhose that have been cut into little strips. These little clips might work pretty well in the place of my nylon strips. These are little plastic clips that can be easily operated one-handed, and they remove easily, too. Since I just received these strips (it's December which is cold where I live) I don't have anything in my garden that I can test them on. My only concern from looking at them theoretically is that while the clip fits easily around most of my admittedly small fingers, they may be too small to go around particularly thick vines. I will add more to this review if I see a need after I've used them for a while, but right now I definitely think they are worth a try as they are easy to use and reusable.

I bought this dvd set to replace my bulky and worn out VHS set which I've had since I ordered them from A & E back in the day. The dvd version looks nice with sharp, clear colors and a wider screen image. I just think this is the closest to perfection any Austen adaptation has come. The movie takes six hours to tell a detailed story in a leisurely fashion. Almost all the major scenes from the novel are included, and most of the dialogue is right from Austen's pen. I've heard lots of complaints that the actress who plays Jane isn't pretty enough, but beauty is so subjective I don't know who would have pleased everybody. And Jennifer Ehle might indeed be prettier than Lizzy should be, but the only complaint I had with her was that she looked way too old. She's supposed to be 20 and Darcy around 25, but they each looked mid-30's to me. Other than that, I have no complaints with the film. I still remember anxiously awaiting each episode to come on tv, and from time to time my husband and I will still get the dvd's out and watch the whole thing again over a couple of nights. It's a good movie with a good cast that stays extraordinarily true to the novel, which, let's face it, is one of the best novels ever!

When I first met my husband and started visiting his parents' home, the family had a favorite outdoor game called Lawn Jarts. Some of you may remember these huge, metal, deadly looking darts that were about as long your forearm. The object of the game was to toss these big darts across the yard into rings laid on the grass. I was always a bit spooked by these things as I was sure that if I accidentally tossed one over the neighbors' fence, I could easily kill their dog. The family informed me that they had been enjoying this game for decades and had worn through several sets, but this would be the last one as they were not longer sold. When our kids were born, the grandparents prudently hid the jarts because they were scared to let the grandkids play with them. So when I saw this set of soft tip yard darts, I thought they might be the perfect way to safely introduce this game to my kids. The set consists of only 4 darts and a couple of plastic rings. When my kids took them out to play with them, they only managed to muster about 15 minutes of interest in them. The darts are ungainly looking things that fly through the air like overweight ducks. They are weighted so that they are always supposed to land with the pointed end up in the air, but we found that while they will teeter over onto their weighted bottoms they are just as likely to topple over sideways on uneven ground. Basically this game bored my kids, and when I went into the house, I came back a few minutes later to find they had abandoned the darts and started playing basketball. They've never been allowed to play with (or even see!) the scary lawn jarts hidden in their grandparents' garage, so I know they weren't comparing the two games (though I was.) Maybe it's that there are only two darts for each person or team to use or maybe it's because the game lacks the subtle sense of possible danger that the jarts had, but nonetheless I can't recommend a game that bored my kids so quickly. Younger kids (elementary or younger) might like the game, but I think more than one set would be needed to make the game move more quickly.

My husband and I rarely make it out to the movie theater, and when we do it's usually taking the kids to a movie they've chosen. My husband had never even heard of this movie when I gave it to him for Father's Day, but he was very interested in the subject matter. I had read a review of it, but it must not have been at local theaters long (if at all) because I seemed to have blinked and there it was on dvd. I do not regret this purchase as it was a wonderfully gripping, moving film about an untold story from World War II. My husband has an interest in the era and enjoys Daniel Craig as Bond, so this movie seemed a natural choice as a gift. We watched it together and agreed it was a story that needs to be told and a movie that needs to be seen. The story follows the three Bielski brothers, Jews who choose to hide from the Nazis (in the forest of their homeland Belarus) rather than submit to being hauled off to death camps. As their ragged band grows, conflicts arise within the group as the two older brothers struggle over their own relationship as well as the role of leader and everyone deals with issues ranging from food, shelter, illness, love, and jealousy. The film is violent by necessity but not gratuitously so. It raises the question of how to fight evil without being evil, and it doesn't blink away from the difficulty and ambiguousness of such a heavy issue. The dvd also includes interesting extras about the actual Bielski family. I highly recommend this film to those who have an interest in the subject matter or just want to see a beautifully acted, complex, and very human story.

My husband, knowing my love of all things Dickens, gave me this set as a Christmas gift, to which I had to say, "Well done!" We watched it together over a few nights, and our kids joined us some of the time, and I'm looking forward to watching it all over again soon. My kids got into the mystery elements of the tale, and my husband liked all the odd characters. As the only member of my household to have read the book, I withhold one star on my review because I felt much of the book's depth was missing. Yes, I realize Dickens' books are so "meaty" it's almost impossible to squeeze it all in, but I ended up having to explain a lot of what was going on to my family as we were watching. They didn't get what was going on with the whole Jarndyce case at all. So overall, I'd say the film was well done and worth buying for one's collection, but I think it could have done a few things better. The comedic characters, particularly Guppy and Inspector Bucket, just about stole the show. My husband and kids sure seemed to think so. I felt that Gillian Anderson's portrayal of Lady Dedlock was lovely, but I didn't much care for the actress who played Esther. I don't want to spoil the mystery, but there was something about Esther's appearance that was crucial to the plot, and this actress lacked those features. (Though I can't fault her emotional portrayal of the character.) The mystery, romance, plot twisting, and humor is designed by Dickens to be crowd-pleasing, and this movie version delivers on pretty much all those levels. I don't think you would be disappointed in this purchase. I know I wasn't!

This book was heavily marketed to churches when it first came out several years ago, and my church participated in promoting the book and using it in large group studies. I had already read it myself, so I didn't join in the studies, but the book is extremely well adapted for that use. The chapters are short and to-the-point in typical Lucado style. Study questions and scripture references at the back of the book make it particularly well suited to a group approach. But it also is an excellent choice for the individual. The book asks the simple question, "What determines a life well-lived?" The answer is to spend your time serving others and addressing at least some of the mountain of needs in this world. The book starts out by citing many depressing statistics about the pain and suffering going on every minute all over our planet and wondering why the church isn't doing more about it. It forces the reader to ponder what future generations might think about our generation and its seeming unwillingness to get out of our comfort zones to really help those in need. If so many of us love Jesus and want to serve Him, why are there so many unmet needs? I'm writing this review after Thanksgiving, and I just heard a news report about near-riots breaking out during the mad rush of Black Friday shopping. What is wrong with our society when we fight over things we want to buy for ourselves while millions of people don't even have their daily needs for food, shelter, and clothing met? Don't read this book unless you want to be inspired and challenged to rise above what settles for normal in our culture and consider ways that you can truly make a difference to people in need.

users.query: Woohoo! The card folder I've had for years has torn plastic holders and are overstuffed with cards. Repair company cards are alongside those of medical facilities. The bank's card is beside the one for an automobile repair shop. Chaos! I purchased two of these folders. Now, I keep related cards in separate folders. Medical treatment facilities are in one folder, business-related cards in another, and ones for personal contacts remain in the old one.

cands.text: I visited Philadelphia's phenomenal Barnes Foundation, a magnificent museum of fine arts, because a friend recommended it. I was wowed by the refined environment that envelopes impressionists, such as Renoir. After an art overload in the museum, I visited the gift shop, where I found "Masterworks". I was reluctant to purchase this ten-pound tome and ship it to my friend. I regretted the decision upon returning to Orlando, and searched Amazon. Aha! There it was, as a "like new" used volume at half the cost. It was only four bucks to ship to Marianne in Sherman Oaks, California, and my friend is thrilled with the book.

I purchased this device only because of an NCIS episode that depicted a scanning device that appropriates credit card numbers. One of the actors used the term RFID, but I thought that was a government agency The product itself is low-quality leather, and I imagine foil inside the lining blocks RFID transmission. I have no way to verify if the product performs as promoted. It is wider than my previous wallet and thicker, perhaps because of extra compartments. This is uncomfortable when sitting, and I decided to use it only when travelling.

Disclosure: The seller contacted me asking that I write a 5-Star review. As a professional book reviewer, I found this appalling. Publishers send free books asking that I post my honest opinion, but no publisher has ever specified the review rating it wants. Of course, the maker of every product wants a highest rating, but begging taints the opinion.

In his fifth forensics nonfiction work, Macavity Award-winning D.P. Lyle answers "morbidly curious questions" from crime writers. The California cardiologist's debut nonfiction book was Edgar-nominated FORENSICS FOR DUMMIES. Nonetheless, Lyle is no stranger to fiction. His six novels include the Dub Walker series, following HOT LIGHTS, COLD STEEL. Lyle also served as consultant to the writers of Law & Order, CSI: Miami, and House. Lyle separates fact from fiction when questioned if a serial killer nurse could inject air to kill a victim. Surprisingly, about a cup of air "would travel into the right side of the heart and block its pumping action." Answering if a heated branding iron applied to a victim could cause death, Lyle provides gruesome details about pain that would be incurred but death is unlikely. "Unless the victim died of shock induced by the severe pain, that is." Questions from writers who want their characters to suffer gunshot wounds or cardiac-like events are categorized and answered with facts and possible scenarios for the authors. Lyle expresses wit with his opinion about a fictional killer that suffers from "paranoid schizophrenia with delusional and psychotic components." Such a person hears voices or feels bugs crawling over him, has a break with reality. "He sounds like an interesting character, but I hope you off him by the end of your tale." For a historical scenario, Lyle offers suggestions about murder methods other than poison in the 1800s. "But what about a hatpin? She could stab the victim in the chest and damage the heart. Or she could drive the hatpin into the victim's ear canal. It would enter the brain and could kill him instantly." When asked if poisons still work for fictional murders, Lyle delves into specifics and scenarios, concluding with "For these reasons, poisons are still rich tools for the writer of crime fiction." More than 200 questions are answered in five parts, the fifth being "Odds and Ends, Mostly Odds." In this comprehensive Q&A book, Dr. Lyle puts authors on the "write" path for their fictional forensics needs. More Forensics and Fiction: Crime Writers Morbidly Curious Questions Expertly Answered Reviewed by L. Dean Murphy

The titular yard on the Florida/Georgia border harbors human bones in seven unmarked graves. Canine Jasper brings home a human skull for his master, Winston Pettis. The only reason Dr. Bill ("Doctor Bill"!) Brockton leaves "The Body Farm" in Tennessee is that Florida forensic analyst Angie St. Claire is studying techniques with him when she is notified that her sister allegedly committed suicide just north of the Florida state line, outside her jurisdiction. Dr. Bill is enlisted as a forensic anthropologist to learn if Angie's hastily buried sister, Kate, could have offed herself with a shotgun.

Angie sets aside grief for her sister's death and drags Dr. Bill into a jurisdictional quagmire. When Jasper brings home another skull and then a femur from nightly forages, a GPS tracking collar is placed on the canine anthropologist wannabe. Only a sinister "big-bellied sheriff" wants this sleeping dog to lie quietly for eternity. The GPS collar disappears but had successfully transmitted the path of a nightly "bone run," which leads Dr. Bill and Angie to unmarked graves a short distance from a notorious juvenile reform school that had mysteriously burned down in the 1960s. Dr. Bill learns that a reform school guard, Seth Cochran (appropriately nicknamed Cockroach), viciously lashed out at boys in the school, but got his just deserts when he died in the fire.

You'd think Dr. Bill would have taken a highly venomous viper in the bathtub of his flea-bag motel as a hint that someone was trying to scare him off the case. But which one: the death of Angie's sister or the unmarked graves? Cherry-hued herrings abound. Then a hidden diary presumed to have been written by one of the reform school boys sheds light and clues as to what really happened---and details unimaginable horrors. Dr. Bill learns first-hand how painful those long-forgotten horrors were.

Despite the difficult subject matter, Jefferson Bass poetically draws from the scenery at the unmarked graves. Resurrection ferns are so named because they die during the dry season, return to life with the first rains. "Were the ferns a cynical commentary on the futility of our efforts to raise these boys from death, or might they be a hopeful portent of progress and justice?"

The writing dynamic duo of forensic anthropologist Dr. Bill Bass and journalist Jon Jefferson educates about forensics without lecturing, sort of a cross between Macavity-winning D.P. Lyle's FORENSICS FOR DUMMIES and Edgar-winning Aaron Elkins's Skeleton Detective series on steroids. It's like watching Abby on "NCIS" weave a forensic fabric. THE BONE YARD is an astounding 5-star thriller sure to be adapted for a blockbuster movie.

Just the facts: According to the authors, this book is "fiction that is deeply rooted in the soil of grim realities," a fact-based novel publishers call "faction." At a notorious reform school, "the Florida Department of Law Enforcement did not excavate or map the cemetery [and] reported to Governor Crist that it found 'no evidence that the school or the staff caused, or contributed to, any of these deaths.'" Former students formed WhiteHouseBoys.org, which "shares numerous accounts of beatings and sexual abuse in the 'rape room.'" Equally troubling is that "Martin Lee Anderson was suffocated by guards just two hours after he arrived at a 'boot camp' in 2006, [which] suggests that banning physical abuse of juveniles isn't necessarily the same as ending physical abuse."

  ---Reviewed by L. Dean Murphy

I purchased the Brother multifunction printer and did not think to order a replacement toner cartridge. As a writer and volunteer for several charities, I print a lot of documents. Six months later when printing a 500-page manuscript, the text became ghostly gray, then joined Casper's invisible friends. Aargh! Living thirty miles from the nearest office supply store--too far to take a chance on a replacement in stock--I ordered a new toner cartridge from Amazon. The cost was 20% below the retailer, no tax, and the free shipping saved several dollars for gasoline. But I learned a lesson from my predicament: purchase two, so that I'll have an extra in an emergency. Fortunately, Amazon expedited the delivery and I received both cartridges three days later. Regardless of which cartridge you buy, I advise purchasing two. You never know...

My grandnephew is an ROTC cadet and future Marine. He had expressed an interest in World War II history, perhaps because my father had served in the Navy during that turbulent era. I purchased for him this excellent combination of photography and detailed history of unsung heroes. What arrived wowed me. There are rare photographs, true, but the recap of military clashes tells far more than I learned in history classes during the 1960s.

I strongly recommend this excellent pictorial history as a gift for anyone who plans a military career. It is a quality hardcover at a paperback price.

Reviewed by L. Dean Murphy, a Bookreporter contributor

At age 21, Emily Porter adjusts after a memory-removal procedure, in a remote Maine village. Readers quickly learn that her real name is Audra Ellison, whod died in a car crash, as part of Emilys new life. Audra immediately tries to reclaim past memories, But its impossible to retrace what you cant remember. Audra learns from Luka Novak that she is a direct descendant of Elizabeth Bthory (Erzsbet Bthory in Hungarian), The Blood Countess. The most prolific female serial killer of all time. In this fictional adaptation, female lineage of Bthory (15601614) are known as Progeny, and have telepathic abilities that plant suggestions in the minds of others not descended from Bthory, not unlike female character Charlie McGee in Stephen Kings FIRESTARTER. Descendants of Bthorys victims are known as Scion, hellbent on eradicating the Bthory legacy. Scion members have the ability to harvest memories of Progenyas they kill them. Thus, Audra/Emily chose to erase her memories of Progeny hierarchy. This character rich (at times overwhelming) creation details Audras extensive search through south-central Europe to locate Bthorys diary that may refute the deaths of Scion forebears, thus freeing Progeny from annhilation by Scion. Drawing from classics, such as L. Frank Baums THE WONDERFUL WIZARD OF OZ (published May 17, 1900), this journey down Audras yellow brick road brings along readers to Budapest, Vienna, Zagreb, Bratislava, Zurich, and other European capitals. Audra/Emily needs to confide in someone, But its hard to trust anyone you don't know. Especially when that person is you. She learns that Luka was a Scion Hunter engaged to kill her and harvest her memory. Why, then, has he not done so? Tosca Lee is the bestselling author of character rich novels (Iscariot; HAVAH; The Legend of Sheba) somewhat based on historical figures. Lee will release the sequel, FIRSTBORN, in May 2017. Reviewed by L. Dean Murphy

Ellen Kirschman is a psychologist who introduces psychologist Dot Meyerhoff, only Doc Dot is a specialistshe works with police officers who experience stress-related issues that may affect their professional and personal lives. And rookie Ben Gomez has those issues with acerbic field training officer, Eddie Rimbauer. Officer Eddie treats Ben abominably, even calling him Safeway, as in a grocery store clerk.

Ben begins to crack under the strain and, along with his pregnant wife April, hes ordered to consult with Dr. Meyerhoff. Ben says everything is hunky-dory, but his wife screams otherwise. Hormonal imbalance due to the pregnancy, Dot thinks. And wrapped in emotional Kevlar, Eddie says, Im the one whos stressed. Being locked up with this kid ten hours a day.

Dot recommends to Chief Baxter that Ben take a few days off, let him have the honeymoon he didnt. Idle hands are Satans workshop and Ben in a fleabag motel Ben bites a bulletliterally. Kenilworths first police suicide.

Dot beats up on herself for not noticing the warning signs. After all, Ben said, Im going to be okay. But she cant leave it at that, and conducts her own undercover psychological autopsy. Dot digs into Bens past and learns that he married into the psycho Patcher family, the patriarch being the DA who files a medical malpractice lawsuit against Dot. Instead of digging into Bens past, she digs her professional grave. But Dot trusts her instincts, something is off. How did Ben ace the pre-employment psych exam? And that exam was approved by her former husband, psychologist Mark Edison.

With plot twists as bizarre as Dots favorite snack (popcorn and wine), events reveal another cause for Ben offing himself.

Having read Kirschmans second novel, The Right Wrong Thing (October 2016), before Burying Ben, I found some characters in the debut book to be somewhat shallow and the writing a bit forced. But Ellen Kirschman is an author to watch. She brings a new perspective to the mystery/thriller genre, and allows the reader to see another aspect of police officers lives.

Kirschman lives in California, is the author of two nonfiction books about first responders, and is working on her third novel.

Reviewed by L. Dean Murphy, a Bookreporter contributor

Following Between Heaven and Texas, bestselling Marie Bostwick releases her latest installment of the Cobbled Court Quilts series. Gayla Oliver is the mother of adult twins, on the downhill slide of middle age and happily married---until she discovers a divorce proposal memo on her husband's computer. A memo! She learns the other woman is "a chit. An embryo. I had sweaters older than her!" But Gayla softens her acerbic stance and realizes that marriage is difficult, "You have to work at it." Her husband, Brian, apologizes, but "People say they're sorry all the time, even when what they really mean is that they're sorry they got caught." Can she mend a torn marriage as easily as sewing two sections of fabric in a quilt? Dual protagonist Ivy Peterman at age 30 is divorced from a scumbag wife-beater, mother of two, and finds it humiliating "to call on my eleven-year-old for tech support." And Ivy fears the unknown, taking chances that could improve her lot. In a sports analogy, friend Virginia cautions her "about missing 100 percent of the shots you don't take." It's not the seams in Gayla's quilts that are coming apart, but the stitches that hold together her marriage. And Ivy has a split-seam thing going on, too. A single mom, she finally quit returning to her abusive husband, when he beat their young daughter. Now, he's out of jail and insists on parental visitation rights. The marriages of both ladies have been...well, torn apart at the seams. Each "had her life turned upside down by a cheating husband." There's a bit of a "Steel Magnolias" thing with these and half a dozen other ladies of diverse backgrounds. They meet at the Cobbled Court Quilts shop, instead of a beauty salon, to discuss issues important to them, and sew metaphoric and real scraps of significant material into a communal crazy quilt. Quilting is the interest these women of different ages and social status share. Quilt-making binds them in a support system, like the many stitches that bind fabric fragments into an artful quilt. Sewing smaller pieces to create larger sections is metaphoric of each lady's assembling broken pieces of her life into a useful, complete treasure. "Making that quilt made me feel capable." Bostwick's novels are inspiration, by setting examples of how her characters overcome adversity. I found inspiration and related to their insurmountable hardships, including my recent carcinoma diagnosis. Regardless of gender, interest in quilting--or not--any Marie Bostwick novel is Hallmark Card-like inspiration that helps anyone ease through a difficult situation. There's little wonder why Bostwick earned the coveted title of New York Times bestselling author. Apart at the Seams, reviewed by L. Dean Murphy, a Bookreporter contributor.

Whenever I visit a historic city, I purchase a coffee table book to remind me of my journey and let visitors know where I've been. What arrived was in good condition, and the photos crisp and clear, as indicated by the cover photo. Yes, photos of the Liberty Bell and statue of William Penn at the towering City Hall building are there, but dozens of sites I had hoped to appear don't. Instead, there are photos of pocket parks and a total lack of narrative. I'll purchase another, more comprehensive book, and donate this to a charity. I advise searching further for a book with more comprehensive depictions of the City of Brotherly Love.

Although all utilities are underground in my gated community, frequent bolts in "the lightning capitol" cause blips in the electric current, which forces the computer to shut down. This can damage the hard drive. I purchased this battery backup surge protector that has about six additional outlets not integrated with the backup charger. The printer, lamp and monitor aren't damaged by electrical interruption. Since I've purchased this device, there have been a dozen blips when my computer was on. Each time, the alarm sounded and I shut down the computer properly. I highly recommend the APC backup.

I had a quality laser printer, but it didn't have scanning capabilities. I downloaded scanning software, and discovered it had an annual subscription fee. Pffft! No way am I going to pay an annual fee that in ten years would have paid for this excellent laser printer. I'm a writer volunteer for several charities, and am involved with the annual writers conference. I need to scan magazine articles and print tons of documents. I can now scan documents and convert them to PDFs, so that other cannot alter the text. It seems that each week I discover another useful feature of this multifunction (MFC) printer. Highly recommended!

Hardboiled detective lore author Raymond Chandler lives on, in the guise of Anthony Award-winning Matt Coyle, creator of the Rick Cahill series.

Having barely survived incidents in 2015s NIGHT TREMORS, Rick now has issues with the San Diego FBI office. He discovers that The FBI had a file on me. Compounding that, neighboring La Jolla Police Chief Tony Moretti --- who now has political aspirations --- tightens a noose around Ricks neck with a pending homicide charge. All the while, Rick faces mortgage foreclosure.

Country singer Brianne Colton dangles a $5,000 foreclosure stay, to unearth evidence that her estranged husband Jim didn't commit suicide. But Rick questions why Brianne --- whose glare could cut glass --- conceals a $2-million insurance policy thats invalidated by suicide. Motive for murder shortly before divorce would remove Brianne as beneficiary?

Rick surmises, however, that LJPD wanted Coltons death to be ruled a suicide and not a murder. The thing is, Jim was a La Jolla cop questioning Chief Morettis methodology, and had placed a 17-minute call to the FBI office shortly before his demise. The bank, Moretti, the FBI. The walls were closing in. Enough weighted evidence on either side to break the scales of justice.

Thickening the mix is that Jim Colton was a former SEAL (Sea, Air, Land: the US Navy military special forces team) investigator tracking a horde of gold that went missing in the Mideast war zone. The SEAL colleagues make appearances, but are they there to help Rick uncover the truth or cover up the cause of Jims death? Had Jim located the gold intending to keep it for himself? Rick doesnt know whom to trust, but his PI nose sniffs out the truth --- despite being shattered by a curvaceous kickass martial arts instructor.

Rick had left a wildfire of burned bridges behind. One of those charred spans is sleazy attorney (redundancy?) Alan Rankin. Chief Moretti is squeezing Rankins short hairs, and the wealthy shyster offers Rick a way to mend the burnt bridge --- and eliminate the LJPD noose constricting Ricks neck.

Dilemma is defined as a difficult choice to be made between two alternatives, especially those equally undesirable. Is there a word to describe the multiple infelicitous choices presented to Rick? Sometimes you have to do whats right even when all the rules say its wrong. Switchback plot turns force Rick to make life-altering decisions, each wrong or right depending upon perspective.

The PI protagonist was acquitted but never exonerated of his wifes murder a decade ago, which continues to haunt him. The characters complete profile can be found in YESTERDAYS ECHO, first in the Rick Cahill series. Each installment sets the hardboiled thriller bar higher, making DARK FISSURES my number one Top Pick for 2016.

Reviewed for Bookreporter by L. Dean Murphy

Having moved to Orlando from Miami, I got lost more times that could be counted. This device is easily programmable, and I find it useful to locate medical facilities, when I have an appointment for the first time. Additional features are the posted speed limit and your actual speed, displayed in red if that limit is exceeded. The Garmin Nuvi also has automatic updates, and indicates when there are traffic delays ahead.

An incident paid for this Nuvi many times over, when driving through Chattanooga. An accident on the Interstate forced all traffic off the highway onto older roads. I stopped for gas and to analyze alternate routes. A convenience store clerk provided a string of directions to get to I-75, but I couldn't recall any after the first four turns. I chose a hotel in Rome, Georgia as a destination, and Nuvi immediately had the magenta arrow pointing in the proper direction. I drove along back roads that have few signs, none of which indicated I was on one of all roads that lead to Rome. Despite the clich, that's not true--unless you have the Garmin Nuvi.

Following An Old Betrayal in the Lenox amateur sleuth series set in the 1870s (and contemporary The Last Enchantments), Charles Finch thrills readers with "one of the most difficult cases Lenox had encountered" in the Victorian era whodunits, his eighth. Aristocrat Charles Lenox has left his Member of Parliament position to form a private detective agency with colleague Lord John Dallington and two others, including Polly Strickland Buchanan. This in an era of "brocaded and upholstered women." But the four detectives can't find clients with a Sherlock Holmes magnifier, especially Lenox. The upstart PI agency is ripped by scurrilous newspaper quips, including uncharacteristic quotes by Scotland Yard inspector Thomas Jenkins, with whom Lenox often had collaborated. Now, Inspector Jenkins has been murdered near the estate of "William Travers-George, the 15th Marquess of Wakefield. The title was among the highest in the land, outside of the royal family. Yet Lenox doubted strongly that there was a man capable of greater evil." The "florid, overweight, and overwhelmed" Sergeant Armbruster is first on the scene, though the maladroit Keystone Kop-ish klutz is a lethargic precinct pencil pusher. Jenkins had left word with Inspector Nicholson to contact Lenox, in the event of his death. They rush to Regent's Park, north of Buckingham Palace, where Jenkins's body was discovered, one shoelace untied and the other triple-knotted. Inside that shoe are a cryptic claim ticket and a two-word note: Charles Lenox. Instead of tying up the case as neatly as the triple-knotted lace, another body and myriad unconnected clues "troublingly out of balance with reality" cause the case to become unraveled as the first shoelace. Has Lenox lost his luster? Lenox encounters motley characters during his insidious investigation, and not only those from London's underbelly called East End. Cloistered nuns, the tony Mayfair district beau monde, and Members of Parliament figure prominently. Even Queen Victoria is rumored to have smoked cigarettes at Balmoral Castle! Predictably, Lenox deciphers coded messages, recondite clues, and barely dodges a bullet fired at close range. Adding enough odd numbers eventually equals an acceptable rounded one. Lenox finally is at par with perpetrators. Perhaps the most enigmatic character involved in the Lenox series is Charles Finch, himself. The author weaves words as intricately as Peter Paul Rubens did tapestries. Dean Murphy reviewed The Laws of Murder for Bookreporter.

The Great Gumshoe is back! Novice private investigator Mortimer Angel --- a former wallet wringer for the IRS, our nations Gestapo --- returns with Jeri DiFrazzia, who is now Morts boss and fiance. Hooker Holiday Breeze again thickens the mix but Ms. Breeze is actually Nevada university engineering student Sarah Dellario, who has an IQ higher than Renos hottest summer day. Sarah/Holiday is in hooker guise searching for her missing younger sibling, Allie, who indeed worked as a prostitute. As stated in the original GUMSHOE, You don't gloss over that kind of weirdness. With Jeris blessing, Sarah (A vamp, but not a vampire) and Mort become a pair of gumshoes searching for Sarahs sister --- and share a bed in a small-town Nevada hotel. Disembodied heads don't find their way to Mort, but youve got to hand it to Super Sleuth. Literally. Via FedEx, someone sends Senator Harry Reinharts unattached hand. When a presidential candidates shaking hand turns up without the candidate, it makes for a real fine story. Affairs get complicated and Jeri calls in her PI mentor, Maude Ma Clary. Ma was the Big Gun. In the first minute I had her pegged as a .44 Magnum. Ma is from the old school of private investigators, and immediately commands respect and admiration, a literary keeper sure to appear in future installments. The plot shifts from finding Sarahs sister to locating Senator Reinharts remaining body parts, especially since he couldn't keep one of them in his pants. Thoughts about this search for Allie were getting bulldozed off a cliff. But Mort and Sarah --- while sharing a bed sans pajamas --- deduce that both cases are somehow related. Moreover, the objectification of Sarah grows as old as Methuselah (Genesis 5:27). A brutally shocking dnouement left me breathless, made me long for a lightning rod. Did I read the last few chapters of another novel? The incongruous conclusion to the authors second installment of this otherwise lighthearted series caused me to question if Mortimer Angel has finally matured. Say it isn't so! Despite the plot peripeteia, this is a bawdily entertaining series, making Mortimer Angel my favorite go-to gumshoe. Reno resident Rob Leininger is the author of Gumshoe (Mortimer Angel), KILLING SUKI FLOOD, and eight other novels. Reviewed by L. Dean Murphy for Bookreporter

The cable provided by the technician who installed the computer could have reached my neighbor's house! I had wound up the unneeded 18 feet and secured it with a rubber band. The band deteriorated and snapped. The cable became tangled with the other electronic spaghetti behind my desk, and it took an hour to unravel the mess. I drove 30 miles--which equates to $10 for gasoline--only to learn that a national electronics retailer wanted $30 for a six-foot cable. That's five dollars a foot!

Thank you, Amazon! For a third of retail price, the appropriate cable arrived in three days.

Following near-death experiences in 2014s ELECTIVE PROCEDURES, tension ratchets when Elle Harrison returns to her position as teacher of Philadelphia second graders. After setting up the classroom a few days before school begins, she stops by the principals office. But draconian Mrs. Marshalls empty eyes gazed at blankness, and her cheeks oozed crimson clots. Gruesome way to start the school year.

Elle has listed her house for sale with Jerry, an egocentric realtor who makes romantic overtures. Returning home, Elle finds freshly vacuumed carpet has a single set of footprints. Was the house shown to prospective buyers? When wine and flowers appear inside her locked abode, Elle vows to have the locks changed. Perhaps she had failed to secure the doors? After all, her dissociative disorder (disruptions of memory, awareness, identity, or perception) causes her to pull an Elle. Too many things causing confusion: another teacher murdered, and Sex and the City-like gal-pal Becky was attacked, at Logan Elementary.

These events unfold when former student Ty Evans, now age 21, obtains early prison release having stabbed his father. Ty conveniently shows up at Elles home to thank her for being the only adult who trusted him. And invite her for coffee. Finally a new man had come into my life. Never mind he was half my age and a convicted murderer.

Elle had taught other Evans family members. A few years younger than Ty, Katie was a model student and now stops by daily to walk home with Seth, age seven, because their mother has alcohol issues. But Seth has been a problem of late: drawings exhibiting rage, hiding in the cloakroom, has bruised arms, and now skin cuts, though hes too young to shave. Is the alcoholic mother to blame, or does Ty have another knife?

With Ty appearing at her front door, and someone coming in through locked doors, impetus to sell the home where estranged husband Charlie had been murdered increases. It was time to let go. To say goodbye to Charlie. With all thats going on in Elles life, she seldom thinks of her late husband, though his essence is still there. The full impact of their life --- and his death --- is found at THE TROUBLE WITH CHARLIE, first in the series.

Whats behind these horrors culminates in helter-skelter chaos. Elles home becomes the center of a tragic universe, as she attracted tragedy and death. That combination is magnified many-fold, as readers are left enchanted with another Elle-oquent thriller.

Reviewed for Bookreporter by L. Dean Murphy

I purchased this guide for an anticipated Seattle trip. Although the descriptions of sites are comprehensive, I discovered that some have changed locations or closed, such as restaurants. Moreover, I had to locate each entry on a city map before heading out each day. Many entries have one site on the north side of town, and the following one on the south side. I spent more time on buses travelling between destination than visiting the sites.

The following year, I planned a trip to San Francisco. A friend recommended TripAdvisor. I checked out that venue and was able to group sites on the city map. I copied each hyperlink and posted it in a document, and identified the address. I grouped sites within a few blocks and identified them, say, as Union Square. This way, I could visit several sites within walking distance. Each day, I took my list to the central site of those I intended to visit. I spent little time on public transportation, and was able to walk a few blocks between most attractions. For those who have Smart Phones, this info is readily available. Unlike Frommers, TA is free. I can easily predict that printed guides may be a thing of the past within a few years. By the time researchers compile information, print the latest volume, that info may be a year old--far too long for fast-changing venues in this electronic age.

Four years ago in TELL NO LIES, charismatic St. Louis prosecutor Jack Hilliard "betrayed Claire and his family, a shadow that followed him wherever he went." He had a one-night fling with fellow attorney, Jenny Dodson, an alluring person of Indian derivation and astounding beauty. Now, Jack catches 16-year-old son Michael 'getting busy' with Celeste, Jenny's doppelgnger. Michael gets into the booze cabinet, and is in no condition to drive 'Cee' home. Jack, hoping to earn his oldest son's respect after the marital booboo, keeps the alcohol and sex a secret from Claire, and takes teen Celeste home--alone. Big mistake! Cee begs Jack to let her sober up in his car for a few hours. Jack had vowed to tell no lies, but "The lies aren't what he says; they're what he doesn't say. And this is when he makes his third mistake." Strike three. Celeste alleges rape, and a DNA conundrum casts doubt about Jack's credibility. Ah, Jack, as Claire says, "Have you learned nothing?" Coincidentally, Jenny approaches Jack after a four-year absence, and "sends a wave of heat through his body like an addict's first hit after a long abstinence." She asks Jack for help with threatening letters. Who sent them, and why? Her former boyfriend, Alex, was convicted of murdering Maxine, and Jenny can't be charged again. But an appellate court may set Alex free, which will put Jenny's neck in a noose--metaphorically--and on death row, for sure. Everything Jenny did "had nothing to do with her feelings for him and everything to do with creating the perfect alibi." Unanswered questions in 'Lies' now haunt Jack during intense courtroom drama. Presumed guilty parties are innocent, or are they? Tables turn like a tornado, as readers become quasi jurors assessing validity of life's prosecution and defense. It is, I feel, essential to read TELL NO LIES before taking on this challenging sequel. The creative present tense omniscient viewpoint writing style puts readers in each character's mindset, and allows the story to flow smoothly. Readers see Claire, Jenny, Michael, and others not from Jack's perspective. This bestseller-bound psychological/legal thriller causes readers to question social issues, and for me, poor choices that affected my life. The author "has a psychological grasp of people that [gives] her an edge." At times, she waxes philosophical with zingers like, "Time is less precious to those who have more of it." Julie Compton is an attorney, has two daughters, and lives in Central Florida with husband, Rick. RESCUING OLIVIA was her second novel. For more information, visit the author's website, Julie-Compton. Compton was named Person of Renown at FWA's October 2011 conference, and selected the top ten short stories for FWA's fourth anthology, MY WHEELS. She is a member of several writers organizations, including Mystery Writers of America, International Thriller Writers, and Florida Writers Association. KEEP NO SECRETS Reviewed by L. Dean Murphy originally for Bookreporter.

Following 2016s The Progeny (Descendants of the House of Bathory), New York Times bestselling Tosca Lee releases the integral sequel that resolves questions about fictional issue of real-life Blood Countess Elizabeth Bathory, the most prolific female serial killer of all time. Known as Progeny, those descendants can control thoughts of common humans, persuade them to do Progeny bidding. In a yin-yang counterbalance, scions of Báthorys victims are known as Uh, Scion. Elite Scion members (led by the Historian) are called Hunters, charged with expunging Progeny. At each death, Hunters can harvest Progeny memories, an internet of sorts that links all Báthory legacy and will help Scion to annihilate the arch enemies. Suave and buff Luka is the Hunter assigned to off Audra Ellison, the most powerful Progeny member. A few months before, in the States, Audra faked her death and intentionally had her memory erased in a clinical procedure, to throw Hunters off her trail. But for what purpose? Now shes in the Old World and lands in more European countries than a Lufthansa pilot. Elements of Audras memory return. She learns that Luka is actually her protector and husband, who has been captured by the Historian. And Audra discovers why she chose memory eradication: to protect someone in this conclusion to the Progeny series. But just who is the title character? Costumed Progeny youth dance their lives away at frenetic Mardi Gras-like galas. Meanwhile, Audra tries to destroy the Historian, before that unidentified being obliterates her, torturing Luka as a means to lure the Progeny monarch. Amongst the three dozen characters that often confuse the inattentive reader, Claudia, Piotrek, computer whiz Jester, and heretic monk Roland swarm around Audra, to protect the queen bee. A key cause for needed protection is Báthorys rumored diary that may trace Progeny genealogy. The Progeny series analogizes the holistic struggle of good and evil. And how opposing sides can come together, sort of a Romeo and Juliet portrayal in a paranormal thriller. In Shakespeares iconic tragedy, the Capulet and Montague families have feuded for so long theyve forgotten why. Only after the deaths of the title characters do the factions make nice with each other. FIRSTBORN is not a tragedy. Its a surprisingly upbeat conclusion to Lees Descendants of the House of Bathory series. Tosca Lee fans will be thrilled to learn that FIRSTBORN has been optioned for film production. Reviewed by L. Dean Murphy for Bookreporter

My neighbors live in England, but have a wintertime home in Florida. Each year for four months, I get my fill of Yorkshire pudding and gin & tonic. Last year, I purchased this British flag to hang in front of the garage door, for their arrival. How pleased were Valerie and Michael after their long flight! I highly recommend this as a gift to visitors from England, something to make them smile. If you have friends visiting from other countries, search Amazon to buy a flag for each of those guests. After all, it's a third the cost of a bottle of wine and something that will last forever, a gift that will remind friends of your thoughtfulness.

FYI, the British flag is called a Union Jack only when it's displayed aboard a sailing vessel, according to Wikipedia.

Following HOME BY NIGHTFALL and THE LAWS OF MURDER, Finchs 10th Charles Lenox mystery --- a series as polished as British sterling --- has multiple subplots that diverge like a river meandering in a delta. Specifically, the Thames, in 1877 London. Only this river is a literary one, filled with red herrings. Queen Victoria has reigned for 40 years, and the Second Industrial Revolution has peaked. The sun never sets on the British Empire.

Former Member of Parliament Charles Lenox has formed a burgeoning investigative agency, along with Britains first female sleuth, Polly Buchanan, and Lord John Dallington. Lenox had developed an interest in solving mysteries 30 years before, at prestigious Harrow. School bud Gerald Leighs father had been killed in a carriage incident and a mysterious benefactor (which the duo dubs MB) pays the Harvard-like tuition and boarding costs. They never detect MBs identity --- until now.

Fast-forward to the new era of electric lighting and Lenox receives a cryptic message from Leigh: The latters life is endangered. It seems someone has left Leigh an eyebrow-raising inheritance, but the solicitor engaged to track down the scientist now living in France refuses to disclose the maker of the bequest. Leigh has returned to London to sign necessary documents, and receive the inherited fortune.

Shortly after, the barrister is murdered, his valise containing documents detailing the bequest has vanished. Many stand to receive the inheritance if Leigh is not alive to do so, and he goes into hiding following two attempts on his life. After a few pieces of tidy detective work, Lenox questions if his school chum killed attorney Ernest Middleton and faked the attempts on his own life as a diversion, proving theres little so dangerous as people who wish you well. Tension ratchets, however, as members of the nefarious Farthings gang are spotted tailing Leigh.

The red herrings swim upstream, into Lenoxs sleuthing agency. Leigh is asked to address the scientific community of the Royal Society, and a member mysteriously summons him to speak in secret. Lord Dallington investigates a Parliament break-in thats too conveniently hushed, and traces onto the towering roof the presumed burglar Labrenz. Labrenz was a Prussian spy, wanted throughout England.

This installment is fraught with the early days and development of Charles Lenoxs interest in detection. The author interlaces word origins, along with afternoon tea or a pint at the pub. Readers learn that a horse-drawn cabriolet is the etymon of cab, as in taxi. Theres even an explanation as to why Brits drive on the left, while those in the civilized world prefer the right.

Although reliving London life of 14 decades ago is satisfying, the detective aspect of this Lenox installment are less so. Still, Charles Finch never ceases to amaze readers with wit and damn good storytelling.

Reviewed for Bookreporter by L. Dean Murphy

That is why I got it. So far, it has not eliminated my IBS, but it certainly should not hurt.  Fennel is listed as one of the herbs for IBS.
The health properties of fennel are warming, carminative, antispasmodic, antidepressant, stomachic, pectoral, diuretic, diaphoretic, aromatic, anti-microbial, pain reducing, fever reducing, and promotes milk-flow in nursing mothers.

Fennel has a long history as a commonly used household remedy for a variety of complaints, especially digestive disorders and it has been used traditionally as a remedy for gas, acid stomach, irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), gout, motion sickness, cramps, and spasms.

Fennel has a diuretic effect, which increases the amount and frequency of urination, which is thought to help remove toxic substances from the body.

Fennel is thought to be an effective herbal remedy for respiratory congestion and is a common ingredient in cough remedies.

It relaxes the smooth muscle lining of the digestive system, and is used for cancer patients after radiation and chemotherapy treatments to help rebuild the digestive system.

Fennel is used as a natural treatment for anemia. Fennel contains iron and histidine, an amino acid found in fennel. Histidine stimulates production of hemoglobin and other components of the blood.

It is common practice, especially in India, to chew fennel seeds after a meal. Some of the components in the plant stimulate secretion of digestive and gastric juices, reduce inflammation of the digestive tract and facilitate proper absorption of nutrients.

Fennel is used as an herbal treatment for diarrhea caused by bacterial action; it is believed that the properties of some components of it are disinfectant and anti-bacterial. Histadine is an example of one of several amino acids in fennel that aid digestion, helping to relieve diarrhea due to indigestion.

The tea is believed to increase milk production in nursing mothers, and may also relieve colic in babies. An infusion of the bruised seeds is a safe and effective natural treatment for flatulence in babies.

When used with urinary disinfectant herbs like arctostaphylos uva-ursi, the herb is thought to be an effective herbal treatment for cystitis.
The plant is rich in phytoestrogens, and is an emenagogue, easing and regulating menstruation by regulating hormonal action in the body. It is believed to be helpful as a natural treatment for amenhorrea, anxiety and depression.

treatment for the symptoms related to snake bites, insect bites or food poisoning. This application is a complementary remedy for symptoms, and must never replace appropriate medical care.

A gargle made from fennel infusion is used as an herbal remedy for relief of hoarseness and sore throats.

The essential oil may be used topically to ease muscular and rheumatic pain and an infusion (steeped tea) of the fennel seeds may be used to prepare a compress as a treatment for conjunctivitis and inflammation of the eyelids.

Besides being used in cooking, fennel is found in many commercial products such as toothpaste, soaps, perfumery, air fresheners, and antacid preparations.

The dried plant is used as an insect repellent; the crushed leaves are used as a flea repellent for dogs and the dried leaves are believed to help keep fleas away from kennels and stables.
Possible side effects::
Pregnant women should not take fennel as a medicinal herb internally as it is a uterine stimulant; however, small amounts used in cooking are safe. Skin contact with the sap or essential oil may cause photo-sensitivity or dermatitis in some people. Ingestion of the essential oil can cause vomiting, seizures and pulmonary edema.

While fennel has a long history of use as a useful herbal remedy, it does contain compounds which are anti-bacterial. Keep in mind that too much of anything can be harmful. Taken in excess, fennel can induce trouble in breathing, increase palpitations and make heart beats irregular. Taken in excess, it may also cause neurotic problems.

It is essential to consult your health care professional when altering medications and you should thoroughly investigate how your medications may interact with each other. Inform your health care professional of any medications, vitamins or herbs that you are taking.
